title: Commentary: Some advice for South Dakota legislators before their next session
description: The next session of the South Dakota Legislature starts on Jan. 12. Between now and the start of the session, lawmakers will need to think about what they want to accomplish. This state’s Legislature doesn’t typically have much extra money available. That’s too bad, because there is plenty that needs funding. Now that South Dakota […]
text:
The South Dakota Senate chamber on Feb. 3, 2026, at the Capitol in Pierre. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)The next session of the South Dakota Legislature starts on Jan. 12. Between now and the start of the session, lawmakers will need to think about what they want to accomplish. This state’s Legislature doesn’t typically have much extra money available. That’s too bad, because there is plenty that needs funding.
There’s no backing away from recidivism reform
Now that South Dakota leads the league in new prisons, it’s time for some long overdue funding to help get inmates ready for life on the outside to ensure that they don’t end up back behind bars.
A task force on that subject has recommended 34 reforms and programs at an estimated annual cost of $1.92 million. That’s almost $2 million a year in a state where the Legislature often doesn’t have much extra money to spend. The $1.92 million figure doesn’t take into account the cost of additional staff needed for the programs.
As much as it pains Republican legislators to consider new forms of revenue, that may be what’s needed to create real, ongoing reform in the prison system.
It’s best to revisit property tax reform
It’s unclear if the property tax reforms approved in the last session are all that popular or effective. So far, the results are mixed. At least seven counties — Custer, Fall River, Hughes, Lawrence, Lincoln, Meade and Pennington — have implemented the county half-percent sales tax with the revenue going to homeowner property tax relief.
South Dakota always ranks among the least taxed states in the nation, yet the thought of adding a county sales tax for property tax relief was rejected by voters in Brown, Codington, Clay and Charles Mix counties. The Charles Mix results may be the subject of a recount.
So far, at least 11 out of 66 counties have taken action, one way or the other, on the new sales tax for property tax relief. It’s not as if the homeowners in the other 56 counties feel comfortable with their property tax bills. Perhaps they’re of a mind that there has to be a way to approach property tax relief that doesn’t depend on taxing renters who won’t reap the benefits of a lower property tax bill.
Follow the law and fully fund schools
There will be plenty of new legislators in Pierre this January. Their mission is to create laws that benefit the citizens of the state. However, if they are anything like the lawmakers that came before them, it won’t be long before they show their true colors. They may have run for the House or Senate, but the job they really want is that of school superintendent.
Their secret identities are revealed in the myriad bills they offer aimed at schools. Last year lawmakers tried, with varying degrees of success, to start charter schools, curb cellphone use in schools, require the state motto on school walls and mandate that students be required to learn about prenatal human growth.
Podcast: Economy, affordability are big issues for session, new state Senate leaders say

On the Legislative Research Council’s website, under the “education” tab in the subject index for bills, there are 59 pieces of legislation. Look closely at the website and there are also tabs for “higher education,” “scholarships,” “school curriculum,” “school districts,” “schools” and “teachers.” Some of the bills are listed under multiple tabs, but it’s obvious that lawmakers have their sights set on the state’s schools.
Under the “education” tab there are 14 bills that deal with school finances or changes to the school funding formula. It’s ironic that so much attention would be paid to school finances because in the last session, the governor’s original budget called for no funding increase for education. Appropriators eventually came through with a 1.4% increase, sidestepping a law that mandates schools get an increase at the rate of inflation or 3%, or whichever is less.
In addition to the last session, lawmakers have used their legislative wiles four times since 2010 to circumvent the law.
Sure, some bills may clean up language in old laws and some may ensure that South Dakota law is in line with new federal regulations. Other than that, lawmakers should leave curriculum changes to the experts, write a check for the funding that’s required by law and then get out of the way.
Figure out the right approach to data centers
Lately, any major project that comes along inspires a group of vocal opponents. No matter the need, the opposition is there for power lines, pipelines and now, data centers. For some reason, new infrastructure seems to bring out the naysayers.
Data center technology is evolving quickly. Innovation in power use, water needs and noise reduction are being made every day because the data center people know that, right or wrong, they are being presented as the bad guys.
South Dakota lawmakers can’t sink into this river of negativity just because it’s the easiest path. Data centers need a cool-headed approach with a clear understanding of what they could mean for the state’s resources and the state’s economy.
Lawmakers have to guard against taking the easy way out and unilaterally opposing data centers just because those who oppose the centers currently have the loudest voices. Leadership means doing what’s best for the citizenry, not what’s easiest.

name: VTDigger
title: Montpelier activates emergency support website for Cummings Street families
description:
City Manager Kelly McNicholas Kury declared the Tuesday fire a level two emergency.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Montpelier activates emergency support website for Cummings Street families.
text:
Fire trucks work to extinguish apartment building units that caught fire Tuesday afternoon on Cummings St. in Montpelier. Photo by Tierney Flavin/VTDigger

Montpelier activated a website Wednesday offering ways to help families impacted by Tuesday’s Cummings Street apartment fire. 
“Montpelier is an amazing community that comes together in times of suffering and hardship to support each other,” said Mayor Marc Gwinn and City Manager Kelly McNicholas Kury in a joint press release Friday. “This generosity makes our little city incredibly special and unique.”
The website allows community members to offer financial or physical donations and provide long-term shelter options for impacted families. 
“Several families were displaced by the fires on Cumming Street,” the joint statement said. “Many of these households were intergenerational and have children in all of our schools.”
Kury dispatched the city’s emergency support function team Wednesday to organize a response. She also declared the fire a level two incident — which is an incident that “requires response by more than one department/response agency,” per the city’s Montpelier Action Plan for Local Emergencies. That plan was established for better preparedness following the floods of July 2023. 
The support team has coordinated the emergency response alongside the American Red Cross, the Montpelier Disaster Recovery Network, the Montpelier Housing Authority, the Montpelier Roxbury Public School District, the Vermont Agency of Human Services and Washington County Mental Health Services. 
The website will be updated with specific needs of the families as they arise, according to a post on the website from Alec Ellsworth, Montpelier parks and trees director.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: What the federal bill to speed up energy projects would mean for you
description: This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here. The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in […]
text:
(Photo by Grist/Getty Images)This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.
The largest renewable energy project ever built in the United States — the sprawling SunZia wind farm and power line in New Mexico — took two decades to build. Its transmission line, necessary to transport the wind power to cities in Arizona and California, faced opposition from birders, the military, and tribes. While some disputes were resolved, tribes’ concerns about the project’s impacts on historic sites have remained unsettled, leading to court battles that still haven’t been resolved even though the line was completed in June.
Such legal challenges commonly delay renewable energy projects and the transmission lines that carry their power to population centers. The threat of lawsuits and resistance from utilities have driven down long-distance power line construction in the United States, limiting the country’s ability to use cheap renewable energy.
The Senate passed a “permitting reform” bill this week that could make it much faster and easier to build transmission lines and renewable energy projects — but it casts a wide net, easing construction for almost all large infrastructure projects. Supporters of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA — including clean energy companies and prominent climate-conscious senators — argue the bill is necessary to clean up the power grid. Critics say it could disempower communities, tribes, and environmental groups while also speeding construction of fossil fuel infrastructure. The bill still needs to pass the House and receive the president’s signature before becoming law.
Here are the answers to some basic questions to help you understand the bill, why it’s such a big deal, and why it’s so controversial.
What would this bill do?
At its heart, the bill is an effort to streamline the federal government’s process for issuing permits for infrastructure projects, including many large-scale energy and transportation projects. Without these permits, developers can’t build infrastructure on federal land, across state lines, or with certain kinds of federal funding. But companies say getting a permit, and keeping it, is a time-consuming, unpredictable, and costly process, even when their project meets all necessary environmental standards.
That’s due in part to the National Environmental Policy Act of 1969, or NEPA, one of America’s bedrock environmental laws. NEPA requires federal agencies to study the environmental, economic, and social impacts of major government actions, including many infrastructure permits. They must consider alternatives to what’s been proposed, solicit input from the public, and publish their findings. A different law called the National Historic Preservation Act requires agencies to carry out similar reviews of projects’ repercussions for historic and archaeological sites.
While NEPA doesn’t explicitly hold projects to a higher environmental standard, it creates a formal process that can educate the public, inform government officials, and open pathways to better outcomes. Still, this process often becomes the source of delays. Opponents of a project can sue an agency, claiming it conducted an inadequate review, potentially forcing the government to redo parts of its analysis and halting construction in the meantime — even if the agency ultimately issues the same permit after redoing the analysis. The motivations for these lawsuits can range widely, from wealthy communities trying to protect their property values to tribes defending their sovereignty and religious freedom.
The bill would speed up environmental and historic preservation reviews, narrow the potential impacts agencies must consider, restrict who can sue over them, and shorten the deadline for doing so. Supporters say that would prevent costly delays, which can be particularly consequential for land-intensive renewable energy projects. Critics say it would reduce public scrutiny and make it harder for communities and tribes to identify environmental harms, protect historic or sacred sites, and push developers toward better alternatives.
The bill would also make several changes aimed specifically at the power grid. It would give the federal government greater authority to override states that block interstate power lines and require regional grid operators to approve lines that improve reliability and affordability. Transmission construction in the United States has slowed over the last decade, even as its importance is expected to grow.
Controversially, the bill would also prevent states from using the Clean Water Act to block power lines or pipelines crossing waterways unless they directly discharge into the water. The bill would not affect the vast majority of projects built on private land within one state.
The SunZia transmission line, viewed during its construction through the San Pedro Valley, Arizona, in September 2024. This photo was taken from aboard a flight operated by Ecoflight. (Photo by Austin Corona/Grist)
Would this bill change my community?
Tribes, states, and local groups would have less power to stop or delay some infrastructure projects, and projects could move forward with less time for public scrutiny. That could mean more power lines crossing landscapes and greater risk that communities’ concerns don’t get adequately considered.
But experts expect the bill to lower electricity costs slightly over the next 15 years by making it easier to move cheap power between regions, while helping states meet clean energy goals. Households and businesses would likely find it easier to sell electricity from rooftop solar and batteries onto the grid.
Most data centers wouldn’t see big changes because of the bill, as they are overwhelmingly constructed on private land whose development is overseen by local and state governments. (Proposals on federal lands exist, though they often involve significant legal issues that this bill would not necessarily change). The bill could accelerate the power and pipeline infrastructure that benefits data centers, but it would also require them to pay for grid upgrades they need and increase transparency around their electricity use. The bill could also make data centers’ power cleaner by making it easier for them to connect to grids with clean energy, rather than building polluting, off-grid gas turbines.

Would this bill be good for the climate?
The bill would enable energy infrastructure generally, meaning fossil fuel projects could grow alongside renewables. The advantage would likely tip toward renewable energy, according to projections from some organizations, though predicting future energy markets is tricky. Some experts believe the bill would make it harder for future administrations to limit fossil fuel projects, making emissions reductions more difficult.
Rhodium Group, an economic research firm, projects natural gas pipelines would continue advancing at roughly their current pace, while renewable energy deployment would accelerate due to faster permitting and greatly expanded transmission. Rhodium’s modeling finds a modest emissions reduction even if natural gas prices drop more than renewables, with larger reductions if renewable energy becomes much cheaper than natural gas.
But arguably the bill’s biggest climate effect would be strengthening future clean energy initiatives: States pursuing clean electricity or electrification would have an easier time building the infrastructure they need, and future federal clean energy incentives could produce better results.
The reverse is also possible. Republicans could take advantage of faster permitting processes to speed up fossil fuel infrastructure while suppressing renewables. The bill attempts to limit presidents’ ability to discriminate among energy sources, although recent amendments slightly weakened those provisions. Some opponents worry these provisions wouldn’t keep President Donald Trump from continuing to suppress wind power, while others worry they will be too successful and prevent Democratic presidents from phasing out fossil fuels.
Who supports the bill, and who opposes it?
Supporters include labor unions, clean and fossil energy companies, a few tribes and tribal energy advocates, centrist policy organizations, and some climate advocacy groups. Clean energy companies have been especially enthusiastic, arguing that permitting and transmission constraints have become some of the biggest obstacles to expanding renewable power.
Opponents include environmental nonprofits, dozens of tribes, rural landowners, civil rights groups, and other climate activists. Some opponents support the bill’s transmission provisions but argue its changes to environmental review would excessively weaken the ability of communities and tribes to scrutinize projects and seek alternatives.
That disagreement has split Democrats and the climate movement. Climate-focused Democratic senators Sheldon Whitehouse and Martin Heinrich co-wrote the bill, while Green New Deal sponsors Ed Markey and Mazie Hirono opposed it. Climate movement veterans Al Gore and Genevieve Guenther have also opposed the current legislation, while climate scientist Zeke Hausfather and utility watchdog David Pomerantz support it.
Neither camp is monolithic, and advocates on both sides offer nuanced explanations of the trade-offs they are or aren’t willing to accept. Many opponents say they support permitting reform but believe Democrats should wait until January, when they will have majorities in both houses of Congress, to negotiate stronger protections for clean energy, communities, and tribes. Some supporters counter that the country needs new clean energy infrastructure now and that there is no guarantee a better political opportunity will arrive.

Will this bill become law?
The bill passed the Senate by a vote of 62 to 33, with 15 Democrats joining all but six Republicans in approving the legislation. Though it moved quickly through the Senate, its chances are less certain in the House. The lower chamber is also controlled by Republicans, but some — including House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie of Kentucky — have signaled concern over transmission provisions. The bill could also struggle if Republicans don’t arrive in Washington to vote, with many staying home after losing races in the midterms.
House Democrats, including top Democrat Hakeem Jeffries of New York, have also expressed concerns about the bill. If a large group of Democrats can convince a handful of Republicans to vote against it, they might be able to defeat it.
Trump has said he supports the permitting reform effort, meaning it should become law if it makes it out of Congress. If BAAJA doesn’t get signed before the new year, however, it will die, and lawmakers will have to start over if they want to pass permitting reform in the next session.
This article originally appeared in Grist, a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change. It was updated with new information after the permitting reform bill passed the Senate.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Why consumers are still powering the US economy — and why this could fizzle
description: Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers. With inflation fatigue, declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back? This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As […]
text:
U.S. consumers have been powering the economy despite inflation and other turmoil. But that may change soon. (Getty Images photo)Holiday shopping season is kicking off, inundating consumers with Black Friday offers. With inflation fatigue, declining real wages and stock market turbulence thrown into the mix, is the U.S. consumer on the verge of scaling back?
This question has long puzzled economists, who wonder why spending has held up even as consumer sentiment slumps. As a researcher of supply chains who has also worked for years at consumer products companies, I’ve run my own studies and have been surprised, time and again, by how spending has continued at a healthy clip even when the economy is faltering.
Most recently, in March 2026, I built a model to assess how the Iran war could affect global supply chains at three, six and nine months out. In the case of consumer behavior, the hit was less than expected. Even though Americans were paying substantially more at the gas pump due to the disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, as well as dealing with tariff-induced inflation and high interest rates, consumer spending held up remarkably well.
I now believe I missed two things: resilience and innovation. More specifically, Americans are continuing to work, whether in formal or gig jobs, and that’s the main factor holding up spending. And as long as consumers have income, they’ll keep finding a way.
What’s changing, though, is that this balancing act is getting harder for many to keep up.
 
What resilience looks like
Resilience and innovation may sound admirable, but in practice they’re often difficult and onerous.
Under “innovation,” some traditional adjustments for consumers include buying cheaper “private label” or store brands, shopping at off-brand and discount stores, or relentlessly hunting for deals. Other adjustments include eating more meals at home rather than going out, or downsizing vacation plans.
“Resilience,” meanwhile, can mean taking on extra work. Economists call this the added worker effect, and it shows up during tough times. During the 2007-09 Great Recession, for example, more married women joined the labor force as unemployment rose among their spouses. In 2026, there’s an uptick in retirees heading back to work as well as an increase in the share of mothers with children who are staying in or reentering the workforce.
These are both responses to the rising cost of living.
More broadly, Americans are using traditional and nontraditional means to make extra cash.
About 1 in 3 workers has had a side hustle in 2026, according to the jobs database ZipRecruiter — whether it’s nanny jobs, side gigs on Etsy, delivering meals for DoorDash or driving customers for Uber. For many Americans, this work is a necessity, not just a way to earn discretionary cash. The increasing need for extra work over the past five years underscores the drop in purchasing power from the salaries many people earn.

Another form of resilience can be seen through volunteering and charitable giving. In my own neighborhood, a food bank that started during the COVID-19 pandemic has helped many in the community over the past five years. Across the country, food bank donations and charitable giving continue to rise despite economic challenges.
According to Giving USA, charitable giving rose to US$617 billion in 2025, surpassing the $600 billion mark for the first time. This increase addresses a growing need for food banks to feed Americans who can’t afford basic groceries anymore. At the same time, the number of donors is dropping.
 
Shoppers are hitting the limit
Consumers are now running out of levers to pull.
Wealthier Americans are continuing to spend at a strong clip, which is why official consumer spending data suggests the economy is steady. But it’s a different picture for the rest.
One in four families are spending more than they make, as seen by rising credit delinquency and auto repossessions, according to the Atlanta Federal Reserve. Whether it’s food, healthcare, rent or cars, Americans are spending a much larger share of their income on necessities than they did 10 years ago.
For especially strapped Americans, like those facing the double whammy of a car payment and a student loan, these trade-offs are especially challenging. A good example are auto loan delinquencies, now near a 10-year high. Losing a car can mean losing a job, with devastating financial consequences. Frontline workers also miss more shifts as gas prices rise.
And this gets to a core lesson for understanding today’s economy: The bedrock for consumer spending remains employment. The stable job market we see right now — with unemployment at 4.1% — is critical. If this healthy job market holds, and interest rates and energy prices ultimately ease, the average consumer will still tread water. But if inflation continues to run hotter than the Federal Reserve would like, and rates rise, Americans’ disposable income will likely shrink — and hurt economic growth in the process.
That could lead to a domino effect: Unemployment rises, reducing the discretionary spending that had been keeping economic growth steady.
The holiday season isn’t necessarily an accurate forward-looking indicator. Shoppers often go to great lengths to make family and friends happy. The big challenge for consumers will start in early 2027. Will the Fed hike rates? Will inflation stay high? Will gas prices come down?
Until these questions are answered, we’re in the “bend but don’t break” phase. Many consumers faced challenging times in 2026, but their resilience has been a surprise on the upside. I’d like to be surprised again in 2027 — but that’s far from a sure thing.

Chris Gaffney is an Edenfield executive in residence and a professor of the practice in the H. Milton Stewart School of Industrial and Systems Engineering at the Georgia Institute of Technology. name: Alaska Beacon
title: Juneauites rally to celebrate certification of the midterms, push for election reforms
description: Dozens of demonstrators gathered at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau on Friday to celebrate the certification of the 2026 midterm elections and call for state and federal leadership to strengthen future elections and protect voting rights. “These were not normal times. They were not normal circumstances,” said Bruce Botelho, former Alaska attorney general [...]
text:
Demonstrators rally outside the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau to celebrate the certification of the midterm elections and call for state and federal reforms on Nov. 27, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Dozens of demonstrators gathered at the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau on Friday to celebrate the certification of the 2026 midterm elections and call for state and federal leadership to strengthen future elections and protect voting rights.
“These were not normal times. They were not normal circumstances,” said Bruce Botelho, former Alaska attorney general and former mayor of Juneau, addressing the crowd.     

Demonstrators rally outside the Alaska State Capitol in Juneau to celebrate the certification of the midterm elections and call for state and federal reforms on Nov. 27, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

“Countless numbers of Americans wondered whether we would have elections in November,” he continued. “And not by interference from some foreign power, but a coordinated pattern of executive orders, federal agency interventions and public rhetoric by President Donald Trump and his administration.”
Botelho listed some of the actions taken by the Trump administration he said were aimed at reshaping election rules and challenging the legitimacy of the midterms, “all of it under the guise of necessary enforcement measures to ensure election integrity and to prevent non-citizen voting.”
That included Trump’s executive order to impose stricter voter registration and mail-in ballot requirements, and mandating proof of U.S. citizenship; rolling back federal protections and civil rights enforcement by the U.S. Department of Justice; pushing for mid-decade redistricting to boost Republicans; threatening to deploy federal law enforcement at the polls; and pushing unsubstantiated claims of voter fraud by non-citizens and calling for his supporters to “cheat like hell” among others. 
“We call on Congress to hold the Trump administration to account,” Botelho said, and thanked Alaska poll workers, poll observers and volunteers “to all those who worked to make sure we had successful elections in Alaska.” 
The rally was organized by Juneau for Democracy, a grassroots group, and Stand Up Alaska, a non-profit social justice organization. The event included songs, speeches and participants adding to a “wish list” of election reforms and signing posters thanking Alaskan election workers that they planned to deliver to the Alaska Division of Elections office down the street from the Capitol. 
In Alaska, demonstrators also called on the incoming state Legislature and the Kreiss-Tomkins administration to take action to investigate several controversial actions taken by the state Division of Elections, and to pass legislation to strengthen state elections.
Botelho and other speakers called for state leaders to investigate the division’s decision to share uncensored voter information with the DOJ. The move prompted public criticism and a lawsuit challenging the decision as a violation of voters’ privacy. The division announced an end to the agreement earlier this week. Attendees called for an investigation into the division’s unprecedented decision to disqualify a U.S. Senate candidate, Dan J. Sullivan of Petersburg, from the ballot, which was overturned by the Alaska Supreme Court. They also called for an investigation into the division removing and then reinstating Republican gubernatorial candidate and former attorney general Treg Taylor to the ballot.     

Anjuli Grantham, dressed as an “accountability elf” – Santa’s favorite helper – speaks to a crowd rallying for elections reform in Juneau on Nov. 27, 2026. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Anjuli Grantham, an organizer with Juneau for Democracy, addressed the crowd as a Christmas-themed character, an “accountability elf” — Santa’s favorite helper. She thanked Alaska reporters and news outlets for their coverage of the election, as well as voters, state attorneys and local, state and national networks for protecting election integrity, added to a “nice list.” On the “naughty list,” she criticized Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom and Division Director Carol Beecher in their roles administering state elections, and Gov. Mike Dunleavy for threatening to stop the certification of the high-stakes U.S. Senate race.
“Something that would have precipitated a real crisis for our democracy,” she said.
She also criticized Dunleavy for vetoing a bipartisan election reform bill earlier this year, and she and other speakers called on the Legislature to take it up again in the next session in January. The initiative would establish a ballot tracking and curing system, pay for postage for all mail-in ballots, boost elections staffing at all rural precincts, update the state’s voter rolls, and others. 
“Take the next bold step!” the crowd sang in a call and response. “You’re voted in. Now let’s begin. Take the next bold step. There’s work to do, we’ll stand by you. Take the next bold step.”
Alaskans saw the highest voter turnout for midterm elections in state history this year — surpassing the previous record in 2014. Results were certified by the division on Monday.
Grantham said in an interview after the event she sees that as a reaction to the Trump administration. “I think there were so many threats to the election,” she said. “And I think a lot of people just said, ‘Like, no, I’m going to do this. You cannot take this right away from me.’”
Botelho, in his remarks to the crowd, said the record turnout shows Alaskans are willing to show up “even when the headwinds that we experience this year are strong.”
“Democracy isn’t something we simply inherit every two years. It’s something we build, something we protect and something we repair together,” he said. “Let’s take the momentum of this election and urge our legislators to again enact these common sense reforms. That way, we can ensure that in Alaska, every eligible voice is heard, and every valid ballot is counted.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: No money for new projects in upcoming transportation plan, county leaders told
description: Maryland's six-year transportation contains no new projects or initiatives, but will continue to focus on safety and maintenance, Transportation Secretary Katie Thomson told county leaders in a series of meetings this fall.
text:
A newly revised six-year transportation plan will continue to focus on safety and maintenance and contain no new projects, county leaders were told this fall. (Photo courtesy Maryland Department of Transportation)Maryland’s six-year transportation contains no new projects or initiatives, but will continue to focus on safety and maintenance, Transportation Secretary Katie Thomson told county leaders in a series of meetings this fall.
That message, delivered as part of Thomson’s annual “road show” meetings with officials in each of the state’s 24 jurisdictions, reaffirmed that somber projections laid out in the draft version of the $21.9 billion plan Consolidated Transportation Program rolled out in September.
“At this point, based on all the feedback that we receive, we do not anticipate any significant changes between the draft and the final,” Thomson said in a recent interview.
“We continue to advance the projects that are identified in the CTP [Consolidated Transportation Program] as priority projects, and that includes funding for further design on the Red Line, advance work for American Legion Bridge, and some of the other projects that you’ve seen … to adjust for inflation and other costs,” she said. “I think that the major projects that you see in the draft will be those that you see in the final.”
State eyes restart of American Legion Bridge replacement, Capital Beltway widening

In addition to her road show visits this fall, Thomson sent a letter to county leaders earlier this month restating her department’s focus.
“I sent the letter because of the uniformity of the messages, both that we, the Maryland Department of Transportation, delivered at each of our tour stops, and the uniformity of messages that we were receiving from the counties and the city of Baltimore, which is recognizing the extraordinary, and unprecedented pressures that we are all experiencing,” Thomson said.
The six-year proposed plan covers fiscal years 2027-2032 and is $200 million less than the CTP approved by lawmakers earlier this year.
The total funding for the period is just 1% lower than the current plan. But it comes at a time when needs continue and the transportation trust fund remains underfunded, stressed by inflation.
Counties face the same uncertainties at a time when state aid they receive from highway user revenue has not returned to levels from before the Great Recession. If left unchanged, the counties could lose more than $100 million in fiscal 2028 as their portion of highway user revenues erodes from a share of about 20% to less than 16%.
“The resounding feedback that we were getting was that everyone’s facing these pressures more extreme,” Thomson said. “It’s not unusual to see inflation in the transportation sector, but this truly is unprecedented.”
In the first eight months of the year, the cost of diesel fuel increased by 41%. The cost of asphalt — a petroleum product — increased by 38%.
The department also cut $26 million from its current year budget.
And while much of those price increases have been driven by the war with Iran, Thomson said in January that they had seen costs on projects increase by 40%.
“So, as we were out talking about why in this CTP there are not major new investments in capital projects, and explaining it’s because, you know, it’s a significant increase in the price of diesel fuel and the increase in the cost of asphalt, other materials, and labor costs that we were not going to be able to make big, major new capital investments,” Thomson said, “and that we were going to focus on the safety of the system and investing our dollars in the state of good repair of the system to the best of our ability.”

title: Alaska Gov.-elect Kreiss-Tomkins announces inauguration in hometown of Sitka
description: Alaska’s incoming governor, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and incoming lieutenant governor, Zac Johnson, are scheduled to be sworn into office the morning of Monday, Dec. 7 in Sitka, with inauguration events continuing in Juneau.  The public is invited to attend in person or view the inauguration by livestream. The swearing-in ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m.[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 2026 candidate for Alaska governor. (Photo provided by the candidate)Alaska’s incoming governor, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, and incoming lieutenant governor, Zac Johnson, are scheduled to be sworn into office the morning of Monday, Dec. 7 in Sitka, with inauguration events continuing in Juneau. 
The public is invited to attend in person or view the inauguration by livestream. The swearing-in ceremony is scheduled for 11:30 a.m. at Centennial Hall in Sitka. The inaugural events will continue at 6:30 p.m. at Centennial Hall in Juneau. 
A full schedule of events will be released soon, according to an announcement by the Kreiss-Tomkins transition team on Tuesday. Volunteers and donations are also being requested at both events. Members of the public can RSVP on the Kreiss-Tomkins administration’s transition website at rebuildalaska.com.
Kreiss-Tomkins was born and raised in the Southeast Alaska community of Sitka, and he represented his hometown district as a Democrat in the Alaska House from 2013 to 2022. At 37, he will be Alaska’s youngest governor when sworn in as the 13th governor to serve a four-year term. 
It will be the first governor’s inauguration to take place in Sitka. Outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy chose his wife, Rose Dunleavy’s hometown of Noorvik in the Northwest Arctic Borough for his inauguration in 2018, but weather diverted the events to Kotzebue. He held inauguration events for his second term in 2022 in Anchorage. Earlier inauguration ceremonies have taken place in Juneau and Fairbanks. 
Sitka was originally inhabited by the Tlingit people, who refer to the community as Sheet’ká. After Russian colonization, it was established as the capital which continued for several decades after the U.S purchased Alaska from Russia in 1867. It was also the site of the ceremonial transfer of Alaska from Russian to U.S. control. Sitka remained the seat of Alaska’s territorial government until the capital was moved to Juneau in 1906.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Small Business Saturday, literacy improvements and rural healthcare: CT politics news
description: Plus: a looming AI startup auction raises data privacy concerns and the Coast Guard academy undergoes renovations.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Hartford reports literacy improvements
Hartford Public Schools reports the number of students starting the year at or above grade level in reading has increased across classes:

Grade 1: 43%, up from 35% last year
Grade 2: 42%, up from 36%
Grade 3: 48%, up from 39%
Grade 4: 42%, up from 38%
Grade 5: 35%, up from 28%

The improvements follow a recent statewide shift toward literacy instruction aligned with the science of reading. Changes include new curricula and more comprehensive literacy assessments. Several districts have praised the results; however, some have called for more attention to preschool and kids fourth grade and above.
— Theo Peck-Suzuki, Education Reporter
Looming AI startup auction raises youth data privacy concerns
The attorney general’s office opposes the upcoming sale of assets from a Silicon Valley startup, arguing that potential bidders will not be required to protect the data of millions of users who interacted with the platform.
Character.AI, which lets users customize AI characters and interact with chatbots, filed for bankruptcy in October. Some of its technology and intellectual property licensing is set to be sold to Disney, but the actual platform, which includes user data, private chats, and other chatbot-collected information, will be auctioned off on Dec. 1.
Attorney General William Tong, joined by a broader coalition of attorneys general, argues that the bankruptcy sale violates the company’s privacy policy, which pledged to protect user data, including more than 2 million accounts registered to minors.
Earlier this year, Connecticut lawmakers passed youth chatbot and data privacy protections intended to help protect residents’ data. Additional parts of the laws are set to go into effect on Jan. 1.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
Coast Guard Academy renovations will include new STEM facility 
The U.S. Coast Guard Academy’s ongoing effort to modernize its buildings will include a new science and engineering facility, bringing additional resources to the New London-based campus.
Earlier this month, the US Coast Guard approved two contracts, including $155M for the construction of STEM West, a new building that will include laboratories, classrooms and design spaces. When completed, the 120,000-square-foot facility will house several academy programs, including marine engineering, naval architecture and civil and environmental engineering. The project is expected to be finished by 2030.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter
CT artists join Small Business Saturday
Across Connecticut, artists will be popping up in almost every town and city for Small Business Saturday, from larger cities like New Haven, Hartford and Bridgeport to smaller ones like Bristol, which are actively working to build up their cultural districts. From Litchfield to New London, Milford to Middletown, creatives are doing their thing to sustain themselves this season.
In its last major study, titled Arts & Economic Prosperity (AEP) 6 and released in 2023, Americans for the Arts found that Connecticut’s arts and culture sector generated $954.1 million, sustained 16,667 jobs, and created $274 million in tax revenue. 
— Lucy Gellman, Arts & Culture Editor
Boosting rural healthcare
The Department of Public Health announced last week a slew of initiatives it will launch with funds from the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion, five-year effort aimed at improving healthcare in the rural U.S.
The initiative with the biggest pot of funding — $7.4 million in the first year of the grant — offers incentives for clinicians who commit to five years of practice in a rural Connecticut town. Enrolled clinicians would receive up to $35,000 per year. UConn Health’s Connecticut Area Health Education Center is finalizing the program structure and applications will open in early 2027.
— Katy Golvala, Health Reporter
Colchester selectmen propose data center moratorium
As backlash to data centers continues to sweep the state, Colchester is the latest town to propose a moratorium on development.
In a recent letter to the town’s Planning and Zoning Commission, the Colchester Board of Selectmen argued that due to strong feedback and consistent opposition from residents, a moratorium should be considered. In recent weeks, residents have voiced concerns about two proposed data centers on Old Amston Road, though a formal application has not been submitted.
The selectmen note that the moratorium would give the town time to better understand the impacts of data centers, adding that state lawmakers are expected to consider a statewide moratorium during the upcoming legislative session. The proposal could be considered at an upcoming Planning and Zoning Commission meeting, if advanced it will then be reviewed at a public hearing in the future.
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: U of I scientist to lead industry partnerships for international fish innovation lab
description: A University of Idaho lab leader will work with another university to connect aquaculture research to business through a new international program funded by the U.S. Department of State.  U of I Aquaculture Research Institute Director Brian Small will lead industry engagement and technology transfer for Mississippi State University’s Feed the Future Innovati[...]
text:
Trout swim in a tank at University of Idaho’s Hagerman Fish Culture Experiment Station in Hagerman. (Courtesy of University of idaho) A University of Idaho lab leader will work with another university to connect aquaculture research to business through a new international program funded by the U.S. Department of State. 
Brian Small, director of U of I’s Aquaculture Research Institute. (Photo courtesy of University of Idaho)
U of I Aquaculture Research Institute Director Brian Small will lead industry engagement and technology transfer for Mississippi State University’s Feed the Future Innovation Lab for Fish, according to a press release. The project is funded by an $8 million award from the U.S. Department of State for the first year of a five-year commitment. 
Small will help connect U.S. aquaculture technology companies with hatchery operators, fish farmers, processors and distributors in participating countries. The partners will “identify technologies that meet local needs and find ways for businesses to use them,” the release said. 
“Research doesn’t help anyone until a business can afford it and make it work,” Small said in the release. “Feed is a fish farmer’s biggest cost, and we can show that diets built on local ingredients perform as well as expensive imports. But that only matters once a feed mill can make them and farmers trust them enough to switch. Industry partners close that gap.”
Demonstrations will allow producers to evaluate improved production systems, hatchery practices and technologies for handling and processing harvested fish, the release said.
The lab will connect U.S. fish egg producers, including Idaho companies that already export certified trout eggs, with hatcheries abroad, giving producers reliable seed stock and U.S. companies new markets, the release said. U of I students will have opportunities to participate through internships or research at partner sites. 
“Hatcheries are an early focus,” Small said. “Many farms in partner countries struggle to get high-quality, disease-free fish eggs.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trinidad Chambliss accounts for three touchdowns as No. 23 Ole Miss beats Mississippi State 41-17
description: Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6), center, holds the "Egg Bowl" trophy awarded the winning team following their NCAA college football game against Mississippi State in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.
text:
Blake Purchase’s interception return to the 1 set up a short touchdown run by quarterback Trinidad Chambliss, and No. 23 Mississippi rallied past Mississippi State 41-17 Friday.
It was the fourth straight Egg Bowl win by Ole Miss.
Mississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) takes a snap from center Brycen Sanders (62) while Mississippi State linebacker Fatt Forrest (0) pressures during the second half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Chambliss ran around left end for a 27-17 lead with 10:30 left in the game as true separation began.
He also threw two touchdown passes, and running back Joshua Dye ran for two touchdowns, all after halftime as the Rebels turned back an upset bid from their beleaguered rival.
The Bulldogs have not won a game against an FBS team since an injury to star quarterback Kamario Taylor against Alabama in Week 5.
Ole Miss (8-4, 5-4 SEC) began the day as a 17.5-point favorite.
Mississippi State running back Fluff Bothwell (24) fights off a tackle attempt by Mississippi linebacker Tah’j Butler (49) on his way to a 16-yard touchdown run during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
“I really challenged them at halftime, and to go 35-7 in the second half in that rivalry… ,” Ole Miss coach Pete Golding said. “It’s always great to win regardless, always good to beat your rival in the last regular-season game and give us a little bit momentum going into bowl game.”
The Bulldogs were only three points back and driving when Purchase got the pick.
“That was the difference in the game,” Mississippi State coach Jeff Lebby said. “We got back in it, were on the plus-41, and the kid makes an incredible play. It was frustrating.”
Golding agreed.
“You felt that momentum starting to slide, then to come back and change the game … that was the dagger,” he said.
After Dye’s 4-yard run gave Ole Miss a 20-10 lead with 4:45 left in the third, the Bulldogs (5-7, 2-7 SEC) answered on Billy Puckett’s 12-yard pass to running back Fluff Bothwell.
Mississippi wide receiver Horatio Fields (11) is tackled from behind by Mississippi State safety Kendel Dolby (3) during the second half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
Bothwell earlier scored on a 16-yard run in the first quarter, and State led 10-6 at halftime.
Chambliss passed 6 yards to Horatio Fields to give the Rebels their first lead, 13-10, with 9:53 left in the third.
A personal foul and defensive holding calls helped boost State to a 40-yard field goal and a 10-6 lead with 1:48 left in the first half.
A scattering of Ole Miss fans booed as the Bulldogs forced Chambliss to take check-down routes and burn time on a 2-minute drill that ended when kicker Lucas Carneiro missed from 62 yards.
Mississippi State defensive coordinator Zach Arnett showed Chambliss a variety of looks in the first half.
Chambliss said he wasn’t rattled.
“We were shooting ourselves in the foot. The plays were there,” he said. “It was only a matter of time, and the plays were going to go our way.”
Run game revival
The Rebels have struggled to run consistently after an early-season injury to starting running back Kewan Lacy, who the school in August promoted for the Heisman along with Chambliss.
Mississippi State quarterback Parker “Billy” Puckett (15) passes under pressure from Mississippi defensive tackle Jehiem Oatis (9) during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. SolisMississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) hands off to running back Joshua Dye (28) during the second half of an NCAA college football game against Mississippi State in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. SolisMississippi State wide receiver Marquis Johnson (2) gestures after catching a pass for a first down against Mississippi during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. SolisMississippi quarterback Trinidad Chambliss (6) throws a pass while sandwiched by two Mississippi State defenders during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. SolisInjured Mississippi State quarterback Kamario Taylor (1) looks at the scoreboard while rolling around the field during the second half of an NCAA college football game, against Mississippi in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. SolisMississippi tight end Michael Smith (82) runs past Mississippi State defenders on his way to a touchdown pass reception in the second half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
It took the Rebels into the second half to spark the run game, but Dye, once the fourth running back on the depth chart, finished with 96 yards on 20 carries.
Ole Miss had 118 rushing yards, with only Chambliss and wide receiver Deuce Alexander as the other rushers.
The Takeaway
Mississippi State: Because of four wins earned with Taylor at quarterback, the Bulldogs, who defeated FCS Tennessee Tech last week, would have been bowl-eligible had they sprung a historic upset.
Mississippi: Ole Miss has won four straight and six of the last seven in the series known as the Egg Bowl.
Poll Implications
Ole Miss expects to remain ranked for a 64th straight week, it’s longest run since 73 weeks from 1957-64.
Up next
Mississippi State: Season over.
Ole Miss: Bowl game TBD.
Mississippi tight end Caleb Odom (4) attempts to fight off a tackle attempt by a Mississippi State defender during the first half of an NCAA college football game in Oxford, Miss., Friday, Nov. 27, 2026.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis

name: VTDigger
title: In the ‘Brave Little State,’ life after flooding goes on
description:
In an upcoming youth opera, performers highlight floods that devastated Vermont almost a century ago — and the lessons that carry into today.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  In the ‘Brave Little State,’ life after flooding goes on.
text:
Members of the Youth Opera Company at their dress rehearsal on Friday, Nov. 27. Photo courtesy of the Opera Company of Middlebury

Elsie Pawul was in preschool when Hurricane Irene swept across Vermont in 2011, leaving her school building flooded. But instead of halting lessons, the teachers forged ahead, going about their daily schedule in a tent on the school lawn.
For Pawul, the flood served as an early reminder. 
“School keeps going,” Pawul said. “Even though the building doesn’t.”
It’s been a decade and a half since Irene hit. Devastating floods in 2023, 2024 and 2025 are a much more recent memory for Pawul and many of her fellow Vermonters. 
But memories tend to lie dormant when it comes to The Great Vermont Flood of 1927, the worst natural disaster the state has ever seen. 
Over two days in early November that year, rising waters killed 84 people, including the lieutenant governor, destroyed 1,285 bridges and cost the state between $30 million and $35 million — or about a half billion dollars in today’s money. 
The year after the flood, President Calvin Coolidge, originally from Vermont, toured the damage and gave a speech about the walloping his state took. In it, he coined a familiar Vermont nickname: the “Brave Little State.” 
It was that moniker that gave the show its name, and that speech that inspired them to look further into the story of the floods, according to Sarah Cullins, the production’s stage director.
It’s those memories that Pawul and the rest of the Opera Company of Middlebury’s Youth Opera Company will rekindle. They seek to highlight a theme that carries through generations: In the wake of catastrophe, life goes on.
This weekend, 12 young Vermont singers will present an opera about a year in the aftermath of the floods. The show will be performed on Saturday at the Faith United Methodist Church in South Burlington and the Champlain Valley Unitarian Universalist Society in Middlebury. On Sunday, the show will be performed at the Lost Nation Theater in Montpelier.
The show is designed to reflect the everyday school experience, Cullins said. Some kids chat about the girl who came to town in the summer. Another girl despises the rigid structure of her choral class. Students cheer when the teacher leaves them unattended, and make fun of their teachers in an opera song. 
Sunday’s opera will begin with a graduation ceremony scene, Cullins said, where the valedictorian reflects on the year after the floods hit. Then it takes the audience back through a year of everyday life at a high school, guided by songs from former operas with composers including Leonard Bernstein, Samuel Barber, Amy Beach and Aaron Copeland. It also features a reenactment of Coolidge’s famous speech.
While the story centers around the year after the flood, said Pawul, an intern and alumna of the opera company, it’s also about regular life.
“All of the everyday things that we did or do don’t just stop because a catastrophe happened,” Pawul said.
Community connection
Each year, Cullins and her team pick a language, composer or musical style for the opera company, she said, which ensures that students who repeat the program can gain different experiences from each session.
This year, they decided to pick American composers as a mark of the nation’s semiquincentennial.
Pawul, who joined the program as a junior in high school, said she enjoyed seeing young people engaging in the art since opera previously seemed like a “huge adult thing” to her. This year, Pawul got the opportunity to write the script from the outline that the team constructed.
“I always had an interest in Vermont history, like specifically Vermont history,” Pawul said. “So it kind of fit in with that, and then I loved most of the songs that we chose.”
She structured the script both around the historical context of the 1920s and the similarities to more recent Vermont floods, Pawul said. She drew on her personal experience as well, since she had witnessed the aftermath of the floods in the past five years.
The biggest connecting factor was the way the community united after the disaster, Pawul said, and the importance of that.
“I think we can do so much with community,” Pawul said. “And I think we either take that for granted or don’t utilize that enough.”
Every student in the production knows someone who was deeply affected by Vermont’s recent floods, Cullins said. It’s not difficult for them to imagine a neighbor needing clothing or other forms of help, or a Vermonter losing their home.
“At the same time, they also know how somehow life goes on,” Cullins said. “And you still go to school, and you still think about the girl you met over the summer, and you still have a graduation, and you have a valedictorian.”

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Post-midterms, presidential hopefuls will step up visits to SC
description: Politicians considering a 2028 presidential run have already been crisscrossing the state. Their visits will ramp up now that the 2028 election cycle is officially underway. And they'll no longer have the excuse of visiting to help South Carolina candidates win their 2026 races.
text:
New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker speaks at the 50th Anniversary Gala for the South Carolina Legislative Black Caucus on Saturday, November 21, 2026 in Columbia. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — When New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker made stops across South Carolina last weekend, he continued to dismiss questions about a 2028 bid. Like other politicians appearing to test the presidential primary waters across the state, he’ll likely get plenty of other opportunities to answer. 
“We’ll see what the future holds. But right now, I’m just happy to celebrate this victory,” Booker told the SC Daily Gazette last weekend on whether his post-midterm tour was related to a presidential run. 
If and when he announces another bid for the White House remains to be seen. He said his latest visit was to celebrate Democrats’ gains in the state and to talk about how the party builds on momentum from flipping a U.S. Senate seat and eliminating Republicans’ GOP supermajority in the state House. 
It was the New Jersey Democrat’s fourth trip to the Palmetto State this year. 
Last Friday, he toured Emanuel African Methodist Episcopal Church in Charleston and a memorial to the nine people massacred at the historically Black church in 2015, then spoke at the Charleston NAACP Freedom Fund Gala. On Saturday, he attended the 50th anniversary gala for the South Carolina Legislative Black Caucus. 
Politicians considering a 2028 presidential run have already been crisscrossing the state. Their visits will ramp up now that the 2028 election cycle is officially underway. And they’ll no longer have the excuse of visiting to help South Carolina candidates win their 2026 races. 
Other Democrats visiting since the election include former White House adviser and Chicago Mayor Rahm Emmanuel, who met with pastors at Columbia’s Grace Christian Church. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg also returned, with stops including a ceremony at the University of South Carolina for the naming of a leadership center after former Columbia Mayor Steve Benjamin. 
SC picks president
Republicans and Democrats in South Carolina like to brag that they pick presidents. Since the state parties began holding presidential primaries here — 1980 for Republicans and 1992 for Democrats — South Carolinians have picked their party’s nominees every time, with one exception for each party.
In both cases, South Carolinians went with a neighbor over a northerner: In 2012, Republicans chose former U.S. House Speaker Newt Gingrich of Georgia over former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney. And in 2004, Democrats chose South Carolina-born Sen. John Edwards of North Carolina over Massachusetts Sen. John Kerry.
In 2028, South Carolina could matter more than ever.
 On the Republican side, South Carolina keeps its first-in-the-South status, following contests in Iowa, New Hampshire and Nevada.  
But South Carolina is first on Democrats’ presidential nominating calendar, with the primary set for Jan. 22, 2028. South Carolina was supposed to be first in 2024, but New Hampshire went rogue.
If there’s no leapfrogging again in 2028, it will mark the first time South Carolinians will actually be at the front of the voting line and for a contest that could truly be a gamechanger. The February 2024 primary wasn’t really a contest, as President Joe Biden’s win against two extreme-longshot candidates was never in question. And ultimately, that win didn’t matter anyway, since Biden withdrew from the race in July and Vice President Kamala Harris replaced him on the ticket.   
But in 2020, it was Biden’s win in South Carolina that catapulted him to the nomination, following a fourth-place finish in Iowa and fifth-place finish in New Hampshire.
He has repeatedly thanked South Carolina Democrats as the reason he won the White House in 2020, even though South Carolina’s electoral votes went to President Donald Trump that November.
Traditionally, presidential candidates don’t return to South Carolina post-primary because it’s presumed the Republican will win. A Democrat has won South Carolina’s electoral votes only once in the last 62 years. Again, the exception involved a fellow Southerner: Jimmy Carter of Georgia in 1976.
But with Democrats’ successes in the midterm, some party leaders believe South Carolina’s votes will be in play past the 2028 primaries.
“When those folks start coming here and testing the waters, they’re coming to a battleground state,” state Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain told reporters the day after the election. “They’re not just coming, in my opinion, to a Southern state that has a different electorate. But I feel like they’re coming to a battleground state.” 
Events that draw contenders
Upcoming events in South Carolina will likely bring out a host of Democrats vying for the White House. 
King Day at the Dome, held at the Statehouse on Martin Luther King Jr. Day, began in 2000 as a protest to remove the Confederate flag from the Statehouse dome. Legislators passed a law later that year bringing it down, though the compromise put a smaller, square version on the front lawn next to the Confederate soldiers’ monument. The NAACP never accepted the compromise, and the annual event continued. In 2015, the flag was removed from grounds for good following the Mother Emanuel church shooting. 
Booker was the keynote speaker earlier this year. Other speakers included U.S. Rep. Ro Khanna of California, another potential 2028 contender.
In 2020, the last time Democrats had a wide-open race for president, Booker dropped out of the field ahead of King Day. 
Participants who marched arm-in-arm that year from Zion Baptist Church, where activities begin with a prayer service, down Main Street to the Statehouse included Biden as well as U.S. Sens. Bernie Sanders of Vermont, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, and Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts; Buttigieg, whose tenure as mayor of South Bend, Indiana, had just ended; and U.S. Rep. Tulsi Gabbard of Hawaii.  
Details of the 2027 King Day at the Dome have not yet been announced. 
In the spring, a must-attend event is U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn’s annual fish fry, a free event held the same night as Democrats’ big fundraiser, the Blue Palmetto Dinner.
This year’s speakers included Khanna and Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, while last year, Govs. Wes Moore of Maryland and Tim Walz of Minnesota addressed the crowd.
For Republicans, the featured speaker for the Silver Elephant Dinner, the GOP fundraising dinner, could be a 2028 frontrunner. Then-Gov. Ronald Reagan was the first Silver Elephant speaker in 1967. Other former presidents to give the keynote address include Richard Nixon and George W. Bush.
In 2023, it was then-former President Donald Trump, who drew a record crowd of more than 1,300 people ahead of his 2024 GOP primary win over former South Carolina Gov. Nikki Haley.
Rep. Russell Fry’s Freedom Fry, which started in 2024, will likely bring Republican contenders to the stage. Next October will mark the first Freedom Fry ahead of a presidential primary. 
This year’s event featured Texas Sen. Ted Cruz, a potential presidential candidate, and Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, who was later chosen by Republicans in the U.S. House later as their caucus leader.
It’s “certainly an event that anybody who is running for president would want to come to,” Fry told reporters Oct. 26. 
Who has been in the state
Beyond Booker, other Democrats considered potential 2028 contenders who visited the state this year — often alongside Rep. Jermaine Johnson, Democrats’ nominee for governor — include Beshear, Emanuel, Khanna, Moore, Arizona Sen. Mark Kelly, California Gov. Gavin Newsom, Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, and Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock. 
Warnock rallied alongside Johnson and Sen.-elect Annie Andrews weeks ahead of the election. Khanna joined Johnson at his final rally the night before the election.
Republicans have also made their way through South Carolina. In the final days ahead of the midterms, Georgia Gov. Brian Kemp and Cruz joined now-Gov.-elect Alan Wilson on his bus tour.
But the dynamics are different for Republicans, since the battle over who will be the nominee to potentially replace Trump will likely include people in his administration who don’t want to be seen as campaigning for the job yet.  
Topping Republican presidential polls are Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Neither has publicly appeared in the state this year. 
Vance was in South Carolina last year on an official visit to a steel plant in Berkeley County to celebrate the first 100 days of the second Trump administration.
No one has officially declared a race yet. But the list could grow quickly in the coming months.   
Democrats, according to a party announcement Monday, will run 12 planned primary debates from June 2027 through March 2028. Republicans have not yet made an announcement about their primary debates.

name: VTDigger
title: Bye-bye box stores, hello flannel flurries
description:
Montpelier’s Flannel Friday kicked off a series of sales and special offers to celebrate the holiday season, and acted as a precursor for Small Business Saturday around Vermont.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Bye-bye box stores, hello flannel flurries.
text:
Main Street in Montpelier on Flannel Friday on Friday, Nov. 27. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger

MONTPELIER — Montpelier’s Friday morning dawned drizzly and cold, but Flannel Friday, an annual downtown event, proceeded as planned. People strolled around Montpelier’s main streets, hopping in and out of local shops with signs advertising their specialty sales.
Flannels abounded, with some people sporting flannel coats, others with flannel collars poking from beneath down jackets, and some wearing flannel pajama pants.
Flannel Friday is part of a two-day chain of events in Montpelier, the second being a nationwide event called Small Business Saturday. It’s a chance for Vermonters and visitors to score discounts on holiday gifts and meet the Flannel Fairy — a winged creature carrying presents for all shoppers sporting flannels — while supporting local businesses.
“We’re investing in our local community rather than sending our money out of the local community,” said Emily Allen, a shopper at Woodbury Mountain Toys on Friday and someone who believes in the importance of shopping locally. Allen grew up in Vermont and now lives in New Hampshire. She was visiting the toy store with her mom.
“So we can help each other by simply getting the things that we need right where we live.”
Toni Cieplensky, a New Jersey resident, traveled to Vermont to visit family over Thanksgiving. She participated in Flannel Friday a few years ago, and was eager to come to the event again.
“I was like, I wonder if they do Flannel Friday still,” Cieplensky said. “I couldn’t wait.” 
She bought a flannel in advance to wear for the occasion.
Alan Johnson and Jen Toce were other participants in the event, with Johnson wearing a flannel scarf around his neck. Toce, the owner of Birchgrove Baking, was taking a much-needed break along with her staff after a frenzied lead-up to Thanksgiving.
“We were open on Thanksgiving Day, and it was just nonstop,” Toce said. “Even, like, we sold out everything. We shut the doors. We still had customers in the store.”
Johnson and Toce strolled through downtown Friday morning after visiting Red Hen Baking Co.

Alan Johnson and Jen Toce pose outside a downtown building on Flannel Friday. Photo captured on Friday, Nov. 27. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger

Small Business Saturday
Communities all across the U.S. and Vermont participate in Small Business Saturday. Montpelier will offer free horse-drawn wagon rides across downtown and specialty discounts at local businesses. 
In Rutland, downtown celebrates with raffles, giveaways, a hot cocoa station and more. Nearby, in Manchester Village, there’s a holiday market at the Equinox Resort. In Newport, the community offers maps of downtown, bingo cards and giveaways, Essex hosts small business pop-up shops, and Burlington features a variety of art fairs and other celebrations including the BTV Winter Market and the Soda Plant Holiday Bazaar. Other similar events are spread throughout Vermont.
For Karen Williams, the owner of Woodbury Mountain Toys, the two events serve as a kickoff for the holiday season and a powerful source of revenue. Last year, Williams estimated that Flannel Friday was her biggest sales day of the year.
Williams said she’s found the community to be very supportive of her shop.
“People are really excited to come into a toy store that is unique and also reminds a lot of people of their childhood,” Williams said. 
The last few years have required deft adaptation, Williams said, between Covid-19 and the floods. But she has also noticed a trend of more adults buying toys, games and puzzles for themselves, perhaps as a way to cope with the news these days. 
And since the pandemic, she’s seen local people bonding together, she added.
“I think that people have almost a better understanding of what it is to, yeah, to be supporting your community,” Williams said.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal court orders authorities to stop making warrantless immigration arrests
description: A U.S. District Court judge ordered federal authorities to stop making warrantless immigration arrests in Montana. The order Wednesday said officers with the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection have a “policy and practice of making unlawful arrests.” It said they won’t stop the illegal acts [...]
text:
The emblem of the United States federal court of Montana (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). A U.S. District Court judge ordered federal authorities to stop making warrantless immigration arrests in Montana.
The order Wednesday said officers with the Department of Homeland Security, Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and Customs and Border Protection have a “policy and practice of making unlawful arrests.”
It said they won’t stop the illegal acts without a court order.
The decision follows a complaint filed by Upper Seven Law on behalf of Jesus Verde Hernandez, three other named plaintiffs, and other individuals in a similar situation that called on federal authorities to stop making illegal arrests.
Upper Seven said it has secured the release of 71 individuals in wrongful immigration arrests since it started such work.
Signed by Chief U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris, the order said the government has an interest in enforcing immigration law, but it said federal authorities still have to follow the law in doing so.
That means if they are making an arrest without a warrant, federal officials need to show the suspect is a flight risk who is likely to run away before the government can get a warrant, the order said.
“Defendants repeatedly have shown they fail to abide by these requirements while making arrests in the District of Montana,” the order said.
Morris granted a temporary restraining order and stopped the federal government, at least for now, from ignoring whether a person represents a flight risk before arresting them without a warrant.
The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a question by press time about whether federal officers would comply with the order.
The judge said federal authorities started “pushing for mass immigration arrests” in January 2025, “resulting in a policy that violates” the Immigration and Nationality Act.
But “courts around the country have concluded that defendants’ policy of arresting people without first assessing the person’s flight risk remains unlawful,” the order said.
It said the feds were using the arrests to try to coerce people into voluntarily deporting.
The court found federal authorities would continue to try to coerce people, even if they had “meritorious claims” for release and without an opportunity to speak with a lawyer, and based on “misinformation” about the immigration process.
The court said the Fourth Amendment prohibits “unreasonable searches and seizures,” and the protection covers citizens and non-citizens.
It said non-citizens “receive constitutional protections when they have come within the territory of the United States and developed substantial connections to this country.”
In a news release about the order, Upper Seven Law, which represents the plaintiffs, said federal immigration officials have arrested individuals in Montana without probable cause for 18 months.
The law firm said it represented a similar class of people in Hernandez v. Crosson, which also contests illegal immigration enforcement.
It said plaintiffs have included an 18-year-old who was on a trip with friends; a 9-year-old arrested with her father; and multiple families with minor children, “upending lives and preventing children from attending school.”
It said others “have been held in cells for 24 hours a day, with no ability to go outside.”
Upper Seven said arrests have occurred at gas stations, work sites and traffic stops, in some cases only because officers determined the individuals spoke Spanish.
In August, the court found the warrantless immigration arrests to be illegal, and in November, it said courts across the country found the same, but federal authorities persisted in making the same unlawful arrests, Upper Seven said.
“The court has repeatedly told federal officials that their conduct is illegal, but the government continues to violate the law,” said Molly Danahy, Upper Seven Law’s litigation director and counsel for the plaintiff class, in a statement. “This injunction is absolutely necessary to stop these unlawful policies and practices.”



Court order
The court order grants a preliminary injunction, or temporary stop, to action by the federal government, which it said is appropriate at this stage of litigation.
The plaintiffs need to establish the following elements to stop the action, and they did so, the order said:

They are likely to succeed on the merits: The court found the government’s policy and practice of warrantless arrests runs contrary to the Immigration and Nationality Act.
They are likely to suffer irreparable harm in the absence of preliminary relief: The court said “it is well established that the deprivation of constitutional rights unquestionably constitutes irreparable injury.” It said the government will continue to violate the law without the order.
The balance of equities tips in their favor, and an injunction is in the public interest: The order said the court weighs the interests of the plaintiffs, the defendants and the public at large. It said the defendants have an interest in immigration enforcement, but they still need to follow the law in doing so, and “it is always in the public interest to prevent the violation of a party’s constitutional rights.” In this case, the court said the balance of equities and public interest “tip sharply” for the plaintiffs.

title: Phebe Shih Chao
description:
War uprooted her childhood, taking her from Shanghai to Hong Kong, Pasadena and Washington. Through all of it, she wrote, “it was reading that carried me through.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Phebe Shih Chao.
text:
Born: 07/05/1930
Shanghai
Died: 10/10/2026
Strafford, NH
Details of service:
A celebration of her life will be held in the spring of 2027. For details, contact maiachaos@gmail.com

Phebe Chao died on Oct. 20, aged 96, surrounded by her loving family at her rural home in Strafford, New Hampshire. She was a beloved and influential Professor of American Literature at Bennington College for 19 years.
She was born in Shanghai on July 5, 1930, the only child of Shih Tao-sheng, a Chinese diplomat, and Anna Chang. Her father named her 菲比, Chinese for “beyond compare” (for which “Phebe” is homophone); and joined with the family name, Shih, or “stone,” made her “a gem beyond compare.”
War uprooted her childhood, taking her from Shanghai to Hong Kong, Pasadena and Washington. Through all of it, she wrote, “it was reading that carried me through.”
She graduated from Sidwell Friends School at the age of 15 and went on to Wellesley. While raising three sons, she earned a B.A., magna cum laude, and an M.A. from the University of Michigan. At 38, she entered Harvard on a Harvard Prize Fellowship, and she went on to earn her Ph.D. in English and American literature.
At Harvard she met Roger Sorkin on a dance floor, where they danced the Lindy to that week’s new record, the Beatles’ “Abbey Road.” She taught literature at Bennington for 19 years, and in 1981, she was a visiting Fulbright Professor at Peking University in Beijing, China.
Her memoir gathers a century of her family’s history, from Shanghai to America. Its title, 夢家 (meng jia), echoes one of the last things her mother, Anna, said on her death bed: That she was “dreaming of home.” 
She is survived by her husband of 56 years, Roger Sorkin; her sons Bruce, Matthew and Stephen Chao and Thomas Ma; her grandchildren Zoë, Maia, Madison, Virgil, Rose and Phebe Chao, Justin and Joshua Ma; and her great-grandchildren Suki, Wilhelmina and Lupina Chao.
