name: Alaska Beacon
title: New app consolidates Alaska tsunami hazard and preparation information
description: Around Alaska, which hugs the shifting and rumbling geological zone known as the Pacific Rim of Fire, tsunamis are ever-present risks in coastal communities. Now the Alaska Earthquake Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks has gathered the latest available tsunami risk and mitigation information into a single source. The Tsunami Map App, which is […]
text:
Mike West, Alaska's state seismologist stands on Oct. 5, 2026, next to an image of a modeled tsunami inundation zone in Seward. The image was pulled from a new app developed by the University of Alaska Fairbanks-based Alaska Earthquake Center, in partnership with other agencies and organizations. The Seward map shows how most of the downtown area of the Kenai Peninsula town would be flooded if there were a severe tsunami. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Around Alaska, which hugs the shifting and rumbling geological zone known as the Pacific Rim of Fire, tsunamis are ever-present risks in coastal communities.
Now the Alaska Earthquake Center at the University of Alaska Fairbanks has gathered the latest available tsunami risk and mitigation information into a single source.
The Tsunami Map App, which is embedded in the center’s tsunami information website, does not provide any new information. What is new is the way it is accessible in a convenient place.
The app links users to detailed interactive maps of nearly 70 communities, pointing out vulnerable areas, inundation zones, designated evacuation routes and more. It’s available as a mobile-friendly web app on the center’s website, not an app available for download. 
Alaska, with its experience with these events, “has been doing really good tsunami things for a long time,” said state seismologist Mike West. He reeled off numerous safety measures, like signage informing people of evacuation routes, brochures tailored for each community.
“But one of the problems is that there’s little bits of information that live all around the place,” he said.
 

A sign pointing out the tsunami evacuation route in Whittier is seen on July 17, 2025. In the background is the Begich Towers, the high-rise building where almost all of Whittier’s 275 residents live. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	Some of that information, though well-researched, may have been overlooked by the public, West said.
He cited one example. “Did you know that there is a dedicated maritime guidance report for Whittier specifically for boat owners?” he said. “That’s been around for some years.”
The app shows expected tsunami inundation zones, as determined by UAF, state and federal scientists, along with community information about hyper-local issues like the most practical streets to take during evacuations. 
Its interactive maps can show individual homes, schools, fire stations and other sites that are important to residents and visitors. It includes the latest accumulated knowledge about known risks from landslide-generated tsunamis, hazards that have been exacerbated by climate change, as well as earthquake-generated tsunamis.
The app is expected to be helpful for city planners, emergency response agencies, mariners, homeowners and even tourists, among others.
Because of Alaska’s seismic history, which includes the most powerful North American earthquake ever recorded and the resulting tsunami damage that killed people as far away as northern California, Alaskans are tsunami-aware – but only up to a point, West said.
 

Vehicles travel on the Homer Spit on Oct. 22, 2025. Homer is among the most tsunami-vulnerable communities in Alaska, and within it, the Homer Spit, a finger of low-lying land that stretches out to Kachemak Bay and holds numerous businesses, is particularly vulnerable. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)
 

	When seismologists now refer to “the big earthquake” or “the big historical earthquake,” many younger residents think of something other than the magnitude 9.2 Great Alaska Earthquake of 1964, West said.
“I am amazed at how many people in Anchorage think of 2018 and not 1964 because generations turn over,” he said. On Nov. 30, 2018, a magnitude 7.1 earthquake struck the Anchorage area, damaging roads and several structures and forcing temporary closures of schools.
Additionally, there are constant waves of transplants for whom tsunami and earthquake information is new, West said. For example, personnel and families stationed at the U.S. Coast Guard base in Kodiak, the agency’s largest base, can turn over every few years, meaning there is frequent retraining of new arrivals, he noted.
Kodiak is among Alaska’s most tsunami-prone communities. It is in a particularly seismically active area, on the Gulf of Alaska coast near where the Pacific plate that is part of Earth’s crust is slipping under the North America plate, another part of the planet’s crust.
The app project resulted from collaboration between the Alaska Earthquake Center and other entities, including the state Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management, the Alaska Division of Geological and Geophysical Surveys and numerous local governments.
There is a caveat about the app’s usefulness. It serves more as a preparation tool than a response tool, West said.
“During a tsunami, now, to be fair, when the siren goes off, that is not the time to be pulling out one’s phone and, you know, searching and pulling up the map and zooming around,” he said.
The Port of Seward, with a docked cruise ship, and much of the downtown distarict are seen on June 19, 2024, from Race Point on Mount Marathon. If a major tsunami were to hit, the port, most of the downtown area and part of the Seward Highway leading north out of town would be inundated, according to scientists’ analysis. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana to receive $239 million in rural federal healthcare money
description: As Montana lands another massive grant for rural health care — $239 million this time — professionals in the field say providers and patients soon will feel benefits from the federal program. The recent Rural Health Transformation Program award was third-highest among all states, following an award in the first round that totalled $233 million […]
text:
The hospital in Ekalaka, a small town in sprawling, rural southeastern Montana, sits at the intersection of two dirt roads. (Photo by Arielle Zionts | KFF Health News)As Montana lands another massive grant for rural health care — $239 million this time — professionals in the field say providers and patients soon will feel benefits from the federal program.
The recent Rural Health Transformation Program award was third-highest among all states, following an award in the first round that totalled $233 million to Montana. Members of the health community say initial funding built the infrastructure to support rural care, and the additional dollars will pay for things such as patient care and EMS services.
The Governor’s Office, in a joint press release with the state’s Department of Public Health and Human Services, said the award will “support efforts to strengthen rural health care, expand access to services closer to home, and help providers build financially sustainable operations.”
In a press release, health department Director Douglas Harrington said the increase in funding was due to the state’s success in the first year of the grant program. The state has now received about $473 million in total from its two applications for the federal money.
“The increased award reflects our first-year performance, a clear plan for Year Two, and the hard work of Montana’s RHTP team,” Harrington of the Rural Health Transportation Program. “In the first year, we built partnerships, committed funds, and put tools in place to support long-term improvements. In Year Two, we will build on that foundation to help rural facilities strengthen their operations, modernize health records, and expand access to care in rural and tribal communities.”
Advocacy organizations, including the Montana Medical Association, say the funding stream has been beneficial.
“We’re really diving in, and all of the partners involved are really taking this as a very important effort and making sure that we can keep Montana healthy,” Montana Medical Association CEO Leeann Sherman said in an interview.
Workforce development is one key area Sherman identified, saying that when looking at the total number of people in the medical profession per capita, Montana is “at least 30 to 40% too low in physician care,” adding that includes nurse practitioners.
She added that the state health department has done a good job addressing the workplace shortages, but that conversation includes other topics such as where people choose to do their medical residencies, as well as student loan debt.
“A lot of people leave Montana to go do residency programs,” Sherman said. “Well, if you move to Chicago or New York or Arizona or somewhere else and you do your residency program, are the odds that you’re going to come back to Montana?”
She added that it’s a conversation that’s happening with them and the Graduate Medical Education Council.
“It’s a huge gap — very huge gap — of physicians and other medical professionals in Montana serving Montana communities,” Sherman said.
Workforce development received $22.1 million from the state’s first grant application, rural facility sustainability got $84.3 million, work geared towards innovative care delivery got $37 million, work to improve community health received $40.9 million and technology modernization was $35.5 million of the initial grant award. Administrative and other costs totaled $13.7 million.
There are questions about the money and how it’s trickling down, Sherman said, who preached patience.
“I think that there’s just an anticipation from people in the community, but also in our profession, that are saying, ‘Where’s the money? What’s happening? It’s been a year from the first (grant award), and now we’re getting awarded the second year, and we don’t see any benefit,’” Sherman said. “And I would just kind of temper that with, absolutely, and there will be transformation coming, but you have to set up an infrastructure, and we have to set up ways to be able to get that money out, and to be able to truly assess where the money needs to go.” 
More than 130 providers, organizations, and agencies received grants in the first year of the award, health department spokesperson Jon Ebelt wrote in an email. 
The second year of the cycle will shift into “operational expansion” across the state, Ebelt said. Investments from the grant highlighted by the state include money going to supporting rural EMS and an expansion of community-based care.
“A lot has happened to give us that foundation,” Sherman said. “And so now you’re going to start to see more and more things being brought to the public. 
The state will be using the second year of the grant to produce community assessments of healthcare needs across the state, modernize recordkeeping, expand tribal healthcare initiatives and continue funding workplace development programs for the medical field.
“This investment builds on the partnerships we established in the first year of the Rural Health Transformation Program to strengthen emergency services, support our rural health care workforce, and help local providers deliver care for years to come,” Montana Gov. Greg Gianforte said in the press release.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa judge calls out ICE for mistakes and for routine encounters ‘gone awry’
description: A federal judge in Iowa has sharply criticized the government for its conduct in jailing a Guatemalan immigrant who was the victim of mistaken identity. “Such an egregious mistake of fact is almost beyond belief,” Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa stated in a recent […]
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement is holding dozens of individuals in Iowa jails. (Main photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images; logo courtesy U.S. Department of Homeland Security)  A federal judge in Iowa has sharply criticized the government for its conduct in jailing a Guatemalan immigrant who was the victim of mistaken identity.
“Such an egregious mistake of fact is almost beyond belief,” Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa stated in a recent ruling. “It continues to bewilder the court how often routine encounters in immigration matters have gone awry,”
In her ruling, Rose stated the “the number of mistakes” law enforcement has made in such cases is concerning and indicated they continue to grow in number.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The ruling stems from a lawsuit filed earlier this month by Santos Fredy Perez Recinos, a Guatemalan immigrant, against U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche and Polk County Sheriff Kevin Schneider.
In his lawsuit, Perez Recinos alleged he entered the United States near Rio Grande City, Texas, in June 2023. Previously released court records suggested Perez Recinos was 20 at the time, although subsequent filings indicate he was 16 when he entered the United States, was taken into custody, processed as an unaccompanied alien child, and then released to the care of his sister.
Court records show that on Oct. 28, 2026, law enforcement officials were attempting to locate and arrest Innocente Perez-Geronimo, who was wanted on a state warrant for sexual assault of a minor, when they instead arrested and then jailed Perez Recinos after concluding he matched the description of Perez-Geronimo.
Perez Recinos sued, with his attorney telling the court his client “was simply living his life when (ICE) picked him up off the street. He never should have been arrested.”
The case went before Chief Judge Rose, who recently issued a ruling giving federal officials 24 hours to release Perez Recinos.



Quotation







The record contains only one reason for his re-detention: law enforcement’s mistaken identification.


– Chief Judge Stephanie M. Rose, U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Iowa


“The record does not contain any allegations that he ever failed to appear for an immigration proceeding or violated any term of his release,” Rose stated in her ruling. “He has no criminal history, and the record does not suggest that he has ever been involved in any criminal activity.”
Rose noted in her ruling that when agents learned they had the wrong man, they contacted the ICE office in Des Moines and “someone in that office told the agents” to keep Perez Recinos in custody and transport him to Des Moines, where an immigration arrest warrant was obtained and Perez Recinos was jailed.
“The number of mistakes law enforcement has recently made in detaining noncitizens is concerning,” Rose stated in her ruling. “And on the undisputed facts of this case, that number continues to grow.”
Rose noted that while agents said they arrested Perez Recinos due to his matching the wanted man’s description, the two men were not the same height or weight, with Perez Recinos being three inches shorter and 20 to 30 pounds lighter.
“Such an egregious mistake of fact is almost beyond belief,” Rose concluded. “Once law enforcement learned of their mistake, they did not remedy it. Rather, they spent the next several hours working to place Perez Recinos — an individual the government previously released into the country on an order of recognizance — into ICE’s custody.”
Rose noted that in response to the lawsuit, lawyers for the U.S. Department of Justice did not cite a statutory basis for Perez Recinos’ detainment and instead chose to “repackage” an argument the court had rejected in a different case just a few weeks earlier.
It is undisputed, Rose noted, that since jailing Perez Recinos, the federal government had not provided him with a hearing at which he could argue for his release on bond – a violation of his due process rights.
Rose also noted that unlike other cases in which the federal government detained individuals on the grounds that there was some material change in the circumstances allowing those people to remain free in the United States, the government didn’t argue Perez-Recinos’ situation had changed at all prior to him being jailed.
“Their only reason for re-detaining (Perez Recinos) without a bond hearing is a mistaken identification,” Rose stated in her ruling. Citing the lack of evidence Perez Recinos was either a flight risk or a danger to the community, Rose ordered the government to release him from the Polk County Jail within 24 hours.
“The record contains only one reason for his re-detention: law enforcement’s mistaken identification,” Rose stated. “The government may detain noncitizens during removal proceedings. But when it releases a noncitizen into the country and allows him to remain free for years, it may not re-detain him without due process.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Judge: Counselor is incompetent and ‘not in the proper mental framework’
description: A mental health counselor who reportedly shared with a client his own theories on government conspiracies and his wife’s alleged infidelities has been sanctioned by the state. The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals alleges that in January 2024, a client of mental health counselor Michael Cox of Davenport filed a complaint with the board […]
text:
(Stock photo by Getty Images)A mental health counselor who reportedly shared with a client his own theories on government conspiracies and his wife’s alleged infidelities has been sanctioned by the state.
The Iowa Board of Behavioral Health Professionals alleges that in January 2024, a client of mental health counselor Michael Cox of Davenport filed a complaint with the board regarding Cox’s conduct.
The complainant alleged that Cox, who has been a state-licensed counselor for 12 years, had used racial slurs and shared with her information about his personal life to the extent that she had become fearful.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In March 2025, the board issued a confidential order directing Cox to complete a comprehensive evaluation of his own mental health. The board says there’s no evidence to indicate Cox ever complied with that order and so earlier this year, it charged Cox with failing to comply with a board order. That led to an October 2026 hearing on the matter before Administrative Law Judge Toby Gorson.
Gorson’s recent decision in the case details the specific concerns raised by the board:
Questionable advice: The client alleged that when she raised the issue of anxious or depressing thoughts she was having, Cox responded by advising her to “tell the thought to f— off.”
Conspiracies: When the client indicated she was having a difficult time handling a school shooting that had taken place at Perry High School, Cox allegedly stated the shooting “didn’t seem right,” and may have been a “set up” or a “government conspiracy.” Those remarks were alleged to be consistent with other reported remarks by Cox about perceived conspiracies and “the evil in this world.”
Self-disclosure: The client alleged Cox frequently complained about his wife cheating on him and having sex with a Hispanic male whom Cox allegedly referred to with a racial slur. The client claimed her counseling sessions eventually were focused more on Cox’s personal issues than on her own problems.
Board records indicate the counseling sessions were remote, conducted via telehealth services, and that the client taped a brief, one-minute portion of their third and final session together.
According to Gorson’s decision, Cox can be heard on the tape talking about “some weird f—ing nefarious plans to try to hurt good people (and) f—ing wedge its way into your mind.” Gorson’s decision states that the recording also captures Cox discussing “the rapist” his wife was purportedly involved with, along with Cox’s characterization of the man as “that f—ing douchebag, that f—ing sp–.”
Gorson says the tape also captures Cox saying of the man, “I told him I’d cut his little d— off,” and then describing the man as a “piece of s—.” According to Gorson, Cox goes on to tell the client about the “stupid evil … something out there gets joy from trying to hurt us and I don’t know what the f— it is.”
Board: Cox claimed to be ‘of sound mind’
According to Gorson’s decision, when a board investigator asked Cox about his comments, he responded by saying he’d obtained his client’s consent to use profane language and that he did so because such language made their sessions more relaxed. Cox also explained that his self-disclosures were intended to “normalize trauma” and show how “everyone goes through it,” Gorson stated in his findings.
Cox allegedly denied using a racial slur or stating his wife cheated on him until the board investigator played the recording for him, at which point he indicated he had forgotten making the comments, Gorson reported. “I know it sounds terrible,” Cox allegedly told the board investigator.
When Cox was asked about his alleged comments referencing the Perry High School shooting, he denied ever discussing the matter, telling the board investigator, “I’m of sound mind” – a comment, Gorson said, the board investigator found odd.
According to Gorson’s decision, the investigator’s interview with Cox ended with the latter admitting he had once been diagnosed with depression and acknowledging he harbored “anger at how negative the world can be,” adding, “I feel terrible for having any – scaring a client. That was not my intent.”
In January 2025, the board has alleged, Cox submitted a written statement in which he said his client had illegally recorded their session, while adding that he was making a “concerted effort not to swear in sessions” with his other clients. Cox also indicated he had completed training on ethics and maintaining professional boundaries with his clients and asked that the board take no disciplinary action against him, Gorson reported.
In deciding that an indefinite suspension of Cox’s license was warranted, Gorson cited Cox’s “demonstrated professional incompetence” and, with regard to Cox’s counseling sessions with the complainant, said that “several lines were crossed, including the frequency and aggressive nature with which he repeatedly cussed.”
Cox, Gorson concluded, “is not in the proper mental framework to carry out therapy sessions for vulnerable clients.” The decision stipulates that Cox can apply to have the indefinite suspension lifted after undergoing the board-ordered evaluation. At that point, the board can then consider whether Cox’s license should be reinstated, Gorson ruled.
Under Iowa law, an administrative law judge’s decision in such matters is considered a “proposed” decision that is only considered final if not appealed in a timely manner. It appears Cox has not appealed Gorson’s decision, which the board recently published as its “final order” in the case.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach either Cox or his attorney Wednesday.

title: Fired from hospital, doctor is fined $1,000 by medical board
description: A northwest Iowa physician fired from a hospital for allegedly failing to check on her patients has been sanctioned by the Iowa Board of Medicine. The board alleges that Dr. Caitlin Mink of Spirit Lake worked at UnityPoint Trinity Medical Center in Fort Dodge for three months before she was fired by the hospital in […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Medicine regulates the state's medical profession as part of the Iowa Department of Inspections, Appeals and Licensing. (Photo by Getty Images, board seal courtesy the State of Iowa) A northwest Iowa physician fired from a hospital for allegedly failing to check on her patients has been sanctioned by the Iowa Board of Medicine.
The board alleges that Dr. Caitlin Mink of Spirit Lake worked at UnityPoint Trinity Medical Center in Fort Dodge for three months before she was fired by the hospital in April 2025. According to the board, Mink failed to complete patient charts in a timely manner and failed to complete her rounds checking on patients.
The board charged Mink with one count of failing to maintain timely and accurate medical records. To resolve the matter without a hearing, Mink and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Mink to complete an educational course of unspecified length on the topic of medical recordkeeping. Mink will also pay a $1,000 civil penalty, according to board records.
The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Mink for comment.
Other Iowa physicians recently sanctioned by the board include:
Dr. Stilianos Efstratiadis of Sioux City: The board recently charged Efstratiadis – board records also identify him as “Efstradtiadis” – with improper management of medical records. According to the board, Efstratiadis failed to properly document patient care by failing to explain “why he used a bare-metal stent for patient S.G.”  The available board records do not elaborate on the nature of the procedure, when it occurred, or the patient’s outcome.
State records indicate the Iowa Board of Medicine opened its investigation into the matter seven years ago, in 2019.  To resolve the matter without a hearing, Efstratiadis and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for the doctor to pay a $5,000 civil penalty. Noting that Efstratiadis’ license is not currently active, the board stated in its order that his license cannot be reactivated until he has demonstrated it would be in the public interest for him to resume the practice of medicine.
Federal records indicate that in 2023, Efstratiadis began working for Phelps Health in Rolla, Missouri. The Iowa Capital Dispatch was not able to reach Efstratiadis for comment.
In 2022, Efstratiadis was accused of negligence in a lawsuit by the estate of Traci Ann Lasher. Accorind to the lawsuit, Lasher died in May 2020 at the age of 53 shortly after being admitted to MercyOne Siouxland Medical Center in Sioux City with shortness of breath and a dangerously slow heart rate. The lawsuit alleged Efstratiadis was the on-call cardiologist at the hospital that evening, and that despite being contacted numerous times by the medical staff he never went to the hospital and examined Lasher. According to the lawsuit, Lasher died eight hours after admission. State records indicate the lawsuit was settled out of court in December 2023.
Dr. Richard Semelka of Iowa City: The board alleges that in May 2025, it received a complaint regarding Semelka and subsequently asked Semelka to provide a response to the allegations. Semelka allegedly failed to provide a substantive response to that and other board inquiries until December 2025 — one month after his Iowa medical license had expired.
At that time, he allegedly informed the board by email that he was “very busy” and had not looked at the complaint. “I am extremely annoyed (at) the whole Iowa thing, so to ask me to take part in something from the Iowa board is not appealing to me,” Semelka allegedly told the board. Board records indicate he told the board that if it were to renew his license at no cost to him, he would be willing to look at the board documents and answer its questions.
The board then filed charges against Semelka, based not on the allegations in the complaint, but on Semelka’s alleged failure to respond to the board’s inquiries. Semelka then submitted to the board documents related to the complaint and asserted that he had originally dismissed text messages and emails from the board, believing they were part of a scam.
The board recently ordered that Semelka be issued a warning and pay a $75 “disciplinary hearing fee.” When asked for comment on the matter, Semelka told the Iowa Capital Dispatch it was “unfortunately a common situation: an organization not taking responsibility for their own shortcomings but removing the speck from their neighbor’s eye.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT to feel the squeeze as spending set to grow beyond revenue
description: A new report warns that the spending in the next fiscal year will grow by more than $1 billion, almost 6 ½ times the projected revenue.
text:
To say state government is headed for an adjustment now that it’s been weaned off billions of dollars in federal COVID grants might be an understatement.
The nonpartisan Office of Fiscal Analysis warned legislators late last week that the cost of programs in the next fiscal year will grow by more than $1 billion, almost 6 ½ times the likely revenue growth of $158 million.
But that revenue growth estimate comes with a qualifier.
It doesn’t include hundreds of millions in extra tax receipts from two key categories. Analysts now say income tax revenues tied to capital gains and business tax payments from smaller partnerships that don’t pay the corporation tax — a category that includes most hedge funds — will yield $419 million more in 2027-28 than had been anticipated earlier.
Those funds technically are captured before they arrive in the state budget by a special savings program Connecticut has used since 2017 to build reserves and help shrink pension debt.
Gov. Ned Lamont remains wary about changing these rules. But many of his fellow Democrats in the new legislative supermajorities are insisting on compromise. Saving less and returning more dollars to the formal budget, they say, could close the projected deficit, enable new investments in education, human services and municipal aid, and finance tax cuts for low- and moderate-income households.
“I’m pretty careful about that,” Lamont said Tuesday, referring to potential changes in budget caps. “We want to make very sure that we don’t spend all of the volatile revenue on long-term tax cuts we can’t afford if the market turns or [on] spending increases we can’t afford if the market turns.”
At issue are caps that have forced unprecedented budget surpluses averaging almost $1.9 billion, or 8% to 9% of the General Fund, since 2017. By comparison, the average budget for two decades prior finished 0.1% in the black, and the single-largest surplus during that 20-year period was 3.3% in 1998.
Critics of the current budget caps, including many of Lamont’s fellow Democrats in the legislature, note it was easier to tolerate limits that forced $1.9 billion yearly from the budget between 2020 and 2026. That’s because the state enjoyed more than $4 billion in emergency federal pandemic grants that could be spent, regardless of cap rules, to replace much of the traditional revenue forced into surplus.
But those grants now are exhausted, and Democrats — who control 116 out of 151 seats in the House and 33 out of 36 in the Senate — have identified many priorities.
Lamont and legislators campaigned for reelection this fall on more than $280 million in new aid to cities and towns. But that required exceeding a state cap that keeps spending in line with household income. And while many lawmakers want to continue or grow that extra aid, Lamont only authorized a one-time waiver of cap limits. In other words, they must either agree to more cap exceptions, or legislators will have to cut other programs to sustain that aid to municipalities.
Analysts say the state budget’s Special Transportation Fund is headed for deficits over the next three years. The STF pays the debt service on the $1 billion-plus that Connecticut borrows annually to rebuild its aging highways, bridges and rail lines.
The state’s single-largest expense, Medicaid, already has suffered from hundreds of millions in cost overruns over the past three fiscal years, and federal assistance for healthcare is scheduled to shrink steadily between now and 2034.
And some leaders of the Human Services and Appropriations Committee are calling for a new state nutrition benefit to assist tens of thousands of residents who’ve lost access to federal Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or SNAP grants.
Rep. Toni E. Walker, D-New Haven, longtime co-chairwoman of the Appropriations Committee, told The Connecticut Mirror last week that while advocates for many programs are seeking more funding, state officials can’t let core services slip badly just because aid from Washington is vanishing.
“The Band-Aid’s off,” she said, adding that since President Donald Trump’s second term began, Washington’s had a “gimme-back attitude” when it comes to funding for states.
Connecticut officials are hoping a new Democratic majority in Congress will reverse that trend, but it remains unclear whether more aid to states is forthcoming.
Further complicating fiscal matters locally, many legislators here ran on pledges to make Connecticut more affordable through state tax cuts. More than half of the 2026 General Assembly co-sponsored a new income tax credit for low- and middle-income households with children. Others want a new income tax credit to offset rising rent costs. Neither was included in the final state budget legislative leaders negotiated with Lamont last May.
Leaders of the state legislature’s Republican minority cautioned this week against wholesale abandonment of state budget caps. Connecticut still carries $29 billion in unfunded pension obligations, one of the largest per capita burdens in the nation.
House Minority Leader Vincent J. Candelora of North Branford said, “It’s really up to [Democrats] to show us how they’re going to lead on this issue,” adding that Republican cost-cutting proposals in recent years that could have mitigated the loss of pandemic grants were “summarily rejected.”
Republicans urged Democrats to scale back state employee raises, eliminate unfilled positions, reduce Medicaid benefits for undocumented residents and seek greater efficiencies at public colleges and universities.
“We certainly offered perspective and suggestions,” said Senate Minority Leader Rob Sampson, R-Wolcott, who added state finances would have been in worse shape sooner but emergency COVID grants “ultimately bailed out the majority in a big way.”
Meanwhile, Lamont’s budget director said that while next fiscal year has some unusual challenges, he’s confident state finances will remain strong over the long term.
Office of Policy and Management Secretary Josh Wojcik said projected deficits two and three fiscal years down the road — after adjustments have been made for the loss of federal grants — are relatively modest.
And he added state finances aren’t buoyed just by healthy income and business tax receipts tied to investment earnings and the stock market. Sales and corporation tax receipts are $270 million greater than originally planned for this year and point to a growing economy.
“We are still seeing growth,” he added. “We are not seeing significant weaknesses across the board.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: University of Iowa researchers test waste tank technology to help mitigate food waste
description: University of Iowa researchers are seeing their technology make its way to the commercial stage, with the hope that it will lead to greater efficiency in waste water treatment and less food waste going into landfills. Zoe Kramin, a graduate student at the UI, joined the university’s Iowa Wastewater and Waste to Energy Research Program […]
text:
University of Iowa researchers are helping waste tank operators better monitor their processes to bring in more food waste. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)University of Iowa researchers are seeing their technology make its way to the commercial stage, with the hope that it will lead to greater efficiency in waste water treatment and less food waste going into landfills.
Zoe Kramin, a graduate student at the UI, joined the university’s Iowa Wastewater and Waste to Energy Research Program in 2023 at the start of a pilot program to improve waste digester monitoring at the Muscatine Water & Resource Recovery Facility. The equipment and tools she and others honed in Muscatine are now being commercialized and adapted for different facilities.
She and other researchers, under the mentorship of UI professor and Iowa Wastewater and Waste to Energy Research Program leader Craig Just, placed light-based sensors in wastewater treatment plant tanks to gather data for an artificial intelligence tool to predict the chemical composition of waste in the tanks and help operators monitor stability.
“In real time, at this pilot study, we were able to have these artificial intelligence models predict every two minutes different chemical parameters,” Kramin said. “Operators could then use those chemical predictions and understand digester stability, and we want to understand digester stability so we can feed digesters as much as possible with different feedstocks.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Muscatine pilot program was completed in summer 2024, Kramin said, and now the team is using the same technology with slightly different equipment to put it to work in farm waste digesters.
Digesters in water resource recovery facilities, also referred to as wastewater treatment facilities, house microbes that turn different wastes into gas for energy, from what Kramin called “municipal biosolids” from sewage and food waste. According to Feeding America, 94 billion pounds of food go to waste annually, and 114 billion meals’ worth of food goes to landfills.
The goal behind the technology is to help operators monitor in real time the state of the chemical processes inside the digesters, allowing them to respond quickly if the ratio of different wastes is off enough to disrupt the process of turning it into energy. Researchers say they hope this will allow the plants to bring in more food waste rather than send it to landfills, where it generates greenhouse gases.
“For me, it kind of comes back full circle of why I got into environmental engineering with Craig in the first place,” Kramin said. “I wanted my science to actually be applied, and I feel like there’s a lot of Ph.D. students who never really get to see that, and so seeing something at a full-scale facility be implemented successfully is like, OK, my research is actually going to have a real world usage, and it is satisfying.”
University of Iowa graduate student Zoe Kramin worked at the Muscatine wastewater plant to put in new tank monitoring technology. (Photo courtesy of Zoe Kramin)
Kramin won $1,000 for her work through the university’s Three Minute Thesis competition. Her next steps include looking at the microbiology of digester tanks, saying she’ “super excited to start getting back to the biology of the whole thing” rather than the chemical and physical properties.
Nirova is the startup company that has partnered with the researchers to commercialize the technology, Just said, and their timeline is “as fast as possible.” The company has had a few successful pilots of its own and is currently working on a business model and price scale that “the market will bear.”
“It’s all about price point. It’s all about getting the installation costs down. It’s about making processes uniform because you have to collect data and build models with this technology to make that all standardized, regardless of the situation,” Just said. “So the technology itself is what it is now. It’s all about just business and making sure that it’s again at a price point and has a certain robustness that will make a viable company out of it.”
Commercialization of technology has always been one of the waste to energy program’s goals, Just said, as it was funded at the start by the Iowa Economic Development Authority to help small community wastewater projects. The program then expanded to include the “waste to energy” concept.
State funding ended for the program this year, Just said, and now it’s running with separate funds. With all of the conversations happening at the state level about water quality and the environment in Iowa, Just said it’s “pretty validating” to see as a “water quality person for three decades.” He hopes that the solutions they’re crafting at the UI will lead to a stronger relationship with the state to tackle problems together.
“I’m a born and raised Iowan, and I want to see Iowa do well, and I want to see the environment in Iowa that I enjoy and that I recreate on and so on and so forth do well,” Just said. “So it’s very satisfying to see that yeah, someone’s willing to take a chance at commercializing this, and then it can spread beyond you know what we do at the university.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT residents spending more money online each holiday season
description: CT sales tax data shows that consumers are spending more money online, at retailers without a storefront, each holiday season.
text:
Black Friday used to draw millions of people out of their warm homes into shivering, winding lines before the sun rose. But each year, more and more money is spent online, and growth in online spending is outpacing in-store growth.
According to Connecticut sales tax data, more money is being spent at non-store retailers, or at retailers without a conventional storefront registered in the state, each holiday season. Holiday spending overall on general retail items, which include anything from electronics to furniture to sporting goods, has also increased in the past five years.
https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/31013664/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script
Last year, $4.8 billion was spent at non-store retailers from October to December, the most spent in the sector since at least 2020, when just $3.2 billion was spent at non-store retailers in the fourth quarter.
Non-store retailers made up more than 44% of all fourth-quarter retail sales last year, up around 8 percentage points compared to 2020.
The fourth quarter is always the busiest time of year for retailers, with sales for the year peaking during the holidays. And in Connecticut, retail sales continue to increase year over year.
https://public.flourish.studio/visualisation/31013743/visualisation.json?ref=embed-script
But Connecticut is not unique. Total spending across the country is expected to reach an all-time high this holiday season, according to Adobe’s holiday shopping report, with online spending also reaching records. And the National Retail Federation estimates a 4.2% increase in spending for 2026.
Cyber Monday, which follows Black Friday, is one of the biggest online shopping days of the season. According to Adobe’s report, consumers spend more than $15 billion in a single day.
Black Friday is expected to see the second-most online consumer spending out of any day in the year.

name: VTDigger
title: Education reform has a trust problem
description:
Vermonters are being asked to remake their school system without being shown how choices are being made.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Education reform has a trust problem.
text:
Dear Editor,
Hello, recently elected legislators: Vermont has a trust problem. You can reorganize school districts by legislation, but you can’t legislate public confidence.
It’s November in Vermont, and we’re deep into stick season. We know what’s coming next: rain in the valley, snow in the mountains and enough uncertainty to keep snow tires at the ready. The forecast for public education is similarly unsettled.
Vermont is undertaking a historic effort to transform its public schools. School districts are exploring mergers and communities are nearly at fisticuffs over school closures. Meanwhile, the rollout of Act 170 has already led to confusion over the rules, responsibilities and the public meetings that communities need to make informed decisions.
Really, that’s more than a communications problem. It’s a trust problem. You can’t ask school communities to make consequential decisions when they don’t trust the process producing the choices.
Policymakers have an opportunity to change course. To help, the next phase of education reform needs three things.
First, show your work. If consolidation is supposed to save money, show the math. If larger districts will improve educational opportunities, explain how. Publish the assumptions, the data and the limitations. School leaders shouldn’t have to reverse-engineer state policy to explain it to their school boards and communities.
Second, make participation meaningful. Public engagement isn’t the same as public consent. Smaller communities need genuine representation, and parents and educators need opportunities to shape decisions, not simply react to them.
Third, be honest about the trade-offs. Consolidation might reduce administrative costs, but it could also increase transportation expenses and weaken local representation. Keeping existing structures might preserve community identity but make programs harder to sustain. There is no magic formula for efficiency.
Vermonters know how to navigate unpredictable weather. We prepare for storms, adjust our plans and occasionally dig ourselves out.

READ MORE

Now we need to apply some of that practical wisdom to education reform. Because the forecast is uncertain, but the need for public confidence is not.
Steven Berbeco,
Winooski, Vt.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Coastal Carolina ups its golf game with new $11M simulation lab
description: Coastal Carolina University celebrated the opening of its new, $10.8 million Professional Golf Management Academic Learning Lab this month.
text:
Students putt at a simulator in the new Professional Golf Management Academic Learning Lab at Coastal Carolina University. (Photo courtesy of Coastal Carolina University)Coastal Carolina University celebrated the opening of its new, $10.8 million Professional Golf Management Academic Learning Lab this month.
Coastal’s PGA Golf Management Program is South Carolina’s only Professional Golfers’ Association-accredited university program and one of just 16 such programs in the country. So, when conversations about updating the school’s nearly 60-year-old golf clubhouse began a few years ago, leadership decided it should have a space that matched the reputation of its degree program.
“In the last probably 10 to 15 years, you’ve started seeing not only are these programs adding in simulators that have data and technology and everything that comes with this industry now, but also golf courses are doing it,” Tyler Bantle, director of player development, told the SC Daily Gazette. “As students were returning from their internships, they were talking about all these experiences that they had working with these facilities, working with this data.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“So, it just made too much sense for us,” he said about the investment.
The university broke ground on the project in March 2024. The two-story facility has the public clubhouse on the ground floor and the learning lab up above.
It includes a repair room where students learn how to repair grips, shafts and rebuild damaged clubs. A classroom can seat almost 75 students for seminars. And the lab features a 25-foot-wide simulator for practice rounds, club fittings, mock lessons and a putting green with projectors showing students the lines of their putt.
“The facility now has essentially everything that a student would need to improve their games, to improve their teaching and coaching abilities,” Bantle said. “It really helps build a baseline for them, so when they go out into the world they’ve had experience with this technology.”

Outside the new Professional Golf Management Academic Learning Lab at Coastal Carolina University. (Photo courtesy of Coastal Carolina University)

“The new Academic Learning Lab will transform how our students learn by placing them in an environment that mirrors a modern golf operation,” added Gil Feagain, director of the PGA Golf Management Program.
With about 280 students enrolled, Coastal’s golf management program is the largest in the country.
It admits between 75 and 100 freshman each fall and ultimately graduates about 40 each school year, Bantle said.
About 80% of those graduates go on to work at a golf course as an assistant golf professional or a teaching professional.
But the program also comes with a business degree, so students may also pursue a corporate or sales job upon graduation.
“We have a network to the top 100 golf courses. We have students who intern everywhere from Pebble Beach to Augusta National on an annual basis,” Bantle said. “And so the biggest power that we can really provide for students is a strong network, so that way they can get started in this industry already with a leg up.”
SC state park reopens refurbished golf course, with new villas in the works

Coastal’s golf management graduates are scattered across the country. But a large percentage opt to go to work in the Palmetto State, including Greenville, Columbia, Charleston, and Hilton Head. At least half a dozen are head professionals or directors of golf in the Grand Strand, Bantle said.
“Anywhere that there’s good golf, there is a Coastal Carolina student or graduate that is there,” he said.
South Carolina has about 350 courses statewide at 300 locations, with some clubhouses supporting more than one course, according to a 2025 study by the state Department of Parks, Recreation & Tourism. That’s about seven courses per 100,000 people living in the state.
Those facilities employ just shy of 12,000 people, with wages totaling more than $300 million.
The courses generate an estimated $1.1 billion in sales. Add in travel costs for golfers coming in from other states, and the revenue grows to $2.2 billion, according to the golf tourism study funded by the South Carolina Golf Course Owners Association.

Furthermore, the state is home to multiple PGA tour stops, including the RBC Heritage on Hilton Head Island, the Myrtle Beach Classic and the PGA Championship, which returns to The Ocean Course on Kiawah Island in 2031.
