name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Bring In The Cavalry: National Guard Deployed in Oʻahu Frog Fight
description: A coalition of coqui frog hunters is refusing to accept defeat against the invasive species.
text:
With a full moon illuminating Pālolo Valley, a hunting party of almost 50 National Guard members, state officials and residents are briefed on the night’s operation. 
Their target: tiny, finger-sized coqui frogs. The mission: Nab as many of the noisy amphibians as possible. 
The hunting party is the largest the valley has ever seen on a single evening, but it’s still outnumbered by orders of magnitude, easily thousands to one.
Enlisting the National Guard is integral to a new all-hands-on-deck approach to Hawaiʻi’s renewed war on the frog, testing what David Day — co-chair of the Hawaiʻi Invasive Species Council — considers a prototype for how Oʻahu and Maui could finally get rid of the invasive pests. 
This brute-force battle strategy comes with an at-least $2 million price tag, one which officials hope will be enough to ensure the frogs don’t make Oʻahu their permanent home. 
The nocturnal frogs’ namesake “co-kee” calls have reverberated through the islands for decades, on Hawaiʻi Island and Maui, though they are relative newcomers to Pālolo Valley on Oʻahu, having arrived around 10 years ago. 
Michael Shiroma’s garage has acted as the forward operating base for Pālolo’s coqui battles for years — but he’s no longer fighting alone. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Just last month Civil Beat reported that invasive species experts were warning that eradication would be impossible without more investment, leaving Oʻahu to become overrun by the Puerto Rican amphibians.
Unwilling to accept defeat, the Governor’s Office stepped in to fund the blitz.
“It’s been said that it can’t be eliminated,” Day told the troops during their pre-hunt briefing. “But we’re going to see if we can prove them wrong.” 
The Few, The Proud
Michael Shiroma’s garage has acted as the forward operating base for Pālolo’s coqui battles for years, though Shiroma has spent much of that time fighting alone. The National Guard members are welcome reinforcements. 
Shiroma is buoyed by their presence, having made desperate calls for help ever since he first heard the frog’s distinctive call coming from Kawamoto Orchid Nursery, his neighbor, in 2017. 
“I get emotional when I see so many people here to help with the situation,” Shiroma said, on the verge of tears. “It’s not just about this noise. This is about trying to stop this environment from being altered forever.” 
Hawaiʻi National Guardsman Tiandrew Taimanao catches a coqui frog in the dense understory of Pālolo Valley. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
It’s a deployment few citizen-soldier recruits could have anticipated when enlisting, or even when most of them were first deployed in August to assist during Hurricane Lala.  
“It’s a bit different to doing our high water rescue stuff.”Sgt. Maj. Randy Delos Santos, National Guard
But Sgt. Maj. Randy Delos Santos, like more than a dozen of his counterparts, is glad to step up to meet the challenge. Coqui duty is optional but more than a dozen have volunteered most nights for the past week, on top of their regular daily duties that include physical training to prepare for other eventualities that also helps them tackle the valley’s rugged terrain. 

A coqui frog hunter closes the lid to a citric acid solution that will smother the invasive amphibian. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)

“It’s a bit different to doing our high water rescue stuff,” said Delos Santos, who recently retired from his job as a federal firefighter. “But it’s still a community service and a great, other approach to serving in the guard.” 
The soldiers have been a quick study in the art of finding the elusive frogs and compete to see who can nab the most. Some have topped 100 in a single evening, which approaches the haul of more seasoned frog fighters.
They use hand-catching techniques refined by Shiroma, which includes either hand-grabbing the frogs or scooping them into a clear tube. Once captured, the frogs are dropped into plastic bottles filled with citric acid, which effectively suffocates them since they breathe through their skin.
Back in September, when invasive species experts started to raise the white flag, Pālolo resident and Coqui Frog Response organizer Sidney Lynch was feeling defeated by the frogs. During the past week, that has changed. 
Eradication seems possible, Lynch said, especially in combination with additional work underway higher in the valley by Pono Pacific, which has been hired by the Department of Land and Natural Resources.  
‘Yes. More. Everything.’
Since the Governor’s Office stepped in last month, the state Department of Agriculture and Biosecurity has joined with the transportation department to put up the $2 million to increase pressure on the frogs. 
That money is going toward hiring contract workers from Pono Pacific to hand capture frogs and cut 1,300 feet of firebreak-like clearings north of the major infestation in the valley and under power transmission lines along Wai‘ōma‘o Stream. The premise for the breaks is simply to break up the frogs’ habitat. 
The additional work also includes placing water tanks in the area, to help workers pull hoses into hard-to-reach areas to regularly spray infested areas with the citric acid solution, which has so-far proven the best weapon in fighting the frogs. 
Cameron Deptula, special advisor to Gov. Josh Green, carefully and quietly catches a coqui frog during Tuesday’s hunt.  (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
The state hopes to contain the spread into forested state land, to stop the frogs from reaching the Koʻolau Mountains and moving north toward the Windward Coast.
In Waimānalo, which has the island’s other large infestation, they have already hopped south, over the ridge and into Kuliʻouʻou.
If the frog hunters succeed in Pālolo, officials say Waimanalo and Kuliʻouʻou are next. Then Maui. 
The state’s show of solidarity and resolve comes as calls for accountability and investment are at fever pitch, as invasive species such as coqui, little fire ants and coconut rhinoceros beetles spread throughout the archipelago. 
The spread is a symptom of a chronic lack of investment and staffing atop infighting among agencies, which Cameron Deptula, special advisor to Gov. Josh Green, wants to tackle head-on. 
On Tuesday, he was among the 50-strong crew catching coquis. So was invasive species council co-chair Day. 

Seasoned frog wrangler Taylor Engle shows a dark, female coqui frog, found on the forest floor. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)

Agencies now are unified in their response, according to Day, who is also first deputy for the Department of Land and Natural Resources. From Day’s experience, there is never politicking on the ground, among workers. 
“So there’s no reason that there should be any at any other level,” Day said. 
Deptula has been one of the architects of the Pālolo strategy, among other things, bringing together the different state departments to finally find a solution.
Among the initiatives is finding a natural predator, called a biocontrol, for the frogs on the Big Island, and rebooting official research into agents that could be more effective than citric acid.   
Deptula’s message is clear: “‘Yes. More. Everything’ – that’s our refrain for all things invasives.”
Taylor Engle, a seasoned frog fighter from Kāneʻohe, has been volunteering in Waimanalo since 2024 and hopes the state’s work in other parts of Oʻahu will start soon. He has also helped in Pālolo, where he helped set up their now 180-strong, frog-focused WhatsApp group. 
“It’s not an ‘either, or’,” said Engle, who works as an aquaculture specialist with the state. “You kind of have to do it all at the same time.”
Vindicated At Last?
On the steep western edge of Wai‘ōma‘o Stream, one of Pālolo Stream’s tributaries, seasoned hunters Engle and Lynch use their well-accustomed ears to listen for male coquis hollering for female attention. 
The frogs’ two-toned calls bounce around the forest, making them especially difficult to find. But not for Lynch and Engle, who know to look for glossy leaved plants like monstera, ti or loulu, among others. They search along the stream’s edge and muddy patches too, where the wet conditions are favored by the females.
Coqui frogs vary in size and can be elusive but many say it takes fewer than a handful of outings to learn their behavior to better track them. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Engle is considered the island’s premier frog hunter, bagging 154 on his best night. He, like many, snatches the frogs with his bare hands before placing them in a water bottle filled with citric solution.
Others opt for surgical gloves along with clear plastic tubing, which they use to trap the frogs. Jonathan Ho, the state’s acting Plant Industry Division Administrator, has his own technique of using his bare hands and empty bottles – the citric is applied later.
“Finding them is one thing. Catching them is another.”David Day, Hawaiʻi Invasive Species Council co-chair 
Some take to it quicker than others, especially given the frogs’ itty-bitty size and slippery skin. 
“Finding them is one thing,” Day said after losing one. “Catching them is another.”
Just in the past two months, between 6,000-7,000 frogs were snagged from the forest. Thanks to Tuesday night’s efforts, when the hunting party caught 1,433 frogs, that’s now risen well past 18,000 kills so far this year. 
On Tuesday, Pālolo coqui stalwarts Shiroma and Lynch work in separate units. Shiroma heads into the steeper terrain with experienced hunters while Lynch works with the initiates. 
With more than 1,400 frogs collected during Tuesday’s hunt, the total caught and killed by volunteers and official invasive species workers is nearing 18,000 this year so far. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026)
Both feel vindicated after months of lobbying the state for more support, especially given that the unified force has lifted their nightly kill count by the hundreds. 
Standing in the understory, on muddy slopes of Pālolo, Lynch remarked on how it has become noticable quieter since the National Guard and state officials injected their resources. But she also attributes the quieter din to the drier weather, which makes the water-loving frogs less active. 
They’re still catching record-numbers of frogs. But is there a chance that the work could actually pay off of Pālolo? 
“I think we can,” Lynch said. “I think there’s a good chance.” 
When the troops rendezvous back at Shiroma’s garage at about 9 p.m., they trade war stories and kill counts. Ho won out with his 172, breaking volunteer Engle’s record. 
The highest among the National Guard was just over 60. And considering the level of friendly competition among the citizen soldiers, it’s likely many of them will rejoin the hunting party after the Thanksgiving holiday, said Delos Santos, the sergeant major. 
Their deployment, partly thanks to the frogs, has been extended through Dec. 20.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Honolulu Police Use Of Force: When, Where And Why Injuries Occur
description: Mental health evaluations were the types of calls most likely to lead to the use of force.
text:
An emotionally distraught woman parked on the side of the H-1 Freeway last April was sobbing and threatening to drive into oncoming traffic. 
A Honolulu police officer who responded to the call was able to snatch her keys out of the ignition, and other first responders soon joined to help. But the woman suddenly opened her door and bolted into traffic. 
Officers followed her, grabbed her and pulled her to the ground. As the woman tried to lock her arms under her body, one of the officers pulled out each arm, one at a time, and put them behind her back to be handcuffed. At the end of the ordeal, she was taken to The Queen’s Medical Center for a mental health evaluation.
This saga was one of more than 12,500 incidents in which Honolulu police officers had to use force over the last five years. Calls involving mental health evaluations represented the largest single category of call during which an officer needed to resort to force, and attempted suicide was a major reason for subjects ending up in an ambulance. 
The use of force data obtained by Civil Beat through public records requests chronicles incidents across Oʻahu between 2021 and 2025. 
While the total number of force incidents fell 13%  in that time period, the percentage of reports involving an injured person went up, from 23% in 2021 to 30% last year. That includes cases in which the officer did not observe an injury but the subject complained of one. 


Less than 1% of reported use of force injuries each year were classified as “serious” or “substantial.” Officers reported being injured in about 8% of cases during the five-year period. The report does not indicate whether or not the force was deemed justified.
Honolulu police officials couldn’t pinpoint exactly why the rate of injuries increased but said it would be part of the department’s annual review of use of force statistics. 
“The Honolulu Police Department prioritizes de-escalation whenever possible to minimize the need for force and is committed to using only the force necessary to overcome the resistance encountered,” Brandon Nakasato, deputy chief of field operations, said in a statement. 
“Through its Annual Use of Force Report, HPD evaluates use of force incidents and identifies potential trends to determine whether changes to policies, training or procedures are warranted, or whether disciplinary issues need to be addressed.”
The department updated its policy in 2023 to require officers to submit a report for any use of force beyond routine handcuffing. 
That same year, the Legislature passed a law establishing statewide standards for use of force reporting. The law doesn’t specify what types of injuries must be reported, but it says all law enforcement agencies must maintain a publicly-accessible policy on use of force and requires all officers to report to a superior if they see another officer using what might be considered excessive force. 
The law also requires officers to promptly provide medical assistance to those injured and requires new police recruits to receive training in de-escalation techniques, mental health response, crisis intervention and first aid. 



Data Dive
Data Dives are Civil Beat's quick takes on numbers and data sets with a Hawai‘i angle. The project is supported in part by the Will J. Reid Foundation.





Read More

Ambulance Transports
Even though the reported rate of injury went up between 2021 and 2025, the number of incidents requiring ambulance transport went down from 85 in 2021 to 45 in 2025. 
HPD’s policy states a use of force report must be filed any time someone is hurt or complains of injury resulting from an officer “guiding, holding, directing, or handcuffing” the person. Reports also must be filed any time a weapon, including a firearm, pepper spray, Taser or baton, is displayed or discharged. 
Most ambulance transports in 2025 were for subjects who were already injured or having a mental health crisis when officers arrived on scene, according to a review of 39 narrative reports obtained by Civil Beat through a public records request. Two reports were withheld due to ongoing investigations and three were withheld because they involved juveniles. 


Eleven of those cases involved someone either attempting suicide or threatening suicide. In one of those cases, a man having a mental breakdown was stabbing himself repeatedly in the chest with a knife when officers arrived and subdued him with a Taser. 
In another case, a man suffering from schizophrenia, PTSD, bipolar disorder and suicidal ideations tried to strangle himself with the harness of an ambulance gurney. Officers handcuffed him to the gurney, and as he struggled against the handcuffs, he cut his wrist, leading the officer to make the use of force report. 
Nineteen of the ambulance transfer cases involved alcohol or drugs. In one case, a drunk and belligerent guest at the Ritz-Carlton Turtle Bay shoved a manager and resisted arrest as four officers tried to pull him off the hotel property. Officers called an ambulance after he started complaining of chest pains and cramping. 
Many people who were taken to hospitals by ambulance after uses of force were in the process of attempting suicide or making suicidal threats when police arrived on scene. Nearly half of the ambulance transport cases in 2025 involved alcohol or drugs. Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2024
Officers tased subjects in four of the cases that resulted in ambulance transport. In four other cases, subjects suffered medical emergencies after fleeing from officers. 
In one case, a man who had been pulled over for having an overly dark window tint on his vehicle fled from officers on foot. Officers caught up with him after a brief foot chase and struggled with him for about a minute, striking him twice in the face before they were able to handcuff him, according to the use of force report. The man’s name was redacted from the record. 
After the ordeal, the man started having difficulty breathing and passed out on the ground. The report says officers administered CPR and an automated external defibrillator while they waited for paramedics to arrive. 
Where And When
Police used force most often in an area within HPD District 1, an area mauka of Ala Moana Boulevard in Central Honolulu. From 2021 through 2025, there were 488 such incidents there. 
The area with the second-highest number of incidents was in central Waikīkī with 372 incidents. 
Police use of force did not directly correspond with the reported rate of violent crime in an area. 
Police Beat 154 in District 1 near Aloha Tower had the highest number of violent crimes reported between Jan. 1, 2021, and Dec. 31, 2025, according to department statistics, but ranked number seven for use of force frequency. 
Officers were more likely to use force on subjects in the evening, with a third of all incidents that resulted in injury happening between 6 p.m. and midnight. 
Some officers were more likely to injure subjects than others when they used force. Officer Logan Nishimura was the most likely to cause an injury with 81 reports, the majority of which occurred in Waikīkī. Officer Jeffrey Chun came in second, causing injury in 79 incidents. 


HPD did not respond to a question about why some officers would use force at higher rates than others. 
The vast majority of use of force incidents do not result in complaints or discipline. Only 14 officers were disciplined for their use of force while on duty between 2021 and 2025, according to Honolulu Police Department reports to the Legislature. 
One of those officers was Chun, who did not attempt to de-escalate a situation and used “unreasonable force” on a handcuffed suspect in 2022, according to an HPD disciplinary report. He served a one-day suspension. The call that precipitated the use of force was for a mental health evaluation. 
Some uses of force have led to lawsuits. 
The Honolulu City Council in October approved a $1.8 million settlement for a father and son after the son, Tevitatonga Cadiente, said he was severely beaten by officers in a case of mistaken identity on Jan. 1, 2024. 
The officers were pursuing a suspect who, like Cadiente, was Tongan. The suspect, Sydney Tafokitau had led police on an islandwide chase and was armed with a rifle. Cadiente was unarmed and walking in the vicinity when officers crashed into him with their police van and beat him, causing a concussion, facial fractures and a burst blood vessel in his eye. 
Tevitatonga Cadiente was beaten by officers after they mistook him for a shooting suspect in 2024. David Croxford/Civil Beat/2024
Officers ultimately shot and killed the actual suspect, Tafokitau. Honolulu Prosecutor Steve Alm declined to press charges against the officers for both their killing of Tafokitau and their beating of Cadiente. 
Two settlements stemmed from lawsuits against one former officer, Cpl. Scott Valdez, who had a history of complaints and criminal charges stemming from his uses of force. 
In one case, the family of Cameron Johnson, who Valdez shot and killed while investigating a stolen vehicle in 2017, was awarded $1 million to settle a wrongful death lawsuit.
Valdez was named in another lawsuit brought by a man who alleged he was severely beaten by Valdez and other officers during a North Shore arrest. The man, Jonah Kaahu, was awarded $120,000 in a settlement.
Prosecutors also charged Valdez twice in 2010 after he allegedly attacked a motorist he had pulled over, but both cases were dismissed after juries couldn’t come to a unanimous verdict. 
In another high-profile wrongful death settlement, the Honolulu City Council awarded $1 million to the family of Micronesian teenager Iremamber Sykap, who was fatally shot by police in 2021. 
Mental Health Checks Are High Risk
About 15% of reported uses of force happened during a mental health evaluation, which was the most common incident type that preceded force. Those kinds of cases also accounted for the most subject injuries and officer injuries: 411 people were injured during mental health evaluation calls and 111 officers got hurt.
The second most likely circumstance to result in an injury was resisting arrest, with 280 subject injuries and 81 officer injuries. 
The Honolulu Police Department has made an effort in recent years to train its officers in crisis intervention. As of June, nearly 300 officers out of about 1,700 had completed a 40-hour crisis intervention training. All recruits also receive mental health first aid training and about eight hours of instruction focused on homelessness, mental health issues and de-escalation techniques. 
Honolulu police Chief David Lazar wrote in a draft of his strategic plan that he intends to increase officer training for crisis intervention and work out a system to divert some nonviolent mental health calls to social service providers. Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2026
Honolulu’s new police chief, David Lazar, noted in a draft of his strategic plan that he wants to expand the number of officers who go through the crisis intervention training program to 25% of the force by December 2028. 
The prevalence of uses of force related to mental health emergencies dropped by about 30% between 2021 and 2025, from 460 incidents to 318. 
Lazar has also made it a goal of his strategic plan to reroute some nonviolent mental health crisis calls to social service providers and other community partners to reduce the strain on officers. Criminal justice reform advocates say they hope diverting that will prevent some of the interactions from escalating to where force is necessary.

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Kaua‘i County Council Now Posts Written Testimony Online
description: The public can now view written testimony without having to submit records requests.
text:
Written testimony submitted to the Kaua‘i County Council is now available online, a move that government transparency advocates say is a win for public discourse. 
The move came two months after Civil Beat reported the council was the only one in the state that didn’t post written testimony online and instead required people to submit public records requests to view them. 
State and county boards have been required to post their board packets — agendas and related materials such as written testimony — online since 2024. 
“This is something to be celebrated, not to be taken lightly,” said Camron Hurt, Hawai‘i state director for Common Cause, a government accountability nonprofit. 
Written testimony can help community members see how much the public is engaging with an issue before a council meeting. It shows who is interested in the issue and what their positions are for and against it.
The first public testimony package posted online for the Kauaʻi council contained submissions from two residents who expressed concerns about a bill that required new homes to be built with wildfire resilience features. The bill was signed into law last week. 
Lyndon Yoshioka, the county’s deputy clerk, said last week that Council Services Division staff worked with the state Office of Information Practices to create the new process, which is for staff to post written testimony as additional agenda packets on the council’s website ahead of the full council and committee meetings on Wednesdays. 
“We’ll continue to look at it and figure out better ways to get that information out to the public,” he said. “It’s kind of a work in progress right now.”
In 2024, a wildfire broke out in South Kaua‘i prompting the evacuation of more than 200 residents. The first public testimony posted on the county council’s website was in response to a bill requiring new homes to include more fire-resistant measures. (Kawika Lopez/Civil Beat/2024) Kawika Lopez/Civil Beat/2024
Before the change in practice, community members had to submit a records request to view written testimony submitted to the council, which the public rarely did. Yoshioka previously told Civil Beat that the division received such requests two or three times a quarter and nearly all requests had been fulfilled the same day. 
Douglas Meller, a volunteer with the League of Women Voters of Hawai‘i, said being able to look at written testimony that others submitted improves public discourse and is a win for public transparency. When he’s following a policy proposal, he’ll look at other testimony to inform his own thoughts and rebut comments he doesn’t agree with. 
Arryl Kaneshiro, who is set to become the new council chair on Dec. 1, said he thinks it’s a benefit for the public to see the written testimony, but it’s made things less efficient for council members.
Council members used to be able to immediately receive testimony sent to the counciltestimony@kauai.gov address. They could then read it, think about it, respond with questions and be more informed for the meeting. 
Now, council members can only view the testimony at the same time the public does, which tends to be a day or two before the meeting.
“I like seeing the testimony ahead of time,” Kaneshiro said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Commentary: Faith communities must reject AI before it is too late
description: This article was first published by FāVS News. The views expressed in this opinion column are those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect the views of FāVS News.  The number of conferences I’ve attended in my life as a participant can be counted on one hand. (I’ve covered quite a few as a […]
text:
The AI threat has emerged at a time when democracy advocates already are deeply concerned about the potential for “ordinary” online disinformation to confuse voters. (Getty Images)This article was first published by FāVS News. The views expressed in this opinion column are those of the author. They do not necessarily reflect the views of FāVS News. 
The number of conferences I’ve attended in my life as a participant can be counted on one hand. (I’ve covered quite a few as a journalist, reporting on the proceedings.)



Admittedly, I’ve frequently considered going to a ComicCon or FanCon, just to see the costumes and experience the level of excitement among the avid devotees to Star Wars, Star Trek, the Marvel Cinematic Universe, etc., but the fees charged to obtain an autograph or have a photo taken with a certain celebrity have always seemed exorbitant. I won’t support such profiteering.
Earlier this year, I did attend a conference that gathered a variety of Catholic professionals to discuss a number of key topics. Of course, the subject of artificial intelligence was included in a number of sessions and, as the discussions progressed, my blood pressure rose.
AI’s harm to people and communities
The men and women in the room agreed AI is doing a lot of harm, with the potential to do far more. Points were made about how AI is literally stealing the work of creatives, and the data centers required to power it are using excessive amounts of energy and water to the detriment of the communities near which the facilities are built.
This includes the noise pollution that disrupts sleep cycles for humans and animals and the cost to residents of those communities through increased utility bills.
Another point made: In the process of “learning” more and more information, AI companies are hiring employees in foreign countries at substandard wages to stare at computer screens for long daily shifts, red flagging images and other materials that are inappropriate. This causes PTSD and other mental health issues for those employees.
Should AI replace human companionship and skill?
Mention was made by the panelists presenting the session of AI systems “babysitting” or providing companionship to the elderly, so caregivers or family members don’t need to be present. For people of faith, how is allowing this a demonstration of love and compassion?
Yet, the majority of people in this same room had no problem using AI for various tasks, using the excuse that it’s already included in many software packages and saves time.
“It’s not going to go away,” said one woman as a justification.
I was, frankly, horrified.
Speaking my piece at the table where I sat, I explained how I don’t use AI, even for something as simple as spell checking. I tapped my skull, noting, “My tools are in here.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
I would rather spend time editing what I’ve written myself, or adjusting the brightness on photos I’ve snapped with my own camera, rather than contribute to a system that has the capacity to annihilate humanity and devastate what is left of our world.
Those seated beside me thought I was being extreme.
But, right is right and wrong is wrong — and AI is wrong, as is using it.
A call to faith communities to quash AI usage 
Weirdly, I’ve known this for decades, ever since science fiction writers like Isaac Asimov, Arthur C. Clarke and others started exploring the possibilities of computers acquiring levels of consciousness that posed an issue for their creators.
The lone sensible statement uttered by one of the panelists at the conference involved the learning process of the AI models that accounts for much of what is termed “slop” seen in AI-generated images or documents: “garbage in, garbage out.”
This garbage needs to be quashed.
If the majority of human beings on the planet would stand against AI — not to mention those same Catholics and members of other religions who stand against the death penalty, protest immigration raids, wars and other injustices — the companies touting AI would languish from lack of customers/consumers.
But, convenience seems to be the order of the day. Too many people see AI as a way to do more with less effort, and they’re OK with that.
By the time they grasp just how wrong they’ve been, it may be too late to do what’s right.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa professor teaches paper making art with international recognition
description: International cultural recognition is pending for a traditional form of Korean paper making — and the University of Iowa is the only U.S. institution to teach about the craft at the master’s degree level. Steph Rue, an assistant professor and artist at the UI’s Center for the Book, received her master’s of fine arts from […]
text:
University of Iowa Center for the Book Assistant Professor Steph Rue teaches papermaking at North Hall during a visit from Korea Educational Broadcasting System. (Photo courtesy of University of Iowa)International cultural recognition is pending for a traditional form of Korean paper making — and the University of Iowa is the only U.S. institution to teach about the craft at the master’s degree level.
Steph Rue, an assistant professor and artist at the UI’s Center for the Book, received her master’s of fine arts from the center in 2015, during which she earned a Fulbright scholarship. She spent time after graduation in Korea learning about hanji, a traditional Korean paper made from the bark of a mulberry tree.
UNESCO, also known as the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization, is reviewing hanji as a potential new addition to its list of “the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity,” which the organization describes online as including arts, knowledge and practices inherited from ancestors and passed down to their descendants into the contemporary age.
Rue said that recognition for the craft will help support those who create the tools for it.
Originally from Sacramento, where she completed her undergraduate education, Rue said she already had some knowledge from a mentor about hanji before coming to the UI, which according to the university houses the only master’s degree program in the UI with coursework on the practice.
“Coming to Iowa seemed like a natural next step in wanting to learn more about papermaking in general and just the craft, but also was a great place for me to deepen my exploration in Korean papermaking,” Rue said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Hanji is made with the inner bark of mulberry trees, in a process that involves dipping a bamboo screen side-to-side into a slurry made of the materials to weave the fibers together and make a single sheet. Hanji Edition, founded by Rue and fellow Korean American printmaker Lars Kim, details the process and produces art books and other products with the goal of introducing people to hanji as a base for print and other art forms.
Appreciation seems to be growing for hanji both in Korea and abroad, Rue said, and the industry has done well in finding different uses for the material and supporting the next generation of hanji makers. Hanji Edition lists the paper’s uses as for art, interior decorations and common household objects. Hanji can also become waterproof when coated with wild sesame oil or be woven into textiles for fabric, clothes and shoes.
However, those handling the “hard labor of keeping this industry alive” are still having a difficult time. Rue said there is only one person left in Korea weaving bamboo screens for hanji and she is over 80 years old. The woman’s husband used to be the “intangible cultural property holder” for the screen making process, Rue said, but he died a few years ago.
Dak, or paper mulberry, tree conservation is also an expensive and laborious practice, Rue said, and many hanji producers are now importing fibers from outside the country.
“I don’t think it’s dying, I think it’s evolving, but I also feel like there could be a lot more support for some of those more vulnerable parts of the industry,” Rue said.
Rue said she hopes the UNESCO nomination and potential designation will help drive support to those areas of vulnerability to keep the art form in its entirety alive and thriving.
The artist attributes much of her understanding and appreciation of craft in general to the Center for the Book, calling the UI program “really special.” It’s also becoming increasingly rare, as the five other MFA-granting book art programs in the U.S. that existed when she started at the UI has now shrunk down to two.
The Center for the Book has been “thriving,” Rue said, in large part due to the support for the arts, writing and books that the UI and Iowa City has provided. She said she hopes that this continues and students like her will keep enrolling, finding their passions and taking them on their journeys after graduation.
“Making things by hand, understanding where we come from and what our traditions are, why we did things the way that we did and how they tie us to our place and land and plants and nature and other people around us, I think that’s what makes us human, and that’s what makes it worth living,” Rue said. “And I think things like art and culture are so vital to why we exist as people.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Wood pellet industry helps keep Mississippi forests green, head of conservation group says
description: Operations resume at Drax in Gloster, Miss., on Friday, Feb. 16, 2024. Some Gloster residents are concerned with the industrial pollution they say is caused by the company that produces wood pellets in the town.
text:
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

Mississippi’s forests are among our state’s greatest treasures. On that point, I agree with a recent Mississippi Today piece attacking the wood pellet industry.
Where we part ways are on the facts, and on what it takes to keep those forests standing.
I have spent my career working to protect and restore this state’s land and water. I helped develop the Wetlands Reserve Easement Program, which has now restored and protected more than one million acres of wetlands and bottomland hardwoods in the Lower Mississippi River Valley. I helped create the Emergency Forests Restoration Program.
I am working with Mississippi’s U.S. Sen. Roger Wicker and U.S. Rep. Trent Kelly to create a new Forest Conservation Easement Program.  I am immediate past-president of the Boone and Crockett Club, founded by Theodore Roosevelt, and my family’s farm in Montgomery County, which I currently own, has been in our family since 1833. Wildlife Mississippi and I led the way to protect Sky Lake near Belzoni, which contains the largest stand of ancient cypress trees on the planet.  
I would not support an industry I believed was destroying Mississippi’s forests. The pellet industry is not.
Start with the claim that our forests are being cut down faster than they can grow back. They are not. The U.S. Forest Service’s Forest Inventory and Analysis program, the most rigorous forest measurement we have, shows Mississippi grows more than twice as much timber each year as is harvested. As former chair of the Mississippi Institute for Forest Inventory, I can tell you our forest resource is growing, not shrinking.
James L. Cummins Credit: Courtesy photo
The real threat to Mississippi’s forests is not harvest. It is the loss of markets. When a forest has value such as trees, people protect it. When it has no value, it becomes a subdivision, a solar farm, a pasture or a row crop field. Most of Mississippi’s forestland is privately owned, and private landowners cannot afford to grow trees no one will buy.
I have seen what happens without markets. On the Theodore Roosevelt National Wildlife Refuge Complex, located in the Mississippi Delta, a stand of bottomland hardwoods was thinned a few years ago. With no mill nearby, pellet or otherwise, the trees were cut and left to rot on the forest floor, releasing their carbon into the air and offsetting nothing.
That brings us to carbon. The article claims burning pellets is worse than burning coal. That comparison looks only at the smokestack and ignores the forest. The carbon in wood was pulled from the atmosphere by growing trees and is recaptured by the forests that replace them, and in Mississippi those forests are growing faster than they are cut. Coal carbon was locked underground for millions of years and is never coming back.
Meanwhile, overgrown, unmanaged forests fuel the wildfires that pour smoke and carbon into the air we breathe.
As a trained biologist, I know that forest management is also wildlife management. Every species needs food, water, shelter and space, and diversity across the landscape is the key to providing them.
Thinning and prescribed fire open the canopy and create young forest habitat. When that management declines, so do the deer and wild turkey that depend on it, along with hunter success, license sales and the funding for our state wildlife agency.
The article also says pellet plants replace natural forests with pine plantations. In south Mississippi, the opposite is happening. One of Wildlife Mississippi’s primary goals is restoring longleaf pine forests that once dominated the region. Too often, landowners who want longleaf cannot get their loblolly or slash pine removed because there is no market for it. The Gloster mill provides that market, and with it, real progress toward the goals of the Mississippi’s State Wildlife Action Plan.  
The concerns of Gloster’s residents deserve to be taken seriously, and I take them seriously. The Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality has held this plant accountable for past violations. In issuing the most recent permit, MDEQ stated there was no evidence presented to indicate health conditions were caused by the plant. Permits are designed to protect people and the environment.
The new permit for the Gloster plant regulates the facility under the federal Clean Air Act, with stricter monitoring and reporting requirements and an automatic shutdown when operations fall out of compliance. If the plant does not meet those standards, regulators have the tools to act.
Finally, counting only the jobs inside the plant fence misses where the money goes. A pellet mill buys low-grade wood from thinning that otherwise has little or no market. That revenue flows to landowners, loggers and truckers across southwest Mississippi, and it pays for reforestation, invasive species control, prescribed burning and timber stand improvement, on private land and on public land such as the Homochitto National Forest.
The choice before Mississippi is not between pellet mills and pristine forests. It is between working forests that pay their way and land that gets converted to something else. I choose healthy, well-managed forests, and the markets that keep them that way.

James L. Cummins is executive director of Wildlife Mississippi, a certified wildlife biologist and a certified fisheries biologist, and immediate past president of the Boone and Crockett Club.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Gov.-elect Kreiss-Tomkins was a Wikipedia power user
description: Two decades ago, an anonymous Wikipedia user edited the page for the then-mayor of Sitka, Alaska, Marko Dapcevich, to say that Dapcevich had, “on several occasions, fought female grizzly bears and eaten their cubs.” Within a few hours, the vandalism had been removed, courtesy of an 18-year-old Sitka resident with a unique Wikipedia handle: Jonathan.s.kt. […]
text:
A screenshot of Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins Wikipedia profile page. Two decades ago, an anonymous Wikipedia user edited the page for the then-mayor of Sitka, Alaska, Marko Dapcevich, to say that Dapcevich had, “on several occasions, fought female grizzly bears and eaten their cubs.”
Within a few hours, the vandalism had been removed, courtesy of an 18-year-old Sitka resident with a unique Wikipedia handle: Jonathan.s.kt.
Fast forward two more decades and that user, Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, has moved on: He’s now the governor-elect of Alaska, set to be sworn in Dec. 7.
But his expansive archive of Wikipedia edits — more than 13,000 between 2005 and 2011, according to the site’s own count — lives on.
And in recent days, it’s drawn national attention, including from the website TechCrunch — headline: “Alaska, your next governor is a Wikipedia nerd” — and from Wikipedia itself. The user-generated encyclopedia’s own newsletter, the Wikipedia Signpost, is set to feature a story on Kreiss-Tomkins, describing him as “the first Wikipedian (that we know of) to be elected governor of any U.S. state.”
A public draft of the Signpost story says that Kreiss-Tomkins “first registered under the username Jarfingle” and “created 134 articles ranging from classical music, public libraries and mountaineering to ferries and footballers.”
“We have records of a bunch of politicians editing their articles to smear enemies or promote themself, but not really any others who just edited to improve the encyclopedia,” wrote one user, 1brianm7, after Kreiss-Tomkins’ election. Kreiss-Tomkins, the user added, mostly stuck to work related to Alaska, Sitka, and Yale University, which he attended, and made the type of incremental edits that Wikipedians describe as “gnoming.”
At the Press, we were curious to see some examples of Kreiss-Tomkins’ contributions. So, we asked for a quick AI review, which highlighted an array of them. Here are a few of our favorites, which were reviewed, confirmed and summarized below by human Press staff.
Kreiss-Tomkins, who was an avid baseball fan, made a host of edits to the page for now-retired Boston Red Sox slugger David Ortiz. Among them: correcting his height, updating and augmenting his 2005 season stats, and deleting a line that called Ortiz a “bum.” “Sheesh, guys, leave this page alone!” Kreiss-Tomkins wrote as he deleted one edit that described Ortiz as having a “horrible arm.”
In 2009, Kreiss-Tomkins cleaned up and trimmed what he described as “adorative, feel-good flim-flam” from a lengthy page for Buckwheat Donahue, a longtime tourism director and colorful character in the Southeast Alaska town of Skagway. (“I sure hope Buckwheat himself hasn’t made any edits on this article,” Kreiss-Tomkins noted in his revision.)
In 2006, Kreiss-Tomkins argued passionately against the deletion of a standalone page for the library in the Kenai Peninsula hamlet of Anchor Point. In response to a user who said that Wikipedia “isn’t a phonebook,” Kreiss-Tomkins wrote that “every small town (or large town for that matter) should have its own article for its library, its high school, etc. because they’re all unique and interesting.” “I’d love to see a Wikipedia with the quantity of a phonebook and the quality of an encyclopedia,” Kreiss-Tomkins added.
Kreiss-Tomkins created pages for the vessels in Alaska’s state ferry system (the Alaska Marine Highway System, or AMHS), which are named after glaciers. Kreiss-Tomkins also created pages for those glaciers. “Hey, I’m finished with creating articles on all the current AMHS vessels! Par-tay!” he wrote after debuting the page for the M/V Tustumena.
He made 93 edits to the page for Sitka, his hometown, including adding a “famous residents” section that included naturalist writer Richard Nelson and novelist John Straley.
Kreiss-Tomkins’ Wikipedia profile page is here; his edit history is here. Send your own discoveries to editor@anchoragepress.com.

This story by Caitlin Justice was first published in the Community News Service on Nov. 15, 2026.
Via Community News Service, a University of Vermont journalism internship, for The North Star Monthly
Under lock and key at the Craftsbury Public Library is a special collection of 93-year-old artist Claire Van Vliet’s handcrafted, limited-edition art books.
Van Vliet’s longtime friend and patron Paul Gruhler has collected these art books for 20 years. Gruhler and his partner, Jane Marlin, donated their Van Vliet book collection to the library early this summer.
“It’s nice to have them where someone could just stumble across them,” Andrew Miller-Brown, an artist who works with Van Vliet, said.
Gruhler said he wanted to keep these books local. This donation, which includes more than three dozen titles, makes the library one of the few locations to offer patrons the opportunity to interact with the books.
“I was very grateful that the library was willing to accept this collection,” Gruhler said.
Susan O’Connell, director of Craftsbury Public Library, was cautious when Gruhler first approached her with the donation. The library is an active place for children after school, and they did not have a place to store the books, she said.
But “after seeing the works, I had a better understanding of what an opportunity this was to expand what we offer to the community,” O’Connell said.
O’Connell brought the idea to the library board of trustees to begin working on a plan to safely display the books.
Local carpenter Jack Sumberg built the cabinet that now holds all of the creations. Sumberg has done a number of carpentry jobs with Van Vliet over the years, making wooden parts for her books.

Craftsbury Public Library in Craftsbury Common is now home to more than three dozen limited-edition books by Newark artist Claire Van Vliet. Photo by Caitlin Justice/Community News Service

The Process Behind the Books
Van Vliet first began publishing her books after founding the Janus Press in 1955. In 1966, Van Vliet moved from California to Newark, Vermont, to continue work at her publishing press.
When starting a new book, Van Vliet starts with just an idea. She then seeks out collaborators, such as authors, poets and artists to help bring that idea to life, Miller-Brown said.
“There’s always a meeting at the beginning to just talk about what she wants and then try to figure out how to get there,” Sumberg said. “It’s always interesting to work with Claire.”
Through Sumberg, Van Vliet declined an interview with The North Star Monthly. But the artist has spoken publicly about her inspiration and creative process over the years. In a 2019 essay for Poets House, a New York City library and meetinghouse, Van Vliet wrote that the physical components of each book can help readers better understand “the essence of the text.”
“The paper acts much the same way as the binding — through the sense of touch as each leaf is fingered, turned — smooth, soft, hard, stiff, pliable, opaque, transparent,” Van Vliet wrote. 
“The placement and spacing of the text along with the shape of the page visually control the movements of the eye.”
Each book is published and produced at Janus Press. It’s a long process to publish a book, and according to Miller-Brown, can sometimes take years.
“There’s all sorts of different stages,” he said. “There will be several projects going at the same time.”
Each of Van Vliet’s works is unique. Her books feature folding paper structures and creatively incorporated texts that are different from a traditional book layout. “Aunt Sallie’s Lament,” which is available for viewing at the library, takes one of these sophisticated forms. Its accordion-like structure features a complex series of cutout paper to mimic the patterns of a quilt, interspersed with poetry written by Margaret Kaufman.
In 1976, Van Vliet received a grant from the National Endowment for the Arts and began experimenting with pulp painting, a technique that uses colored paper pulp to create images.
“The things that make her books unique are the quality, attention to the details, the materials and the construction, combined with the care she puts into selecting the authors and artists, or if she’s the artist, how they go together,” Miller-Brown said.

Janus Press books from the Gruhler Collection fill the new display cabinet at Craftsbury Public Library, including Claire Van Vliet’s edition of Aratus’ “Phaenomena,” open to a southern-hemisphere star chart, and the quilt-patterned “Aunt Sallie’s Lament” on the shelf above. Photo by Caitlin Justice/Community News Service

Built to Last
In 1989, Van Vliet was awarded a MacArthur Fellowship for her innovative designs. Van Vliet’s books are bound together with woven and interlocking paper structures so that no glue is needed. Van Vliet binds the limited editions — about 100 to 120 copies of each book — with a small team.
“She’s very careful about what materials are used, and how they’re put together so that they will not wear out quickly from being open and closed,” Miller-Brown said.
The 93-year-old artist is still working out of Janus Press today.
“She loves doing the work and she likes hanging out with the people who do the work with her,” Miller-Brown said.
See Them Up Close
The Craftsbury Library is taking precautions to keep Van Vliet’s books safe. The librarians can remove the books from the cabinet upon request so that people can interact with them up close.
The library hosted Miller-Brown on Nov. 8 to give the community an overview of the Janus Press. Visitors attended the talk to learn more about the creation of Van Vliet’s books.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico ski industry eager to see if El Niño can still deliver
description: After two lean years, New Mexico ski area managers eagerly await a change in the weather and look hopefully to what El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or El Niño, might bring.
text:
An aerial view of Pajarito Mountain after overnight snow, with freshly whitened trails cutting through snow-covered forest. 
(Photo courtesy of Pajarito Mountain)
As the first dustings of snow reached New Mexico’s mountains, ski area staff, skiers and snowboarders have become increasingly optimistic about the possibilities of plentiful snowpack as they readied resorts to open on or near the Thanksgiving holiday weekend. After two lean years, ski area managers, in particular, eagerly await a change in the weather and look hopefully to what El Niño-Southern Oscillation, or El Niño, might bring. Historically, the pattern favors stormy winters in the Southern Rocky Mountains. 
“Everything looks really good and everyone is agreeing that this could be a winter of winters,” said Jasen Bellomy, general manager of Pajarito Mountain Ski Area, outside Los Alamos. 
But climate researchers caution that other forces in play — namely, increasing global temperatures — could tamper with how well this El Niño matches its predecessors. The results matter for ski areas looking to open terrain and lure guests with the promise of powder days, but also for everyone downstream hoping that snowpack might provide temporary reprieve from the drought that’s been wringing out the Southwest for decades.
“El Niño tends to bring wetter winters to the Southwestern U.S., but warming may change what that extra precipitation means on the ground,” Andy Hoell, research meteorologist with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration Physical Sciences Laboratory, wrote in response to emailed questions. “Warmer temperatures mean more of it falls as rain instead of snow, snowpack melts earlier, and more water evaporates from soil and reservoirs.”
Ski area managers are eagerly waiting to see if and how much snow this El Niño might bring.(Photo by Elizabeth Miller)
Last winter, New Mexico saw record low snowfall for the second winter in a row. A high-pressure ridge blocked moisture from reaching the mountains and allowed warm air to gather, according to Julien Ross, the New Mexico forecaster for OpenSnow, a weather service focused on connecting skiers with powder days. New Mexico reported its warmest winter on record. Rain fell in places that historically would have seen snow.
“Last year, we kept waiting for that storm, and it didn’t come and didn’t come,” Christy Germscheid, executive director of the nonprofit trade organization Ski New Mexico, said. “We couldn’t even make snow, it was so warm.”
Skiers and riders caught the news stories about no snow in the Rockies, and visitation dropped by 17% from the 2023-24 winter, according to Ski New Mexico. That meant jobs lost and tourist dollars failing to appear at local restaurants, hotels, stores and transportation services in an industry that generated $600.6 million in the record-setting 2023-24 season. So, Germscheid, who lives near Angel Fire Resort, was encouraged to see the temperature at 34 degrees Fahrenheit at 4 p.m. in early November. The October and early November rainstorms that soaked the state resembled the way El Niño drives winter storms, Ross said, a sign that the pattern was setting up as expected.
“Even when we don’t have a banner snowfall year, there’s still great skiing and it’s still great to get out in the mountains,” Ross said. “But of course, we’re all hungry for a really banner snow year and kind of hope this is the one.”
Forecasting the future relies on the past. For El Niño, meteorologists look to historical “analogs,” or previous years when conditions set up similarly to what buoys, floats and satellite data have observed in the Pacific Ocean this year. But several of the analog snow years for this season date to the 1970s and 1980s, and since 1970, average annual temperatures in New Mexico have increased by 3.7 degrees Fahrenheit. Four of the 10 warmest winters on record have occurred since 2000. 
Climate models differ on whether those analog years will offer relevant comparisons or if global warming will scramble the signals, said Jeremy Klavans, a climate scientist at the University of Miami who has studied how global warming affects El Niño. NOAA’s latest seasonal temperature outlook called for near-normal temperatures in New Mexico in December, January, and February, but climate scientists still have questions about these interactions.
“The balance between global warming and El Niño, it’s going to teeter on that line,” Klavans said. “It’s really hard for us to answer that question: Is it going to be 33 degrees and everything’s going to come as rain or is it actually going to be freezing?”
New Mexico’s ski areas have invested millions in snowmaking equipment to bring a reliable start to ski season amid unreliably snowy winters.(Photo of Ski Santa Fe by Elizabeth Miller)
High elevation lowers the temperatures at several ski areas, including Ski Santa Fe and Taos Ski Valley. For lower-elevation and more southern ski areas, such as Sandia Peak Ski Area, Ski Apache and Sipapu Ski and Summer Resort, whether temperatures will be cold enough for the light powder skiers crave remains an open question.
El Niño begins changing the weather with a 0.5-degree Celsius increase in ocean temperatures. In November, the National Weather Service reported the relevant portion of the Pacific Ocean was 4 degrees Celsius warmer. The sizable temperature difference means this “super” El Niño could resemble some more recent analog years like 1983 and 1997, Klavans said. Essentially, this El Niño is strong enough to override some regional changes that are making for a hotter, drier Southwest, he said, including the shifts in wind patterns that have driven storms, and with them, moisture, away from the Southwest for the last 30 years. 
But even if this winter does see heavy snowpack, the region will likely continue to see less precipitation, as it has since the 1990s. In years to come or with weaker El Niño events, global warming is poised to win.
“We’re still amidst this declining precipitation trend,” Klavans said. “When we look back 10 years from now, we’ll see a nice blip of a hopefully good ski season, a hopefully wetter winter, but it will look like a blip in that trend.”
A single wet winter won’t significantly ease longer-term impacts from drought, including low reservoir levels and depleted aquifers, said Andrew Mangham, senior service hydrologist with the National Weather Service. The region needs several years in a row of persistent summer and winter moisture to make those gains. The National Weather Service expects El Niño to linger just until March.
At this point, few ski areas in New Mexico are willing to run on faith in nature alone. Ski areas are spending between $300,000 and $500,000 each year on snowmaking equipment and infrastructure upgrades, according to Ski New Mexico, manually replacing what may no longer reliably fall from the sky. This winter, that includes Pajarito, which was able to firm up a Nov. 27 opening day in part by adding snowmaking to 11 trails. The increase is expected to double the number of days the ski area’s chairlifts run, but more critically, without it, Bellomy said, Pajarito would likely soon cease to operate. 
“Obviously, the climate crisis is real and it is existential to our business, so we have to figure out how to adjust,” said Rebecca Hagler, senior resort marketing manager with Taos Ski Valley, which now has snowmaking on 99% of its beginner and intermediate terrain. 
So, skiers will enjoy it while they can. Conditions look to be setting up like the 2023-24 winter, which brought 36 inches of snow to Taos Ski Valley in just 24 hours. That news has Hagler hoping to ski a favorite run that hasn’t opened in two years.
“We’re excited about the possibility, and that big, deep, light desert powder that has been sparse,” Hagler said. “The hype is absolutely very real.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Brandon Presley says he will not run for Mississippi governor in 2027
description: Democratic gubernatorial candidate Brandon Presley speaks during Mississippi Economic Council's 2023 Hobnob at the Mississippi Coliseum in Jackson, Miss., Thursday, Oct. 26, 2023.
text:
Brandon Presley, the Democratic candidate who narrowly lost the 2023 governor’s race, will not run for governor or any other public office in 2027, he announced in a video. 
“Although I know in my heart that we could win and the political fires within me haven’t burned out completely, it’s just simply not the right time for us as a family,” Presley said in a video he shared with Mississippi Today. “But now is the time for me to make this announcement so that others can make preparations for next year.”
The announcement settles a question that has hung over Mississippi politics since Democrat Scott Colom’s stunning U.S. Senate victory over Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith this month. Colom’s win, which shocked the nation, raised expectations that Presley, a longtime Democratic force in the state, might try again next year. 
Presley, a former Northern District public service commissioner and former mayor of Nettleton, lost the 2023 race to Reeves by around 25,000 votes. At the time, it was considered a remarkable feat that a Democrat came close to ousting an incumbent Republican governor in a Deep South state. 
If Presley had jumped into the race, it was widely expected that he might clear the field of any major Democratic opposition and raise a significant amount of money in a quest to become the first Democrat to win the Governor’s Mansion since Ronnie Musgrove’s election in 2000. 
Reeves is term-limited as governor, and four Republicans so far have announced they will seek the state’s top office next year: Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, former House Speaker Philip Gunn, Attorney General Lynn Fitch and State Auditor Shad White. 
Lt. Gov. Delbert Hosemann and billionaire businessman Tommy Duff have also said they’re considering running for governor as Republicans.  
Presley’s announcement, though, leaves the Democratic field wide open in a race with no incumbent. 
So far, only two Democratic candidates have announced they’re running: former Mississippi Highway Patrol trooper Ivana Williams and civil rights advocate Priscilla Williams Till.
But neither of the two Democrats has ever held elected office, and other candidates are almost certain to jump into the race now. 
Presley said he would work with Colom, U.S. Rep. Bennie Thompson and other Democrats to ensure Democratic candidates are elected in Mississippi next year and that he will be “on the field pushing and fighting for the progress” of the state for a long time. 
“To national Democrats watching our state, don’t let this moment pass,” Presley said. “Invest in the South, and the South will deliver. Mississippi just proved that to the nation and to the world.” 
Candidates have from Jan. 4 to Feb. 1 to file paperwork to run for statewide office.

name: VTDigger
title: New tax brings in over $100K for Little City so far
description:
The check brings optimism that the town will over-perform its original revenue projections.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  New tax brings in over $100K for Little City so far.
text:
The Vergennes skyline in July 2020.  File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

This story by Sophia Keshmiri was first published in the Addison Independent on Nov. 19, 2026.
VERGENNES — The Little City’s first local option tax check came in at $122,998.95. This initial quarterly disbursement projects annual revenue that will far exceed the $200,000 officials conservatively predicted could be generated earlier this year.
“I’m excited for the money, but it’s one of those things where I’m hesitant to see what the next six months bring,” Mayor Chris Bearor said in a phone call on Friday. “I think we’re definitely going to be ahead of what our estimate was.”
Vergennes residents approved the additional 1% levy on sales, rooms, meals and alcohol last March on Town Meeting Day, becoming one of three towns in Addison County that charge it (Middlebury and Bristol are the other two). Just 51 of Vermont’s 247 municipalities have implemented the tax, the revenue from which is split 75%/25% by the state and municipality.
The bulk of Vergennes’s first check, $106,528.91, came from sales and use. Meals and rooms accounted for $16,470.04.
When voters approved the local option tax in March, they also agreed that the funds would “be used for municipal, non-education operational and capital expenditures, including municipal infrastructure, as identified by the City Council, for the benefit of the taxpayers of Vergennes,” per the ballot article.
At that time the city council indicated that 2028 Town Meeting Day discussions would include getting input from residents about how to use the funds.
While the city was experiencing a tough budget season this spring, city councilors indicated at that time that the local option tax could be a way to make up for some of the shortfalls in that spending plan — namely, cuts to paving and sidewalk work.
During a recent city council meeting, Alderman Mel Hawley was optimistic about what this first check, received on Nov. 9, could mean for the other three quarterly disbursements the city will receive within a year.
“If those sales and all of that continues throughout the fiscal year, we’re coming close to $488,000, let’s call it a half a million bucks,” he said. “This is really good news.”
Deputy Mayor Dickie Austin was cautiously optimistic.
“I would just temper our enthusiasm a little bit,” he said, noting that the recent check reflects spending during the time of year “when we get the bulk of our influx from tourism by contributing to that local option tax.”
“…The best chunk of the year we got it. It still means we’re on track to significantly beat the estimated (200,000),even (300,000).”
While Hawley thinks the first few months of 2027 could be slower, he predicts the holiday season could be just as, if not more, fruitful than this summer and leaf-peeping season were.
“I think a lot of it is e-commerce still. So I’m going to say that with Christmas coming, I think that those Amazon trucks and whatever are going to be busier,” he said. “My crystal ball is that the next quarter would not surprise me at all that it’s more than 122. And then it might soften after that, but we’ll see.”
Alderman Jamie Dragon’s take was that check number one is a good indicator of how Vergennes businesses are doing. “It’s a nice note of the health of the businesses in our town,” he said. “The higher that number goes, the healthier our salespeople are, right? So that’s, you know, storefronts getting filled.”

title: WA state lawmaker preps for 2027 race for a top Snohomish County job
description: Weeks after winning a third term in the Washington state House of Representative, Republican Sam Low is gearing up for a 2027 campaign for Snohomish County assessor. Low, who is in his third and final term as a Snohomish County Council member, plans a formal announcement Monday.  He said he is interested because the assessor […]
text:
Washington state Rep. Sam Low, R-Lake Stevens, speaks on the floor of the House on March 5, 2025. (Photo courtesy of Legislative Support Services)Weeks after winning a third term in the Washington state House of Representative, Republican Sam Low is gearing up for a 2027 campaign for Snohomish County assessor.
Low, who is in his third and final term as a Snohomish County Council member, plans a formal announcement Monday. 
He said he is interested because the assessor deals with housing and property taxation issues that he’s worked on as both a council member and legislator.
“It’s a political office and I’ve got plenty of political experience,” he said, adding that he’s demonstrated “trusted and proven leadership” in his elected positions.
If he wins next year, he said he would decide after the 2028 legislative session whether to continue as a state representative.
Low is the second candidate in the race. Quinten Schmit of Lake Stevens, who has worked in the Snohomish County Assessor’s Office for more than two decades, launched his campaign earlier this month.
Schmit is the Residential Appraisal Manager, overseeing the division responsible for valuing more than 265,000 residential properties. He’s endorsed by his boss, the current assessor, Linda Hjelle.
Quentin Schmit, a 2027 candidate for Snohomish County Assessor. (Photo courtesy of Schmit campaign)
This is his first run for a major political office, though he said he was a Democratic Party precinct committee officer more than a decade ago.
“I don’t see this as an ideological fight,” he said in an interview. “It is about experience. I know this work in and out.”
Schmit said he’s running to bring experienced, steady leadership to the office, make the assessment process easier to understand, and ensure residents can get clear answers to their questions.
“Property assessments affect every homeowner and business in Snohomish County, and people deserve to know that their property is being valued fairly and accurately,” he said in a statement. 
In the Legislature, Low represents the 39th Legislative District that comprises portions of Snohomish and Skagit counties.
He was elected to the House in 2022 by unseating an incumbent Republican, Robert Sutherland. Low’s been re-elected twice, and garnered nearly 55% of the vote in the Nov. 3 election.
For the past decade, he’s served on the County Council representing the 5th District, which includes Lake Stevens, Snohomish, Monroe, Sultan, Gold Bar, and Maltby.
In 2016, he beat a Democrat appointee, former state lawmaker Hans Dunshee, to complete an unexpired term. A year later, Low won a full council term, then won re-election in 2021 and 2025. Under county term limits rules, he cannot run again in 2029.
Low has an annual salary of $72,494 as a lawmaker and roughly $159,000 as a county council member. His county salary will rise to $165,831 next year. The assessor’s job will pay $180,921 in 2027 and rise by 3% in 2028.
Low says his constituents know he holds down two political posts.
“The Legislature is a part-time job. Almost every legislator I know has a regular job outside the Legislature,” he said.
The county assessor is a nonpartisan office. Low will look to capitalize on his greater name recognition and reputation of working productively with Democrats at the local and state levels.
“I will have strong bipartisan support,” he said. “I don’t think anyone can dispute that I can work in the assessor’s office in a nonpartisan way.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
