description: Students at Florida State University are more willing to engage in cordial political disagreements than they think their classmates would be, a survey conducted last month found. According to FSU’s Institute for Governance and Civics, “There is more room for debate and discussion on campus than students assume.” The survey asked students whether they would [[...]
text:
The Integration Statue stands in front of the Florida State University Student Union. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)Students at Florida State University are more willing to engage in cordial political disagreements than they think their classmates would be, a survey conducted last month found.
According to FSU’s Institute for Governance and Civics, “There is more room for debate and discussion on campus than students assume.”
The survey asked students whether they would respond with a negative remark or in a hostile way to a student “openly expressing political views that you strongly disagree with.”
Just 2% of students responded they’d be “very likely” to be negative and 13% said they’d be “somewhat likely.”
The survey asked students to guess what percentage of FSU students would be “somewhat or very likely to respond negatively toward a student who openly expressed political views they strongly disagreed with” by making a negative remark or being hostile. Students’ average guess was that 51.9% of other students would be negative or hostile.
“In short, students overestimated negative reactions by 37 points,” the university said. 
“When students expect negative reactions, they refrain from speaking, which diminishes the value of their education and the college experience,” Ryan Owens, director of the institute, said in a news release. “But our survey shows there is greater opportunity for open dialogue than students anticipate. Students should take notice. They can – and should – speak and debate more than they do now.”
The survey was sent to 7,000 students and 683 participated during September and October. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The survey asked several other questions, and the results break responses down by gender, race, political party identification, political ideology, and class year in school.
For example, it asked whether “[b]eing able to freely express and hear controversial social or political views is an important part of the college experience.” Nearly half, 48%, of students said strongly agreed, while another 45% agreed or somewhat agreed.
Republicans were more likely to strongly agree, while Democrats were more likely to agree or somewhat agree. The same pattern was true for liberal versus conservative students. 
Freshmen were more likely to strongly agree than seniors, while seniors were more likely to somewhat agree.
When asked whether students should be able to “openly express unpopular opinions without fearing negative consequences from the university’s faculty, staff, and leadership,” overall, 93% of respondents net agreed while 4% net disagreed.
In asking that question again but replacing the university imposing consequences with “consequences from other students,” 88% net agreed and 8% net disagreed. Within that, 57% of Republican students strongly agreed, while 27% agreed and 10% somewhat agreed. Among  Democratic students, 33% strongly agreed, 27% agreed, and 23% somewhat agreed. 
A group of Florida International University students drew reprimands this year for protesting the university’s involvement with immigration enforcement. Those punishments were withheld last week, following a lengthy legal process.
When asked, “If a majority of FSU students on campus oppose an invited speaker, the speaker should be disinvited,” 53% net disagreed, 32% net agreed, and 15% were neutral. Students who identified as Democrats agreed at a higher rate than Republicans, with 46% net agreeing and 40% net disagreeing. For Republicans, 18% net agreed and 69% net disagreed. 
Students seemed uncertain about how many students agreed with their politics. The table below shows the results to the question asking students whether they agreed or disagreed that “[t]he majority of students at FSU hold political views similar to my own.”
“To what extent do you agree or disagree with each of the following statements? The majority of students at FSU hold political views similar to my own.” (Screenshot from FSU’s survey results)
A similar spread happened on the next question, which asked about a majority of faculty holding similar political views.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Former Kansas educator gets help with 1st Amendment lawsuit tied to support for transgender rights
description: National organization supports free-speech lawsuit by former Kansas school paraprofessional who raised transgender issues with member of Kansas House.
text:
Attorneys representing former Edwardsville Elementary School paraprofessional Barbara Williams filed an amended First Amendment lawsuit challenging her March 6, 2026, firing for raising transgender rights issues with state Rep. Carolyn Caiharr, R-Edwardsville. (Kansas Reflector/Submitted)TOPEKA — A national organization advocating for secular public schools joined a civil rights lawsuit against the Bonner Springs-Edwardsville school superintendent who recommended dismissal of a paraprofessional for sharing views on transgender politics with a visiting member of the Kansas House.
Former aide Barbara Williams was disciplined for criticizing Republican Rep. Carolyn Caiharr’s support for anti-transgender legislation mandating people use restrooms aligned with their sex assigned at birth when in public facilities. In the March exchange between Williams and Caiharr before classes began at Edwardsville Elementary School, Williams repeatedly told Caiharr “trans rights are human rights.” Williams also objected to the state devoting public tax dollars to private schools.
Caiharr, who serves in the House and as the mayor of Edwardsville, was at the elementary school to judge a door-decorating contest related to Read Across America. In two brief conversations that Williams estimated lasted approximately five minutes, and beyond earshot of students or parents, the paraprofessional raised the transgender and private school issues with Caiharr.
“Ms. Williams did not shout, use profanity, threaten anyone or block Representative Caiharr’s path,” the amended lawsuit says.
Superintendent Richard Moulin issued a formal letter the same day, March 6, suspending Williams without pay and recommending the school board terminate her employment. The school board voted three days later to dismiss Williams.
In the letter, Moulin said Williams was disciplined for “expressing personal opinions” to a “community guest” and the paraprofessional’s conduct was harmful because of “its impact on the integrity and reputation of the district.”
In August, Williams filed a wrongful termination lawsuit. The American Humanist Association, in conjunction with Lawrence attorney Max Kautsch, filed an amended complaint Tuesday on behalf of Williams in U.S. District Court. The revised version of the lawsuit claimed the school district violated Williams’ First Amendment right to expression and her 14th Amendment right to due process.
The updated complaint dropped Unified School District No. 204 board members from the case, but alleged the superintendent unlawfully retaliated against her and fired her for sharing opinions with a legislator before school instruction had began.
Amitai Heller, legal director with the American Humanist Association, said U.S Supreme Court precedent clarified public school employees didn’t lose all of their free speech rights by accepting a job. An off-the-clock educator has the right to express opinions on LGBTQ+ rights with a visiting legislator given the Supreme Court’s determination a public school football coach had the right to pray at the 50-yard line after a game, Heller said.
“No one should be fired for participating in the democratic process,” said Alexandria Huiskens, staff attorney with the American Humanist Association. “Telling a lawmaker how you want them to govern during your off hours is quintessential First Amendment speech. The district fired Ms. Williams because they didn’t like her message, and that’s precisely why the Constitution protects it.”
In court documents responding to the original version of Williams’ lawsuit, defense counsel Gregory Goheen said none of the plaintiff’s claims was viable.
Goheen said Williams was terminated by the school board in accordance with state law. That action didn’t trample on Williams’ freedom of speech guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution, he said.
“Plaintiffs’ rights under the First Amendment, as a public education teacher, are limited when she is acting in the course and scope of her employment,” the school district’s response said. “This action is frivolous and insubstantial, having been filed without probable cause or reasonable investigation, entitling defendant to its costs, including reasonable attorneys’ fees, incurred in defending this action.”
Williams, who defines herself as a humanist, said she believed in equal treatment of transgender people and the value of public institutions.
“In that moment this past March, in the presence of a lawmaker who has taken action to undermine my beliefs in the past, it felt morally and ethically paramount that I speak up and say something,” Williams said. “Silence was not an option. I filed this lawsuit because I don’t want to see the district punish anyone else for exercising their freedom of speech.”
Williams was employed at Edwardsville Elementary School from fall 2024 to March 2026 as a paraprofessional in a behavior support classroom program.
Caiharr, who won a full term in the Kansas House in the November election, was appointed to serve as a state representative in 2025.
During the 2026 legislative session, Caiharr voted for Senate Bill 244, which requires Kansans to use restrooms in public facilities that corresponded to the individual’s sex assigned at birth and to list their designation at birth on a Kansas driver’s license. Democratic Gov. Laura Kelly vetoed that bill, but the Senate and House, with Caiharr’s support, overrode the governor.
Caiharr also voted for House Bill 2468 to increase the cap on state tax credits obtained by making donations to private school scholarship funds. The governor vetoed the legislation.

title: Podcast: Christmas takes over the South Dakota Capitol

name: VTDigger
title: After yearlong dispute, Vermont state employees required to return to the office in January
description:
“We feel like, not only is this a huge financial hit to us as employees who work from our home offices, but it's costing the state,” said one Department of Environmental Conservation employee.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  After yearlong dispute, Vermont state employees required to return to the office in January.
text:
State employees enter the state office complex in Waterbury in Oct. 2025 as the Vermont State Employees Association opposes Gov. Phil Scott’s return to work mandate. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Vermont’s state employees will be required to return to in-person work at least three days per week beginning Jan. 10, 2027.
The final timeline for Gov. Phil Scott’s controversial return-to-office mandate, which was communicated to staff by email on Nov. 13, followed a bitter, circuitous conflict with the Vermont State Employees’ Association. 
Scott first signaled his intention to introduce such a requirement last summer, saying that the change would improve collaboration in state government, and make public officeholders more accessible to Vermonters.
The announcement was met with backlash from state employees’ union leaders, who argued the move bypassed a required bargaining process, and would impose inappropriate burdens on its members. The mandate has also drawn criticism from prominent Vermont Democrats, including House Majority Leader Rep. Lori Houghton, D-Essex Junction, and former gubernatorial candidate Amanda Janoo.
After the policy was implemented last December, it was initially struck down in April by the Vermont Labor Relations Board, which said the governor had indeed failed to bargain in good faith about the mandate.
Scott, blasting both the decision and the board itself, took the case to the Vermont Supreme Court, which ruled unanimously in his favor on Sept. 25. The governor had stayed well within the bounds of his authority under the law, the state’s highest court said.

READ MORE

“The Governor’s assessment of the operating needs of his administration was reasonable, and it is not up to this Court to assess the wisdom of that decision,” wrote Associate Justice Nancy Waples in the decision.
Earlier this month, state Human Resources Commissioner Kristin McClure announced the Scott administration had settled on a timeline and procedure for the renewed in-person work mandate. All existing remote work arrangements would be “null and void” as of Jan. 10, she said in an email to staff which a spokesperson provided to VTDigger.
Such agreements had become widespread during the Covid-19 pandemic. A staff survey last fall indicated that over 3,000 of Vermont’s 8,000 state employees still worked from home three or more days per week. Before 2020, only about 9% of the workforce had worked more than one day per week, an earlier survey indicated.
“The decision to require some level of in person work is not based on individual performance or productivity,” McClure said in her email. “As an enterprise, the State needs a workforce that is more regularly and consistently connecting in person in support of Vermonters.”
Steve Howard, executive director of the 6,000-member state employees’ union, said in an interview last week that he expected a substantial number of employees to resign in the coming months as a result of the policy. The most highly qualified employees, he said, will have the easiest time finding roles elsewhere.
The Department of Human Resources had “seen nothing that would indicate the potential for large-scale departures,” the department’s spokesperson Ted Fisher said. 
Data from last December, after the policy was implemented for the first time, did not appear to show a mass exodus of employees. But Howard said the attrition could occur over the course of months as staff begin to find the required commute untenable, or are unable to find necessary housing or childcare near the office.
Employees can still ask to work virtually up to two days per week, but such arrangements are entirely at the discretion of supervisors, according to guidance McClure provided to staff. If they don’t have an approved telework request, staff must be onsite for all their working hours, the document says. 
McClure also recommended that supervisors review such agreements every six months “to make sure that telework plans continue to dovetail with the work needs of the unit,” according to Fisher.
Some officials in state government — like game wardens or correctional officers — have always worked onsite due to the nature of the job, Fisher said in an email Monday.
Last year, the employees’ union also raised concerns about office capacity, with staff showing up in person on one occasion to demonstrate a Waterbury complex’s space limitations.
“We know there are a very small (single digit) number of entities with ongoing space challenges,” Fisher said in a Tuesday email, adding that the Department of Buildings and General Services “continues to work closely with them.”
Previously, Scott’s administration had also outlined a period of roughly nine months for out-of-state workers to come into compliance with the return-to-office mandate. Such a policy was not laid out in McClure’s email.
As of last September, more than 500 state employees worked outside Vermont.
Shannon Jenkins, a financial specialist with the Department of Energy and Conservation who lives in Cabot, said the move seemed both burdensome and inefficient. She can’t afford to move to the Montpelier area, she said, so for her the change means buying a new car, paying more for gas to fuel her new 40-minute commute and leaving her 8-year-old alone for part of the evening.
“We feel like, not only is this a huge financial hit to us as employees who work from our home offices, but it’s costing the state,” Jenkins said, through expenses such as office rent, equipment and building services.
She also argued that state employees living in and contributing to a variety of communities across the state, rather than being clustered around the capitol, is inherently valuable. 
“It just removes us from our communities,” Jenkins said of the return-to-office mandate.
Howard said he hopes that Vermont’s next governor will have a “modern view of today’s workforce,” and reverse parts of the policy. In the meantime, he said the union may raise the issue again when negotiating its contract next year.
“This is a mess,” Howard said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Old Tallahatchie courthouse preserved as Emmett Till museum
description: A crowd gathered inside the historic courtroom in Tallahatchie County on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in anticipation of the ribbon-cutting for the new courthouse.
text:
The historic courthouse where Emmett Till’s killers went on trial is becoming a full-fledged museum.
It’s a plan 20 years in the making.
In 1955, two of Till’s killers went on trial in the Tallahatchie County Courthouse in Sumner. An all-white jury acquitted them, and months later, they admitted they had killed the 14-year-old Black youth from Chicago. That injustice helped propel the Civil Rights Movement.
READ MORE: Delta barn where Emmett Till was slain is bought as a ‘sacred site’
READ MORE: The writer and killers ‘stole the story of Emmett Till from his mother and family’
After the Philadelphia Coalition successfully pushed for the 2005 prosecution of Edgar Ray Killen for orchestrating the 1964 killings of three civil rights workers, a biracial group of 18 Tallahatchie County residents decided they, too, would work on racial reconciliation. 
The Rev. Willie Williams speaks to the crowd before the ribbon-cutting of the new courthouse on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026. Credit: LaDerek Thompson/Emmett Till Interpretive Center
“For 50 years, there was silence about the Emmett Till case,” said the Rev. Willie Williams, a member of the Emmett Till Memorial Commission. “People tried to erase the case, as if it never happened.”
As a step toward that reconciliation, Jerome Little, the first Black supervisor of Tallahatchie County, suggested restoring the historic courtroom. The group agreed that work could be a part of telling the truth and honoring Till and his mother, Mamie Till-Mobley, whose decision to have an open casket so the world would see what was done to her son served as a catalyst to the movement.
The group held a 2007 event at the courthouse where commission members delivered a public apology to the Till family for what happened. Across the county, officials built commemorative markers related to the Till case.
The commemorative marker built at Graball Landing, where Till’s body was recovered in the Tallahatchie River, was repeatedly shot and vandalized. So were the markers that followed. In 2019, the Emmett Till Interpretive Center replaced them with a bulletproof marker.
Tallahatchie County received more than $4 million to restore both the courtroom and the courthouse. “It was in dilapidated condition,” said Williams, the board chair for the center.
In 2015, the opening of the restored courtroom drew national fanfare. “There was a sense of joy on that day,” Williams said.
Inside the courthouse, county officials have continued to use their offices, and judges have continued to use the courtroom. Renovation on the rest of the courthouse continued.
In 2023, the courthouse and Graball Landing became part of the National Park Service’s Emmett Till and Mamie Till-Mobley National Monument.
The new Tallahatchie County Courthouse was built with a $1.85 million grant from the National Park Foundation. Credit: LaDerek Thompson/Emmett Till Interpretive Center
On Nov. 14, Tallahatchie County officials held a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a new courthouse, which was built with a $1.85 million grant from the National Park Foundation.
“A Mississippi courthouse sparks lots of feelings,” Ollie Gordon, president of the Mamie Till Mobley Memorial Foundation, said in a statement read at the event. “Today my family is grateful the old courthouse is preserved as a national monument, where generations will remember what once passed for justice there.”
She said she prayed for those who serve there to receive wisdom to see, humility to hear and the courage to act. “A courthouse can be dedicated in a day,” she said, “but the people who serve in it must dedicate themselves to justice every day.”
Patrick Weems, executive director of the Emmett Till Interpretive Center, speaks to the crowd before the Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, ribbon-cutting at the new courthouse. Credit: LaDerek Thompson/Emmett Till Interpretive Center
Patrick Weems, co-founder and executive director of the Emmett Till Interpretive Center, called the new courthouse “a real capstone of Jerome Little’s vision to both honor Emmett Till and to bring resources in to have a functioning county space.”
He anticipates the historic county offices will be transformed into offices for the National Park Service. And since the courtroom will no longer be used for trials, exhibits can be erected there and throughout the courthouse, he said.
The visitors’ center will remain across the street from the courthouse, he said.
Williams hopes this museum will inspire young people to pursue justice. 
“One day this community will be proud it happened,” he said. “It doesn’t solve everything racially, but we have accomplished something we can be proud of — Black or white, Democrat or Republican.”

name: California
title: California’s philanthropic funders need to give bravely to counteract federal cuts
description: Foundations and donors should increase support for California nonprofits serving immigrants, low-income and racial communities losing federal funds, says a philanthropy executive.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

Connie Chung Joe
Connie Chung Joe is the president and CEO of Asian Americans/Pacific Islanders in Philanthropy.


Last year I was leading a legal and civil rights organization, Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California, during one of Los Angeles’ most tumultuous times in recent history.
There were wildfires decimating our communities, immigration raids against our clients, attacks on culturally specific organizations and threats or cuts to our funding.
Now, as I lead Asian Americans/Pacific Islanders in Philanthropy, a race-explicit organization on the philanthropic side, I work with private funders who resource that same nonprofit work. From this vantage, I have a new perspective on who is making a difference during these times when nonprofits face unprecedented challenges.
Money remains the most direct support foundations can offer, but most give less of it than they could. Federal rules require private foundations to pay out roughly 5% of their assets each year. Most foundations treat that 5% floor as a ceiling.
They could do better.
The California Endowment has signed the Level Up pledge, a national campaign asking foundations to increase their grantmaking by 20% or raise their payout to at least 8%. The California Endowment doubled its payout to 10%, which means up to an additional $160 million is being given out per year. 
In a moment when there are sweeping federal funding cuts — such as H.R.1, the so-called Big Beautiful Bill, that will slash healthcare and food benefits for millions of low-income Californians — coupled with rising needs for nonprofit services, that philanthropic commitment helps fill critical gaps. 
Public voice matters too. The California Wellness Foundation, under CEO Richard Tate, rolled out a new framework built around three words: race, money and power. It states that a Californian’s race and income remain among the strongest predictors of how long they’ll live, so the foundation commits to funding work that names and confronts that gap directly. 
While many institutions have retreated under federal attacks on immigrants and diversity efforts, Cal Wellness has stayed vocal, keeping immigrant communities and racial equity central to its work. Their visibility tells nonprofits doing work on the ground that they aren’t alone and signals to other funders that a courageous position is available to them, too.
Foundations need to invest not only in the work of nonprofits, but the people behind the organizations.
While I was at Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California, Joanna Jackson, CEO of Weingart Foundation, championed a peer leadership program called the Sisterhood Trust. Social justice leaders at the Community Coalition, TransLatin Coalition, Brotherhood Crusade, CARECEN, Khmer Girls in Action and Asian Americans Advancing Justice Southern California created this space of mutual support to work on wellness, prevent burnout and strengthen Los Angeles’ leadership bench to sustain the progress we’ve worked so hard to achieve.
Two statewide surveys of nonprofits released this year — one covering Los Angeles County and one covering the Bay Area — also found that burnout among executive directors and staff ranks among the sector’s top management challenges.
Philanthropy needs to support and work alongside nonprofit leaders who carry this work on their shoulders, especially when the community needs these organizations more than ever.  
Nonprofits are the infrastructure that keeps California’s communities running when government fails to come through. Rebuilding that infrastructure with fewer public resources starts with private funders willing to listen to the people closest to the work, and to give more money and use their voices courageously. 
These California funders are already doing it. More should follow.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: Utah has a wild pig problem, lawmaker says. His solution may surprise you
description: Some states encourage hunters to kill wild hogs to control the population, but a Utah lawmaker says the state should do the opposite.
text:
A still image from trail camera video shows wild pigs rooting in the dirt at the SunRiver Golf Club in St. George in April 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources). Some states encourage hunters to kill wild hogs in an effort to keep the population small and prevent the pigs from destroying crops, trampling landscapes and passing viruses to livestock, wildlife and even humans.
But now that the animals have made their way to southern Utah, Rep. Rex Shipp says the state should do the opposite. The Cedar City Republican suspects sport hunting is what brought the invasive species to Washington County in the first place. 
“I think there must be some folks out here that are trying to get a population started so they can hunt, but we don’t want it,” Shipp told Utah News Dispatch. “They cause more damage than what good they do, you know? We got plenty of other things to hunt.”
Shipp is reviving a bill he unsuccessfully ran earlier this year for the upcoming 2027 legislative session that would make hunting feral swine a third-degree felony. A conviction would carry up to five years in prison and a $5,000 fine. 
Wild pigs stayed up past midnight at the SunRiver Golf Club in St. George in April 2026, according to a still image from trail camera video. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources).
In the last year and a half, state wildlife managers started hearing about wild pig sightings along the Virgin and Santa Clara rivers in Washington County. Since then, they’ve been working with state agriculture officials and the Shivwits Band of Paiutes to trap and euthanize more than 100 feral hogs, said Dax Mangus, the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources’ southern region supervisor.
They’ve also collected DNA that suggested some of the animals came from Oklahoma, which raised their suspicion that they didn’t migrate to Utah on their own. 
Wild hog populations can expand quickly, Mangus said, since they can have multiple litters a year. In southern Utah’s warmer temperatures, they’re less likely to succumb to cold weather. 
“At first thought, you might think, ‘Oh, well, if we hunt these pigs, that’ll help get rid of them,’” Mangus said. “But it actually ends up kind of doing the opposite. If you create a big hunting community around feral pigs, suddenly you’ve got people doing all kinds of things to try to maintain huntable pig populations.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Trail cameras have made it easier to track down the hogs, and so has a GPS tracking device placed on just one animal at a time. 
“They call it a ‘Judas pig,’” Mangus explained. Because the animals are social and seek each other out, he added, “that pig led us to other areas where we found additional pigs, and then we were able to remove those ones as well.”
Feral hogs were brought to the United States as food for settlers in the 1500s, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Today they’re a combination of escaped domestic pigs, Eurasian wild boars and hybrids of the two, and can carry at least 30 viral and bacterial diseases and even more types of parasites. 
They can also be aggressive and have at times attacked farmers, golfers and hikers. 
In Utah, their presence is “not a gigantic issue at this point, but we sure don’t want it to turn into one,” Mangus said.
With consent from a landowner, anyone can kill a wild pig in Utah under current state law. Shipp wants to change that to stipulate that trapping, killing, transporting — or even just keeping a live feral pig — fits the felony offense. 
A still image from trail camera video shows a wild pig at the SunRiver Golf Club in St. George in April 2026. (Photo courtesy of the Utah Division of Wildlife Resources).
He wants to give authorities the power to seize trucks or cars used for those purposes, then sell them at auction within a month. Under the bill, the state and landowners protecting their property would still be allowed to kill the animals. 
Last week, the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Environment Interim Committee voted to endorse Shipp’s proposal as a committee bill, giving it prioritized consideration during the Legislature’s upcoming session that starts Jan. 19.
Troy Forrest, deputy commissioner at the Utah Department of Agriculture and Food, told the panel last week that trail video has captured more than pigs, showing at least one person that appeared suspicious. 
“With law enforcement’s help, we’ve been investigating them,” he said without offering details. 
The legislative proposal has support from the Utah Farm Bureau. The earlier version had broad backing from state lawmakers, Shipp said, but ran out of time in the final hours of the 2026 legislative session.

name: Nevada Current
title: Nevada AG, immigration advocates monitor suit to block housing rule targeting mixed-status families
description: A Trump Administration rule that would strip “mixed-status” families from housing assistance in Nevada and across the nation is scheduled to take effect next month, though a new multi-state lawsuit is seeking to block it. Nevada did not sign on to the multi-state lawsuit, but Attorney General and Gov.-elect Aaron Ford is monitoring the lawsuit […]
text:
Photo by Kent Nishimura/Getty Images)A Trump Administration rule that would strip “mixed-status” families from housing assistance in Nevada and across the nation is scheduled to take effect next month, though a new multi-state lawsuit is seeking to block it.
Nevada did not sign on to the multi-state lawsuit, but Attorney General and Gov.-elect Aaron Ford is monitoring the lawsuit and “supports the coalition in their efforts to block this new rule that would divide families,” spokesman John Sadler said in a statement to Nevada Current. 
22 states sue feds over rule stripping housing aid from mixed-status immigrant families

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development announced earlier this year that it would seek to reverse a rule that allows undocumented immigrants to live with family members who have legal status and are receiving housing assistance. Benefits are currently prorated for mixed-status families.
HUD this month announced it finalized the rule and would put it into effect Dec. 14. On Monday, 22 states announced it would sue to block the rule change. 
 “The decision to not join this lawsuit was based on the programs’ structure in Nevada,” Sadler said. “In our state, they’re the purview of regional organizations like (the Southern Nevada Regional Housing Authority) and nonprofits.”
Mixed-status households are made up of people with varied immigration statuses, including legal residents and U.S. citizens.
An estimated 9% of households in Nevada have mixed-status families, the highest proportion of any state according to the Pew Research Center. 
An 2024 analysis from the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities found that 150 mixed-status families receive housing assistance in Nevada. 
Nevada, as with the rest of the country, has experienced an affordable housing shortage. Without providing any evidence, the Trump administration has repeatedly blamed the crisis on immigrants. 
In a February press release announcing the proposed change, HUD Secretary Scott Turner said households should prepare to “pack your bags” when the rule is finalized.
In the lawsuit filed this week, states argue that “HUD lacks authority to rewrite federal law to exclude families this Administration disfavors from federal affordable housing programs.”
Local housing and immigrant groups admonished the proposed rule change. 
Noé Orosco, coordinator of the Nevada Immigrant Coalition, previously told the Current that the proposed rule was a “shameful attempt to scapegoat immigrants for the ongoing housing affordability crisis.”

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: DFL Sen.-elect Mark Legvold to wear many hats in the Senate: veteran, firefighter, farmer, educator
description: Sen.-elect Mark Legvold, who defeated first-term Republican state Sen. Bill Lieske, has exactly the resume Democrats needed after losing working-class voters badly in 2024: He’s a veteran, firefighter, farmer and educator.  Legvold, 56, graduated Northfield High School in 1989 and enlisted in the Air Force, serving five years on active duty before returning [...]
text:
Mark Legvold, DFL-Northfield, said he’ll focus on reducing the cost of living for Minnesota families, while bolstering public education and the state’s agricultural economy. (Courtesy photo)Sen.-elect Mark Legvold, who defeated first-term Republican state Sen. Bill Lieske, has exactly the resume Democrats needed after losing working-class voters badly in 2024: He’s a veteran, firefighter, farmer and educator. 
Legvold, 56, graduated Northfield High School in 1989 and enlisted in the Air Force, serving five years on active duty before returning to Minnesota in 1995, when he joined the Air National Guard. 
Legvold worked as a teacher and school administrator for St. Paul Public Schools. He returned to military service full-time, becoming a fire chief at Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport. He retired in 2023 and farms alongside his father on the family’s Northfield-area corn and soybean operation. 
“I still felt compelled to serve other people after doing it for 33 years, and wanted to make my community and my country a little bit better place,” he said. “So I decided to run for office.”
District 58 covers a swath of southeastern Minnesota, including Northfield, Dundas, Lonsdale, Farmington and parts of Rosemont and New Prague.
Legvold said he’ll focus on reducing the cost of living for Minnesota families, while bolstering public education and the state’s agricultural economy. 
This interview is a part of a series on rookie state legislators. It has been edited for length and clarity.
Tell us about yourself.  
I went to college while I was in the service and eventually chose elementary education as my major. When I reached the point where I needed to student-teach, my family had grown to include my wife and two kids, so we moved back to Minnesota for me to finish my education.
I started working in St. Paul Public Schools while serving in the military part-time. I earned my master’s degree in school administration and my principal’s license from the University of Minnesota while continuing my military service.
In 2007, the guard asked if I’d take a full-time position. I became the fire chief at the Twin Cities airport. By then, I had three kids.
Along the way, I became a single parent in 2010. Then I met my wife, Lisa, through her kids, and we eventually got married. We’ve got a family of six, all paired up with a lovely significant other, and five and one-third grandkids.
What made you decide to run for office?
My degree from Hamline University is in political science and elementary education, so I’ve always been politically interested. But in the military, we’re not politically active. We vote, we protect democracy, but we’re not influencing.
My last job, especially, was very politically adjacent. I had a lot of experiences seeing how things are shaped in our global and local politics by good policy work, so, yeah, I was interested.
I also served during the first Trump administration, which was incredibly difficult. I knew when he got elected a second time, it was going to be just plain hard, to put it mildly.
Why do you think you won?
Good, hard work. We started the race over a year and a half before the election, and we were knocking on doors, introducing myself, getting out and meeting people where they were, listening to folks and putting in the hard work that people in public service should do.
Did you learn anything new about your district on the campaign trail?
Absolutely. What I learned first and foremost is that politics is local, and relationships come down to the doorstep. People are genuinely kind and decent, and very understanding of somebody standing on their doorstep, even if you don’t agree politically.
For the most part, folks are good. They just want a better life, and they care about how we get there.
Looking ahead, what are some issues you want to work on?
Making life affordable for every Minnesotan and figuring out how we get there is really going to matter. 
People are struggling to afford their health care, but they’re also struggling to afford gas in their tank, food on their table, clothes on their backs and a roof over their heads. So, making Minnesota a more affordable place, providing a great public school education that’s available for every single kid in Minnesota, and making sure our economy thrives. 
And that means, for me as a family farmer, making sure we protect our family farms and that the folks in agriculture are able to thrive. Twenty four percent of our state’s economy relies on agriculture. So if farmers aren’t doing well and people in agriculture aren’t doing well, then the rest of the state isn’t doing well. 
What issues do you think you might disagree with your party?
Economic growth might be one area where I disagree, as well as health and human services, or just human services in general.
I am a strong supporter of environmental initiatives and taking good care of our air, land and water, so I don’t think we’re going to see a lot of disagreement there. But how we do that is going to matter.
Time and again, folks out in the rural areas of our district, especially, want to see us compromising with our Republicans out there. They want to see how we involve everybody who has been elected to office in solving the complex problems we’re facing.
With us going into a session where we do have a trifecta in place, I still want to make sure that we’re working with Republicans who are reasonable, come to the table and want to solve these problems. I just don’t have time for extremism, and neither do the people in our district.
What is something about your background that you know the majority of the public would be kind of surprised to learn?
I was a single parent for a time, with three teenagers at home while working a full-time job and farming. (Levgold is divorced.) I didn’t necessarily share that much on the campaign trail.
I understand the hard work it takes to be a single parent, and I’m really proud of our blended family.
As a single parent, how does that shape how you’re entering the next legislative session? With those experiences behind you, did it make you think about things differently?
It really has. It’s not just about what I went through, but what every single parent goes through while trying to build a better life.
My wife is a great role model and mentor. She was also a single parent of three before we blended our families. She went to school full-time while raising three kids and maintaining a household. Without some of the help she received, she wouldn’t be where she is today.
She’s a physician assistant who worked hard and had help along the way. I keep saying it: When you put your money where your people are, it makes our world and our state a much, much better place.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC colleges’ $2.2B in requests include defense, nuclear and cancer facilities
description: A defense research center, a nuclear workforce training center and more money for a cancer hospital are among SC colleges’ budget asks.
text:
Clemson University's ROTC units parade during the schools annual Military Appreciation Game day. (Photo courtesy of Clemson University)COLUMBIA — A new national security research center, a nuclear workforce training center and more money for a top-tier cancer hospital are among items on South Carolina colleges’ budget wish lists for the coming year.
In all, public colleges, including the state’s 16 technical schools, are seeking nearly $2.2 billion in additional state aid from taxpayers for the fiscal year starting July 1, according to a review of budget requests posted online.
Agency requests are rarely fully funded. The governor’s office and legislators use them to draft their budget plans.
The state’s three large research universities account for almost half of public colleges’ total ask, with Clemson University leading in dollars requested.

Money for defense and military programs
The Upstate school wants $368.7 million total, including $110 million to build a national security focused center on its acclaimed automotive research campus and $14 million more annually to run it.
The money would build a home for the center formed in March.
“The investments would give Clemson the facilities and talent to pursue larger federal and industry research partnerships and help more students enter South Carolina’s aerospace and defense workforce,” spokesman Joe Galbraith said.
The 65,000-square-foot building would include laboratories, offices, meeting rooms and incubator space for defense-related startups. Plus, there are plans for an outdoor test space for unmanned vehicles and aircraft.
Establishing a National Security Institute at Clemson University reflects the school’s “rising relevance to national security priorities and its capacity to serve as a strategic partner to the federal government, the armed services and the defense industry,” according to a statement from the college.
Clemson touts already having an annual federal research portfolio of more than $30 million with the Department of Defense.
Lockheed Martin laying off 10% of Greenville workforce

And it boasts proximity to Lockheed Martin, located 40 miles away in Greenville, which builds F-16s for the international market.
Clemson’s new center will focus on developing materials that can stand up to harsh conditions, such as high-speed flight and fibers for high-powered lasers, as well as artificial intelligence.
Clemson also wants $42.5 million for a new combined ROTC center.
Most of that — $37.5 million — would renovate Holtzendorff Hall, which dates to 1915 and is located on the historic parade ground where the former, all-male military colleges’ corps of cadets drilled.  The remaining $5 million would be annual dollars to pay for staff and programming.
The renovation would bring Clemson’s separate ROTC centers for various military branches under one roof. The hall would have classrooms and offices, as well as simulators for tactical training.
Going nuclear
Meanwhile, in the Midlands, the University of South Carolina is seeking $336.7 million in funding for its main Columbia campus.
That includes more than $100 million for a previously announced center to train a workforce for the nuclear power industry, should White House-led efforts to build more nuclear power plants across the country come to fruition.
USC, Westinghouse sign agreement for nuclear workforce training center

The school also wants $75 million to move its pharmacy school onto its new downtown medical campus.
Across the entire USC system, requests total $550 million. Larger projects at the system’s six other campuses include a $60 million expansion for nursing schools in Aiken, Beaufort and Spartanburg, as well as a $20 million marine and environmental science center in Beaufort.
And USC and Clemson, as well as South Carolina State University, are again asking legislators to pump more money into a workforce development partnership with South Carolina’s federal nuclear laboratory. The three schools are jointly seeking another $40 million, with $16 million each for USC and Clemson and $8 million for SC State.
The Legislature last funded the so-called Battelle Alliance at the Savannah River National Laboratory with $40 million in the budget year that started July 1, 2023.
Cancer treatment and rural health
In the Lowcountry, the Medical University of South Carolina is returning to the General Assembly to ask for another $175 million to put toward its proposed $1 billion cancer hospital.
The Legislature approved the first $175 million of the state-owned medical school and hospital system’s request in the current budget. Now hospital administrators are looking for the second half of its request from last year.
MUSC Health seeks $350M for new, top-tier cancer center

MUSC is chasing a Comprehensive Cancer Center designation from the National Cancer Institute.
If approved, the center would be the first of its kind in South Carolina.
Patients seeking this top level of care currently must travel out of state to centers in North Carolina, Georgia and Tennessee.
The hospital system also is seeking $10 million to take its cancer treatment efforts into more far-flung parts of the state.
“A key priority is expanding access to cellular therapy across the state, especially in rural communities. These personalized, targeted treatments use a patient’s own cells or donor cells to deliver therapies throughout the body or restore function,” MUSC’s budget request reads.
The annually recurring funding would cover the cost of rural clinical trials, infusion machines to deliver the treatments and research.
In a different rural health related initiative, the hospital system is asking the state for $5 million to open a dental clinic on its Lancaster hospital campus.
Tuition and more
Two other Lowcountry schools round out the top five college budget requests.
The Citadel wants $218.7 million, mostly for building renovations on the military college’s campus. And College of Charleston wants $80 million, including $67 million for a nursing school, business school and visitors.
And all of South Carolina’s colleges, including MUSC and technical schools, continue to ask the Legislature for more money in exchange for holding tuition rates steady for in-state students.
This year’s ask would add $133 million more to public college budgets.
So-called tuition mitigation is annual funding and stays in the budget year after year, the total amount growing with each new increase.
This fiscal year, South Carolina’s 17 public colleges, not including technical schools, split $406 million total in tuition mitigation. Yearly increases in the tuition aid since 2019 have cumulatively provided $1.6 billion to the public colleges.
This latest round of funding, if approved, would add to that.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Commentary: Treating homelessness as a crime doesn’t work
description: Everyone deserves a safe place to live, but for many Michiganders, even full-time work doesn’t pay enough to afford basic needs, including housing. To address the homelessness resulting from this structural problem in the economy, some communities are misguidedly turning to the criminal legal system. We at the Michigan League for Public Policy urge them […]
text:
Man sleeping on the street outside the Fort Cass People Mover Station in Detroit, Michigan in June 2026 (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)Everyone deserves a safe place to live, but for many Michiganders, even full-time work doesn’t pay enough to afford basic needs, including housing.
To address the homelessness resulting from this structural problem in the economy, some communities are misguidedly turning to the criminal legal system. We at the Michigan League for Public Policy urge them to focus on investments in affordable housing and supportive services rather than further punishing people our economy has left behind.
To afford a two-bedroom apartment in Michigan, a full-time worker must earn $25.53 per hour – an increase of 47% over 2020. Meanwhile, the average renter wage remains under $20 per hour. And people earning the minimum wage must work 74 hours a week to cover rent and other basic living expenses.
Being unable to afford a home shouldn’t be a crime, but our country has a long history of treating it that way. This approach has gained even more traction in recent years, even though it’s never proven effective in reducing homelessness.
Owosso vigil honors two people found dead as residents raise concerns over homelessness

In 2024, a U.S. Supreme Court decision gave local communities wide latitude to ticket and jail people who are unhoused, even when there isn’t shelter space for them. Since then, hundreds of cities, including five in Michigan, have passed laws further criminalizing survival activities by people who are homeless.
Then came a presidential executive order conflating mental health disabilities with homelessness, and calling for the weakening of protections against involuntary commitment. The order also directs federal agencies to abandon humane, evidence-based practices and prioritize funding for communities that rely on the arrest and incarceration of people who are unhoused and disabled.
But these crackdowns won’t reduce homelessness or make our communities safer, because they’re based on false stereotypes.
Many people experiencing homelessness work despite facing barriers related to health, transportation and discrimination. Recent research shows that more than half of adults staying in homeless shelters and 40% of those who are unsheltered are formally employed.
For many, job loss is what triggers a fall into homelessness. Forty percent of Michigan households struggle to pay for the basics. The U.S. doesn’t provide the same level of protection for workers and their wages that other well-resourced nations do, so when people get laid off or can’t work due to illness or injury, it can be catastrophic.
Locking up people who are homeless doesn’t improve public safety, either. The overwhelming majority of crime is committed by people who actually have housing. Across the nation, people who are experiencing homelessness are known to account for less than 5% of jail bookings, and they’re far more likely to be the victim of a violent crime rather than the perpetrator.
Here in Lansing, where the League is based, we’re seeing what happens when people are deemed unworthy of safety simply because they’re struggling to survive: five of our unhoused neighbors have died in less than a year. Homicide has been determined in three of these deaths and has not been ruled out for the other two.
Lansing City Council hears calls for emergency homelessness response, delays action

None of us should look away from homelessness or blame people who are unhoused for their plight. Homelessness is just the extreme endpoint of a convergence of broader social forces that is making life increasingly difficult for all but the wealthiest among us.
People who are unhoused are not the reason our groceries, utilities, healthcare and housing are getting more expensive. They aren’t the reason the middle class is shrinking, or that families are falling further into debt and feeling more anxious about how they will live in retirement.
We need to look to the corporate interests and policymakers who have built an economy that leaves so many families just one missed paycheck or unexpected expense away from losing their homes.
Income inequality is growing, and today, the wealthiest 1% of Michigan households have incomes nearly 22 times greater than the bottom 99%.
While we’re all spending more to put food on the table and fill our gas tanks, corporate profits are soaring. The world’s largest and most profitable corporations are paying workers poverty wages while their CEOs enjoy salaries hundreds of times higher.
It’s time to stop punishing those with the least and focus on real solutions: worker empowerment, a robust social safety net and affordable housing for everyone.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Affidavit ballot scramble increase calls for Mississippi early voting
description: Election Commissioner Madison Hill processes affidavit ballots at the Rankin County Election Commission in Brandon on Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, as the U.S. Senate race between Democratic candidate Scott Colom and the incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith remained uncalled.
text:
As voters across Mississippi arrived at the polls on Election Day only to find their names missing from the poll books, they were forced to cast affidavit ballots, leaving them frustrated and wondering whether their vote would count.
Mississippi is one of three states without early voting, which funnels most voting into a single day. Advocates say that magnified the chaos this year and forced many voters to cast a affidavit ballots, and delayed final results of the midterm Senate election. 
Candidates, advocates and voters now say Mississippi should join the overwhelming majority of states by allowing some form of early voting to reduce the number of affidavit ballots cast during an election and correct some mistakes ahead of time.
“We have been singing this song for as long as I can recall, but definitely if we had early voting, that would be helpful and truly we wouldn’t have as much of the chaos,” Democratic Rep. Timaka James-Jones of Belzoni said. 
James-Jones, a former county circuit clerk, said early voting would reduce the number of affidavit ballots and she believes voters who cast affidavit ballots are likely to be in the same position next time because the underlying problem never gets corrected. 
Instead of early voting, Mississippi has absentee voting. To vote absentee, a voter must list one of about 10 legal excuses for not casting an in-person vote on Election Day. For example, a voter can cast an absentee ballot if they plan to be out of town on Election Day or if they are a college student.
One of the major opponents of early voting is Republican Gov. Tate Reeves. On Election Day, he wrote on social media that he and First Lady Elee Reeves voted “IN-PERSON. On Election Day. With a Valid Photo ID. Just like every other person in America should be required to do.” 
His opposition has been decisive before. Senate leaders ended the 2025 session without sending Reeves a bill that would have expanded pre-Election Day voting, and he would likely have vetoed it. He had called no-excuse early voting bad for election integrity after the Senate passed that bill.
But it appears even his own party is leaving him behind. 
The Mississippi Republican Party sent a mailer out before the election encouraging voters in large print to “vote early” for GOP candidates. In smaller letters toward the bottom, it said “vote absentee before October 31 or head to the polls on Election Day, November 3.” 
President Donald Trump before the election also said on social media that in-person early voting was “UNDERWAY NOW” in Mississippi, which was inaccurate.
Senate Elections Chairman Jeremy England, a Republican from Vancleave, has pushed early voting legislation through the Legislature for years, but it’s failed to advance out of the Capitol. He has said constituents are frustrated and confused to learn Mississippi has no early voting. 
Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson is responsible for administering parts of the state’s elections and provides training to county election officials.
He recently told reporters that he is “an old school guy who loves Election Day” voting at the precinct but doesn’t oppose early voting laws. He argued that in-person absentee voting already functions as a form of early voting
Wakinya Clanton, the state director of the Southern Poverty Law Center, also supports early voting, but she said the state’s vote-counting system needs a complete overhaul, including same-day voter registration. 
“We need early voting without stipulations,” she said. “You don’t need an excuse to vote. If you’re a Mississippian, you should be able to participate in the election.”
The Mississippi Legislature will convene on Jan. 5 for its regular session.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Gainesville Elementary ranks among Missouri’s top rural schools for academic growth
description: GAINESVILLE — An elementary school in rural southern Missouri ranks among the state’s top performers for academic growth in English language arts, an achievement its superintendent credits to improved instruction, dedicated teachers and efforts to address challenges students face outside the classroom. According to Saint Louis University’s PRiME Center 2026 [...]
text:
Gainesville students prepare supplemental food bags for the district’s weekend food program, which serves approximately 200 students each week (Courtesy of Gainesville R-V School District).GAINESVILLE — An elementary school in rural southern Missouri ranks among the state’s top performers for academic growth in English language arts, an achievement its superintendent credits to improved instruction, dedicated teachers and efforts to address challenges students face outside the classroom.
According to Saint Louis University’s PRiME Center 2026 academic growth report, Gainesville Elementary School ranked 15th among 251 rural elementary schools in Missouri for three-year growth in English language arts, earning a growth score of 89.9. The rankings reflect student performance from the 2022-23 through 2024-25 school years.
The score measures student growth rather than overall proficiency. The report found that 55.1% of Gainesville students tested proficient or advanced in English language arts.
Superintendent Justin Gilmore, now in his seventh year leading the Gainesville R-V School District, said the recognition reflects an approach that places students’ academic, physical and emotional needs at the center of the district’s work.
“We’ve taken a holistic approach,” Gilmore said. “We have to take care of kids’ basic needs before we can ensure they’re ready to learn.”
Located in Ozark County, Gainesville is a community of approximately 700 residents. Gilmore said economic challenges facing local families have influenced the district’s approach to education.
To strengthen instruction, district leaders researched curricula used by high-performing Missouri schools and took teachers to visit those districts to observe classroom practices firsthand.
“We took teachers to visit other districts and see their approaches in action,” Gilmore said. “We have phenomenal teachers, and we trust them to help lead those decisions.”
The district also provided Language Essentials for Teachers of Reading and Spelling (LETRS) training, a professional development program focused on the science of reading, including phonics and foundational literacy skills.
“It was an eye-opener,” Gilmore said. “Some of what we thought we knew about how children learn to read wasn’t as accurate as we believed.”
While identifying curriculum changes and teacher training as important developments, Gilmore cautioned against attributing academic growth to any single strategy.
“You can’t just say, ‘We chose a new curriculum and everything changed,’” he said. “It’s the whole approach.”
Supporting students beyond the classroom
Gilmore said the district has increased its emphasis on addressing students’ basic needs, including employing two grant-funded community resource specialists who connect families with assistance.
The district participates in Care to Learn, a program that addresses needs related to hunger, health and hygiene. Its Youth Empowerment Project (YEP) also engages high school students in community service, including preparing supplemental food for students to take home on weekends.
Misty Cullipher, a community resource specialist and YEP coordinator, said her work involves helping families navigate housing difficulties, food insecurity and unexpected expenses.
In one recent case, the district assisted a single mother of four whose work hours had been reduced. The family received help with extracurricular expenses and $500 toward a utility bill, Cullipher said.
The district also maintains laundry facilities and a private shower for students experiencing housing instability or other hardships.
“We have a private shower in our community resource room,” Cullipher said. “That provides a little more dignity and confidentiality.”
Cullipher said the goal is to ensure students feel supported and prepared to participate in school.
“We believe in supporting students beyond the classroom,” she said. “Everything we do to help them feel ready to learn also helps them feel loved, seen and cared for.”
 Students helping students

One of the district’s largest initiatives is its weekend food program, which has grown from serving approximately 60 students a week when Cullipher took over four years ago to about 200 today.
During the previous school year, the district distributed approximately 7,900 food bags.
High school students involved in YEP help prepare the bags, which are distributed to students from preschool through high school.
Cullipher said a partnership with Convoy of Hope, a humanitarian organization based in Springfield, has expanded the district’s resources to include household necessities such as laundry detergent and toilet paper.
For Gainesville High School seniors Ella Barber and Karlie Cole, both YEP leadership team members, volunteering has provided an opportunity to help classmates while gaining a greater awareness of the challenges some families face.
Barber said she initially joined because she wanted to volunteer alongside friends.
“We started out just wanting to get out of class and spend time with friends while packing food bags,” she said. “But it turned into something much more meaningful.”
Barber said students help prepare food bags, organize clothing and complete other tasks behind the scenes.
“I really like being able to see the difference we’re making,” she said.
When students have access to food, clothing and hygiene resources, she said, they can focus more on school and extracurricular activities.
“They can focus on being kids,” she said.
Cole became interested in YEP after attending a meeting where older students described the program’s activities.
“I was impressed that we could help students without making them feel embarrassed,” she said. “We provide food, clothing and household items every week.”
Cole acknowledged that packing food bags can become repetitive, but said its purpose keeps her motivated.
“Sometimes packing food bags feels repetitive,” she said. “But at the end of the day, knowing those kids are getting what they need makes it worthwhile.”
Gilmore said opportunities for students to serve others are central to the district’s educational philosophy.
“We want our students to read, write and do math,” he said. “But we also need them to be kind, to care for others and to have empathy.”
 A personal commitment to Gainesville

For Gilmore, the district’s efforts to support students are rooted partly in his own experiences growing up in a family that faced financial difficulties.
“I grew up poor, so I understand what that experience is like,” he said. “My family eventually moved out of poverty, but those experiences have stayed with me.”
Gilmore said he has had opportunities to work elsewhere but chose to remain in Gainesville because he wants local children to have educational opportunities comparable to those available in larger districts.
“My goal has always been to stay in Gainesville,” he said. “I want us to be the envy of rural schools. I want our kids to have the best of everything we can provide.”
Gilmore said the district has secured more than $6 million in grants over the past seven years to support improvements and opportunities that would otherwise be difficult to finance through local resources.
Still, he emphasized that academic rankings and standardized test results are only part of what he considers a successful education.
As a parent himself, Gilmore said he wants students to leave school with more than the ability to perform well on academic assessments.
“At the end of the day,” he said, “I want our students to leave Gainesville not only with a good education, but with compassion for others and a desire to make a difference in their communities.”

title: Feds offer new agreement framework for states working with satellite providers in broadband program
description: LINCOLN — New federal guidance for how states should work with large satellite internet providers under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment, or BEAD, program is raising eyebrows among local broadband advocates. The National Telecommunications and Information Administration released a new model agreement Monday meant to “simplify the contracting proce[...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025, just hours before a federal government shutdown. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)LINCOLN — New federal guidance for how states should work with large satellite internet providers under the Broadband Equity, Access and Deployment, or BEAD, program is raising eyebrows among local broadband advocates.
The National Telecommunications and Information Administration released a new model agreement Monday meant to “simplify the contracting process” with satellite providers and expedite services to eligible BEAD locations. According to an NTIA statement, some national satellite companies have been slow to sign state contracts, as different states have imposed “a patchwork of obligations” beyond the basic federal requirements.
BEAD is a nationwide broadband expansion program that began under the Biden administration. In late 2025, state lawmakers learned of changes coming to BEAD through President Donald Trump’s “Benefit of the Bargain” initiative.
A BEAD on Nebraska broadband: State reopens provider applications with over $300M still in limbo

Nebraska has received roughly $57 million of the $405 million it was initially awarded, with the leftover dollars being held as “non-deployment funds” that may or may not come to the state.
Currently, about 23% of Nebraska’s BEAD technology is satellite, according to a previous statement from the Nebraska Broadband Office. Nebraska Department of Transportation — which encompasses the Broadband Office — spokesman Jay Omar said the office was in the middle of evaluating its response to the latest guidance.
“NBO is currently evaluating all options in response to the recent guidance around the Model Zero Outlay Agreement and will share decisions in the coming days,” Omar said of the changes announced Monday.
According to the NTIA statement, states can use the model agreement for Low Earth Orbit satellite providers that agree to meet BEAD service and testing requirements, but decline BEAD subsidies. States that choose to not use the model agreement will be responsible for finding a different provider who can serve locations at a comparable cost.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Emily Haxby, a Gage County farmer and vocal critic of the changes made to the BEAD program under the Trump administration, said the model agreement will mainly impact Nebraska’s working relationship with Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite company. She said she believes the model agreement would remove the accountability measures meant to ensure that Starlink serves Nebraska’s BEAD locations.
“SpaceX is giving up the subsidy and minimizing exposure, which makes sense because their entire BEAD award nationwide is less than two weeks of revenue for the company,” said Claude Aiken, chief strategy officer for Nextlink, another internet provider participating in Nebraska’s BEAD implementation. “The long-term benefit for them is keeping other providers from receiving subsidies for these locations.”
While Haxby said she suspected supporters of the latest changes would frame the model agreement as a cost-saving opportunity, she noted that Starlink was already serving Nebraska locations and wasn’t in need of BEAD subsidies in the first place. She said she doubts Nebraska would be able to find another company that can offer comparable or cheaper costs.
“(Nebraska) could have absolutely done better, but I will give them a little bit of a benefit when I tell you that the NTIA and them changing the rules did not help us at all,” Haxby said. “Quite frankly, they should just keep their grubby paws out of it.”

name: WyoFile
title: Elite female athletes forged on the anvil of the Teton Mountains
description:
Jackson Hole History Museum features the "Mountain Elite" exhibit. The six black-and-white prints will hang in the lobby serving as an appetizer to a Dec. 17 conversation with groundbreaking female athletes.
The post Elite female athletes forged on the anvil of the Teton Mountains appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Visitors to the Jackson Hole History Museum this holiday season can view photographic portraits of groundbreaking Wyoming women athletes featured in WyoFile’s “State of Equality” series.
The 11-by-14-inch prints will hang at the museum through Jan. 2 and will be an appetizer to a free Dec. 17 evening “Beers and Banter” panel discussion. The forum is scheduled to feature three of the Teton County athletes — Grand Canyon boatwoman Lorna Corson, Yosemite rock climber and alpinist Catherine Cullinane and Exum Mountain Guide Jessica Baker — along with moderators.
WyoFile’s overarching series “America at 250: State of Equality,” featured 17 articles or commentaries and was published this summer and fall. Shepherded by WyoFile Managing Editor Tennessee Watson, the series examined Wyoming’s historic role as the Equality State and the degree to which it lives up to the moniker.
Six profiles of elite female athletes who were forged on the anvil of the Teton Mountains make up the “Mountain Elite” subset of the project. Each profile included a portrait made in the athlete’s natural environment.
The photographs were made by this author with a medium-format camera on black-and-white negative film. Each frame measures about 2-by-3 inches. The format provides a finer quality image than the smaller, ubiquitous 35-millimeter size of most film and digital cameras.
The portraits were printed on silver halide paper in the Art Association of Jackson Hole’s darkroom in the Center for the Arts. Silver infused photographic paper renders rich, smooth tones generally superior to modern ink-jet printers that paint a digital image on the surface of the paper.
Art Association of Jackson Hole Photography Associate Jon Stuart supervises the development of an 11-by-14-inch black-and-white print for the “Mountain Elite” exhibit. (Angus M. Thuermer Jr./WyoFile)
The Art Association’s Photography Associate Jon Stuart and Studio Manager Jen Hoffman supervised the printing and mounting of the images.
The History Museum is open from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday starting Dec. 1. Admission is $12 for adults, $10 for seniors and students.
In addition to the museum’s regular gallery and showroom, a special photography exhibition “Jackson Hole 1955,” is also on display through the holidays. That show features large prints from Kodachrome images by Orson L. Arvin. The collection shows “the valley during the post–World War II auto tourism boom …  before the ski resort and rapid development began transforming the community in the 1960s,” according to the museum’s description.
Doors to the free Dec. 17 Beers and Banter “Mountain Elite” program open at 5:30. The program will run from 6 p.m. to 7:30 p.m.
