name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: He once pumped gas at Yellowstone. Now he’s running the national park.
description: This story was originally published by WyoFile on Nov. 25, 2026. For three summers during college, Barclay Trimble traveled from his native Texas to Yellowstone National Park, where he worked pumping gas at the Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge service stations. It represented his first meaningful encounter with America’s national park system. Trimble hiked an[...]
text:
Interim Superintendent of Yellowstone National Park Barclay Trimble assumed his duties in October 2026. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)This story was originally published by WyoFile on Nov. 25, 2026.
For three summers during college, Barclay Trimble traveled from his native Texas to Yellowstone National Park, where he worked pumping gas at the Old Faithful and Fishing Bridge service stations.
It represented his first meaningful encounter with America’s national park system. Trimble hiked and backpacked and explored on his time off hours and loved the experiences. And while today Trimble jokes that it’s “the one job that I never thought would show up on a resume,” he’s been reminded of that era during his first month in the role of Yellowstone’s acting superintendent.
Conservation groups, Forest Service add new public land near Yellowstone National Park

Trimble, a veteran National Park Service employee who has served in parks ranging from the Grand Canyon to Denali to Cape Hatteras National Seashore off the coast of North Carolina, filled the role that former superintendent Cam Sholly vacated in September.
At the helm of the country’s first national park, Trimble oversees 2.2 million acres of rugged landscapes, wildlife and geologic marvels that draw more than 4 million annual visitors — making it America’s third-most-visited park in 2025.
Since he started in October, Trimble has been working to get up to speed and understand the dynamics, issues and relationships that are critical for Yellowstone, he said.
“A lot of what I’m doing right now is still listening mode,” Trimble said. “I’m trying to learn from the park staff, I’m trying to learn from the state and federal partners, from the gateway communities and our tribal partners.”
Lion Geyser erupts in Yellowstone National Park. (Photo by Jacob W. Frank/National Park Service)
And in the window of time he had before park sections began closing for the winter season, Trimble said, he got out to tour around, even visiting some of those old haunts from his gas station days.
“It’s good to come back and dust off the memory banks,” he said. “For me it really is kind of like coming home.”
 With decades of national park experience, Yellowstone’s interim superintendent settles in

Trimble brings a breadth of experience gained over 35 years in the agency. He served as acting superintendent of Grand Canyon National Park, worked in the Intermountain Region in Colorado and in Washington, D.C., and was the deputy regional director for the Southeast Region. Before coming to Yellowstone, he was the superintendent of Mammoth Cave National Park in Kentucky, which is home to the longest known cave system on Earth.
He’s happy to be back in the Mountain West, where he had spent about half of his career, he said.
Gardner River floodwaters in 2022 obliterated many stretches of Yellowstone National Park’s North Entrance Road, which runs from Gardiner, Mont., to Mammoth Hot Springs, Wyo. (Photo by Kyle Stone/National Park Service)
Sholly left the superintendent role after eight years to work at the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation. He left a legacy of strengthening infrastructure, addressing worker housing and protecting the park’s wildlife and ecosystems. He also steered the park through crises like historic flooding and the COVID-19 pandemic, along with the more typical mishaps like bison gorings, visitor bottlenecks, tourists wandering off boardwalks and geothermal explosions.
Trimble takes the reins on several ongoing projects, like rebuilding a new permanent North Entrance Road. After a catastrophic 2022 flood destroyed the former North Entrance Road, crews quickly constructed a temporary highway to connect the towns of Gardiner, Montana, and Mammoth Hot Springs. The new road will replace that with a highway engineered for longevity, according to the park.
“So all the planning and compliance is done on that, and we will be moving forward on going out to bid and trying to award a contract, and hopefully starting on that” in 2027, Trimble said.
Work on a new Yellowstone River Bridge near Tower Junction finished in the last couple of weeks, and the park has projects ongoing to improve employee housing.
Still, Yellowstone faces challenges in maintaining its inventory of buildings, roads, trails and campgrounds. The Park Service estimates $1.2 billion in deferred maintenance and repairs in Yellowstone.
In October, the park announced the creation of a $105 million conservation and stewardship fund, the result of what it called the largest single private gift in the park’s history. Tallgrass, a Colorado company building an AI power hub near Cheyenne, seeded the donation.
Among the projects the effort will fund is a $35 million visitor center at Norris Geyser Basin, which Trimble said will be a major undertaking.
In general, Trimble’s philosophy when it comes to helming a national park is that “it’s not an island. It takes others for us to be successful,” he said.
Gateway towns, state agencies and tribal partners are among the organizations crucial to Yellowstone, he said.
In that vein, he said, “one of my top priorities is really just kind of getting out, having those conversations, building that trust, and continuing whatever I can do to help strengthen those partner relations.”
 Other leadership changes at Yellowstone National Park

Trimble isn’t the only new Yellowstone administrative face. Kristen Kosick became the park’s deputy superintendent in September, replacing Mike Tranel, who retired.
Bison bask in the sunlight on July 8, 2024, at Yellowstone National Park. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Kosick previously worked as chief of Michigan State Parks. Before that, she spent 15 years working for the National Park Service — including five years in Yellowstone as the fee program manager and chief of staff.
The National Park Service has launched a process to name a permanent superintendent, meanwhile.
Yellowstone is now downshifting operations in preparation for winter. Three of the four entrances have closed for the year, and park crews are preparing for the start of snowmobile and snowcoach travel, which begins Dec. 15.
The park tallied 4.7 million visitors through October. The highest year on record was 2021, when the park reported 4.8 million visitors.

description: A nonprofit that broadcasts government meetings around Alabama is testing an updated version of its platform that will incorporate artificial intelligence to retrieve information requested by users. text:
Construction crews continue work on the new Alabama State House on Monday, Nov. 23, 2026. The Alabama Channel said it will beta test an updated version of its website that keeps recordings of government meeting to make it easier for users to retrieve relevant content. (Ralph Chapoco/Alabama Reflector)A nonprofit that broadcasts government meetings around Alabama is testing an updated version of its platform that will incorporate artificial intelligence to retrieve information requested by users.
The Alabama Channel plans to unveil the updated version during the coming legislative session, which starts in February. Users can ask the platform about a specific topic, from healthcare to criminal justice, and the system will then apply artificial intelligence to search through its archives to identify people who spoke about the issues at specific meetings archived on the site.
“Now, you will actually be able to go in and say, ‘What did my representatives say about this topic I care about this week, or what did they say in the last three years?’” said Tara Bailey, director of The Alabama Channel, an initiative established by the League of Women Voters of Alabama, in an interview Monday. “It is actually going to go back into our footage that we have already captured and pull some of that information as well.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The system currently allows users to enter keywords that will then search the transcripts of recorded meetings that are available within the site. Incorporating AI is the most recent update to an application that began in 2022.
“We just started it as an archive of videos,” Bailey said. “We just wanted it to be a searchable archive and thought that we would just do the House and Senate, and legislative meetings.”
The Alabama Channel records the video feeds from the chamber floors and some committee meetings and publishes a transcript of what was said during the proceedings.
The program has expanded to include meetings of state agencies like the Alabama State Board of Education and the Alabama Department of Environmental Management. The system also records legislative meetings that happen outside the legislative session, such as the Contract Review Committee and the Joint Legislative Prison Oversight Committee meetings.
The initiative began on a shoestring budget with a couple of grants, one from the national organization of the League of Women Voters, according to Bailey. Traffic on the site has increased from almost 1,200 views per day at its peak during the 2023 legislative session to almost 1,800 views per day during the 2026 special session that dealt with redistricting, according to a graphic from Bailey.
A new grant will allow the program to pay for cameras and allow it to cover meetings of the Forever Wild Land Trust, which purchases land in the state for public use, four times a year.
Aside from the AI feature, the updated interface will better be able to identify lawmakers and other officials who are speaking in the recordings. The goal for the update is to make it easier for users to find information. Bailey likened the search to evaluating the performance of someone who is hired for a job.
“This is a way for people to check up on their representatives, to understand what laws are happening, to be empowered and go and talk to their representatives about things they want to see happen,” Bailey said.
Bailey said the channel wants to add other features that will help increase civic education, such as information on how bills move through the Legislature.
“Eventually, we want a teacher to be able to go to The Alabama Channel and pull down lesson plans that they can use for the classroom that pertain to what they need to be teaching based on the standards,” Bailey said.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: The anti-abortion movement is facing a reckoning
description: This story was originally reported by Shefali Luthra and Grace Panetta of The 19th. Meet Shefali and Grace and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. Heading into the 2028 presidential primary, Republicans are looking for a reset after catastrophic midterm losses and Democrats are energized coming off a historic wave. But […]
text:
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis waves to a person who asked for his signature on their DeSantis sign following his speech May 30, 2023 at Eternity Church in Clive. DeSantis helped enact a six-week abortion ban in his home state and is reportedly exploring a 2028 presidential bid. (Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
This story was originally reported by Shefali Luthra and Grace Panetta of The 19th. Meet Shefali and Grace and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
Heading into the 2028 presidential primary, Republicans are looking for a reset after catastrophic midterm losses and Democrats are energized coming off a historic wave.
But what both have in common: They’re still figuring out how to talk about abortion in 2028.
Republicans have long allied themselves with the anti-abortion movement, but the national ban many of those groups back is tremendously unpopular — enough to dissuade many front-runners from endorsing major abortion restrictions. Meanwhile, this year’s blue sweep expanded the number of Democrats who identify as personally “pro-life,” and the party’s moderate wing is encouraging its voters to be open to candidates talking about abortion differently in order to win in deep red states.
For both parties, the field is wide open, and Republican and Democrat contenders alike are beginning to test different messaging to voters.
If Democrats win both the presidency and control of Congress, they could have enough votes to pass a federal law enshrining abortion rights, something party leaders since the fall of Roe v. Wade have repeatedly said would be a top priority if they gained full control of Washington.
Abortion is poised to help shape the 2028 presidential election. Molly Murphy, a longtime pollster and president of Impact Research, said her organization found that abortion, while not the top issue in a midterm cycle dominated by concerns about the economy, was still a factor for over half of voters in battleground congressional districts and in Maine’s Senate race.
“So if it mattered in 2026, it matters more when they’re making decisions about who they want to be the president,” she said.
 The Republicans’ approach

Republicans’ effort to appeal more to national voters could upend the party’s long-standing partnership with the anti-abortion movement.
Polling from The 19th and YouGov shows that a large majority of voters want abortion to be legal. And polling conducted by Impact Research, a Democrat-aligned firm, found that in battleground states, most voters said lawmakers should work to pass federal protections. Anti-abortion ballot measures have repeatedly failed to garner majority support, including in more conservative states such as Ohio, Kansas and Missouri.
As a result, anti-abortion strategists and policy analysts say the GOP — which has for decades backed abortion restrictions — is publicly shifting away from the national bans its members supported just a few years ago. It’s similar to President Donald Trump’s approach; in 2024 he said abortion should be left up to individual states, and he has frustrated anti-abortion activists by ignoring many of their requests for federal limits on abortion medication.
“What we’re seeing is Republicans coming to some kind of grip with reality, when it comes to, OK, you can’t be a total no exceptions — you can’t be a hardliner and hope to have a future at the national level,” said Patrick Brown, a scholar at the Ethics and Public Policy Center, a conservative think tank.
It’s part of a larger Republican effort to find a message that may be more appealing to voters than enacting a strict national ban.
“They know they’re in a losing position, and they are trying to figure out — how do they waffle?” said Celinda Lake, a Democratic pollster and strategist.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who is reportedly exploring a presidential bid and helped enact a six-week abortion ban in his home state, recently said that the national anti-abortion movement has been caught “flat-footed.” He suggested that an effective conservative message would approach the issue differently based on an individual state’s politics, saying, “Mississippi can have a different message than New Hampshire.”
“I don’t really see much of a message at all on this,” DeSantis said days after the midterm elections. “I think the issue has lost a lot of salience, obviously partially because the left has won in most of these states at this point and the pro-life movement really hasn’t done much to fight that.”
It’s not yet obvious how other potential Republican presidential contenders might approach the issue. Vice President JD Vance — who has spoken frequently about his opposition to abortion — has been viewed by abortion opponents as a key ally in the White House and possible champion if elected president. But since the GOP’s midterm shellacking, Vance has not yet indicated how he would approach abortion if made the Republican nominee. His post-election remarks have instead focused on immigration policy and the ongoing military conflict in Iran.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also viewed as a potential 2028 contender, backed national abortion restrictions as a senator from Florida. But in 2022, months after the fall of Roe v. Wade, he told a reporter that he supported a ban in Florida but believed the issue should be left up to individual states.
But there isn’t clear agreement that avoiding the issue is a successful strategy for Republicans. In addition to winning back both chambers of Congress, Democrats also made huge gains at the state level, flipping control of many governorships and state legislative chambers now responsible for setting abortion policy. Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, a major national anti-abortion group, blamed Republican leaders and consultants for shying away from the issue, depressing a key segment of the Republican base.
“The only tangible results of this strategy were turnout problems, missed persuasion opportunities, and hundreds of thousands of dead babies in the strongest pro-life states,” the organization said in a post-election memo.
Strategists, activists and analysts agree that the Republican presidential primary represents an existential question for the future of the anti-abortion movement. Andrew Shirvell, founder and executive director at Florida Voice for the Unborn, said the anti-abortion movement as a whole has “soul-searching” to do. He argued that national anti-abortion groups have been overly focused on Congress and trying to get an abortion ban passed at the federal level, which he said is infeasible.
“The same movement leaders go back to the same nonsense,” Shirvell said. “I’m telling you this straight up. We’re never going to get a national abortion ban passed through Congress, no matter who the president is.”
Shirvell said he wants to see 2028 GOP presidential candidates who will be “a leader for a culture of life” and can restore morale among the grassroots base of the anti-abortion movement.
“What we need, and what I’d like to see, is somebody that’s going to articulate the pro-life cause using their bully pulpit of the presidency to motivate the movement to do the hard necessary work on the state and local level,” he said. “Because that’s where I foresee the movement is really going to be focused on for the next 10 to 15 years.”
As Brown put it: “The pro-life movement is not in a good place, and I think we all know that.”
 The Democrats’ approach

In 2024, then-Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential bid was defined by her full-throated embrace of abortion rights as “freedom.” The messaging in 2028 will likely take a bigger tent approach.
Central to that is tying abortion to cost-of-living concerns and, in some cases, a shift away from “culture war” issues or “identity politics.”
Abortion wasn’t a big topic at post-election Democratic gatherings like Crooked Media’s CrookedCon in Washington, D.C., and What’s Next, a conference of party strategists and 2028 hopefuls hosted in Denver by center-left group Majority Democrats.
But Lis Smith, a veteran Democratic strategist and adviser to Majority Democrats, said on a panel at CrookedCon that signaling moderation on the issue helped Democrats who support abortion rights win key midterm races in deep-red and purple states.
Sen.-elect Adam Hamilton in Kansas, a Methodist pastor, calls himself “pro-life with a heavy heart” and said he supports keeping abortion legal despite feeling “moral tension” around the issue. Sen.-elect Scott Colom, who pulled off a massive upset victory in Mississippi, says he’s “personally pro-life” but that he believes in reproductive choice.
“The big lesson to me from all of this is not left or right or moderate or populist,” Smith said. “There’s no one way to be a Democrat, and a big tent of voters requires a big tent of candidates. And we should stop trying from stages like this to tell people, ‘This is the prescription for the future of the Democratic Party,’ and let people in different places go out and show us what it is.’”
Mini Timmaraju, president of abortion rights group Reproductive Freedom for All, said she wants to see 2028 contenders talking about expanding abortion access on the trail. Timmaraju is hoping to see action “in the first 100 hours” of the new Congress to repeal the Hyde Amendment, which bans federal dollars from funding abortions in most cases, and wants 2028 Democratic presidential contenders to push for its abolishment.
“What we’d like to see is very clear commitments from Democrats across the board on plans to restore abortion rights in all 50 states, plans to remove discriminatory barriers to care, like the Hyde Amendment, and bonus points for comprehensive plans on issues like a right to contraception and IVF protections,” Timmaraju said on a call with reporters.
When Democrats launch their campaigns in South Carolina, the first state scheduled to hold a Democratic primary, many voters will expect to hear about abortion in some form, said Charleston-based political strategist Renee Harvey, pointing to the state’s six-week ban.
“We are the only early state with an abortion ban,” she said. “The first time they talk to voters, they are going to be campaigning in a state where the consequences of Dobbs are not hypothetical.”
But effectively campaigning on the issue will mean tying it to other voter concerns, she said, such as the cost of living and health care availability.
“Reproductive freedom is not separate from those kitchen table issues,” she said. “I don’t think anyone can claim to care about the cost of living while ignoring the cost of forcing women to give birth.”
In that context, some potential 2028 Democratic presidential contenders have begun testing out their own framing on abortion.
Harris, who campaigned heavily on the issue in her failed presidential bid two years ago, appeared at the end of October on a podcast hosted by Reproductive Freedom for All to argue that restoring abortion rights would also require changing political institutions such as the Supreme Court and Electoral College.
A spokesperson for Harris suggested those remarks were part of a larger focus on reproductive health, also pointing to a September appearance at a birth center alongside Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed in Detroit, where she criticized the Trump administration’s cuts to diversity, equity and inclusion programs as well as federal cuts to Medicaid, the health insurance program for low-income people.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin, a Michigan Democrat, appeared on another episode of the same podcast to argue that voters perceive support for abortion bans as a sign of extremism — and suggested that the right to end a pregnancy should be considered a cost-of-living issue.
Andy Beshear, the Democratic governor of Kentucky, devoted a chapter of his recent book, “Go and Do Likewise,” to his experience campaigning for exceptions to abortion bans alongside Hadley Duvall, a young woman from the state who had an abortion as a child after being raped by her stepfather.
“In all the debate surrounding the question of abortion, almost all of it cast in religious terms, Hadley speaking out on behalf of others was the most Christlike action I had ever seen,” Beshear wrote.
Georgia Sen. Jon Ossoff, who cruised to reelection this fall, highlighted his state’s six-week abortion ban during his campaign, including in a speech where he described women “bleeding out in Georgia labor wards because they didn’t get prenatal care.” Multiple women’s deaths in Georgia have been attributed to the state’s ban.
For Democrats, Lake said, “it’s a winning issue for candidates where there is a contrast.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Afghan family in NC faces immigration and medical uncertainty over federal delays
description: Sahar Amir’s wife, daughter and son spoke little after they loaded bags into a van and set off into the night. Inside the vehicle headed from Kabul, Afghanistan, to the Pakistan border, the atmosphere was grim.  Amir — not his real name — was an attorney in Afghanistan. From 2009 to 2011, he worked with […]
text:
A child looks at the aircraft as he moves towards his flight during an evacuation at Hamid Karzai International Airport, Kabul, Afghanistan, Aug. 24, 2021. (Photo by Sgt. Samuel Ruiz / U.S. Marine Corps)Sahar Amir’s wife, daughter and son spoke little after they loaded bags into a van and set off into the night. Inside the vehicle headed from Kabul, Afghanistan, to the Pakistan border, the atmosphere was grim. 
Amir — not his real name — was an attorney in Afghanistan. From 2009 to 2011, he worked with the U.S. military processing supply procurement for Bagram Air Force Base. For almost a decade after that, he was a prosecutor with the Office of the Afghanistan Attorney General, in the Department for the Elimination of Violence Against Women. While in that office, he led multiple high-profile cases against government officials, religious figures, even Taliban members accused of raping girls and young women. His victories at trial put perpetrators behind bars for years at a time.
“He was known for his courage, confidence and determination,” recalled a former colleague who now lives in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. “Cases involving members of the Taliban, terrorists or violent extremists accused of violence against women were often assigned to him.”
When Kabul and the country fell to the Taliban in August 2021, foreign friends told Amir to wait at home and avoid wading into the chaos at the Kabul airport.  They promised to help him get out of the country. But the help never arrived. By  January 2022, he needed to flee. The only person Amir could confide in was his father, a man in his 80s.
“My dad said, ‘Do not talk with anyone. Just leave the country,’” Amir said. 
That night at multiple Taliban checkpoints, money changed hands, and the van continued into the darkness, arriving at the border around 6 a.m. The guards there began to argue with Amir, accusing him of working for the government.
“I said, ‘Brother, I was a taxi driver.’” Amir recalled. “He said, ‘No, no, no, you are not taxi driver. Tell us the truth.’ I said, ‘What I am saying is this: I am not (with the government).’”
Amir said he and the Taliban border guard went on like this for almost 45 minutes when his daughter began to cry. 
“He said, ‘Okay, leave him, leave him. His daughter is crying. Leave him,’” Amir said. With another bribe, the guard waved the van through the border. The family entered Pakistan. 
Amir, it turns out, was predicting his own future. After three years of applying for visas to Germany, Canada, Australia, in January 2025 the U.S. granted him entry on a Special Immigration Visa. Now he’s a Lyft driver around Raleigh, hustling to support his family while his children go to school and his wife, who speaks little English, keeps their small apartment in order.
He was making do until summer 2026 when he was diagnosed with cancer and required surgery to remove his kidney. The family got support from North Carolina Medicaid to cover health care. Their assistance from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program had already ended in February.  
On Oct. 1, though, all the medical support ended. A new federal rule, created by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, stripped medical care from Amir, his family and another 10,500 refugees and others in North Carolina who were admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds. According to the state Department of Health and Human Services, a total of 12,500 lost food aid earlier in the year. 
Now Amir wonders how he’ll manage any further cancer treatment. 
Sitting in limbo
Before the administration of President Donald Trump, refugees who arrived in the U.S. would be connected to local resettlement agencies. The newcomers would have a year or so to apply for green cards and begin their path to citizenship.
In 1996, Congress restricted which new arrivals to the U.S. qualified for Medicaid, establishing so-called public charge rules. Most immigrants who’ve arrived here, even through traditional lawful channels, have had to wait for five years before they can get Medicaid and other benefits. However, Congress created an exception for refugees, along with asylum seekers, people who had been victims of human trafficking or domestic violence, and others admitted to the U.S. on humanitarian grounds. Those immigrants also were eligible for subsidies on the Affordable Care Act marketplace to purchase health insurance.
Families like Amir’s, with Special Immigrant Visas, were exempt from public charge rules. They received streamlined entrance from a country that was grateful for their help during the Afghanistan conflict.
In October, that all changed. With very limited exceptions, all those people lost access to any assistance — even the ability to receive an income-based subsidy on an ACA plan. Now, the only way for people in the Special Immigrant Visa pool to get benefits is to receive a green card.
“But since probably about mid-2025, the Trump administration has paused many green card applications, so people are no longer receiving those,” said Jennifer Taylor from Refugee Hope Partners, a Raleigh-based nonprofit that has helped refugees from more than 80 countries. “They’re just kind of in limbo, waiting.” 
Taylor explained that since that time, almost no refugees have been admitted to the U.S., except for white Afrikaners from South Africa. Around the world, everyone else continues to wait. 
Amir’s family arrived on Jan. 2, 2025. Had his family’s flight been delayed just a few weeks, until after Trump’s inauguration, they would have been refused entry. On his first day in office, Trump signed an executive order essentially shutting down all refugee entries to the U.S. 
Even though Amir and his family submitted their green card paperwork while still in Pakistan, they’ve waited, along with thousands of other Afghan refugees who helped the U.S. military during Operation Enduring Freedom, the 20-year Afghan conflict. 
“As Afghans who stood alongside the United States, supported it and worked closely with it, I expected America to provide us with full support in return,” said Amir’s former prosecutor colleague, who’s now a housewife in Louisiana. “We came to the United States legally, after going through a long waiting process. Unfortunately, instead of receiving the support we expected, I feel that the U.S. government is treating us as if we were criminals.”
In the past, Taylor said, families like Amir’s and his former colleague’s would have gotten green cards within six months to a year of arriving in the United States, and it was a “pretty normal process. 
“It went smoothly. Now what’s happening is they’re just not receiving it,” she said. 
“Even when they talk to their lawyers or different things like that, the whole process is stalled.”
At times, Amir’s frustration with the lack of progress for his green card bubbles over. 
“Please see in the system, I am active. I am already in,” he said, shuffling through several inches of forms and other paperwork. “Please just issue my green card.”
Without that green card, Amir can no longer get Medicaid or SNAP benefits. The bank balance he showed on his phone was $475. He had an unpaid credit card balance, and the rent was due in less than a week. 
Money is hard enough but without Medicaid, Amir wonders how he can afford  follow-up care for his kidney cancer. 
Frightening diagnosis
In early 2026, Amir began to feel pain in his lower back. 
“I had seen him for back pain earlier in the year, and he had a history of kidney stones,” said Matt Oettinger, a family physician who works at NeighborHealth, a community clinic based in Raleigh. 
NeighborHealth has a good reputation among local immigrants and refugees, and resettlement agencies frequently send people there. About 40 percent of the clinic’s patients speak languages other than English, including the Dari and Pashto languages widely spoken in Afghanistan. 
At first Oettinger treated Amir for kidney stones, but the pain persisted and worsened. One of Oettinger’s colleagues ordered an image and found a mass. 
“We got him in to a specialist pretty quickly,” Oettinger said. 
That July, Amir had surgery at WakeMed to remove his cancerous left kidney.
“They think that they got it all. Right now, the prognosis is good, but they need to continue watching,” Oettinger said. “He has other chronic medical problems, too, that he needs care for.” 
Including post-traumatic stress. 
Oettinger said that about 500 NeighborHealth patients — 5 percent of its total customers — lost their Medicaid coverage in October. 
Federal rules prohibit the clinic from providing free care, but patients can pay on a sliding scale. Despite those low-cost services, Amir said that without Medicaid it will be hard to afford the follow-up treatment. At the same time, he wants to pay his share.
So, Amir’s done what many other Americans have: He set up a GoFundMe campaign.
Twin fears: the Taliban & ICE
NC Health News agreed to identify Amir with a pseudonym and not show his face in photos because he said his family in Afghanistan — father, siblings and their families — could be at risk. 
Now, though, Amir worries about a risk closer to home as he drives people around Raleigh: Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 
“They are arresting people,” he said about ICE. “They arrest the people, and they take to jail, and then they will send you to Louisiana” where the U.S. is holding detainees before deportation. 
Refugee Hope Partners’ Taylor said many Afghan refugees share Amir’s hesitation about revealing his identity. While technically Amir and his family are in the country legally, she said she wasn’t certain that would keep ICE from picking up any of them. 
“Fear is one of the biggest things that we see,” Taylor said. “Just fear of the unknown, fear of what’s next, fear of ‘what happens to my family if we end up getting deported or detention’ or things like that.
“They left home for a reason. They left their country for a reason, and they cannot go back.” 
Amir describes his biggest worry about ICE: “They will deport me directly to Pakistan, and Pakistan will deport directly to Afghanistan.”
That’s already happening. Pakistan is in the process of pushing refugees back into Afghanistan. According to The New York Times, Pakistan’s government has forced the return of more than 2.7 million Afghan citizens to their home country since 2023.
Amir cannot return there, despite his desire to see family members again. The Taliban has released most of the people he helped put in prison, and they’d be out to get him.  
Even before the Taliban’s return, Amir faced the wrath of the people he prosecuted. He showed NC Health News photographs of his house in Kabul pockmarked with bullet holes after masked men shot at it at the conclusion of one of his high-profile cases. The head of the office for Elimination of Violence Against Women gave him firearms and weapons training. Two bodyguards became his constant companions.  
Leslie Schneider, a Virginia prosecutor, was an international legal adviser in Afghanistan with a gender justice assistance project before 2020. She told NC Health News that it was very hard to prosecute the types of cases Amir worked on. 
“There was such a resistance for getting justice for women who were victims of crimes that the top people who worked with [the former head of the office], they all had some degree of security presence,” she said. 
Amir’s former colleague told NC Health News: “His work was important not only for enforcing the law, but also for protecting women’s rights and helping victims seek justice — regardless of the power or influence of the accused.” We did not name her at her request.
She recalled that in Afghanistan, handling such cases involved “serious personal risks.” 
And now, under the Taliban, no one is doing that work. 
‘Simple taxi driver’
Schneider remembered Amir, if not the specifics of his case. She said that she and other Americans who worked in Afghanistan are haunted by the memories of many of their former comrades left behind and frustrated about their circumstances in this country.
She said she hears from Afghan refugees in situations similar to Amir’s almost every month.
They have so much to mourn. Amir remembers the killing of his 21-year-old cousin who was a CIA interpreter in Kandahar province. Amir was just a few meters away when he witnessed a suicide bomber blow himself up. And, in August 2021, when the Taliban returned to Kabul, he saw his life’s work shattered. 
In Afghanistan, Amir was important, respected, well-off, potent. On his phone he keeps photos of himself standing with former president Hamid Karzai, with the vice president, with provincial leaders, presenting at international conferences. 
Now, he describes himself as a “simple taxi driver,” making $150 on a good day and struggling to pay the rent. Before his surgery, he could work 12 hours a day. Now he can only manage eight or nine hours before the pain overwhelms him. 
But he remembers what he was like in court in his home country, speaking forcefully, delivering justice for women who had been wronged. He would love to keep arguing cases. He said he would love to serve the U.S., a country which, despite his struggles here, he says he loves. 
First, though, he has to stay alive. And without consistent health care, without Medicaid, that may not be possible.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Voter turnout surged in many states in the midterms, but not in Arkansas
description: The story of the 2026 midterm elections was defined in part by increases in voter turnout, especially in the South. Voters angry at persistent affordability issues and mid-decade redistricting that broke up several majority-Black congressional districts showed up at the polls, driving historic Democratic gains in traditional Republican strongholds like Missi[...]
text:
A line of voters wait to cast a ballot on the last day of early voting at the Pulaski County Regional Building in Little Rock, Arkansas on Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Ainsley Platt/Arkansas Advocate)The story of the 2026 midterm elections was defined in part by increases in voter turnout, especially in the South. 
Voters angry at persistent affordability issues and mid-decade redistricting that broke up several majority-Black congressional districts showed up at the polls, driving historic Democratic gains in traditional Republican strongholds like Mississippi, Texas and South Carolina.
Arkansas told a somewhat different story.
No statewide or federal offices flipped blue, with Democratic gains limited to legislative and local races. While some areas saw increases in turnout, an analysis of Arkansas’ election data shows voters generally stayed home more than they usually do during midterms, which already see lower turnout than presidential election years. 
The Arkansas Advocate’s analysis used election data provided by the Arkansas secretary of state’s office. It compared turnout in 2026 to the 2022 midterm election, and the two major political parties’ share of votes in this year’s U.S. Senate race to the 2024 presidential election.
Here are three things that stood out:
  Top Trump-winning counties stayed home 
The drop in turnout was especially pronounced in some counties that voted for Republican President Donald Trump by the widest margins in 2024. Three of the five counties with the largest drop in turnout compared to 2022 were among the top five counties who voted for Trump by the widest margins in 2024.
Searcy County, which gave Trump 85.4% of the vote in 2024, saw its midterm turnout drop from 55.5% in 2022 to 38.8% in 2026’s general election. That amounted to the largest percentage drop among Arkansas’ 75 counties, and was only 1 percentage point above turnout in March’s primaries. Primary turnout is generally lower than turnout during a general election.
Laurie Gross, the former Republican commissioner on the Searcy County election commission who was decertified by the state board of election commissioners last year due to issues with the procurement of equipment used during the 2024 election, said there weren’t many races on the general election ballot that people cared about.


Gross said she suspected county voters had little interest in the federal and statewide races. There were the national issues, such as the war in Iran, that could have been a factor, but she said locals also remained bitter over legislation signed by Republican Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders that restricted local government’s ability to regulate cryptocurrency mines.
“Searcy County is kind of unusual in that we are a red county, we’re very Republican, but our voters are more … independent-type voters than they are hardcore Republican voters,” Gross said. 
The same could be said for many of the rural counties in hilly north Arkansas, Gross noted. But the former election official said she couldn’t say definitively why her county stayed home more than usual this year.
“There’s no way to know why somebody didn’t vote unless you ask the person who didn’t vote,” she said.
  Northwest Arkansas Democrat wins accompanied by thousands of new voters on rolls 

Despite earning a larger share of cast votes in every county in this year’s Senate race than they did in 2024’s presidential contest, Democrats’ gains were confined to the Legislature — though they came close to flipping U.S. Rep. French Hill’s central Arkansas congressional seat. Those gains were concentrated in northwest Arkansas, with other pick-ups in central Arkansas and Jonesboro.
Increases in voter registration could be seen in many of the areas where Democrats flipped seats. Benton and Washington counties, where tens of thousands of voters have been added to rolls since 2022, were the epicenters of Democrats’ 11-seat gain in the Legislature. The two counties saw some of the sharpest leftward swings in the state.


“We’ve had pretty much a steady growth” in voter registration over the years, said Dana Caler, a longtime elections administrator for Benton County. That was especially true in the smaller cities and suburbs.
“We were actually a little lower on our turnout this year,” she added, referring to a midterm year.
Faulkner County, the home of a Republican-held state House district that flipped blue, gained 1,449 voters over the same period. Craighead County, where Democrats flipped another seat, saw a gain of 1,212 voters. 
  Turnout gains in south Arkansas come with caveat 

Arkansas counties along the Mississippi River were among the few that saw modest gains in turnout — though accompanied by sharp drops in the number of registered voters.
Voter turnout is calculated by dividing the number of ballots cast in a county by the number of registered voters.
Desha County was one of two counties that flipped Democratic in 2026 after voting for President Donald Trump in 2024. Forty-nine percent of the county’s registered voters cast a ballot in 2026, compared to 44% in 2022.
The former chair of the county’s Republican Party, Jamie Sims, said in an email that he was saddened by the flip. Sims, who resigned as chair in September after moving to a different part of the state, said local races for county judge and clerk likely contributed to turnout there.
But there were also far fewer registered voters in the first place.
Like many rural counties in Arkansas over the last two decades, Desha County’s population has continued to shrink, with the average age of its residents increasing from 38.3 years in 2010 to 41.6 in 2024. Since 2022, when it had 7,100 people registered to vote, the county shed more than 1,000 voters from its rolls.
But because there were only 222 fewer ballots cast in the county in 2026 compared to 2022, according to unofficial data from the secretary of state’s office, the voter turnout still moved upward.
Similar drops in voter registration, accompanied by a much smaller decrease in the actual number of votes cast, could be seen in other Delta and south Arkansas counties where turnout was higher. In Union County, voter rolls shrank by more than 2,500 — but only saw 289 fewer ballots cast.
Crittenden County lost a similar number of registered voters, but saw 231 more people cast votes in 2026 compared to 2022.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Mason County data center named one of biggest potential polluters in the US
description: The Mason County Monarch Compute Campus could be one of the most polluting data centers in the country, according to a recently released report by the Sierra Club.
text:
The site map for the Monarch Compute Campus data center in Mason County, West Virginia. Nscale expects the data center to be in operation in January 2027. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection)The Mason County Monarch Compute Campus could be one of the most polluting data centers in the country, according to a recently released report by the Sierra Club. 
The data center, located next to a house subdivision, could produce 11 million tons of CO2, more than 600 tons of “hazardous air pollutants” and nearly 300 tons of formaldehyde, according to the report called “Artificial Intelligence, Real Pollution: How Data Centers Became a Top Climate Threat.” 
Elaine Matheny, an organizer with Mason County United, said the pollution emitted from the data center could exacerbate health issues for those living in the area. 
“We are concerned. The health risks are obvious,” she said. “People with asthma, people with breathing problems, COPD, they’re all going to be going to the doctor more.” 
Matheny also warned that the pollution won’t be limited to the immediate area around the data center, which has already experienced flooding during construction. 
“It’s going to be a very hazardous project to the area and beyond,” she said. “Ripley, Ravenswood. I don’t think the people living around here realize how it’s going to affect Point Pleasant, which is not very far.” 
Nscale, the developer of the data center, did not reply to a request for comment Wednesday. 
Nicholas Preservati, director of the West Virginia Office of Energy, said the emissions cited by the Sierra Club only reflect a scenario where the data center is operating at full capacity. 
“The numbers in the Sierra Club report come from the maximum emissions allowed under the facility’s draft air permit, not from actual operations,” Preservati said in a statement. “Those maximums are inline and in some cases below what existing power plants already emit. Even so, the Sierra Club acknowledges there are limitations to their study.”
The Sierra Club sourced its information through air permits filed with the state and based on the assumption that the data center will be used at 90% of its capacity. 
The report warns that CO2 emissions, accepted by most scientists as the cause of climate change, are projected to increase because data centers are reliant on natural gas, on-site diesel generators and coal fired plants to run. 
The report predicts that if data center development keeps its pace, any gains at reducing greenhouse gas emissions over the last 15 years will be erased in the next three years. 
“This report is not an argument about the ethics of AI; it is about how the machines behind it are powered and how those decisions will impact our future, unless we enact guard expediently,” the report states. “It is a call to affirmatively stop locking in fossil fuels before it is too late.” 
The Monarch Campus will run on more than 800 gas-powered turbines, according to the report. 
Preservati said the health concerns need to be viewed in the context of the bigger picture of health in the Mountain State. 
“West Virginia has some of the highest rates of heart disease, diabetes and drug overdose deaths in the nation,” he said. “Any serious discussion about the long-term health of West Virginians must also consider the effects of poverty, unemployment and a lack of economic opportunity.”
“We can change that through economic development. More good-paying jobs mean more West Virginians can support their families and more resources to improve healthcare, provide clean drinking water and fix our aging infrastructure,” Preservati added. 
Matheny said her group has been showing up at West Virginia Department of Environmental Protection hearings and speaking and monitoring the construction site to report any violations they see. 
She said the data center could use less harmful power generation means, but the legal landscape created by House Bill 2014, the state’s data center law, has stripped people from pushing for that. 
“There’s alternatives, but we have no right and no vehicle to even comment before this all started,” she said. “That’s really been the thing that has most people angry.” 
Preservati pointed out that HB 2014 doesn’t exempt data centers from following state and federal environmental guidelines. 
“Anyone who wants to build in West Virginia must still meet every state and federal environmental permitting requirement,” Preservati said. “The state has reviewed Monarch’s air quality permit application and preliminarily determined that it meets all applicable requirements. Any future projects will undergo the same thorough review.” 
Matheny noted the fight against the data center has turned out people from across the political spectrum, from libertarians to liberals. And she believed that’s why the two delegates representing Mason County lost the county. 
Del. Jonathan Pinson and Del. Jim Butler, who both voted in favor of HB 2014, were able to retain their seats by winning slivers of neighboring counties they represent. Following the election, Butler lamented during a presentation at the November Interim session of the Legislature that the biggest issue is communication with the public. 
“I’m skeptical of all the economic development stuff, but when I see something that’s going to work and I buy into it, I’m sticking with it, and I’m sticking with the decisions we’ve made here,” he said. 
But HB 2014 contributed to the wins of several Democrats across the state, including delegate-elect Lucia Valentine in Berkeley and Jefferson counties. She’s representing a district that borders the Penzance data center. 
Valentine said she doesn’t have specifics at the moment, but she anticipates introducing legislation to address pollution and other issues. 
“In addition to restoring local control over projects, we need protections for air quality and public health,” she said over text message. 
While Republicans haven’t been vocal on the potential pollution issues surrounding data centers, a few high ranking members are beginning to second guess the legislation. 
Last week, Treasurer Larry Pack announced his legislative priorities for 2027. The Treasurer included reforms to the taxation portion of HB 2014, which diverted tax monies that typically go to counties into state coffers. 
He also said other portions of the bill should be revisited, too. 
“There’s no question that I believe there needs to be more transparency. There needs to be local input,” Pack said.
And Tony Hodges, the co-chair of the West Virginia Republican Party, posted on X that President Donald Trump had said, “make them pay your community” in regards to data centers. 
“He did not say make them pay your state. He said make them pay your ‘community.’ House Bill 2014 has a glaring mistake. It must be fixed,” he posted.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Lawmakers are reaching across the aisle for Michigan’s trails system
description: Spanning more than 13,000 miles across the state, Michigan’s trails system offers hikers, bikers, equestrians and snowmobilers plenty of space to blow off steam. While many know Michigan as the Great Lakes State, the state has earned another nickname – the Trails State – due to its extensive network of outdoor trails, which are maintained […]
text:
Multi-use trail in Sleepy Hollow State Park, DeWitt, Michigan (Photo by Susan J. Demas/Michigan Advance)Spanning more than 13,000 miles across the state, Michigan’s trails system offers hikers, bikers, equestrians and snowmobilers plenty of space to blow off steam.
While many know Michigan as the Great Lakes State, the state has earned another nickname – the Trails State – due to its extensive network of outdoor trails, which are maintained in collaboration between state and local governments 
Brought together by a desire to promote and enhance the various trails crisscrossing the state, lawmakers in the Michigan House and Senate are reaching across the aisle to establish the Michigan Trails Caucus, chaired by Rep. Parker Fairbairn (R-Harbor Springs). 
Speaking with Michigan Advance, Fairbairn said he began talking with the state’s various trails groups in the wake of the 2025 ice storm, discussing the ways the storms impacted – and continue to impact – the trails system to this day.
A common theme in these discussions is just how difficult it is to keep up with trail maintenance.
“They only have so many volunteers. The equipment, in a lot of cases, is outdated and becoming obsolete if they’re not already. And you know, they receive money from the state to help manage the trails,” Fairbairn said. 
Grooming Michigan snowmobile trails. (Photo by Marla R. Miller/Michigan Advance)
In these cases Fairbairn said money is often a real problem. In founding the caucus, he hoped to look through the Department of Natural Resources’ budget to see how funding for trails is being spent.
However, the caucus’s purpose is twofold, Fairbairn said, with education on Michigan’s trails system serving as the other key focus. 
“My hope is we’ll have different organizations who work and deal with the trails come in and present to the caucus or present to other people interested in trails and educate them on issues that snowmobile groups are having and issues that these bike groups are having,” Fairbairn said. 
As of Nov. 17, Fairbairn said the caucus had 25 members.
While the caucus won’t be able to address every issue, members will at least be educated on the importance of Michigan’s trails and how various organizations are helping them, Fairbairn said.
Trails leading out from Oval Beach in Saugatuck, Michigan on Aug. 21, 2024. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)
In a statement to the Advance, Rep. Will Snyder (D-Muskegon), one of the caucus’s vice chairs, pointed to the state’s trails as a great resource for residents, as well as a draw for tourists. 
“As a legislator, I’ve been a champion for expanding tourism opportunities, and supporting our trails system is another way of bolstering tourism in Michigan,” Snyder said. “In the Muskegon area, we’ve been working with Laketon and Fruitland townships on a trail system expansion that would connect local trails to the Fred Meijer Berry Junction Trail, which, in turn, is tied together with most other regional West Michigan trails.”
While Snyder did not anticipate much action in the Legislature during the lame duck period that follows the election, he said the caucus would continue to grow its ranks and develop its vision for the state’s trails in the next legislative session beginning in 2027.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia vies to host NASA’s first U.S. space academy in Hampton
description: Virginia wants to become home to NASA’s first United States Space Academy in Hampton, a move that would strengthen the commonwealth as a training ground for a multidisciplinary space workforce.   This comes after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August directing the establishment of the academy, creating a new federal educational enterpris[...]
text:
The Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport at the NASA Wallops Flight Facility on the Eastern Shore. (Photo courtesy of MARS)Virginia wants to become home to NASA’s first United States Space Academy in Hampton, a move that would strengthen the commonwealth as a training ground for a multidisciplinary space workforce.  
This comes after President Donald Trump signed an executive order in August directing the establishment of the academy, creating a new federal educational enterprise. Multiple states, including Texas, Pennsylvania, Louisiana and Maryland, have submitted proposals. 
Virginia’s proposal is rooted by a 600-acre campus at NASA Langley and Fort Monroe, with  Wallops satellite campus and a goal of welcoming 300 cadets in 2028.
“Virginia is a world leader in aerospace innovation and national defense, and the commonwealth is best positioned to be the future home of the United States Space Academy,” said Gov. Abigail Spanberger in a statement on Nov. 16. 
She said that with Virginia’s “unparalleled defense footprint” and “world-class research assets,” she is confident Virginia can meet the federal government’s ambitious goal and begin training the first class of cadets by 2028. 
NASA’s invitation to states calls for “a NASA-led, civilian Federal academic institution that combines rigorous technical education with disciplined leadership development, civic responsibility, and a lasting commitment to public service.”
The invitation adds that the academy will prepare the future multidisciplinary space workforce, including astronauts, engineers, operators and scientists, to “advance American interests across the aerospace sector.”
In its proposal, Virginia said NASA Langley would provide the academy’s research, engineering, flight, innovation and technical core, while Fort Monroe would support residential life, instruction, leadership development, ceremonies, administration and public engagement. 
Virginia Spaceport Authority’s Mid-Atlantic Regional Spaceport (MARS), located at Wallops Island, would also serve as a satellite learning campus, providing field-based experience in payload integration, space launch and range operations, mission planning, flight safety, uncrewed systems and post-mission analysis.
Virginia’s proposal outlines a path to welcome approximately 300 cadets in 2028, using existing academic, residential, laboratory and student support capacity. 
“Through adaptive reuse of existing facilities and a network of industry, research, and academic leaders, Virginia will work with NASA to rapidly realize its vision and meet its needs,” Secretary of Commerce and Trade Carrie Chenery said in a Nov. 16 statement. “Together, we will build an academy capable of cultivating our next generation of space visionaries.”
Virginia’s congressional delegation has all signed on in support of the proposal to bring the academy to Hampton. Multiple universities also support a unified academy curriculum spanning fields such as aerospace engineering, aviation, cybersecurity, data science and power systems.
House Technology Committee Chair Cliff Hayes, D-Chesapeake, said landing the academy would be “spectacular” for Hampton Roads, the commonwealth and the nation.
“Hampton Roads has long helped defend America’s interests on the seas with the world’s largest naval base and through the air with Oceana Naval Air Force presence,” Hayes said in a statement. “With the United States Space Academy, we have an opportunity to help prepare the scientists, engineers, and innovators who will advance America’s interests among the stars.”
NASA is located in Washington, D.C., and has operations across the country, including Wallops Flight Facility and Langley Research Center in the commonwealth.
This project is Virginia’s most prominent new federal-site competitions since the FBI headquarters fight that began almost a decade ago. Ultimately, the project was awarded to Maryland in 2023, under President Joe Biden’s administration. 
But last year, Trump reversed course after being elected and kept the FBI in Washington, D.C. His administration later lost in court after Maryland challenged the decision.
An announcement on where the academy will be headquartered is expected in late December.

title: Virginia provides White House with 6th National Christmas Tree
description: Virginia is once again at the heart of the century-long tradition of lighting a national Christmas tree at the White House. For the third year in a row, the George Washington and Jefferson National Forest supplied a red spruce that will be displayed at the Ellipses at the White House throughout the season. The tradition […]
text:
Forest Service employees make final preparations before harvesting a 36-foot red spruce in Highland County, Virginia,  selected as this year's National Christmas Tree. (USDA Forest Service photo by Preston Keres)Virginia is once again at the heart of the century-long tradition of lighting a national Christmas tree at the White House. For the third year in a row, the George Washington and Jefferson National Forest supplied a red spruce that will be displayed at the Ellipses at the White House throughout the season.
The tradition of erecting a Christmas tree on the grounds of the nation’s capital began back in 1923 when First Lady Grace Coolidge allowed local schools to put up a tree on the Ellipses. President Calvin Coolidge pushed the button to light up the tree in front of a crowd of thousands.
Virginia has provided the tree in 1939, 1940, 2012, 2024, 2025, and now in 2026. The 36-foot tree was picked from the mountains of Highland County and has been taken to Washington for the Dec. 3 lighting ceremony in President’s Park. 
“Our farmers, our producers, and our forests are truly the pride of the Commonwealth, and I’m so glad they’re being celebrated,” Sen. Mark Warner posted on X.
In the past, trees were cut to be put on display. Now, the tree is kept alive and planted on the grounds and sometimes used for multiple years. The tree from Virginia in 2012 was kept through 2018.
“We are honored to share this magnificent red spruce with the nation as the National Christmas Tree and to showcase the natural beauty and heritage of Virginia on a national stage,” said Acting Forest Supervisor Troy Morris. 
Red spruces are found in the high elevation and cold parts of the Southern Blue Ridge. There have been efforts to restore these trees and the surrounding ecosystems after extensive logging between the 1880s and 1930s, as well as wildfires. 
Groups like the Southern Appalachian Sprue Restoration Initiative and the U.S. Forest Service have worked to plant seedlings – with up to 8,000 red spruce seedlings to be planted in 2027 near Mount Rogers.
The spruces rely on cold weather for survival, so the warming climate puts these unique forests at risk. 
The restoration initiative reports that the forests provide habitat for a number of species that are only found in these types of environments and have been listed as species of concern, such as the spruce-fir moss spider, Carolina northern flying squirrel, as well as other birds and salamanders.
The tree will be on display on the White House grounds starting on Dec. 5.

title: Virginia health officials say communities have ‘stepped up’ to combat measles uptick
description: The recent death of a young child who tested positive for measles has Virginia health officials redoubling efforts to bolster immunity, and communities with higher unvaccinated populations are responding, they said.  Dr. Maria Almond, director of the Piedmont Health District, said her staff conducted outreach and vaccinations throughout the summer to tame an[...]
text:
An MMR vaccine is administered. (Photo by George Frey/Getty Images)The recent death of a young child who tested positive for measles has Virginia health officials redoubling efforts to bolster immunity, and communities with higher unvaccinated populations are responding, they said. 
Dr. Maria Almond, director of the Piedmont Health District, said her staff conducted outreach and vaccinations throughout the summer to tame an outbreak that began in Buckingham County and spread into Cumberland County. 
“Once (the localities) became aware of what was spreading … and the significant severe effects of the illness in many people, they worked to reduce opportunities for spread,” Almond said. “This was not easy but with increasing immunity over several months, eventually the community was able to snuff out the spread.”
Of Virginia’s 230 cases so far this year, the bulk occurred between May and June, with many cases attributed to that region. Throughout July and September, statewide cases were between one and two per month. 
Public health officials warn of rise in measles, as Va. hantavirus patient under monitor

But as cooler weather has kept people indoors those numbers have increased with 51 cases reported between mid-October through November . Almond noted a “current uptick” specifically in Charlotte County.
She said holiday travel and gatherings could compound transmission spread in unvaccinated populations.
“The Charlotte County community has stepped up with increased requests for vaccination over the past several months, each person vaccinated contributing to the protection of the community,” she said. 
Measles, a highly contagious virus spread through the air, causes a high fever, runny nose, bloodshot eyes and a rash. Measles weakens the immune system and can result in dangerous complications like pneumonia, brain swelling, or a nervous system infection — all possibly deadly. 
The death this month of a child under the age of 4 was the first reported death from measles in Virginia in nearly 50 years. To protect the identity of the child and their family, the state has not released any details of their death or where they live.
About 90% of cases affect people who are not vaccinated against measles. 
Sixty-seven percent of cases statewide have been in minors under 18 years of age. Fifty-two percent of those have been children under 12.
The resurgence of measles has followed several years of anti-vaccine rhetoric on social media and from within the federal government, including U.S. Secretary of State Robert F. Kennedy Jr., leading to confusion and hesitancy for some parents. 
Once considered eliminated in the U.S., the Pan American Health Organization determined last week that the country no longer meets those standards. For nearly 20 years, the U.S. had averaged 150 measles cases nationwide per year and only three deaths between 2001 and 2018. 
As measles vaccines are typically given when people are young, the Virginia Department of Health suggests people who are unsure of their status can check through a records request in a VDH portal. 
Vaccines are widely available at pediatrician offices, pharmacies and local health departments. Local health departments also offer free or low-cost options for eligible people. 
The process for children entails two doses, spaced 28 days apart. 
Health officials consider people born before 1957 who have had measles as a child to be immune, but any adult or child born after that who has not had the disease and has not been vaccinated should seek the doses, VDH immunization director Christy Grey suggested. Blood tests can also determine if a person has a measles immunity and adults, unless they are in a higher risk group, could obtain one dose of the vaccine if needed. 
With nearly 6,000 confirmed cases nationwide as of late November, Almond emphasized how “incredibly contagious” it is. 
“Nine out of 10 people without immunity will become ill if in close contact with someone with measles,” she said. “When a case lands in a cluster of those who are not vaccinated, it will spread quickly and with ferocity.”
