name: Nevada Current
title: Data centers’ electricity use is soaring — especially in these states
description: This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here. It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet […]
text:
(Image: Craig Mitchelldyer / Getty Images / Grist)This story was originally published by Grist. Sign up for Grist’s weekly newsletter here.
It takes a lot of electricity to power the sprawling computing campuses undergirding the artificial intelligence boom: a lot for servers, a lot for cooling the chips, a lot for networking, and a bit for keeping the actual lights on. Yet translating “a lot” to real numbers pinned to individual facilities requires usage data, something that data-center operators are loath to disclose.
A Harvard-led study published this week in Nature Sustainability gets us closer to these numbers. Researchers extracted locations and building footprints for as many U.S. hyperscale data centers as possible, ultimately cataloguing 403 of the warehouse-sized facilities across the country. Translating power capacity to theoretical electricity usage, the authors estimated these facilities gobble up roughly 82 terawatt-hours of electricity annually, the equivalent of nearly 8 million homes. They suggest this electricity is associated with about 26 million metric tons of carbon dioxide emissions.
The 82-TWh estimate corresponds to about 2 percent of U.S. electricity. Though noteworthy in its own right, that figure shrouds high state-to-state variability, with many states boasting data-center electricity shares in the double digits. When viewed as a fraction of the retail electricity sales reported to the Energy Information Administration (EIA) in 2024, Oregon’s studied data centers used the equivalent of 18.6 percent of the electricity sold in the state. In Virginia and Iowa, data centers consumed 15.5 and 13.1 percent, respectively.

While data-center electricity consumption remains a national issue, electricity prices and utility planning look very different from state to state. And the speed of hyperscale buildouts means these figures can change quickly.
In Oregon, for example, the state’s data-center share of electricity use grew from about 3 percent in 2015 to about 23 percent in 2025, according to analyses presented to the state by energy economics firm ECOnorthwest and the University of Virginia. The group estimated that data centers were associated with approximately 96 percent of the state’s electricity sales growth between 2020 and 2025.
Data centers can “no longer be understood as a marginal component” of Oregon’s electricity demand, the authors wrote — and in the Wild West of hyperscaling, it’s a component poorly matched to current regulatory structures. In its most recent biennial energy report, the Oregon Departmentof Energy noted that the state “currently lacks a policy mechanism to address emissions from data center load growth.”





Many states are grappling with the ramifications of recent data-center buildouts. Because the Harvard study was limited to hyperscale facilities the authors could verify, its electricity-use estimates are likely undercounts. In Virginia, for example, the study’s 142 included facilities account for about 15 percent of the state’s electricity sales — itself a staggering sum. But Dominion Energy, the largest seller of electricity in the state, has estimated that data centers purchased 28 percent of the electricity its Virginia subsidiary sold last year.
Currently, there is no federal apparatus to track or check these figures, as surveys of utilities’ sales tend to label customer segments as merely residential, commercial, industrial, or transportation-related. In March, Senators Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley wrote to the EIA, arguing: “Without this data, policymakers, utility companies, and local communities are operating in the dark.” The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, the infrastructure permitting bill currently under consideration in the Senate, would direct the agency to explicitly measure data-center electricity usage.
Hyperscale electricity can also be understood in terms of the planet-warming gases emitted during its generation. Together, the facilities catalogued by the Harvard researchers emit more annually than the carbon-dioxide equivalent of countries like Jordan, Kenya, and Guatemala.
State context matters here, too, since emissions estimates depend on a given state’s grid, which vary by energy mix. The Nature Sustainability study’s authors used federal power-plant data to estimate the average per kilowatt-hour emissions for each confirmed data center. The resulting rates range from Washington’s hydropower-heavy 10 grams of carbon dioxide per kilowatt-hour to Virginia’s fossil-fuel-backed 325.
Yet even grid averages fail to capture the growing phenomenon of on-site power plants. Frequently gas-fired, these generators are built at or near hyperscale campuses to generate electricity directly for the data centers themselves. Electricity usage from on-site power can be harder to measure, given it is often “behind the meter” — that is, the electrons might never touch a public grid. As of June, about 2 GW of gas generators powered four data centers around the country, including Elon Musk’s xAI sites in Memphis, Tennessee. There are 143 GW of gas plants currently proposed to power data centers around the United States, according to the Environmental Integrity Project (EIP), a watchdog group.
Most of this proposed gas could push the hyperscale buildout outside the Harvard study’s map. West Virginia, for example, hosts exactly zero of the data-center campuses confirmed by the Nature Sustainability study. Yet the state is second only to Texas in proposed direct gas capacity, with more than 15 GW tagged by EIP.
If built, these projects could reshape the geography of U.S. data centers — and make their electricity use less visible in utility-sales and grid-demand data. Behind-the-meter power doesn’t show up as utility purchases.

It’s possible many of these proposed plants will never actually break ground; only about two dozen of the 74 proposed plants tagged by EIP are currently permitted for construction under the Clean Air Act. Yet if the recent supercharged data center build-out offers any indication, applications for new on-site facilities will continue to roll in.
“What we’re seeing is already striking, but it’s only a snapshot of a rapidly expanding industry,” said Gianluca Guidi, lead author of the Nature Sustainability study, in a statement. Forget 2 percent: The electricity and emissions estimates offered by his team “could already be substantially larger now in 2026.”
 


The Nevada context
The Public Utilities Commission of Nevada has moved to approve three methane gas power plants in the last three months to power data center projects at and near the Tahoe Reno Industrial Center in Storey County. 
NV Energy told regulators rapid data center growth in the states has outpaced available regional generation capacity.
Tract Capital Management and its subsidiary Fleet Data Centers are pushing two behind-the-meter methane gas-powered plants, the Peru Ridge and South Valley power plants. 
If approved, the Peru Ridge and South Valley gas power plants would generate more than 360 megawatts of electricity using methane gas-fired engines, or enough power to serve about 396,000 homes, according to filings.
More high-emissions gas-fired power plants are likely being planned in northern Nevada with the massive expansion of a methane gas pipeline in the region. Switch, a major data center developer in Nevada, has also proposed a 510-megawatt gas-fired power plant. It would be one of a dozen new delivery points tied to a gas pipeline expansion planned by the Great Basin Gas Transmission Company. 



This article originally appeared in Grist, a nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to reporting on climate change.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Why Gov. Landry now calls data centers ‘digital factories’
description: Landry’s nomenclature preference follows President Donald Trump’s executive order that required the federal government to change all documented references of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence.”
text:
Entergy Louisiana CEO Phillip May, right, accepts a copy of an executive order Gov. Jeff Landry signed Thursday, June 25, 2026. The order calls aims to protect Louisiana utility customers from the high costs of electricity related to increased demand from data centers. Louisiana Economic Development Secretary Susan Bourgeois joined the governor for the signing ceremony at the State Capitol. (Photo by Greg LaRose/Louisiana Illuminator)Gov. Jeff Landry says his administration has started to refer to data centers as “digital factories” because he believes the new term aligns more closely with the facilities’ use.

“What started off as a data center, which used to be where you would just store things, has now become a digital factory. They make a widget,” Landry said at a turkey giveaway in St. Bernard Parish the day before Thanksgiving. 
“Those are digital, virtual products. They’re digital widgets,” he said.

The change in language comes as data centers and the artificial intelligence industry they support have become increasingly unpopular across the country. In elections held earlier this month, communities approved at least 44 ballot measures that restrict data centers and only one that favored their operations. 
Landry’s nomenclature preference also follows President Donald Trump’s executive order in September that required the federal government to change all documented references of artificial intelligence to “super intelligence.”

While Democrats in Congress gear up to push a national data center moratorium, Louisiana remains bullish on the projects. Landry recently placed new restrictions on tax breaks data centers receive, according to The Times-Picayune, but several new facilities are still in the works for the state. 

The “widgets” data centers create include applications for the platforms Claude and ChatGPT that make artificial intelligence accessible to everyday users as well as any programs individuals might design for themselves using AI, Landry said. 

“What happens inside those mass facilities is the creation and the ability for those processes to unfold. So to call them just simply a center is really disingenuous,” Landry said. “They actually make things. They create jobs and they create value.” 
“Without the digital factory, you wouldn’t be able to do any of those things,” the governor added.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT looks to next steps after ruling on ICE: ‘We’re not backing down’
description: Advocates and lawmakers said they are exploring the ways in which CT's existing laws and new proposals can offer residents protection.
text:
The news last week that four provisions of a law intended to regulate U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement action in Connecticut were blocked by a federal judge was “not a surprise” to some immigration advocates. But, they argued, it didn’t erase the impact of state officials’ willingness to take action in the face of President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.
“I think it underlines our state, and especially our legislators’ willingness to still pass policies that could be challenged because they were the right thing to do, and send a message to residents — immigrant and non-immigrant — that is is where Connecticut stands,” said Constanza Segovia, organizing director for Connecticut For All and co-founder of Hartford Deportation Defense.
She said when the laws were passed, including the provision that aimed to stop agents from wearing masks or other facial coverings when they interface with the public, advocates were aware there would be pushback.
But Segovia, other advocates and some lawmakers said they are exploring the ways in which the state’s existing laws and new proposals that might come up in the 2027 legislative session can offer residents protection in response to safety concerns related to federal immigration enforcement actions.
In the meantime, though, Carolina Bortolleto, an organizer with Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants, said the ruling still “leaves Connecticut less safe” because “no one wants masked agents running around neighborhoods.”
Senate Bill 397 was passed in 2026 and quickly was challenged by the U.S. Justice Department. The federal government called the law “blatantly unconstitutional,” saying that the state has no authority to tell federal agents what they can and cannot do. The government also argued that the law goes against the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution, which says that when state and federal laws clash, federal laws override those of the states. Judge Vernon Oliver agreed.
The state law, Oliver wrote, “plainly imposes conditions on how federal officers must conduct and present themselves during the course of their federal duties, and it subjects them to criminal and civil penalties if they do not abide by those state-imposed conditions.” 
“But the Supremacy Clause ensures that federal operations are not chilled by state prosecution and that federal officers are immune from state prosecution when acting within the scope of their federal authority,” he added.
ICE officials did not return a request for comment.
Yet even in the wake of the decision, some immigrant rights advocates like Bortolleto were sounding a note of optimism. A provision of the bill that requires ICE agents to have a warrant in locations like schools, hospitals and places of worship remains in effect.
“I think that’s really important because I think that section of the bill is what goes the longest way to making immigrant folks feel safer,” she said. Bortolleto said that she hoped that during the legislative 2027 session that begins in January, doctors’ offices could be added to the list of protected areas.
Advocates also say that agents have frequently been observed wearing masks in the state even when that portion of the law was in effect.  
Miguel Castro, a member of the Meriden Middletown Immigration Alliance and second vice chair of the Connecticut Hispanic Democratic Caucus, noted the injunction is temporary and he still has hope that Connecticut will ultimately succeed. 
“Our state still has an opportunity to go back to the court process and challenge this as it is sits today,” he said. “It is a responsibility of the state under the 10th Amendment of the Constitution, using the sovereignty of our state, that it is our duty and fiduciary responsibility to protect the members of our community, and that’s what we intend to do.”
Dealing with masked agents presents a variety of concerns, advocates say.
“It’s a traumatic experience to see someone or a group of people with masks on, and they are carrying weapons, and you are by yourself and you have nothing to defend yourself with,” said Juan Fonseca Tapia, a co-founder of Greater Danbury Unites for Immigrants. “All you’ve got is a phone.” That phone can be used to record agents and provide evidence of abuses, but when those agents are masked, advocates say it can complicate accountability. The bill also sought to make officers wear identification, a provision that was blocked by Friday’s ruling. 
Segovia said it would be a priority in 2027 to look for regulatory loopholes that disenfranchise immigrants and people of color, and make sure they are closed.
Supporting working-class immigrants means “supporting expansive healthcare policies that include everybody, regardless of immigration status,” Segovia said. Lawmakers should “make sure that nobody can touch our kids’ ability to go to public schools and public universities, regardless of their immigration status,” along with other key rights like renter protections.
Segovia’s group is among those pressing the Lamont administration to put $10 million toward legal aid and emergency cash assistance for immigrants impacted by ICE enforcement. 
House Speaker Matt Ritter, D-Hartford said that he is interested in having that discussion in the new year. Ritter said the attempt to regulate ICE activity was worth pursuing, but ultimately there are “just limits to what the states can do.” He said it’s time for the Democratic majority in Washington to step up.
“It’s not me throwing my hands up in the air saying, ‘we’re going to give up.’ We’re going to do everything we can to be helpful,” he added. “But there’s 259 Democrats in the House and 56 in the Senate, and if they need help learning how to pass bills I’m glad to go down there and try to help them.”
Rep. Steven Stafstrom, D-Bridgeport, a key backer of Connecticut’s law as co-chair of the legislature’s Judiciary Committee, said he was disappointed with the ruling. But “we’re not backing down,” he said. 
Stafstrom said there are still legal remedies to holding agents accountable for abuse of use of force.
“One of the things that was blocked was having the inspector general do investigations into abuse of use of force, but just because that piece was inexplicably blocked, doesn’t mean Connecticut won’t continue to enforce state laws, it will just fall to individual states attorneys for the judicial districts to do that,” he said.

name: Mississippi Today
title: ‘Mississippi Snakes,’ decades in the making, offers a close look at these spellbinding reptiles
description: Authors Terry Vandeventer and Robert Young with their book, Mississippi Snakes, in September at the Mississippi Book Festival in Jackson.
text:
Authors Terry Vandeventer and Robert Young set out to unravel perhaps the most complex relationship between man and animal: that between man and snake.
“Few people have a take ‘em or leave ’em attitude when it comes to their feelings regarding snakes,” the introduction to their book “Mississippi Snakes” reads. “Whatever feelings one may harbor about snakes, these emotions are often deep-rooted and intense.” 
Some people might consider these remarks understatements, which underscores the challenge Vandeventer and Young undertook in writing a book for “the masses” that offers a doorway to a greater understanding and humane treatment of these complex, fascinating creatures. 
The result is 400 pages of detailed, informed observation and analysis set out in a fluent, familiar style laced with wry humor and play. The book is superbly illustrated with photographs, drawings, and maps, and provides readers with authoritative, up-to-date information for the more than 50 kinds of snakes that make their home in the Magnolia State. 
The cover of “Mississippi Snakes.” Credit: University Press of Mississippi
What’s more is “Mississippi Snakes” offers a fascinating, kaleidoscopic perspective on the people and culture of Mississippi from a snake’s-eye view, as it were. During over 30 years of field work, the authors met Mississippians of all stripes, “anglers, hunters, amateur and professional naturalists, farmers, country-store owners, foresters, and old bluesmen sitting on Delta porches,” who added their own beliefs and stories to the cultural narrative of snakes. This narrative is further enriched by snakes in story, song and notions derived from both the Old World and the New.
A primary emphasis of “Mississippi Snakes” is on the identification and natural history of Mississippi snakes. Each profile of the over 50 species and sub-species of snakes in the state provides distinguishing characteristics (as well as common variants), a natural history that includes common names and their origins, habitat, distribution (with detailed state maps for each species), temperament, behavior, reproduction and whether the species is venomous or not. 
The identification of venomous snakes and the rare instances of snakebites are treated in separate sections, both of which implore the casual naturalist, hunter or fisherman to leave snakes alone. The authors point out that many snakebites are due to someone trying to kill or capture a snake, venomous or not. Though full of information, the species descriptions are shorn of the technical language and nuances of scholarly publications to make identifying snakes in the field fast and effortless. 
This reader-friendly style permeates the entire book and is a joy to read. As biologist William Lamar observes in his eloquent preface, Mississippi is “nothing if not a land of stories.” 
He continues, “The authors share with us the incomparable folklore surrounding its snakes, some of it partly based on fact or misunderstanding, with a tranche — like so much gossip — lodged firmly in the realm of fantasy.” 
In the Choctaw language, “‘sinti means ‘snake,’ while ‘sintollo’ is the word for ‘beloved snake’ and refers to all rattlesnakes,” the authors write to illustrate the differing perspective Native Americans had on the natural world. 
A cottonmouth figures prominently in “True Evil,” a novel by Mississippi author Greg Iles, and Faulkner describes his protagonist stepping on two “moccasins” while rescuing people from rooftops during the Great Mississippi Flood of 1927. Snakes often find their way into Mississippi blues, “literally or metaphorically,” among lyrics that “reflect love lost, rejection, unfaithfulness, and as is typical of most blues songs, a touch of risqué innuendo.” The authors offer samples in “Crawling King Snake,” “Cottonmouth” and “Black Snake Moan.” 
Snakes appear in the names of places throughout the state, such as the two Rattlesnake Creeks, one in Lauderdale County and another in Carroll County. The practice of snake handling receives a thorough, enlightening examination, and the Lake Washington “Snake Grabbin’ Rodeo,” during which harmless water snakes are caught and released, receives a nod.
“Mississippi Snakes” reveals this diligence in every sentence. The scholarship behind this work is impeccable, the research comprehensive and thorough. “Mississippi Snakes” provides both professionals and the casual outdoorsman or backyard naturalist a concise, accurate field guide, and we have every reason to believe that the authors’ hopes of the book finding its way “into the college classroom as a definitive reference on Mississippi snakes” will be realized in short order. 
As for the authors’ other “grand dream,” that the book will “perhaps strike a spark in the curious mind of some youngster who will hopefully, someday, grow up to write an even better book,” that certainly might happen, but a better book than “Mississippi Snakes” will be a long time coming.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: A Black Friday dispatch from your correspondent in the retail shopping epicenter of Kansas
description: Welcome to Black Friday, the American retail shopping holiday defined by percentages.  During the final hours that Kansas stores were open before Friday’s annual merchandise onslaught, I visited Town Center Plaza, the outdoor mall in Leawood. The stores were doing their final transactions Wednesday — taupe sweatpants, peppermint hand lotion, dainty bracelets[...]
text:
Black Friday shopping can be broken down to a brutal contest of percentages, writes our columnist. (Photo illustration by Eric Thomas for Kansas Reflector)Welcome to Black Friday, the American retail shopping holiday defined by percentages. 
During the final hours that Kansas stores were open before Friday’s annual merchandise onslaught, I visited Town Center Plaza, the outdoor mall in Leawood. The stores were doing their final transactions Wednesday — taupe sweatpants, peppermint hand lotion, dainty bracelets, AI glasses — before opening early the day after Thanksgiving. 
Along with shopping areas in Overland Park, Prairie Village and Olathe, Town Center Plaza helps cement Johnson County’s reputation as the retail hub of Kansas. If you can’t find it in a Johnson County store on Black Friday, your best bet will be online. 
If possible, Town Center Plaza provides an even more exotic melange of stores than the 1980s malls of my childhood. In one short walk, I passed an aerial arts space where you can perform by hanging from the ceiling using silks; a golf simulator experience; an anime store with figurines, games and trading cards; and a Barnes & Noble. There are stores dedicated to candles, cookware, lingerie, mattresses and sportswear. 
Even more than election day, Black Friday at Town Center Plaza and across America demands your calculator and a mastery of statistics. In almost every store Wednesday, the deals were announced in percentages.
Pottery Barn Kids arranged a table of Hanukkah decor for 40% off. 
Banana Republic was sure to remind shoppers that their 40% off “includes cashmere.”
At LaserAway, a sign advertised a whopping “75% off Laser Hair removal.”
Some deals came with caveats. 
Disingenuously, Sunglass Hut bragged about “30% off entire store” before adding “Brand exclusions apply.”
Meanwhile, at Macy’s, the shopping area’s only department store, percentage discounts dotted nearly every countertop or shelf holding merchandise: “60 percent off” chocolates and “30 percent off” jackets and “70 percent off” Christmas tree ornaments. Macy’s red-and-black signage (so intense!) perched on clothing racks, resembling weathervanes fastened to Kansas barns and forever interrupting sightlines in the store. 
Also at Macy’s, I found a predictable element of any department store visit: the silver-haired husband waiting for his wife. 
This particular gentleman was playing the part almost too on-the-nose. He was sitting, not in a chair, but on a sleek modular white display case, surrounded by posh DKNY purses that were for sale. 
His cellphone speaker blared a parade of short-form videos at maximum volume. He hunched over it, oblivious to the shoppers around him. In a mash, he held his wife’s coat, a shopping bag and one of his wife’s potential buys. 
After 20 minutes of circling the store, I returned to find him still on display, still on his phone and still crumpling — almost beyond recognition — everything he was holding. 
It was unclear if he had been discounted along with the purses. 
At most stores, Black Friday discounts had already started Wednesday or even Tuesday. Alo, the high-end store for swanky athleisure wear, didn’t have a single discount sign Wednesday. However, when I asked an employee, she said everything had already been discounted at the same price that would be offered Friday and through the weekend. 
Even with early sales like these at many stores, Town Center was sedate Wednesday. Some stores had retractable crowd control stanchions set up, but during my visits to more than 20 stores, I only saw one person waiting in line at a cash register.
The deals were there. The shoppers were not. 
The shopping area had the atmosphere of a party that technically had started, but not actually. All of the cocktails and hors d’oeuvres were sitting out and waiting for guests. The music was playing. The host was ready. But really no one had arrived. 
Maybe more than the discounts, shoppers enjoy the sport of jostling with others to snag the deal in the peak action of Friday morning. Maybe people were finishing their last hours of the work week on Wednesday afternoon rather than shopping. Or, perhaps it’s the Black Friday shoulder-to-shoulder competition of getting the last available red flannel button down (“size extra small, if you have it”) before your rival shopper.
Or, less likely, shoppers might enjoy using their vacation day on Friday to browse a department store at 6 a.m. (If so, good news: Macy’s opens four hours early and closes an hour late for Black Friday.)
As I walked through stores at Town Center Plaza, I wondered at the intricate piles of clothing. At the Buckle, for instance, one modest circular table offered 20 towers — hats, t-shirts and pants — with two stacks cantilevered over the edge. No need to go searching for a metaphor for the US economy.
Set against the white walls, Black Friday will again be a retail triumph of America’s glorious and gluttonous sartorial architecture.
At the Gap, jeans posed in every possible configuration. Responsibly stacked and folded. Fastened by clips. Sorted into cubbies. Looped on hooks. Suspended by belt loops. Most extravagantly, hanging upside down and rolled up from the cuff. 
Each store also had its seductive mannequins and models ready for the holiday. Photographs of each brand’s models decorated the walls above the clothing racks and in the front display windows. At the Gap, a phalanx of mannequins — each with their own multi-layered outfit — greeted shoppers seductively at the door. 
Seductive seems the right word to me here in two ways — first, because of the models’ coy and sultry looks, but also for the way the models and mannequins seduced us normal-shaped shoppers. “Buy this,” they suggest, “because it’s easy to look this great.” 
Like the stores themselves, the sidewalks of the outdoor mall were mostly empty. Shoppers sprinted through the cold directly to their intended store and then right back to their preheated SUVs. In one case, I heard a clutch of three women decide, as they set off for their car, that it was much easier to drive to their next store. 
I overheard their next destination. It was a 30-second walk away.
At the other end of the parking lot, I encountered a mother and daughter leaving their car for Blue Chip Cookies & Ice Cream. The mom, with a very particular Johnson County intensity, wore a sweatshirt with foot-high lettering on the front, proclaiming, “JOY.” Her daughter, scowling for a moment, struggled to keep up.
Yet, as she fast-walked ahead of her daughter, she hectored her: “Hurry up! Why are you taking so long?” 
With that, I wish you a joyous Black Friday indeed.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Nearly every candidate who ran on childcare won. Now comes the hard part.
description: This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th. Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. Almost every Democrat who flipped a Republican seat in the midterms had the same thing on their platform: childcare. A decade ago, a plan for childcare was nowhere to be found […]
text:
The Downtown Children's Center in St. Louis. (Photo by Rebecca Rivas/Missouri Independent.) 
This story was originally reported by Chabeli Carrazana of The 19th.  Meet Chabeli and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
Almost every Democrat who flipped a Republican seat in the midterms had the same thing on their platform: childcare.
A decade ago, a plan for childcare was nowhere to be found on political priority lists. Now, it’s almost a requirement for Democrats, and even some Republicans, running for office. In contested seats this midterm elections, Republicans offered solutions like a tax credit for childcare expenses or incentivizing companies to offer childcare.
Democrats went even further on the issue than they ever have, with breakout candidates including Michigan Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed and Colorado Rep.-elect Melat Kiros calling for universal childcare, a policy seen as radical until 2025, the year it became reality in New Mexico and a central plank in the platform of New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
Childcare was often relegated to the side because it affected a small percentage of the electorate. But this cycle, it was folded into overall affordability, said Elliot Haspel, a national child care expert who has written two books on the subject.
“If you make it this avatar of how unaffordable family life has become in America, then all of a sudden it’s got an enormous amount of narrative power,” Haspel said.
Democrat Lindsay James, who flipped a Republican House seat to become one of more than a dozen freshman mothers joining the House this upcoming Congress, said childcare came up again and again in rural Iowa, where options are limited. Her family spent a year on a waiting list to get into a center.
“Everywhere I go, people are talking about the cost-of-living crisis in this district,” James said. “And it comes in the form of the cost of groceries, gasoline, utility bills, the cost of health insurance, the cost of childcare.”
In almost every state, childcare costs top family budgets alongside rent and mortgage. In some families, childcare is the top expense. In a September poll from The 19th and YouGov, 52 percent of Americans said they wanted the government to spend more on childcare.
For many years, though, the issue was viewed as something the government should not take on for middle- and even higher-income families. In 1971, when President Richard Nixon vetoed a bipartisan bill that would have created a national childcare system, he argued the government’s involvement should be kept to “an absolute minimum.” And that’s how it went for 50 years, until COVID-19 reshaped the nation’s understanding of the role childcare plays in helping working parents stay in the labor force. State and local governments have shown that we can go further, and voters have shown they want more of it.
“Childcare is no longer seen as a personal problem that women have to fix, but an economic one that the nation needs to solve. Childcare is the linchpin of affordability,” said Reshma Saujani, the founder and CEO of Moms First, an organization pushing for affordable care and other family policies. “It’s also not an issue that’s on page 15 of a candidate’s platform. It’s the issue they’re getting elected on.”
Now, there’s a solid chance substantial childcare legislation could pass at every level of government. Here’s what we could see in the next two years.
 Childcare at the federal level

U.S. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., spoke to advocates outside the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, Dec. 6, 2023, about $16 billion in childcare funding requested by the Biden administration. (Samantha Dietel/States Newsroom)
After the election, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat from New York expected to be the next speaker of the House, said the top issues voters want Congress to confront are costs, corruption and care. “That’s healthcare, childcare and elder care,” he said. Jeffries will likely be joined by Rep. Katherine Clark, who has been a leading voice on childcare in the House for years. Now, she’s poised to become the first woman House majority leader, which means “she will have so much influence in setting the agenda,” Haspel said.
On the Senate side, Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has laid out the five areas Democrats want to go after now that they have a majority in the chamber: “healthcare, electric costs, groceries related to the tariffs, and how much you pay for childcare and housing.” Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Patty Murray, who have been key authors of major childcare proposals for years, will also have new seats of power. In the next Congress, Warren will be the chair of the Senate Banking Committee and Murray will take over as chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee.
In a speech Tuesday, Warren made it clear that she intends to advance childcare policy she’s been pushing for years. Democrats can move forward on their priorities through a reconciliation package that won’t require a single Republican vote, she noted. Potential avenues they could pursue: “reverse the healthcare cuts the Republicans put in place, expand healthcare coverage, and fund universal childcare — all with a 51-vote majority in the Senate,” she said.
Longtime childcare candidates will also no longer be among the few in their respective chambers. During the campaign cycle, six of the eight Democrats who flipped Senate seats had childcare plans in their platforms (Maine’s Troy Jackson, Ohio’s Sherrod Brown, South Carolina’s Annie Andrews, Texas’ James Talarico, Iowa’s Josh Turek, and North Carolina’s Roy Cooper). In the House, 44 Democrats flipped Republican seats so far and about half of them had childcare proposals, including Pennsylvania’s Bob Brooks and Michigan’s Christina Hines, who both advocated for universal pre-K.
It’s not a question now of whether childcare will come up at the federal level, but how.
If the next Congress decides to go for a more modest childcare proposal, it could look like a federal version of what Jackson proposed earlier this year when he was running for governor of Maine before switching to a Senate campaign. Jackson offered a plan that would make childcare free for families earning up to 125 percent of the state median income, or about $145,000 annually for a family of four.
Or it could look like what Texas’ Talarico suggested in his campaign: capping tuition for 3- and 4-year-olds in pre-K at 7 percent of the family’s total income, which is what the Department of Health and Human Services has set as the benchmark for affordability. Talarico also wants to boost funding for Head Start and the Child Care and Development Block Grant, the two federal programs that subsidize care for the nation’s poorest children. Talarico also proposed offering childcare facilities federal tax breaks and companies that support childcare a tax credit.
Because overriding a veto takes two-thirds of each chamber, Democrats have to consider how President Donald Trump may respond to a bill that reaches his desk. The president said during an Easter lunch reception at the White House that “the United States can’t take care of day care. That has to be up to a state.”
Haspel believes Democrats have a path forward with a “skinny” reconciliation package that is just focused on care priorities such as passing some form of federal paid parental leave, improving the child tax credit and perhaps doubling or tripling the funding in the childcare block grant so more families can access subsidized care. Something like that would mean the president would have to “think really hard about vetoing,” Haspel said.
Saujani hopes politicians push for something even more ambitious than they did last time Democrats tried to expand childcare through budget reconciliation. Under President Joe Biden, a package called Build Back Better that would have created a universal pre-K program never passed the Senate.
“We need to think even bigger than we did with Build Back Better. Don’t just dust off Biden’s plan and run it back. The opportunity here is to be bolder and more ambitious about what families actually need,” Saujani said.
If the next Congress goes more ambitious, it could lean into the universal childcare ideas that candidates like El-Sayed talked about extensively on the campaign trail. In an interview with “60 Minutes,” El-Sayed argued that the way to address the issue of falling birthrates and encourage people to have children is for the government to be an active player in lowering costs for families.
“You need to be invested,” he told “60 Minutes.” “That means you have to address the rising cost of having kids. So if your argument is that we can’t have childcare, we can’t have healthcare, we can’t subsidize housing, we can’t do these things, do not be surprised when all of a sudden we age past the point at which we are viable.”
 Childcare at the state and local level

As federal aid ran out, advocates called on lawmakers to fund the Child Care Counts program using state dollars in Wisconsin. (Baylor Spears | Wisconsin Examiner)
In state gubernatorial races, five Democrats flipped Republican seats, and all five had at least one childcare proposal on their platforms: Nevada’s Aaron Ford, Texas’ Gina Hinojosa, Georgia’s Keisha Lance Bottoms, Iowa’s Rob Sand and Ohio’s Amy Acton. In gubernatorial races overall, a majority of candidates who had some form of childcare proposal on their platform won, including all six candidates (all Democrats) who proposed universal childcare, according to an analysis by Bank Street College of Education.
In some states, governorships and legislative control also flipped, setting up Democrats to control the legislative and executive branches and giving candidates who support broader childcare proposals an opportunity to make inroads.
Experts are closely watching Wisconsin, Minnesota and Michigan, three states that now have a Democratic trifecta and that have been leaders in childcare policy for years. Wisconsin, in particular, may be interesting because there was a prolonged fight over childcare funding there between outgoing Democratic Gov. Tony Evers and the Republican-controlled legislature in recent years. Evers wanted to expand state funding significantly but ultimately had to reach a compromise with the state legislature for a smaller amount.
Now, the legislature is set to be under control of Democrats and David Crowley, who Evers endorsed, will take over as governor. Childcare policy expert Julie Kashen called Crowley a childcare “champion.” On the campaign trail, Crowley proposed a system under which all kids under the age of 5 have a spot in the state’s childcare subsidy program, and any costs not covered by the subsidy are capped at 7 percent of the family’s income.
“The new trifecta is really going to make a difference there,” Kashen said.
If Wisconsin moves to expand childcare, that could produce momentum in neighboring Minnesota and Michigan, states that have both already made substantial upgrades to their childcare systems to try to bring down costs.
“Do the Midwest states start competing for some form of universal childcare?” Haspel said, or does something similar happen in the West, where Nevada and Arizona now have Democratic trifectas near New Mexico? Both, he thinks, are possibilities.
Another open question now is whether any cities will follow in the model Mamdani created in New York. Los Angeles and Washington, D.C., both elected new democratic socialist mayors who have stated commitments to improving childcare. In L.A., Mayor-elect Nithya Raman wants to address the problem by improving supply, making it easier to open a center or expand an existing one.
In D.C., Mayor-elect Janeese Lewis George is focused on lowering costs. Her proposal includes capping all childcare payments at 7 percent of family income — families earning less than $100,000 a year would pay no more than $600 a month in childcare. Lewis George’s proposal was one of the most comprehensive this cycle, with ideas around how to boost more childcare supply, such as placing programs in existing public schools, and pushing to increase provider pay to be on par with public school teachers.
In crafting her plan, Lewis George told The Washington Post she took lessons from what New Mexico did. And during her victory speech last week, she called the issue out again as a top priority: “We will make childcare affordable and within reach,” she said.
Plans like Lewis George’s are bold, Saujani said — a sign that childcare has finally risen to the top of the priority list.
“The Overton window is opening, and we’re finally seeing politicians willing to imagine something bigger,” she said. “We shouldn’t be begging for scraps or settling for incremental improvements. Let’s make childcare free. Let’s have some imagination again.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Looking for a Christmas tree? Here’s what’s grown in Georgia, including some sustainable options.
description: The holiday season is upon us, which means that — for all who celebrate — it’s time to start looking for a Christmas tree. Chuck Berry, the owner of Covington-based Berry’s Tree Farm and the president of the Georgia Christmas Tree Association, said most farmers sell the majority of their supply in the five days […]
text:
Cypress, pine and fir trees are for sale at Berry’s Tree Farm, a Christmas tree farm based in Covington, Georgia. Photo courtesy of Chuck Berry.The holiday season is upon us, which means that — for all who celebrate — it’s time to start looking for a Christmas tree.
Chuck Berry, the owner of Covington-based Berry’s Tree Farm and the president of the Georgia Christmas Tree Association, said most farmers sell the majority of their supply in the five days after Thanksgiving.
“It’s a pretty unique operation because it comes real quick and it also goes real quick,” he said.
Georgia has nearly 100 farmers who grow Christmas trees in-state, according to the Georgia Department of Agriculture, which publishes an annual map of Christmas tree farms across the state.
“Majority of what’s grown now in Georgia is in the cypress family,” Berry said. “But there are some farms that also offer cedar and pine. And then a lot of farms also bring in Fraser fir from North Carolina.”
Mark Czarnota, an associate professor of horticulture at the University of Georgia, said a wide variety of Christmas trees are grown in Georgia, such as Leyland cypress, Arizona cypress and red cedar trees. Those species, he said, can be grown just about anywhere around the state, and are fairly hardy and drought tolerant.
El Niño could mean snow for Georgia this winter, but it’s not a sure thing

But other types of trees, including Fraser firs and white pine trees, need a significant level of elevation to be able to grow. The ones that are grown in Georgia are mostly found in the state’s northern counties.
“You need to get above 1,000 feet above sea level to really have those trees perform okay,” he said. 
In recent years, Czarnota also said he has noticed an increase in people looking for more environmentally friendly ways to deck their halls for the holidays.  
“I see a lot of movement towards people purchasing live plant material that they can plant in their yard when they’re done with it,” he said.
Some Georgia farmers have also found creative ways to bring a tree into their home without having to cut one down or buy an artificial one: Christmas tree rentals.
Elizabeth Beak, the owner of Joy To The Earth Tree Farm, has allowed Georgians in the Atlanta area to “foster” tree saplings for the holiday season since 2022, providing about 50 families the opportunity to have a live tree in their house without chopping one down.
Unlike other types of live Christmas trees, she said, families don’t need to put their tree in the trash after the holidays or have a yard to plant a potted tree in.
“The tree instead comes back to the farm,” she said. “It continues to grow. It provides habitat throughout the year out at the farm.” 
A rented Christmas tree from Joy To The Earth Tree Farm is brought inside and decorated for the holidays. Photo courtesy of Elizabeth Beak.
Several families, she added, have fostered the same tree for several years in a row. This year, the farm is not offering rentals, but will instead be planting the first cohort of trees in the ground for the first time, with some trees going in the yards of their foster families and others to be planted in parks around Atlanta.
The rental program will return next year with a new set of saplings, Beak said.
The process of renting a tree and returning it to the outdoors, she added, provides benefits that go beyond just the holiday season.
“They can provide habitat for our wildlife,” she said. “They can help our soils. They can help with flooding. They can help with fresh air. They can beautify just all sorts of different things.”
Still, she said, her family has held on to their artificial tree that they purchased before starting the farm. They display it alongside a live tree each year, she said, mostly because it seems more wasteful to throw it away. If she had the choice now, she said she would prefer a tree rental.
“A lot of [artificial trees] are made far, far away in a different country, they’re using a lot of plastic and things like that,” she said. “And plus, you have to store them.”
But Czarnota, the UGA horticulture professor, said tree shoppers shouldn’t worry too much about the environmental impact of cutting down Christmas trees from a farm.
“You’ve got to remember the tree is replanted,” he said, adding that many communities have programs to turn Christmas trees into mulch to use around people’s gardens. 
Because Christmas trees are an industry, buying a real tree also helps support Georgia farmers, Czarnota said. 
“It’s not like you’re going through a clear cut in the forest and putting in a parking lot or a development,” he said. “Usually the land’s reused multiple times for tree plants.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: CT has built something healthcare can’t afford to waste
description: Connecticut has an opportunity to turn connected health information into more coordinated care and healthier communities.
text:
Connecticut has spent the past several years building the connections needed to make health information sharing a reality across the state. Now comes the more important work: putting that information to use in ways that change lives.
As healthcare providers face growing demands to address disparities and do more with limited resources, timely access to reliable health information has never mattered more.

Michelle Puhlick

As I step into the role of interim executive director of the Health Information Alliance, Inc. (HIA), I see an opportunity to build on the foundation we’ve established through Connie, Connecticut’s statewide Health Information Exchange, and turn connected data into more informed decisions and better health outcomes. We’ve built the infrastructure. Now, we’re focused on what it can make possible.
I’ve been part of Connie’s journey since before it launched in 2021, helping establish the operational foundation and connections for statewide information sharing. This transition is built on years of collaboration and a shared vision for what Connie can become. We’re now entering the phase where that groundwork starts to pay off, as we put the data to work for patients and providers in even more meaningful ways, and I’m committed to carrying that mission forward with energy and focus.
Connie now connects more than 4,000 provider locations across Connecticut, helping healthcare providers, payers and public health entities securely share information that supports coordinated, high-quality care. We’ve expanded participation among skilled nursing facilities and pharmacies, connected our first behavioral health electronic medical record systems and brought our first emergency medical services provider onto the network.
These milestones give care teams more opportunities to see the bigger picture and make informed decisions. They also reflect our participants’ trust in Connie and Connecticut’s collective commitment to improving care.
 Additionally, we’re:
 • Demonstrating Connecticut’s leadership in addressing health information exchange challenges nationwide, with Connie among just nine organizations selected nationally for a pilot grant to advance electronic consent management for patients receiving behavioral health care.
 • Helping providers improve race, ethnicity and language data, enabling more complete, accurate information to inform efforts to make healthcare more equitable.
 • Developing tools that give home and community-based services providers access to timely health information to support more coordinated, whole-person care.
These accomplishments give us a strong foundation, but I believe our greatest opportunity lies ahead. Our next phase is about putting the information and infrastructure we’ve built to work in more meaningful ways.
That means using data to help identify patients who may benefit from earlier intervention, strengthening public health response and supporting more equitable outcomes across Connecticut. It also means continuing to improve data quality and expand the network while ensuring the organizations that depend on Connie can realize its full value.
Rural health will be an important focus. Through Connecticut’s Rural Health Transformation Program, we’re working on initiatives to help providers identify rural patients at risk of avoidable hospitalizations and unnecessary emergency department visits. Better information and earlier insights give care teams more opportunities to intervene before a health concern becomes a crisis.
We’re pursuing this work in partnership with the providers, state agencies and community organizations that understand Connecticut’s needs firsthand. Technology alone cannot solve the challenges facing healthcare. Progress depends on listening to providers and patients and acting on what they tell us as we build practical solutions together. That includes guidance from our Clinical Advisory Council, Patient and Family Advisory Council and the feedback we gather at community events across the state.
My commitment is to carry forward Connie’s mission while continually asking how we can do more with the foundation we’ve established. Our leadership team and staff remain focused on supporting our participants and state partners, and the services and relationships people rely on will continue. 
What will evolve is how we use our capabilities to create even greater value for the people and communities we serve.
I’m proud of what we’ve built so far, but I’m even more energized by what comes next. Connecticut has an opportunity to turn connected health information into more coordinated care and healthier communities. With our partners, we intend to help make that opportunity a reality.
Michelle Puhlick is interim executive director and COO of the Health Information Alliance, Inc., the operating entity charged with running Connecticut’s Health Information Exchange, Connie.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Is the ‘Connecticut Option’ a good one?
description: Gov. Ned Lamont wants a state-designed health insurance model that will lover costs. Will it work?
text:
Rising health insurance premiums remain a growing concern for Connecticut households. For 2027, average increases of 11.3% and 15.1% have been approved for individual and small-group health insurance plans, respectively. 
Connecticut needs policies that make health insurance and healthcare services more affordable, especially for people living with chronic diseases.
The problem of high healthcare costs in Connecticut is not new. Historically, healthcare costs have gone up faster than household income in Connecticut. A 20-year comparison of average healthcare cost increases and median household income growth shows a 2.8-percentage-point difference: 4.8% compared with 2%. This means healthcare costs increased more than twice as much as household income. 
Health insurance premiums are rising for several reasons. Medical services and prescription drugs are becoming more expensive, and people are using more healthcare services. Insurance companies are also paying more for medical claims than they expected. Changes in federal financial help for people buying health insurance can also affect premiums.
Many Connecticut residents are already struggling with healthcare costs. A 2025 survey of over 1,400 adults found that about 64% had trouble affording healthcare during the previous year. Also, 61% reported delaying or going without healthcare because of cost. So, what does this mean for people living with chronic conditions?
Chronic conditions often require ongoing care. People living with diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, or chronic kidney disease may need regular visits with healthcare providers, lab tests and medicines to manage their conditions and prevent serious health problems. Missing or delaying these services can make their conditions worse and may even put their lives at risk. For these individuals, high insurance premiums add to the financial burden of paying for medicines, frequent visits with healthcare providers, and medical equipment they may need. Moreover, paying for healthcare while also meeting basic needs, such as food, housing, and family expenses, can make life more difficult.
Although the Connecticut Insurance Department has made efforts to reduce the yearly premium increases requested by insurance companies, there’s still more to do. The state must put in place policies to ensure that people with chronic conditions can get the medicines, medical equipment, and follow-up care they need without having to pay more than they can afford.
Gov. Ned Lamont has proposed the “Connecticut option” as a possible solution to high healthcare costs in the state. This would be a state-designed model managed by private insurance companies. It would include a network of healthcare providers offering quality care at lower costs, which people would be encouraged to use. The Office of Policy and Management has been directed to study whether the plan could work under Public Act 26-68, and the governor plans to propose legislation in 2027.
Organizations such as the Connecticut Hospital Association have raised concerns about the Connecticut option. They worry that the plan could limit patients’ choices of healthcare providers and lead to higher healthcare costs. These concerns are especially important for people living with chronic diseases, who may have regular healthcare providers familiar with their conditions and treatment needs.
As the state studies whether the Connecticut Option could work, officials should consider these concerns and work toward a plan that lowers healthcare costs without limiting patients’ access to healthcare providers. Legislators should also consider these concerns when reviewing the proposed plan.
Dorothy Wilson is a graduate student at the Elisabeth DeLuca School of Nursing, University of Connecticut.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Are Fairfield teenagers getting the mental health care they need?
description: Having mental health resources does not automatically mean every teenager knows about them, feels comfortable using them, or can access the right care.
text:
Growing up in Fairfield, I saw how much mental health can affect a person, a family, and an entire community. I had multiple friends who struggled with their mental health, and some died by suicide. I have also struggled with my own mental health.
These experiences have shown me how important it is for people to feel comfortable asking for help and know where to find it. Fairfield has brought people together to discuss mental health, especially after difficult experiences and losses. These conversations are important, but we also need to make sure teenagers know how to find support. Having resources available is one thing. Knowing how to access them and feeling comfortable using them are different things.
Fairfield should make it easier for teenagers to understand their mental health options and access support without feeling embarrassed or unsure where to begin.
When I have needed mental-health support, I have struggled to find a therapist in Fairfield who was the right fit, including someone who offered talk therapy or cognitive behavioral therapy. I have ended up looking in nearby towns, including Westport, Norwalk, and New Milford. My experience does not mean Fairfield lacks mental-health providers, but it has made me question how easy it is to find the right support when someone needs it. 
 For teenagers, this process can feel even more overwhelming. They might not know which services are available, how to contact a provider, whether their family can afford treatment, or what information will remain private. Some may fear judgment from friends, while others may not realize they need help. Parents may also struggle to know where to start. When someone is already having a difficult time, figuring out how to get support should not become another challenge. 
Research supports these concerns. A 2021 review by Jerica Radez and colleagues found that stigma, embarrassment, confidentiality concerns, costs, transportation, and limited knowledge can affect whether young people seek mental-health care. A 2022 study by Alice Villatoro and colleagues also found differences between how adolescents approach mental-health help for themselves and how they recommend it to peers. Encouraging a friend to seek help may feel easier than asking for it personally.
Schools can be part of the solution. Research by Mylien Duong and colleagues found that school-based mental-health services were used by about 7% of youth in the general population and about 22% of youth with elevated symptoms or diagnoses. Schools cannot solve every mental-health problem, but they can help students understand what support exists and how to take the next step. Students should not have to search through multiple websites or depend on word of mouth to learn where to turn.
Fairfield Public Schools already share social-emotional learning resources, and the town has a Collaborative for Youth Mental Health. These are important starting points. Instead of automatically creating more programs, Fairfield should examine whether teenagers and families can easily find and use the resources already available.
 Fairfield Public Schools, town officials, families, and local mental-health organizations should work together on three steps. First, they should create one clear, regularly updated guide to local resources, including how to make appointments, available cost and insurance information, and where to ask about confidentiality. Second, schools should regularly discuss mental health in age-appropriate ways and explain how students can seek support. Third, students should have a way to share their concerns anonymously so community leaders can better understand what prevents them from getting help. 
 These efforts should be evaluated over the next school year. Schools could ask students whether they know where to find support before and after these changes. This would help show whether the information is reaching young people instead of assuming that making resources available means students are using them. Listening directly to students would also help Fairfield understand which changes would be most useful. 
 Some may argue that Fairfield already has mental-health resources and community programs. That is a fair point. However, having resources does not automatically mean every teenager knows about them, feels comfortable using them, or can access the right care. Improving access does not mean ignoring what Fairfield already does. It means building on existing efforts and identifying what still gets in the way of young people. 
 Mental health should not become a community conversation only after a tragedy. Teenagers deserve to know where to turn before they reach a crisis point. Fairfield can build on the conversations already happening and make support easier to find and use. Sometimes, helping someone starts with making sure they know help is available and that they do not have to figure everything out alone. 
Maddie Reed of Fairfield is a fourth-year Human Services major at Elon University interested in youth well-being, mental health, and improving access to support for adolescents.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Are you shopping as you read this? Black Friday moves to different days, ways to buy
description: Black Friday might not be the “shopping extravaganza” it once was, but that doesn't mean people won't be spending for the holidays like always -- and then some, with total sales expected to top $1 trillion this year nationwide.
text:
Shoppers will be spending for the holidays, but the traditional Black Friday scrums won't be as much a part of the season, which has stretched out over a longer period and moved to online and other platforms. (Photo by Getty Images)Black Friday might not be the “shopping extravaganza” it once was, but that doesn’t mean people won’t be spending for the holidays like always — and then some, with total sales expected to top $1 trillion this year.
The National Retail Federation predicted in October that retail sales during the November and December holiday season will grow 4.2% more than the 2025 rates. Total spending is set to hit $1.013 trillion compared to last year’s $972 billion.
But with additional holidays like Small Business Saturday and Cyber Monday, and weeklong deals at online shopping platforms like Amazon, the sales have moved past the exclusivity of a single day as the years go on, economic experts say.
University of Maryland marketing professor Jie Zhang said retailers have begun introducing sales earlier each year. Tariffs, rising gas prices and inflation continue to drive up the cost of living, making consumers less willing to buy and retailers less willing to discount.
Zhang, who specialized in retail management, said this year’s average discounts are projected to be similar to last year’s, which were already scaled back after hits to the nation’s economy.
“[Retailers] just simply could not afford to offer really deep discounts anymore because many of them absorbed a substantial part of tariffs … unfortunately, this year they’re not seeing much relief,” she said. “Because of that … some retailers might feel the pressure to actually raise prices and then offer discounts. The prices consumers end up paying, even with the discounts, are certainly higher than they have ever been.”
While the NRF is predicting sales will increase this holiday season, consumers shouldn’t take the growth rate at face value, said Henry Boyd, a clinical marketing professor at the University of Maryland who has a focus in consumer spending. The higher totals don’t factor in higher prices and costs of goods due to inflation and tariffs.
“You’re going to probably buy less stuff, but the stuff you buy is more expensive,” Boyd said in an interview last week.
The Maryland Retailers Alliance noted in a November press release that the outcome for Maryland retailers might be more of a mixed bag. According to the organization’s annual member survey, about 64% of participating businesses experienced lower sales in September and October compared to the previous year. The other 36% said they expect their sales to decline this holiday season.
Alliance President Cailey Locklair said these numbers could largely be influenced by the small businesses that make up a sizable portion of Maryland retailers. Small businesses tend to be more cautious about their forecasts, as online shopping and larger retailers become and tend to be more popular during sales events.
Consumers are also becoming more comfortable using artificial intelligence as a way to surf the internet for the best deals, which has the power to change consumer habits and increase the holiday spending activity, Boyd noted.
“We take it for granted: information at your fingertips,” he said. “It used to be the hardest part was figuring out where is the deal. You can do that now instantly.”
The national foundation’s additional late-October report notes that online shopping continues to rank as the top method, but the percentage of individuals planning to shop online has begun to decrease, with only 52% of consumers –  compared to last year’s 56% –  saying they plan to do so.
“It’s online fatigue. So much of our lives now are lived online,” Locklair said. “For a lot of people, it’s not just shopping; it’s an experience. It’s a whole-day adventure.”
Consumer behavior isn’t the only thing that drives the holiday season. Retailers are beginning to prioritize different marketing strategies during the busiest months for their income, Zhang said.
In addition to the holiday no longer being limited to a singular day of shopping, she said large retailers are starting to stagger sales to draw consumers in. This is where a retailer hikes up their prices, offers a sale for a short time period and gets rid of it before reintroducing a similar sale, giving the illusion of better discounts.
“For retailers, the end-of-the-year holiday shopping season is the single most important shopping season for their business,” Zhang said. “Because of that, competition amongst retailers has become more and more fierce over the years.”
But Boyd said that even with an influx of ways to shop online or grab the best discounts using AI platforms, shoppers still tend to appreciate the social experience holidays like Black Friday provide.
Even if people aren’t in a line wrapped around the store early Friday morning, people won’t be ditching the brick and mortar stores, he added.
“It’s like a form of entertainment,” Boyd said. “For a lot of folks, the magic lies … with your family, you’re with your friends… you look at a couple things, you grab something to eat, and those are the memories.”
