name: VTDigger
title: Alburg Springs border station to close for renovations with upgrades set for other Vermont crossings soon
description:
Work is also being planned at the crossing on Interstate 89 as well as smaller facilities in Richford, Derby and Norton over the next several years funded by a tranche of pandemic-era federal dollars. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Alburg Springs border station to close for renovations with upgrades set for other Vermont crossings soon.
text:
A Canadian Customs and Excise sign sits in Haut-Richelieu, Quebec across the U.S. – Canada border seen from Alburgh on Thursday, January 15, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
One of the ports of entry along Vermont’s border with Canada is set to close for renovations next month. Meanwhile, similar upgrades are being planned at four other border stations across the state in the coming years. 
U.S. Customs and Border Protection said the Alburg Springs station, in the Grand Isle County town of Alburgh, will close to traffic starting the afternoon of Friday, Dec. 11. That’s the crossing on Alburg Springs Road near the shore of Lake Champlain. 
The other border crossing in town, just north of Alburgh’s village center and about a 15-minute drive away, will remain open during the project, the federal agency said in a press release last week. Work is expected to last 12 to 14 months.
At Alburg Springs, the government plans to renovate the interior of the 1937 building and update its mechanical, electric and plumbing systems, according to a project webpage. Outside, the project will add a new bullet-resistent booth for officers and new gates to control traffic, the page says.
“These improvements are designed to enhance security and better support officers in carrying out their mission and daily operations,” Customs and Border Protection said in the release.
Danielle James Choiniere, Alburgh’s town clerk, said Wednesday she was not aware of any local residents who were upset about the upcoming closure.
“I haven’t heard that it’s a big issue,” she said. “Probably the consensus would be: There’s always another border crossing in Alburgh.”
There are a number of homes on Alburg Springs Road close to or across the street from the border station. Some members of the Alburgh Selectboard, at a meeting earlier this month, said they worried the construction could make it difficult for town crews to clear snow from the road in front of those homes. Amanda Costello, the town administrator, said at the meeting she would raise the potential plowing issue with the project’s manager. 
The road will remain open during construction up to the point it reaches the border, Choiniere noted Wednesday. 
Alburg Springs’ upgrades are set to cost between $9 million and $11 million, per the project webpage. The money was set out in the 2021 federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, a slice of more than $3 billion for upgrades at 26 ports of entry along the United States’ northern and southern borders. 
That includes upgrades at four other border crossings in Vermont.
To the east, planning work has been underway for years on a project that will rebuild the large border crossing on Interstate 89, at Highgate Springs. It’s the most-used crossing in Vermont and consistently ranks among the top three busiest ports of entry in New England, according to project plans.
Plans call for expanding the number of personal vehicle inspection lanes from five to seven and adding a second inspection lane for buses. They also call for replacing the main port building, which houses offices and interview rooms, as well as the existing building nearby for commercial vehicle inspections.
The government is currently finalizing the design of the new facility, according to a project webpage. It’s set to cost between $211 million and $257 million and be mostly completed by the summer of 2030, the website says. Unlike at Alburg Springs, though, it will remain open during construction.

READ MORE

The project’s webpage says the Highgate Springs crossing needs to be enlarged to accommodate an up to 30% expected increase in traffic passing through now that the Canadian government has expanded the A-35 highway south of Montreal nearly all the way to Vermont’s border.
Farther east, construction is set to begin in May at the port of entry just north of Richford’s village center on Route 139. That project, set to cost between $36 million and $44 million, will also demolish and replace the existing port of entry facilities. Plans include a new building that is more energy efficient, additional lanes for vehicle travel and bullet-resistant officer booths, according to project details online.
The future station’s expanded footprint requires tearing down a private home south of the existing facility and displacing the person living there, planning documents state.
Those documents also estimate that the crossing would be closed for about two years for construction. 
The government is still in the planning process, too, for upgrades at the crossing on Beebe Road in Derby, known as the Beebe Plain station. That project, set to cost between $10.5 million and $13 million, includes expanding the canopy over the vehicle inspection area, interior building renovations and other changes, a project webpage says.  
The page says the government expects to make a construction award in June with work to be largely completed by October 2028. It was not immediately clear whether or not the station would stay open during construction. 
Yet farther east, the crossing off Route 114 in Norton is also slated to get demolished and replaced with a new, more modern building. That project, which would also add on a new vehicle travel lane and adjust the current traffic pattern, is set to cost between $80 million and $95 million. Construction is expected to start next fall and be mostly completed by the summer of 2031, according to a project page. 
The Norton facility would stay open during construction, per project plans.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Judge denies financial support to son of former Gov. Matt Bevin
description: A judge has denied the request of former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin’s estranged son for support, possibly bringing an end to a long-running family legal saga that the judge deemed “heart-wrenching” and temporarily landed Bevin in jail for contempt of court. In the order issued late Wednesday, Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson summarized the […]
text:
Jonah Bevin, right, and one of his lawyers, Melina Hettiaratchi, listen during a court hearing in Louisville, March 25, 2025. (Photo by Michael Clevenger, Courier Journal, via press pool)A judge has denied the request of former Kentucky Gov. Matt Bevin’s estranged son for support, possibly bringing an end to a long-running family legal saga that the judge deemed “heart-wrenching” and temporarily landed Bevin in jail for contempt of court.
In the order issued late Wednesday, Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson summarized the 18-month court  battle in which Jonah Bevin, 20, one of four children Bevin and his ex-wife, Glenna, adopted from Ethiopia,  sought support for what he alleged were years of neglect and abuse.
The 16-page order released late Wednesday found that while the case raised “complex” and “novel” legal questions, state law does not provide for an adult child to require support from parents. Nor did the parties provide sufficient evidence to warrant such an award, Johnson said.
However, finding that Matt and Glenna Bevin acted in “bad faith” through delaying disclosure of their financial information and other actions, Johnson ordered them to pay $65,683 in legal fees to Jonah’s lawyers, John H. Helmers and Melina Hettiarachi.
Johnson ordered Matt Bevin to pay the majority of the costs, $47,216, finding that he “engaged in the most time-wasting conduct and tactics and has the most financial resources.” Glenna Bevin is to pay the rest, her order said.
Matt Bevin, a businessman, estimated his wealth in the millions of dollars when he ran for governor. The Republican was elected in 2015 and served one term before he was defeated by current Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, a Democrat.
The Bevins filed multiple, unsuccessful appeals throughout the family court cas, and Matt Bevin failed to appear in person as ordered at hearings earlier this year, ultimately leading to his arrest on a contempt of court and causing him to spend two weeks in jail before the Kentucky Court of Appeals freed him.
Jonah in May 2025 sought to intervene in his parents’  divorce case, alleging he was abandoned at age 17 in a brutally abusive facility in Jamaica closed by child welfare authorities. After authorities closed the facility, Jonah said the Bevins failed to help with his return to the United States and he was placed in custody of the Jamaican foster care system until outside advocates helped arrange his return.
He had asked for support from the court as well as help in furthering his education. His lawyers said a high-school degree purportedly provided by an online academy, was not valid and insufficient.
At a court hearing in July, Glenna Bevin testified that Jonah, one of the couple’s nine children, had a difficult childhood and was at times threatening and aggressive. He attended a series of youth residential facilities starting at age 13 until he ended up at the facility in Jamaica, the Atlantis Leadership Academy.
It drew international attention when celebrity Paris Hilton — seeking to highlight what she said is an abusive “troubled teen” industry — flew to the country to show support for the youths, including Jonah, removed from the facility.
At the July hearing, Glenna Bevin said her ex-husband made most of the decisions about Jonah’s placements and handled the finances. Matt Bevin did not attend the hearing despite a court order for him to do so.
The judge, in her order, questioned the selection and quality of  placements for Jonah.
“It seems from the testimony, none of the institutions were evidence-based, mental health programs, and they were selected by word of mouth,” Johnson’s order said.
Further, Matt Bevin claimed Jonah had a high-school degree from an accredited program, but never provided proof of that to the court despite claiming he would do so, her order said.
While the order appears to bring the case to an end, it could be appealed.
Lawyers for the parties did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: How Americans, including Minnesota librarians, are saving the history Trump is trying to erase
description: Republished with permission from Capital & Main.  In January, park rangers removed 34 interpretive panels from a slavery exhibit at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia. The signs, which described the lives of the nine people George Washington enslaved at the presidential residence there, were unceremoniously taken down — in some cases leavi[...]
text:
HARPERS FERRY, WEST VIRGINIA - SEPTEMBER 16: A visitor views exhibits related to slavery at the John Brown Museum at the Harpers Ferry National Historical Park September 16, 2025 in Harpers Ferry, West Virginia. According to a report in the Washington Post, the Trump administration has instructed the Department of Interior to remove signs and exhibits related to slavery at multiple national parks. (Photo by Win McNamee/Getty Images)Republished with permission from Capital & Main. 
In January, park rangers removed 34 interpretive panels from a slavery exhibit at Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia. The signs, which described the lives of the nine people George Washington enslaved at the presidential residence there, were unceremoniously taken down — in some cases leaving the dried glue in place — to comply with President Donald Trump’s Executive Order 14253, titled “Restoring Truth and Sanity to American History.” The order calls for the removal of signs that “inappropriately disparage Americans past or living” from the country’s national parks. Apparently, telling visitors about our first president’s slaves ran afoul of that.
When Trump issued the order in March 2025, Molly Blake, a social sciences librarian at the University of Minnesota, worried about the information that might be lost as a result. She began talking with colleagues at the university, including Jenny McBurney, a government publications librarian, about what they could do. Even if they couldn’t stop park rangers from tearing down the signs, maybe they could archive them for posterity. Within a few months, they would launch Save Our Signs, a nationwide effort to preserve what the government was trying to erase.
Blake and McBurney couldn’t go to all 63 national parks, of course, let alone the hundreds of historic monuments and sites overseen by the National Park Service. “We knew we had to get the public involved,” Blake said, so they invited parkgoers to photograph signs to be recorded in an online archive. The response has been overwhelming.
To date, members of the public have sent Save Our Signs more than 17,000 photos shot at 428 sites, from Ellis Island and the Japanese American internment camp at Manzanar to monuments dedicated to the memory of Emmett Till, whose killing helped spark the Civil Rights Movement. They’ve also sent reports and photos from parks where the signs have already been removed, which become part of the archive’s “Censorship Tracker.”
“The folks that we hear from are saying things like they love our parks, they  support our parks, they want to maintain the really high-quality educational materials they’re seeing there,” McBurney said. “They want us to remember our history, the good and the bad.”
 A daunting task
Even for the combined forces of the American public, however, there are a lot of parks and land to cover: More than 85 million acres across 50 states. And nobody knows where the government might strike next.
“They’re not hiding it,” said Alan Spears, senior director of cultural resources at the National Parks Conservation Association. “They’re also probably not putting out press releases saying that this stuff has happened. You can just show up on Monday or Tuesday of this past week, [and] the signs are gone.”
Because of the uncertainty, SOS encourages parkgoers to photograph everything. “One of the signs that was removed just noted that it’s a good idea to refill your water bottle because it’s better for the environment than using plastic,” Blake said. “I wouldn’t have guessed that that would have been targeted, but it was.”
Since the order was issued, park employees have removed or modified more than 100 signs at 41 National Park Service sites, from California’s Muir Woods National Monument (for mentioning climate change and the park founders’ connections to anti-immigrant policies) to Wyoming’s Grand Teton National Park (for calling attention to explorer Gustavus Cheyney Doane’s participation in a massacre of more than 150 Indigenous people).
Monitoring all those signs is as daunting for the Interior Department, which includes the Park Service, as it is for SOS. The department relies on park rangers and other employees at each site, instructing them to look for signs that might not be doing an acceptable job of reminding parkgoers of this country’s “unmatched record of advancing liberty, prosperity, and human flourishing,” as Trump’s order puts it. Park staff are expected to remove or alter such signs within 120 days of the executive order.
 Snitch signs
A confidential Park Service database, leaked in March and containing internal communications among park staffers, showed rangers wrestling with difficult questions about what exactly the order requires. Did signage about the return of California condors from near-extinction disparage hunters? one ranger asked. Another wondered whether signs about graffiti at Utah’s Arches National Park violated the directive to emphasize the park’s “natural beauty.”
For SOS, the leak provided a list of parks that might be targeted for sign removals if they hadn’t been already.
“Right now, we have on our website a map of parks that, based on the leaked dataset of what might be targeted, are parks that are priorities for us,” Blake said. “It was called out on this leaked spreadsheet as a place that there might be censorship happening. We really want more photos there.”
One of the challenges for Save Our Signs is the ambiguity of Trump’s order as well as Secretarial Order 3431, which Interior Secretary Doug Burgum issued to implement the executive order. Consider the orders’ ban on “inappropriate disparagement” of Americans. Is it OK for signage at a Till site to disparage the men who tortured and lynched him? Can park signs at civil rights monuments in Birmingham, Alabama, and Little Rock, Arkansas, disparage the white supremacists who opposed the Civil Rights Movement?
“Inappropriate disparagement” of Americans is “a really confusing turn of phrase,” McBurney said. “Especially in the early days, nobody knew what that meant.”
The secretarial order also requires parks to post notices telling visitors how to report supposed violations, an effort that has largely been a bust. The QR-code-enabled notices, prescribed in a section of Burgum’s order titled “Encouraging Public Participation,” were soon dubbed “snitch signs” by detractors, thousands of whom submitted sarcastic comments and jabs at the Trump administration. “There are some people who reported, ‘I think there needs to be more about Indigenous history here,’” Blake said.
 Legal conflicts
The watchdog group Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility (PEER) filed a Freedom of Information Act request last year to find out how the executive order was being implemented. The Interior Department never responded, so PEER sued to get the records in June.
Tony Irish, a longtime Interior attorney who left the department last year and joined PEER in May, said, “There’s a number of terms [in the order] that, even for me, with my background in Interior programs, isn’t clear.” He wonders how these orders might run afoul of federal law, including the National Park Service Organic Act of 1916, which created the service, and the National Historic Preservation Act of 1966. “There’s other sites, particularly ones like Little Big Horn, where Congress has specifically directed the agency to provide a viewpoint from the Native American tribes that were impacted by the events there,” Irish said.
It’s not just Park Service signs that are being removed and altered. Trump’s order calls for the removal of offending signs throughout all 500 million acres of Interior Department lands, comprising roughly one-fifth of the country. Park Service sites are getting most of the attention because Americans are more inclined to visit them, Irish said, but the Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Land Management oversee even more acreage. PEER is suing the department for information about the order’s impact on those lands too.
There have been impacts on wildlife refuges and the Bureau of Land Management, Irish said. “Part of why we want to get these records is to see just to what extent.”
 Insidious alterations
Little is known about the fate of many of the lost signs. When a district court judge told the Trump administration to provide an inventory of removed materials, the partial list from the Interior Department included 18 items that had been “discarded.”
Few parks employees are inclined to talk about where the old signs might be, let alone which others are slated for removal, Irish said.
“We’ve seen … circumstances where employees have made their personal feelings known that have led to swift reactions from the department,” he said. “So I would suspect there is some fear of being open about that.”
Some of the replacement signs sanitize or dilute the history laid out in the originals in ways that aren’t immediately obvious.
“These are really insidious,” said Save Our Signs’ Blake. “The differences are really subtle. In one case, a sign about Black soldiers during the Civil War, a reference to the fact that the military remained segregated until after World War II, that sentence was quietly taken out. So you could read something like that and not realize this has been censored.”
This whitewashing of history at park sites reverses decades of progress at the national parks, Spears said.
“We spent the last 30 years trying to raise up some of these untold stories so that we can have a better understanding of the contributions that all of us have made,” she said. Spears called the current shift “disheartening and anger-inducing.”
Save Our Signs continues to document the loss as signs across the country continue to come down. Blake said the effort is capturing an important moment in our history when an accurate telling of our past is itself under attack.
“Best-case scenario, the signs that have been censored will go back up, and this will be a way to study what happened,” she said. “Worst-case scenario, if this censorship continues, we want to be documenting it so that people can see what has been changed.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: Washington faith leaders split over I-638 transgender sports ban
description: This article was first published by FāVS News. The recent success of a Washington state ballot measure, passed with the help of Christian organizations and banning transgender girls from competing in sports that align with their gender identity, has drawn religious ire from other communities. Supporters of Initiative 638 say that it upholds the binary […]
text:
Ahnaleigh Wilson, 17, of Eastmont High School, center, and Frances Staudt, 17, of Tumwater High School, right, speak with the media about Initiative 638 at Let’s Go Washington’s election night watch party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. (Photo by Ryan Berry/Washington State Standard)This article was first published by FāVS News.
The recent success of a Washington state ballot measure, passed with the help of Christian organizations and banning transgender girls from competing in sports that align with their gender identity, has drawn religious ire from other communities.
Supporters of Initiative 638 say that it upholds the binary of gender that they see in the Bible. Religious opponents of the law, which is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 3, argue that it dehumanizes and demonizes a specific portion of the population in violation of the biblical requirement to love all.
The initiative, which is being challenged in courts and defended on the state’s side by a contracted law firm, requires girls who want to play in school sports to undergo a genital check, a hormone test for testosterone levels or a chromosome test to determine their sex assigned at birth. Washington has not restricted trans students from participating in sports that align with their gender identity for nearly 20 years.
The law was championed by Let’s Go Washington, a political action committee working to pass conservative-leaning initiatives in the state. Supporters of I-638 say it protects fair competition in girls’ sports, citing a hypothesis that teenagers who were born male have a biological advantage over those who were born female.
Opponents say it both marginalizes trans students and will discourage cisgender girls from playing in sports due to the invasive medical procedures.
Religious ire
Several mainline denominational groups and religious networks have spoken out against the passage of the initiative, which was approved by a vote of 56%.
The Episcopal Diocese of Spokane and the Episcopal Diocese of Olympia released a joint statement two days after election day, lamenting the results of the vote “and its impact on our transgender and non-binary siblings” as well as cisgender female athletes.
“Throughout the recent mid-term campaign, much anger, suspicion and fear-mongering has been directed toward the trans community,” the statement read. “These children of God have been dehumanized.”
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
The dioceses’ stance on the issue came from the character of Jesus Christ, according to Bishop Gretchen Rehberg, who oversees the Episcopal Diocese of Spokane.
“Jesus is constantly going after the outcast,” Rehberg said, or the ones that “society deems not as important.”
“The idea of, ‘there are no outcasts, there’s only the beloved,’” is a “gospel value,” she said, adding that it is against the character of Christ to discriminate against anyone.
More mainline Christian denominations speak against I-638
The bishops of several synods in the Evangelical Lutheran Church in America also released a statement decrying the initiative.
“Every child is a beloved child of God. Every child,” it read. “To transgender girls, nonbinary and intersex children and youth, we want to say this directly: You are beloved. You are not a problem to be solved. You are not a political argument. You are a person created in God’s image, with gifts to share, friendships to enjoy, and a life that matters.”
Prior to the initiative’s passage, many religious organizations from a variety of backgrounds and denominations joined in on the opposition campaign, titled “No Hate in Washington State.”
Wayside United Church of Christ in Federal Way was one of the organizations explicitly opposed to the initiative.
“We have a lot of belief that people — trans people, and gay people and straight people and cis people — are all beloved children of God,” Amy Johnson, minister for sexuality, education and justice at the church, said. Nationally, the United Church of Christ has stood for transgender youth, gender equality and “the dignity and belovedness and sacredness of trans folks” for a long time, she added, and the Washington initiative seemed to be in opposition to those principles.
Jewish faith communities oppose I-638
Temple Beth Am in Seattle also publicly opposed the initiative. Shelly Cohen, a member of the temple who spoke on her own behalf, said she supports the rights of transgender and gender non-conforming people “based on simply the fact that we are all created in the image of God.”
“This is who we are, and there is a lot of diversity in who and how we are,” she said, adding that she thought the initiative violated the inherent dignity of transgender girls and cisgender girls with its medical exams.
Cohen said that some readings of Jewish documents, like the Talmud, which discusses Jewish law and theology, reference the existence of up to eight different genders. Some key biblical stories are also seen as including characters with sex changes, according to some Jewish traditions.
“Gender is not as fixed as some people would like you to believe,” Cohen said.
Another reason Cohen opposed the initiative was because she viewed it as scapegoating a small group of people, which caused her, as a Jew, to worry. The Washington Interscholastic Activities Association has said it is aware of about 10 transgender middle and high schoolers who play public school sports in the state.
“I think we have a responsibility when we see something like that to stand up and say this is wrong,” Cohen said of the law.
Religious support
The initiative was not without people who rallied behind it for religious reasons.
The Family Policy Institute of Washington, a conservative Christian advocacy organization, advocated publicly for the law. The Washington State Catholic Conference officially endorsed it.
Neither organization responded to a request for comment
John Respold, a pastor at the nondenominational church Mosaic in Spokane, supported the initiative based on his theology.
“I think that the distinction between male and female is biblical and kind of rooted in human nature,” he said, adding that his reading of the Bible presented a gender binary.
“I think that the Bible pretty well presents it, that we are different bodies that are intended to represent, partly, the presentation of God and creation here,” he said, adding that “we’re to glorify God with our bodies.”
To change one’s gender, in his mind, is “usurping the role that God has in creating and forming a human body.”
“I think it goes against creation,” he said. “I think it goes against God’s involvement in creation.”
Respold said that Christians who are opposed to changing one’s gender are not a “hateful bunch of people.”
“We’re willing to lay our lives down for everybody,” he said, adding that he was “not willing to sacrifice other people’s dignity for what I would perceive is really the confusion of the few.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico nonprofit brings music, joy and connection to people with neurological conditions
description: Musical group Healing Harmonies helps people with neurological issues come together.
text:
Ruthie Francis (center) from Shiprock joins a session on music, movement and brain health, led by Healing Harmonies founder Nicole Gallegos during the State of New Mexico's Conference on Aging held in October, 2026, in Glorieta. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)When Nicole Gallegos founded Healing Harmonies New Mexico in 2022, the group was a small way for people with neurological conditions to come together, make music and connect with others. Today, the nonprofit organization has about 80 members who rehearse and perform with Gallegos in the Albuquerque area.
Healing Harmonies brings together people with dementia, Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s, ALS, stroke, traumatic brain injury and other neurological disorders or changes and their caregivers, and creates a space for them to “rediscover” their voices through socialization, cognitive engagement and vocal strengthening.
According to experts, one in four New Mexicans are projected to be aged 65 or older by 2030, meaning the state will soon have one of the largest elder populations in the country. In the same timeline, the Parkinson’s Foundation reports that 1.2 million people will be living with the disease across the U.S. And according to the Alzheimer’s Association, 46,000 New Mexicans lived with the disease in 2020, with 642 people dying from the disease in 2024. 
Earlier this week, the State of New Mexico announced it had recently completed an approximate five-year plan to address dementia and brain health in the state, with includes goals for caregiving, education, policy, services and workforce development. According to the report, approximately 46,000 New Mexico residents aged 65+ live with Alzheimer’s, and 20% of adults 45+ report cognitive decline, though few seek evaluation.
“We want New Mexicans to know that support is available, whether you’re navigating a new diagnosis or providing help to a loved one,” Aging and Long-Term Services Department Secretary Emily Kaltenbach said in a statement. “This roadmap gives us a path forward to prioritize those supports and help those living with dementia and their families maintain their quality of life.”
During a recent mental health workshop held in Santa Fe, aging experts voiced concern over social isolation among older adults and the need for earlier screening for mental health and cognitive changes. 
Aging experts call for expanded early detection of mental health conditions in older New Mexicans

“I feel like all of us can run into it with brain changes or with aging; we can just develop sometimes an apathy or some depression, especially when we’re talking about mild cognitive decline or any of those other neurological changes,” Gallegos told attendees during a presentation at the state Aging and Long-Term Services Department’s annual Conference on Aging held in October in Glorieta. “Something that I think about myself is these steps — make it small, make it easy and do something together…Just think, ‘I don’t need to accept that feeling of sadness or loneliness.’”
Healing Harmonies founder and Executive Director Nicole Gallegos leads a session at the October 2026 New Mexico Aging Conference in Glorieta. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)
Gallegos is a licensed speech-language pathologist and certified vocologist with Corrales Voice & Speech Therapy. She held a session at the aging conference in which she asked attendees to sing along to “You Are My Sunshine” while moving their arms and clapping in time, combining music and physical movement. By the end of the session, nearly everyone had joined in and a happy buzz spread around the room as people laughed and talked about the experience.
According to the organization’s website, Healing Harmonies and Gallegos’ approach uses music as a catalyst for improved memory and breath support, as well as social connection.
“There’s so many, so many tough, really tough diagnoses where we know someone might not be alive in a year from now. And I think even for the family member, being able to support them and bring some joy in that moment, I think just being around other people who are experiencing the same things that they are is huge,” Gallegos told Source NM. “But also, we just laugh a lot. We try to keep it really positive so that it’s a really uplifting space.”
She said the nonprofit is working to expand into other communities in the state by connecting with other people who could start their own Healing Harmonies choir. Gallegos told Source NM that she has connected with interested people in Los Alamos and Santa Fe, but funding is the barrier for expanding right now.
Healing Harmonies members sing at the New Mexico Aging Conference held in October, 2026, in Glorieta. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)
“It doesn’t cost much to do it, but it adds up just to be able to maybe have a musician come out or rent space for rehearsals. I don’t feel like we’re far off though,” Gallegos said. She added that the group is also working to meet the needs of more people by expanding virtually. “That way at least people, if they’re homebound, could join us. Or if they’re in a very remote part of New Mexico.”



Healing Harmonies has two performances in Corrales scheduled in December. On Dec. 5, the group will take part in the 7th Annual Pay What You Please Trees event, where attendees can pick a Christmas tree and proceeds are donated to charities, including Healing Harmonies. On Dec. 12, the group will perform a free holiday concert at San Ysidro New Church featuring Christmas classics, plus some tunes by Elvis Presley and Dolly Parton.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: This year, I’m giving thanks to NJ politicians committed to NJ, not the White House
description: Nearly every recent governor of New Jersey has thought they could make it to the White House. Is Gov. Mikie Sherrill one of them?
text:
Nearly every recent governor of New Jersey has thought they could make it to the White House. Is Gov. Mikie Sherrill one of them? (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)No New Jersey resident has been elected to the White House in over 100 years, yet that hasn’t stopped our high-profile pols from flirting with the idea that they may be the one who finally gets catapulted to the presidency again.
Chris Christie, our Republican former governor, is on an I-told-ya-so tour in an attempt to get his name before voters and donors as a potential 2028 presidential candidate. U.S. Sen. Cory Booker, a Democrat, sprinted to the pivotal state of South Carolina for two visits soon after Democrats dominated on Election Day earlier this month.
It sure looks like our new governor, Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, thinks she’s in the mix, too. Politico New Jersey reported this week that she presented her own agenda to the 13 Democrats who will represent our state in Congress starting in January, which feels like an unsubtle bid by Sherrill to place herself in the center of the 2028 conversation (the letter also went to Democratic leadership of the Senate and House). Sherrill’s term as governor doesn’t end until January 2030.
We’ve been here before, mostly to the detriment of New Jersey residents. Christie spent so much time out of state running for president during his final years as governor that his approval rating here tanked and never recovered. Booker ran for president in 2020, spending an awful lot of time talking to voters in places like Iowa while he was ostensibly representing New Jersey in the Senate (he dropped out before a single vote was cast).
And of course Sherrill’s predecessor, Phil Murphy, tried to make us think he was in the running to become Kamala Harris’ vice presidential pick, an idea laughable on its face that nonetheless generated some headlines for Murphy.
I asked Sherrill’s office whether her letter to our incoming members of Congress indicates she’s more focused on D.C. than the state she’s governing.
“With Trump still in the White House, Governor Sherrill knows that this moment demands that we leverage every single tool we have, and how important it is for the state and Congressional delegation to work together. She looks forward to partnering with them to deliver for New Jersey and ensure we get our fair share of resources, especially given the impact of federal cuts on our state budget,” Sherrill spokesman Sean Higgins said.
Micah Rasmussen, director of Rider University’s Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics, told me there’s evidence that nearly every Garden State governor since Woodrow Wilson has been mentioned as a potential candidate for president, with varying degrees of plausibility.
Why is that? Rasmussen said it boils down to ego, national attention, and moola.
“For the last 79 years, New Jersey governors have constantly heard the same refrain: that they are the most powerful governor in the nation,” he said. “So when they hear talk about how governors make good presidents, they think that means them. And let’s face it, our proximity to the media’s center of the universe has traditionally meant that whenever there’s any kind of crisis, New Jersey governors are front and center, whether it’s a snowstorm or 9/11.”
Considering the 2028 presidential campaign has essentially started, we’ll find out soon enough what role, if any, Sherrill thinks she’ll play. As we give thanks today, may I offer my own thanks to the many New Jersey elected officials who are fully focused on the Garden State and not eyeing a move to 1600 Pennsylvania Ave. I hope Sherrill is on that list.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Hospital system expands food aid, mobile health services in rural South Jersey
description: Inspira Health is expanding food aid and mobile health services in a region that lags the state in many health outcomes.
text:
Inspira Health community health workers Whitney Robinson and Samantha Darnall are pictured outside the community resource van. The program launched in the summer to provide mobile health screenings and serve as a rolling food pantry. (Photo courtesy of Inspira Health)A South Jersey hospital system is finding new ways to keep people healthy in a region where health outcomes lag the state at large.
Earlier this month, Inspira Health opened a food pantry at its Mannington hospital, its first such program in Salem County. Some 300 people have already received help through the site, according to senior vice president and chief strategy officer April Venable.
For Inspira, the goal is not just providing medical treatment, but reducing barriers to good health.
“People go to the doctor and tell them they have a ton of barriers that clinical care won’t solve,” Venable told the New Jersey Monitor.
New federal rules proposed for food stamps are inhumane

Inspira already operated food pantries at hospitals in Cumberland and Gloucester counties, part of a program it launched in 2020. Patients who struggle to afford food can visit these sites to talk to a community health worker and take home fresh fruit, vegetables, and other healthy foods.
In the summer of 2026, Inspira also launched a van service that serves as a rolling food pantry and healthcare screening site, a spot for blood pressure checks or skin cancer screenings at farmers markets, college campuses, and community events.
Inspira is clear it can’t alone solve every problem for patients, who may also need help with housing, child care, or education, Venable said.
“But we do feel that we’re an important piece of the pie and we should have a process, so when we screen people for difficulties we have a process to hand off,” she said.
Inspira — which has hospitals in Elmer, Mannington, Mullica Hill, and Vineland, along with clinics throughout the region — said these programs were prompted by input the system received from residents as part of a multi-year community health assessment, which highlighted the depth of food insecurity in the region.
Inspira’s plan for a van that can be used for mobile food aid and other services makes sense to Triada Stampas, the CEO of Fulfill Inc., a food bank that supports pantries and soup kitchens in Monmouth and Ocean counties, feeding about 150,000 people each month.  Demand at these sites has increased by one-third over last year, she said, and a survey of its users shows only half own a car.
“Putting the food where people are already going is one of the strongest options we have,” Stampas told the New Jersey Monitor.
She added that food insecurity is often a sign that families have other needs.
Fulfill also runs a mobile pantry, which Stampas said has been well received. Food bank operators are also exploring other options, like home delivery services and food lockers, refrigerated containers that people can access with a code to collect groceries, she said.
The goal is to provide free, healthy food choices in easily accessible places where people are already going, Stampas said.
“It’s cheaper to move food to people than it is to move people to food,” she said.
One in eight New Jerseyans faces hunger at times, according to national advocates Feeding America, including 1-in-6 children here. The federal food stamp program provides benefits to about 430,000 households, helping to feed roughly 860,000 people here, with benefits that average less than $200 a month, but reductions in federal funding are expected to shrink its reach in the coming years.

title: Read President Abraham Lincoln’s proclamation upon declaring a national day of Thanksgiving
description: Editor’s note: At the urging of magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale, President Abraham Lincoln declared an annual national holiday of Thanksgiving in 1863. Here’s the proclamation:  […[...]
text:
Abraham Lincoln Memorial in Washington, D.C.Editor’s note: At the urging of magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale, President Abraham Lincoln declared an annual national holiday of Thanksgiving in 1863. Most remarkably, Lincoln made his proclamation at the height of the bloodiest war in American history. Bit of trivia: The text was written by Secretary of State William Seward. Here’s the proclamation: 
The year that is drawing towards its close, has been filled with the blessings of fruitful fields and healthful skies. To these bounties, which are so constantly enjoyed that we are prone to forget the source from which they come, others have been added, which are of so extraordinary a nature, that they cannot fail to penetrate and soften even the heart which is habitually insensible to the ever watchful providence of Almighty God. 
In the midst of a civil war of unequalled magnitude and severity, which has sometimes seemed to foreign States to invite and to provoke their aggression, peace has been preserved with all nations, order has been maintained, the laws have been respected and obeyed, and harmony has prevailed everywhere except in the theatre of military conflict; while that theatre has been greatly contracted by the advancing armies and navies of the Union. 
Needful diversions of wealth and of strength from the fields of peaceful industry to the national defence, have not arrested the plough, the shuttle or the ship; the axe has enlarged the borders of our settlements, and the mines, as well of iron and coal as of the precious metals, have yielded even more abundantly than heretofore. Population has steadily increased, notwithstanding the waste that has been made in the camp, the siege and the battle-field; and the country, rejoicing in the consciousness of augmented strength and vigor, is permitted to expect continuance of years with large increase of freedom. 
No human counsel hath devised nor hath any mortal hand worked out these great things. They are the gracious gifts of the Most High God, who, while dealing with us in anger for our sins, hath nevertheless remembered mercy. 
It has seemed to me fit and proper that they should be solemnly, reverently and gratefully acknowledged as with one heart and one voice by the whole American People. 
I do therefore invite my fellow citizens in every part of the United States, and also those who are at sea and those who are sojourning in foreign lands, to set apart and observe the last Thursday of November next, as a day of Thanksgiving and Praise to our beneficent Father who dwelleth in the Heavens. 
And I recommend to them that while offering up the ascriptions justly due to Him for such singular deliverances and blessings, they do also, with humble penitence for our national perverseness and disobedience, commend to His tender care all those who have become widows, orphans, mourners or sufferers in the lamentable civil strife in which we are unavoidably engaged, and fervently implore the interposition of the Almighty Hand to heal the wounds of the nation and to restore it as soon as may be consistent with the Divine purposes to the full enjoyment of peace, harmony, tranquillity and Union.
In testimony whereof, I have hereunto set my hand and caused the Seal of the United States to be affixed.
Done at the City of Washington, this Third day of October, in the year of our Lord one thousand eight hundred and sixty-three, and of the Independence of the United States the Eighty-eighth.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Colom once displayed leadership, as well as grit and tenacity, on the Millsaps College basketball team
description: Scott Colom, right, played basketball for Millsaps College during the 2003-04 season.
text:
Twenty-five years ago John Stroud, the Ole Miss basketball great and former NBA player, recruited Scott Colom to Millsaps College and coached him during Stroud’s last two seasons at the Jackson school.
Rick Cleveland
Colom went on to earn a law degree and become a district attorney in four counties. He won a U.S. Senate election in Mississippi this month, unseating Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith.
I asked Stroud, who now works in private business in New Albany, what he thought back then Colom would wind up doing later in life.
“Well, my first guess wouldn’t have been United States senator,” Stroud answered. “But I knew he would be successful. I knew he was really, really intelligent, and I knew he was a leader. I knew he was a people person. Scott will talk to anybody about anything. I knew for sure he would make something of himself.”
Stroud will tell you up front young Scott Colom was not a great basketball player, even at the NCAA Division III level. He was a back-up point guard, better at guarding on defense and setting up the offense than at scoring points himself. 
Scott Colom, right, plays in a Millsaps College basketball game during the 2003-04 season. Credit: Courtesy of Millsaps College
“What I most remember about Scott is that when I would come into the locker room before a game to talk to the team, Scott was already talking to them, already coaching them about what we needed to do to win,” Stroud said. “When I say he was a leader, he really was. He was an enthusiastic leader. I believe he’ll be a great senator.”
Colom came to Millsaps from Columbus, where his parents were lawyers and one of his best friends was Thomas Adams, a doctor’s son who was two years older and already at Millsaps. Thomas Adams was a four-year starter and star, now a member of the Millsaps Athletics Hall of Fame.
Thomas Adams Credit: Madison Public Schools
Says Adams, now the principal at Madison Middle School, “Our families were close. We spent a lot of time together growing up. We played together, went to church together. Either I would spend the night at their house or Scott and Andrew (Scott Colom’s twin brother) would spend the night at our house.”
While Andrew chose to attend Ivy League Columbia, Scott picked Millsaps, at least in part to play basketball with Adams.
“I remember Scott and his family would drive down to our games to watch Thomas play,” Stroud said. “They had played together in high school. Scott could have gone to college anywhere because of his academics, and in his family, academics came first, but Millsaps gave him a chance to do both.”
Asked to describe Colom as a player, Adams responded, “He was always so competitive. He’d scrap and claw to make the team better. He was all about the team.”
When Stroud left Millsaps for private business, Tim Wise, who had played at Millsaps and was the school’s all-time assists leader, was elevated from assistant to head coach. Wise remembers Colom, as a smart, strong, physical guard, “who played a lot that first year I was the head coach.”
“Scott was a team player, the kind that who get a group of guys going in the right direction,” Wise said. “He was a great encourager, the kind of guy who makes the guys around him better.”
Colom decided not to play his senior year of eligibility, opting to concentrate fully on academics to prepare for law school. He eventually landed at the University of Wisconsin, where he flourished. But, says Wise, “I always thought he would come back to Mississippi and made a difference, which he has.”
John Stroud
Stroud and Colom remain good friends and talk often. Even so, Stroud says, he marveled at Colom’s successful campaign. 
“I mean the president of the United States comes down to campaign for his opponent, and Scott goes to the event and walks down the line of people waiting to get in, shaking hands and greeting folks,” Stroud says. “Who else does that? But if you know Scott Colom, you’re not surprised.”
Adams, his childhood friend and former teammate, certainly was not surprised.
“Scott has taken the same mindset he had on the basketball floor into the political arena. He’s always been a competitor,” Adams said. “When he got in the race, I thought he was a long shot, but I went to some of his campaign events and saw how he connected with people, how hard he worked. He just wasn’t going to be denied.”
Wise joked that Colom’s election gives Stroud a unique status.
“I told John not many people can say what he can,” Wise said. “He coached a senator in Scott. There are only a hundred of those. A few years before, he coached Tate Reeves, the governor. There are only 50 of those. He coached two of 150. I wonder how many coaches there are in America who can say that. Not many, I suspect.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri prepares for SNAP purchase restrictions as court battles continue
description: Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change. To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received […]
text:
The restrictions planned for Feb. 15 will impact the almost 5,000 retailers who are authorized to accept SNAP benefits in Missouri (Steph Quinn/Missouri Independent).Missouri plans to give nearly 5,000 retailers a list of candy, sugary drinks and desserts that shoppers will no longer be able to purchase with federal food benefits starting Feb. 15. But grocers worry the list could quickly become outdated as products change.
To create the list, the Missouri Department of Social Services has received permission to forgo competitive bidding and make a one-time purchase of a Missouri-specific product database from global market research firm NielsenIQ.
The restrictions, approved by the federal government at the state’s request last year, will prohibit purchases of candy, prepackaged, shelf-stable desserts, sugary beverages and energy drinks through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP. They will also apply to a program called SUN Bucks that gives families of eligible children a one-time benefit of $120 to buy groceries during the summer.
The list is intended to help almost 5,000 SNAP retailers statewide implement the changes consistently, according to the department’s single feasible source purchase notice.
“Without this centralized procurement, approximately 4,944 SNAP-authorized Missouri retailers would each need to independently acquire the data, risking inconsistent implementation and federal noncompliance penalties,” according to the department posting. 
But the Missouri Grocers Association, which advocates for the state’s grocery industry, says that unless the department provides regular updates to the list, retailers will struggle to implement SNAP restrictions uniformly as product formulations change and manufacturers release new products. 
Dan Shaul, the association’s executive director, told The Independent he also worries retailers will be punished for inconsistencies that will be difficult to avoid.
“Yes, we’ll go ahead and program that list in,” Shaul said. “But then how do we make changes as our products change? I don’t think people understand the depth of product changes or (Universal Product Code) changes from retailer to retailer. Those things change constantly.” 
Missouri’s plans are unfolding against the backdrop of federal court battles over the legality of SNAP restrictions in 23 states where the U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved waivers. 
A class action lawsuit filed Nov. 18 and led by the National Center for Law and Economic Justice seeks to strike down proposed and current SNAP restrictions in 18 states, including Missouri, arguing federal officials lacked authority to use waivers to undertake such large-scale change to SNAP. 
The lawsuit builds on the center’s ongoing legal challenge of SNAP restrictions in the five other states where USDA approved waivers. A judge blocked  those waivers, in Colorado, Iowa, Tennessee and West Virginia in June, though the USDA has appealed the decision. 
Missouri’s updated waiver, approved by USDA in June, defines candy as products that combine sugar or artificial sweeteners with “chocolate, fruit, nuts, caramels, gummies and hard candies…in the form of bars, drops or pieces.” The definition excludes items that contain flour or require refrigeration.
The waiver prohibits the use of SNAP benefits to purchase energy drinks, as well as “soda, juice, punch and tea,” which are defined as containing more than 10 grams of sugar per serving or 50% or less of vegetable or fruit juice. But SNAP participants can use benefits to buy beverages containing milk and sports drinks marketed to increase hydration.
The waiver’s ban on SNAP purchases of pre-packaged, ready-to-eat desserts does not include items baked fresh in grocery stores that aren’t considered shelf-stable.
To qualify for SNAP, Missourians can earn a gross income of no more than 130% of the federal poverty level, or $41,796 per year for a family of four before taxes and other deductions.
As researchers study the impacts of SNAP restrictions, the effectiveness of the waivers at improving nutrition remains unclear.
Kate Bauer, a professor of nutritional sciences at the University of Michigan School of Public Health, told The Independent that while studies conducted before the first waivers took effect showed little impact on participants’ diets — suggesting people used resources besides their benefits to buy restricted products — more recent research suggests SNAP restrictions can decrease purchases of sugary drinks.
Bauer said she worries SNAP restrictions will heighten existing stigma against people who use food benefits.
“A big concern for me is that with these restrictions and really a lot of confusion over what foods and beverages are eligible, that stigma would increase,” Bauer said.
 A “good day one list”

Shaul said several other states are using product lists from NielsenIQ and that “it’ll be a very good day one list.”
But, he said, “my responsibility now is to try to find (retailers) tools beyond the day one list that will allow them to comply” with the coming SNAP changes.
In an email to The Independent, Baylee Watts, the department’s media director, said the department could not disclose the cost of the contract because procurement is still underway.
But Watts said “requiring each store to independently license and maintain this product data would cost Missouri retailers an estimated aggregate of more than $7.4 million — and that figure excludes additional fees for larger retailers.”
The department’s single feasible source posting also indicates that because of the “urgent federal implementation timeline,” a competitive request for proposals would have been “impractical and detrimental to compliance efforts.”
The department applied for federal permission to restrict SNAP purchases at the behest of Gov. Mike Kehoe in a September 2025 executive order. The department postponed the original start date of Oct. 1, 2026, to better support Missouri retailers, Kehoe said in a June press release. Retailers had warned they needed clearer guidance to enforce the new restrictions.
Watts said the list the department plans to provide “is designed to eliminate guesswork.”
“Rather than requiring individual store owners to manually audit tens of thousands of inventory items, this standardized electronic dataset allows retailers and their point-of-sale (POS) software providers to perform direct, batch updates across their systems,” Watts said.
Shaul said the association is searching for a solution that would provide a dynamic list, so that product changes won’t require manual updates to retailers’ systems.
The definitions in Missouri’s SNAP waiver, Shaul said, are “up for interpretation.
“I would hope that the department would interpret it the exact same way as every retailer in the state that has SNAP,” Shaul said. “That is not going to happen.
 Fundamental changes

Neither of the two Missourians named in the class action lawsuit filed Nov.18 have funds other than their SNAP benefits to purchase food, according to court documents.
Nicole Noblet, of Kansas City, has celiac disease, gastroparesis and, her doctor suspects, hypoglycemia. Her conditions make it difficult for her body to absorb sugar from solid foods, so she uses soda or energy drinks to raise her blood sugar. 
Gerard Rogers, of Springfield, has diabetes and sometimes uses candy bars to manage low blood sugar, according to the lawsuit.
Katharine Deabler-Meadows, a senior attorney working on the lawsuit, told The Independent many SNAP participants don’t have other resources they can reallocate to buy items restricted by state waivers.
“Probably the simplest and most classic example that we’ve run across as we’re talking to people about these waivers is a person who is diabetic who relies on soda or candy to manage blood sugar crashes when they’re working or running errands or caring for their children,” Deabler-Meadows said. “…They’re going to have to choose: Do I manage my chronic health condition, or do I not buy something else that my household needs?”
Deabler-Meadows said throughout the history of SNAP, USDA’s definition of SNAP-eligible food has matched the definition in the federal Food and Nutrition Act and has been consistent across states. 
Changing this definition of food through federal regulations — and making different changes in different states — is “a fundamental change to the way this program works” and a “backdoor method to restrict access to SNAP,” Deabler-Meadows said.
“This is not the sort of change that can or should be done by an administrative agency through the waiver process,” she said. “This should be done via open debate in Congress.”
 Getting on the same page

Bauer said research shows programs that incentivize purchases of healthy food can improve the quality of people’s diets.
She gave the example of Double Up Food Bucks, which allows SNAP participants to get twice as much fresh produce when they use their benefits to buy fruits and vegetables.
“People want to eat healthy, and they want to feed their kids fruits and vegetables,” Bauer said. “They know what’s healthy. That’s not the limiting factor. The limiting factor is the amount of money they have.”
Bauer also pointed to difficulties retailers could face implementing SNAP restrictions. One recent study shows that since states began implementing the waivers this year, slightly fewer convenience stores are accepting SNAP benefits.
Shaul said he wants to make sure grocers making a good-faith effort to comply with the coming SNAP restrictions don’t get penalized for noncompliance.
“We’re going to continue to work with the department to try to get to a point where everybody is in the same — I won’t even say the same page, but the same book,” Shaul said. “I’d love to be in the same chapter.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Commentary: The real story behind that Thanksgiving turkey that prompted the Kentucky Capitol haz-mat response
description: Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces. The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible flesh-rot that despised humankind. It wasn’t just a […]
text:
This is not the maintenance worker who responded to an unusual post-Thanksgiving emergency outside the Kentucky Capitol Annex. That incident went unphotographed, as far as we know, though not forgotten. (Getty Images)Frankfort’s small army of state workers, fresh from four days off for Thanksgiving on Dec. 1, 1997, slipped from their cars in normal morning sun and almost as one looked to the sky with twisted, stricken faces.
The Capitol Annex parking lot seemed misted with some indelible flesh-rot that despised humankind. It wasn’t just a smell but a Presence. It sucked life from you; your soul departed and you knew it would not return. Your eyes glazed toward opaque. You could not breathe but for shallow, burning gasps that presaged death rattle.
Of all possible causes, you wouldn’t at this moment imagine a turkey.
Yet. Over there, 30 feet yonder, a maintenance lad in a white haz-mat suit with a stout black bag and a muscular garbage picker crept toward a thing on the Annex lawn. It looked like a yellowed stew of plastic and flesh. It seemed to glow and quiver. Some brave parking-lot sufferer managed to croak out toward the creeping lad, “Dear God, son … What … Why?”
“Some a-hole threw a turkey on the lawn,” the lad said, in a voice that echoed death. It was a sentence as final and direct as, “They launched the nuclear missiles.”
When he’d kissed his wife goodbye that morning, the young man had no clue what this day would bring. He was about to be a hero. He retrieved the turkey. He lost his sense of smell. “Like starin’ at the Sun and goin’ blind,” he told the Workers Comp Board weeks later, I heard. It was a metaphor nailed down tight.
So this is a story I’ve been badgered to tell since then. It started when Rep. Jim Callahan of Southgate gave me a Thanksgiving turkey.
Jim was House Democratic Caucus chairman. In the happy event he liked you, you could have no finer friend in the stinging spin-drift of the Kentucky legislature. If he didn’t, he was one of the few people who could and would get you fired. A man to be trusted and feared. A perfect politician.
I had just lately and reluctantly been put in charge of the Legislative Research Commission’s Public Information Office, a communications shop whose future was in doubt because of some early Republican restiveness. They didn’t find the office deferential enough. It likely wasn’t.
I made it my strategic purpose in life to become indispensable to Jim, so he (and the House Dems, then lazy with a comfortable majority) would protect me against the new restive Republican hordes. I succeeded with Jim, the caucus obeyed his instructions re: me, and in late 1997 Jim started rewarding me for my many good works with appreciated tokens like holiday meats.
The day before this particular Thanksgiving — five days before the maintenance lad’s heroics — Jim’s lanky assistant presented me with my first turkey, laid the sweaty sucker on my desk, bagged in plastic, pristine, frozen and promptly forgotten.
Forgotten, that is to say, in my windowless, steam-heated office, 80 degrees at least, with four black holidays awaiting it and a billion turkey-flesh bacteria awakening to yawn, scratch themselves, and eat.
Flash forward: 9:27 p.m., Payton Residence, Louisville. Sat. Nov. 29.
Quick scene:
“Aw, MAN! NO!”
“What?”
“I forgot the damn TURKEY!”
“What turkey?”
“The one Jim C. gave me three days ago that’s sitting on my desk like a bomb about to explode, if it hasn’t already! I have to get it.’
(Indistinct squabbling).
Even quicker scene:
“You’re not driving a hundred miles round-trip to Frankfort in the dead of night to retrieve a turkey that’s wrapped in plastic and perfectly fine. No.”
Note to young husbands: There are many days coming in your marriage when you simply look at your wife’s slant eyes and surrender. I surrendered. Fifty miles east, the turkey-flesh bacteria ate and ate.
The rest of the weekend was like waiting for biopsy results. Monday morning I drove to work early, dreading what I’d find, hoping against hope the turkey hadn’t exploded but otherwise wanting to get things cleaned up and tended to as best I could before anyone else arrived. Pretty sure I was first in the parking lot slammed by the Presence, the living thing I’d birthed.
The Kentucky Capitol and Annex are in the author’s hometown of Frankfort along the Kentucky River. (University of Kentucky Libraries, Special Collections Research Center, Post Card Collection)
But hope withstood its first assault. As a Frankfort native, I was accustomed to its distilleries, specifically the smell of its distilleries burning mash. The signature smell of the Kentucky River valley. In many ways, Frankfort is a smell. It’s not necessarily a good smell; many find it rank. But all share in it. Every redneck boy, every doctor’s son, every lawyer’s daughter and governor’s privileged kid walks out on fall mornings into its egalitarian embrace. It is hillbilly Marxism: Share the stink.
So for no more than half a second I thought/hoped this stink might be mash. For the second half-second I thought, “Whew, did they throw some rotting sheep cadavers into the mash vats this morning?” Then of course I knew: Turkey. Hissing from my office. Into the Annex HVAC system. Leaking out the old building’s windows. Filling the river valley. Soon to make me the laughing stock of Frankfort. Republicans would say this proved my liberalism.
I try to be relatively accurate in memoirish accounts like this (facts are critically important until they interfere with a good laugh). So I’ll admit the next half hour is a blur that resists disinterment.
The grotesque bird was still on my desk, its plastic bag ripped open by the force of its eruption. I recall an echoey dripping sound onto the floor, a yellowish oozing slime, thick like molasses, that seemed alive itself (remember, it teemed with a billion chomping necrobiomes). It looked like some bad special-effects alien from the first season of Star Trek in 1966.
I cannot remember how I managed to scoop up the carcass itself, make some quick impossible decision about disposing of it, and rush it down the still-deserted Annex hall to the bronze entry doors, where I flung it mightily onto the front lawn and the Presence began spreading in earnest, as did its legend.
At some point the heroic haz-mat kid was called, he gave the remains their final scoop, yet the smell snaked through the Capitol campus (HVAC circulation and filters are eternal, and the river valley itself a thermal trap). Many workers went home for an extra day or two of Thanksgiving celebration. Every sentence at home began “You won’t believe…”
Me, I suffered the derision I deserved, and have at least once a year for 27 years been hectored into telling “Scott’s Turkey Story” to wildly laughing, knee-slapping audiences. I’ve hated it every time, knowing they’re not exactly laughing with me, and sworn for many years I’d “write it up” and just hand the sucker out at every such request.
So now I’ve done that. Here you are. Don’t ask again.
But.
Coda: There is more to the story, and it’s good, but it doesn’t belong to me. It belongs to a fellow Capitol staffer who worked a mysterious deskless job for people who seemed powerful. His name recalls that of a major world capital. He would “borrow” your desk without asking if he needed one. Jim Callahan gave him a turkey every year too.
This is a grand fellow, as all in politics must be, but a bit absent-minded, as most in politics are. To his credit though, and unlike me, he miraculously got his gifted bird to his car that afternoon. Threw it in the trunk. Promptly forgot it.
A week or so later, troubled by some mystery problem with the car — couldn’t quite put his finger on it, snap, snap! — he dropped it off at the repair shop.
From memory:
FRANKFORT STATE JOURNAL
Police Reports 12/8/97
Police responded at 8:19 a.m. to call from Willie and Joe’s Auto Service on East Main of a suspected dead body, decomposed in trunk of customer’s vehicle. Officers opened trunk, discovered turkey.

title: Cost of Thanksgiving dinner went up 6% from last year
description: A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people costs on average $58.63 in 2026, which is a 6% increase from the cost in 2025, according to the annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation.  The biggest cost increase from 2025 to 2026: turkey. The Thanksgiving centerpiece was 10% more expensive, according to the grocery shopping survey, […]
text:
The cost of a Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people increased 6% in 2026 according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. (Photo by Cami Koons/Iowa Capital Dispatch) A Thanksgiving dinner for 10 people costs on average $58.63 in 2026, which is a 6% increase from the cost in 2025, according to the annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. 
The biggest cost increase from 2025 to 2026: turkey. The Thanksgiving centerpiece was 10% more expensive, according to the grocery shopping survey, with an average price of $23.68 per 16-pound bird in 2026. 
Farm Bureau reported the cost of the meal is nearly $3.50 higher than 2025’s meal — but in inflation-adjusted figures, that’s a difference of about 38 cents, or a 2% increase. Last year’s Thanksgiving meal was also the lowest cost, according to the survey, since 2022. The 2026 average cost is similar to the cost of the meal in 2024. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
According to Gov. Kim Reynolds’ turkey pardoning proclamation, Iowa is seventh in the nation for turkey production, raising about 12 million turkeys annually. 
The Farm Bureau report said strong demand for turkey and tight inventories have led to increased prices for turkey in 2026. U.S. Department of Agriculture outlooks from October predicted turkey prices will continue to increase in 2027 and showed an increase in turkey production in 2026 compared to the year prior. 
Iowa Secretary of Agriculture Mike Naig read a proclamation from Gov. Kim Reynolds pardoning Early and Bird. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The highly pathogenic avian influenza continues to impact the turkey industry. While Iowa has had fewer than 10 cases in 2026, a Sac County commercial turkey flock of about 44,400 birds had a case of bird flu at the end of October. The virus impacts poultry production and supply, but turkey and chicken products remain safe to consume. 
Reporting from Stateline noted that labor shortages caused by changes to immigration policy also contribute to higher turkey prices. 
Turkey wasn’t the only item on the menu that increased in price this year. Boneless ham, milk, dinner rolls, sweet potatoes, russet potatoes, frozen peas, frozen green beans, cranberries and cubed stuffing also went up this year from last year.
Farm Bureau said there are myriad factors driving price increases that “aren’t a complete surprise.” Higher input costs including diesel fuel, fertilizers and labor make food production more expensive. 
A regional analysis of Thanksgiving meal prices show feasters on the East Coast will pay the highest price for their meal, with an average cost of $61.57 for the 10-person meal. Midwesterners will shell out $56.89 for the meal, which was more expensive than shoppers in the South, but slightly cheaper than Western states. 
The cost of vegetable trays and frozen pie crusts declined in 2026 compared to 2025, according to Farm Bureau. Heavy whipping cream also decreased from the year prior. 
Farmers receive a relatively small share of the food dollar, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. The latest data showed farmers make, on average, just under 13 cents per dollar spent by U.S. consumers on domestically produced food.
Farm Bureau said this means when consumers pay higher prices at the grocery store, it might translate into higher revenues on farms but they can be “quickly offset” by mounting production costs. 
A National Farmers Union analysis of the farmer share of the dollar shows farmers receive less than 10 cents per consumer dollar spent on Thanksgiving foods like turkey, sweet corn, stuffing and dinner rolls. 
National Farmers Union President Rob Larew said in a statement that the consumer price only tells “part of the story.”
“But higher grocery prices don’t mean farmers are earning more,” Larew said. “When a handful of powerful companies dominate agricultural and food markets, farmers and families are left with fewer choices and less power. We need a fairer food system that works better for everyone.”

title: Health insurers are dropping Idaho Medicare Advantage plans that cover tens of thousands
description: Nearly a third of Idaho seniors who have private Medicare coverage are set to lose those health insurance plans next year. More than 60,000 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that are set to be canceled statewide or in their county, according to federal data analyzed by Idaho health insurance brokers.  With a week […]
text:
With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help. (Photo by Getty Images)Nearly a third of Idaho seniors who have private Medicare coverage are set to lose those health insurance plans next year.
More than 60,000 Idahoans are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans that are set to be canceled statewide or in their county, according to federal data analyzed by Idaho health insurance brokers. 
Your Health Idaho is in open enrollment. Insurance premiums hikes might be tamped down.

With a week and a half left in Medicare open enrollment, insurance brokers are encouraging Idaho seniors to read mailed notices from their insurer to understand if their plan is being canceled, and reach out for help.
“It’s actually causing a lot of panic with seniors,” Coeur d’Alene based broker Malia Rogers said.
This year, she said seniors are navigating plan cancellations, trying to make sure their medical providers are still accepting their Medicare Advantage plan, and checking that their prescriptions are still covered.
“Don’t try to do it on your own, because there’s so many things … to watch out for,” Rogers said. “My recommendation is to find a broker. Brokers have a trained set of eyes, and we never charge for our services, so our services are free.”
Nearly half of the people who are on Medicare in Idaho are enrolled in Medicare Advantage plans, which tend to cover extra benefits than traditional Medicare. 
Some seniors are being hit harder by the cancellations because their Medicare Advantage plans were tailored to their needs. Marcia Benton, a broker in Meridian, said some people in North Idaho won’t be able to find comparable plans. Rural areas, she said, will also be hit hard. 
 If your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, what can you do?

Open enrollment for Medicare ends Dec. 7. 
In a statement last month, Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron encouraged Medicare members to tap free help from a licensed agent or a Medicare counselor with Senior Health Insurance Benefits Advisors, a state service available by phone at 1-800-247-4422 or online at https://doi.idaho.gov/shiba/about-shiba/ask-shiba/.
“While some carriers are exiting the market, Idaho still offers a competitive selection of plans and strong consumer protections,” Cameron said.
But if your Medicare Advantage plan is being terminated, you may be able to switch to another plan or traditional Medicare after through a special enrollment period.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Insurers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with inflation, broker says

State insurance officials say the scalebacks in Idaho and across the nation are caused by a mix of regulations, federal pay structures and rising costs. This is the second year of major Medicare Advantage cancellations in Idaho, but brokers say that less Idahoans are enrolled in plans being terminated this year than last year. 
Insurance carriers haven’t seen federal pay rates keep up with sharp medical inflation, Benton said. She called the Medicare Advantage market unstable and said plan closures can result in higher costs for consumers.
“But we do need to stop having these closures. Because moving mass amounts of people from plan to plan is not good for any carrier,” Benton said.
UnitedHealthcare is closing two Idaho plans, along with withdrawing from several counties across the state. About 16,500 Idaho seniors are enrolled in the plans affected. In a statement, a spokesperson for the insurer said its moves in Idaho are meant to “help ensure long-term sustainability of our plans.”
“UnitedHealthcare is making targeted changes to our Medicare Advantage offerings for 2027 to help ensure long-term sustainability of our plans,” the spokesperson said. “We are here to support members through any necessary transition and remain committed to helping everyone understand their options.”
Other health insurers that are canceling plans in Idaho could not be immediately reached for comment.
