Hiki ke pālua ka waiwai o ka ʻoihana mahiʻai o ka mokuʻāina inā ua māmā mai nā lula pekelala pili ponoʻī iā Hawaiʻi e ʻoi aku ai ka papaha no nā mahiʻai e kūʻai aku ai i nā hua ma ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa.



Civil Beat stories ma ka ʻōlelo Hawaiʻi 
'Ka Ulana Pilina' is an ongoing collection of news articles and opinion pieces written in the Hawaiian language to better connect with our Indigenous readers, identify underreported stories and improve our engagement with an underserved community.





Read All

Pēlā mai ka Hawaiʻi Institute for Public Affairs ma ka moʻolelo hope iho nei, kahi i wānana ʻia ai ka lilo o ka $800 miliona kālā i nā mahiʻai ma ka waiwai e loaʻa paha mai ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa i kēlā me kēia makahiki — he huinanui i ʻoi aku i ka waiwai pau loa o ka ʻoihana kāʻokoʻa.
Nānā ʻia ʻo Hawaiʻi he ʻāina ʻē ma ka ʻōnaehana pekelala e hōʻoia ana i ka palekana no nā mea ola e kū nei, he mea e ʻāʻumeʻume nei nā mahiʻai me nā lula pekelala ʻoʻoleʻa, a wahi a ka hui noiʻi, he mea e hiki ke hoʻonōhie ʻia no ke kōkua i ka mahiʻai ʻana. Ua hoʻokumu ʻia ia mau lula no ke kaupale ʻana iā ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa mai nā ʻelala mahiʻai he nui wale o Hawaiʻi, e laʻa ka nalo, he mea nō naʻe ia e pilikia nei nā mahiʻai o ka pae ʻāina ma ka mālama ʻana i ko lākou kaʻawale mai nā mākeke o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, wahi a ka moʻolelo.
Pāpā ʻia ma lalo o kekahi mau lula nōhihi ka hoʻouna ʻia o nā hua ʻai a lauʻai he nui i ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa e laʻa ke cacao. ʻAʻole hiki ke hoʻouna ʻia ka hua ʻai maoli inā ʻaʻole hoʻomaloʻo a hoʻomākaukau mua ʻia. (Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025) Kevin Fujii/Civil Beat/2025
E pono e lilo kēia he hopohopo ʻoihana hoʻokele waiwai no ka mokuʻāina, wahi a ka moʻolelo. He kōkua nui ka lapaʻau ʻana i kēia pilikia no ka mokuʻāina, e ʻae ana i nā mahiʻai e komo ma nā mākeke hou me nā hua hou a kahiko pū, wahi a Cameron Deptula, kekahi o nā mea kākau o ka moʻolelo.
Ua hoʻohiki nā alakaʻi mokuʻāina e hoʻonui i ka nui ʻai e hoʻoulu ʻia ma ka pae ʻāina a me ka lawa o ka ʻai no nā makahiki he nui, ua lilo nō naʻe nā ʻāʻumeʻume me ka pipiʻi o ka ʻāina, ka hana ʻana a nā kānaka, ka wai, a me ka nui wahi he ālaina. He 0.4% o ka ʻoihana hoʻokele waiwai o ka mokuʻāina ka ʻoihana mahiʻai, ma kahi o ka $554 miliona i ka makahiki 2025.
Ma ka mokuʻāina ka mole o ka nui o ia waiwai ʻoiai, kākaʻikahi ka haʻalele ʻana o kahi mea iā Hawaiʻi.
“Hoʻouna ʻia aku ka ʻuala kahiko, ka hēʻī, basil, a ʻo ia wale nō paha, wahi a Brian Miyamoto i ʻōlelo ai, ka luna hoʻokele hoʻokō o Hawaiʻi Farm Bureau.
Pōkole ka papa helu o nā hua a lau ʻai e ʻae ʻia. No nā mea hou, e laʻa nā ʻano maiʻa a hua ʻai ʻālani ponoʻī, aia ma ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono nā hōʻoia ʻana e loʻohia ai nā ʻāina mahiʻai i ka wā e hoʻāʻo ana e hoʻonui i kahi e kūʻai ʻia ai nā hua, wahi a Deptula.
E pono e lilo ka hoʻēmi ʻana i nā luhi o nā lula — ʻo ka nui, ʻo ka hoʻēmi ʻana i ka nui manawa e ʻāpono ʻia ai kahi hua hou, a he ʻelima makahiki i kekahi manawa — he makakoho, wahi a Deptula, he mea e noho nei he aʻoaʻo kūikawā i ke Kiaʻāina Josh Green.
Ma ka nui, e pono ko Hawaiʻi e hoʻonui i ka palekana o nā mea ola e huli ai ka manaʻo o ke aupuni pekelala no ka hoʻomāmā ʻana i nā lula a me ka hoʻopōkole ʻana i ka wā ʻāpono no nā hua a lau ʻai hou, wahi āna.
Aia he ʻelua hale mahiʻai ma ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono: ʻo Mahi Pono ma Maui no nā lemi, a ʻo Volcano Wasabi ma Hawaiʻi mokupuni.
Aia ka nui o ka nānā ʻia o nā hua a lau ʻai i ka nui o ka makaʻu i ka hopena e loaʻa paha no nā hua a lau ʻai o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, ma ka nui loa. For nā lemi, he nui loa nō ia, keu hoʻi ma nā wahi e like me Kaleponi. No laila, inā ua makemake ʻo Mahi Pono e hoʻouna he lemi ʻokoʻa i ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa, e pono ana e komo hou i ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono.
“ʻO ka pololei, ʻaʻole nānā ʻia ke ʻano o ka pea, ke ʻano o ka manakō,” i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Ken Love, ka luna hoʻokele hoʻokō o Hawaiʻi Tropical Fruit Growers.
A no Volcano Wasabi e hoʻoulu nei i ka wasabi ma Hawaiʻi mokupuni, ua hoʻomaka ka ʻōnaehana ʻāpono he ʻehā a ʻoi makahiki aku nei me kahi loiloi i ka makaʻu i ka hopena no nā ʻelala. No ka loiloi e koi ʻia ai ka noiʻi hohonu i nā hopena e pili pū ana me nā ʻelala ma luna o nā mea ola, he ʻelua paha makahiki ka lōʻihi o ia hana. A he ʻelua hou aku makahiki no ka ʻōnaehana loiloi i kō ʻole a i kēia.
Wānana ʻia ma ka moʻolelo ka pā a lilo o ka ʻoihana ma ka $760 miliona kālā, a he $40 miliona a ʻoi kālā ma ka hōʻoia ma mua o ka hoʻouna ʻana a me ka hahai lula.
“ʻAʻole nō nānā ʻia inā he ʻāina mahiʻai nui a kahiko kou nona nā lako e hana pū ai me nā kānaka loaʻa o ke kālā a no ka ʻimi i ke kākoʻo kānāwai, ʻo ia paʻa nō ia o nā ʻōnaehana liʻiliʻi a nui pū,” wahi a Deptula.
A laila, loaʻa nā lula hou aku e pākuʻi ʻia, ʻo ia hoʻi nā kiʻina koi ʻia, e pā ai paha ka maikaʻi o ka hua a lau ʻai, a pau ai ka pono. No ko Hawaiʻi mau manakō e pono e mālama ʻia i loko o ka wela ma mua o ka hoʻouna ʻia, makehewa ka hoʻouna ʻana a haʻalele i ka mokupuni, i ʻōlelo ai ʻo Love.
ʻOiai penei, he ʻelua wale nō ala no nā mahiʻai: ʻO ke kūʻai wale nō ma Hawaiʻi a ʻo ka ʻimi i nā ala e hoʻolilo ʻia ai ia mau mea he mau lako no ka hakakau i loaʻa ʻole nā ʻelala.
He ala nā kiʻina mālama e laʻa ka pepehi ʻelala a mūhune ma ka wela e hōʻoia ʻia ai ka loaʻa o ka nui kālā e hiki i nā mahiʻai a e hoʻēmi ʻia ai ka ʻōpala ma ke kiʻi i ka hua a lau ʻai i kū ʻole i nā lula o ka nānā ʻana. He ala pū nō naʻe ia e emi ai ka makaʻu i ka hopena no nā mahiʻai e lilo ana paha ka hua a lau ʻai ma muli o ka manawa i lilo i nā lula hoʻokaʻawale pekelala, wahi a Deptula, ʻo ia kekahi o nā kumu i hoʻokaʻawale ai nā ʻelele kau kānāwai i ke kālā ma nā miliona ma luna o nā hale mālama meaʻai ma ka mokuʻāina.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Miyamoto o ka Farm Bureau, ua kūkā ʻia kēia pilikia ma Wakinekona me ko Hawaiʻi mau ʻelele ʻahaʻōlelo. Ua hāpai pū ʻo ia i ke kuhina o ke Keʻena Mahiʻai o ʻAmelika Hui Pū ʻIa.
Ua ʻōlelo ʻo Love, e pono ka mokuʻāina e hānai mua i kona poʻe iho nō. Hoʻouna aku ka mokuʻāina he 20 miliona paona ʻālani a he 45 miliona paona maiʻa, wahi āna.
No laila, i loko nō o ka maikaʻi o ka hoʻonui ʻana i nā mea e hoʻouna ʻia aku ma kekahi mau ʻano, e pono pū e lilo he mea maʻamau nā papahana e ʻimi ana i nā pani no nā mea e hoʻouna ʻia mai i Hawaiʻi. Ua kākaʻahi iho nei ko Love hui he 12,000 kumu ʻālani a pūmaiʻa ma lalo o kahi papahana o ia ʻano e “kaulike” ai, wahi āna.

(Photo courtesy of Providence City Council)Free parking at designated metered parking spaces in Providence returns for the holiday shopping season starting Saturday, with up to two hours of free parking through Jan. 1, 2027.

A free “Candy Cane Express Train” will operate on the evenings of Thursday, Dec. 3 and Friday, Dec. 4, and make stops throughout downtown. On Saturday, Dec. 5, a downtown holiday trolley will make stops at shops, restaurants, and festival events between Biltmore Park, Downtown, Federal Hill and Track 15. 
A holiday market will run throughout the weekend, at Grant’s Block, located at the corner of Westminster and Union Streets, featuring entertainment, workshops and a showcase of local artists and small business.
The Providence Rink will open Friday, Nov. 27, for public skating and ice bumper cars through March. The rink will also host free ice skating performances on Dec. 4.
City Hall will host its annual Hanukkah Spectaculah on Monday, Dec. 7, from 4:45 to 6 p.m., with a menorah lighting, traditional foods, art activities and live klezmer music.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: The dream of farming is alive and well in New Hampshire — but it’s still a tough row to hoe
description: Sustainable, local, farm-to-table food can sound especially appealing in a world of hyper-processed products and periodic food-safety scares.  That’s just one of several ideals cited by some of the newest small-scale farmers to take the plunge into the world of New Hampshire agriculture. “Food security is the main goal here,” said Walter Alce, who dreams […]
text:
Running a small farm in New Hampshire requires a strong community and support system, said Jesse Wright, field specialist in agricultural business management with UNH Extension. Here, she speaks with new and aspiring farmers during an Extension New Farmer School session in Rochester on Oct. 14. From left: Walter Alce, Maria Elena Potter, Deborah Stacy, Sam Monohon, Wright, and Lisa Aquizap. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Sustainable, local, farm-to-table food can sound especially appealing in a world of hyper-processed products and periodic food-safety scares. 
That’s just one of several ideals cited by some of the newest small-scale farmers to take the plunge into the world of New Hampshire agriculture.
“Food security is the main goal here,” said Walter Alce, who dreams of running a self-sustaining family farm with his wife and four children — and who, last year, took a major step toward that goal when he purchased Elm Farm in Francestown.
It’s not an unusual dream. Others across New Hampshire also aspire to work the state’s land to produce crops and livestock for their families and neighbors. But for those new to the field, there’s lots to learn about the realities and limitations of farming in New Hampshire. And sometimes that journey comes with hard lessons along the way, experts and new farmers said.
Standing in a wood-heated greenhouse, Sam Monohon, co-owner of Nerdy Turnip Farm, addresses a group of new and aspiring farmers on Wednesday, Oct. 14, at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester. Monohon has co-owned Nerdy Turnip Farm for four growing seasons. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Food and community
Small family farms make up about 86% of all agricultural operations in the U.S., according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. In New Hampshire, that proportion is similar. According to 2022 data from the department, the median size of the state’s farms, by land area, is 37 acres; that year, the average operator took home $6,568 in net profit.
New and aspiring farmers come from diverse backgrounds, drawn to farming for many different reasons, said Jesse Wright, field specialist in agricultural business management with the University of New Hampshire Extension. 
With Caroline Beaton, Wright helps run the extension’s New Farmer School program, where some of those fledgling farmers gather. The class welcomes recent retirees and young adults; transplants and lifelong New Hampshire residents; and people who have dreamed of farming their whole life alongside people suddenly plunged into the field when they, say, inherited a family member’s land or married into a farming family, Wright said. 
Many, like Alce, were drawn to farming as a way to provide healthy food or other natural products for their family and community.
“This is where science and food and community and practicality all kind of meet together,” said Sam Monohon, who for four years has co-owned Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester, where New Farmer School students arrived for a tour of the grounds this fall.
Kale plants soak up October sunlight at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Finding a field to plant in
One of the first and biggest barriers many aspiring farmers face is land access.
The high cost of property and limited amount of well-suited farmland coming onto the market are major hurdles for many, Wright said. 
“If you don’t have space, or a space that’s well suited to growing, it’s kind of a non-starter,” she said.
Alce and his wife searched for over three years before finding the right property that could support the chickens, pigs, cows and other livestock they wanted to raise. Navigating fluctuating interest rates and a competitive market for land was a frustrating and drawn-out process, he said.
At the same time, it felt like the puzzle piece that would make everything else fall into place.
“Land is something you can’t make more of,” Alce said. “You find the land, then anything else, and everything else, is possible.”
In the end, Alce said, success came down to “being in the right place at the right time and sending out the right email.”
But for others — some of whom cannot afford to purchase land themselves or struggle to find a suitable property — newer, creative approaches to secure land access can help, said Beaton. These include joining forces with other aspiring farmers to make joint land purchases; renting fields instead of buying land; and working with land trusts and other groups to access agricultural conservation land. 
A turnip launched by Sam Monohon, co-owner of Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester, sails over new farmer Allyson Traeger’s head and into the waiting hands of Robbin Ray, media relations director with the University of New Hampshire, on Wednesday, Oct. 14. Monohon welcomed new and aspiring farmers to her property for a tour that day as part of the “New Farmer School” program run by UNH Extension. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Sowing spreadsheets
Like the matter of land, many other parts of the high barrier to entry for beginning farmers are also financial. In a broad sense, one thing most non-farmers may not realize is the sheer amount of business savvy required to run a successful farm, Monohon said.
“Every farmer that I know is secretly a giant spreadsheet nerd,” she joked. “Doing the farming is kind of a small piece of what it ends up being, when you own the farm or when you manage or run the farm.”
Rising costs have also hit farmers, and the price of production for crops and livestock can be staggering for those just getting into farming. For Alce, that realization hit him when he first began looking into raising chickens.
“I think most of us don’t know the true cost of food,” Alce said. 
Government subsidies for large-scale farms can obscure the true cost of food and make it hard for small farms to compete, Alce said.
Turnips are ready for harvest at Nerdy Turnip Farm in Rochester on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
Wright recalled a conversation with an aspiring farmer and New Farmer School participant who calculated the total cost of producing their goods, from seeds to fertilizer, feed and labor, and concluded that to charge anything over the actual cost of production would price out members of their community.
Farmers must also contend with the normal costs of running a small business: accounting and payment processing, wages for their laborers and insurance, to name a few, Monohon said.
Marketing is a major task for farmers, who must cultivate a reliable customer base in addition to their crops and products. For many, this means reluctantly posting on social media.
“The shiny, beautiful, outside thing is the growing of the things, and the less fun thing is the number crunching and the Facebook posting,” Wright said.
Affording health insurance for themselves as well as their employees is a major burden on many beginning farmers and, in some cases, a barrier to entering the field, Beaton said. 
To make it work, many farmers work a day job. Alce and his wife both work 9 to 5, while Monohon’s husband, Caleb, works full time, allowing the couple and their two toddlers to access health insurance through his work. Many other participants in New Farmer School also said they work day jobs, have a family member who does or are retired.
It’s a difficult reality that can bring up complicated feelings for farmers. 
“There’s a lot of imposter syndrome feelings that I get,” Monohon said. “… It is a difficult thing to do without that kind of tie into society. Farming can kind of make you self reliant, but Caleb and I have not figured out a way to be entirely just on the farm.”
It’s a common struggle, Wright said: Aspiring farmers enter the field with big dreams and wholehearted visions for their future, while societal barriers make those dreams difficult to realize. 
Helping farmers access resources and promoting programs like incubator farms, extension trainings and community support is crucial to helping lessen the burden, as is transparency about the difficulty of the endeavor, she said.
It’s possible to achieve the dream of a small, sustainable farm successfully, she said, but not without multifaceted community support.
“I think we have to be done pretending that you can have a small farm in New Hampshire and support a family, support a lot of folks’ vision for what life can look like without some of these background levers being pulled,” she said. 
Tomatoes that dropped from the summer’s plants and escaped harvest lie on the floor of a greenhouse in Rochester on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)
A committed lifestyle
Beyond the finances, living as a farmer requires near-constant commitment.
One thing that some New Farmer School participants are dismayed to learn is that farmers “can’t necessarily go on vacation,” Beaton said. 
Alce said he decided against raising dairy cows after talking to other farmers, who told him they were a seven-day-a-week commitment. It’s knowledge-sharing and discussions like that, he said, that have helped him gather experience and avoid pitfalls as he gets his footing.
Contending with the unpredictability of growing is one of the biggest struggles of the farming life, said Monohon. Weather, pests and a revolving array of unforeseeable circumstances — like fungus or equipment problems — can turn plans upside down. 
But for Monohon, after four years of running the farm, the plunge has proven worthwhile. After the trial-by-fire days of navigating both farm ownership and parenthood for the first time, Monohon said, she feels a new era beginning. And though her day-to-day is still full of challenges, seeing the farm take on a life of its own has been both fulfilling and exciting.
“There’s something really wonderful about it,” she said. “… I have my little chunk of land that I’m going to do with what I can to make the greatest positive impact on this greater problem, and help protect my family and my friends and my community in future years.”
New and aspiring farmers stand among pieces of twine used to support tomato plants in a greenhouse at Nerdy Turnip Farm, in Rochester, on Oct. 14. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)

title: With weeks until federal law changes, here’s what you need to know about hemp-based THC
description: With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years. Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparin[...]
text:
A change in federal law coming next month could change the market for hemp-based THC drinks, seen here at a St. Paul market. (Photo by J. Patrick Coolican/Minnesota Reformer)

With just three weeks until a strict new federal definition of hemp takes effect, business owners and consumers are scrambling to understand what the changes will mean for the availability of the intoxicating hemp-derived products like gummies and drinks that have been widely available for years.
Minnesota’s top cannabis regulator said his office is preparing for either possibility: that the law takes effect, or Congress delays or overturns it.
U.S. Sen. (and Gov.-elect) Amy Klobuchar introduced a bill Tuesday with GOP Sen. Tim Sheehy of Montana that would loosen the definition of hemp and create a regulatory framework for intoxicating hemp products.
If things feel like they are in flux, it’s because they are. Here’s what you need to know about the new hemp law, what could yet happen and what it means for you.
How did we get here?
It all started back in 2018 when the federal Agriculture Improvement Act – better known as the Farm Bill – legalized hemp products containing up to 0.3% by weight of delta-9 tetrahydrocannabinol (THC), the primary compound in marijuana that produces a high.
That meant all sorts of hemp-derived THC products, such as gummies, beverages and topical ointments, were legal nationwide, as long as they met that 0.3% THC threshold. These products quickly became available in stores nationwide, but Congress did not create any mechanism to regulate them, leaving that to the states.
Some states, like Minnesota and Indiana, created their own regulations for hemp. But many others did not, and these products were essentially unregulated in many places.
In November 2025, Congress attempted to put the toothpaste back in the tube by passing a new definition of hemp that will outlaw most intoxicating hemp products in much of the country. Under the new rules set to take effect Dec. 11, any product containing more than 0.4 milligrams of THC per container will be considered marijuana under federal law. That standard is so strict that many nonintoxicating products, such as a topical balm containing the cannabinoid CBD, along with trace amounts of THC, will also become federally illegal.
What happens next in Washington?
Without further congressional action, the new law goes into effect next month, though a handful of bills have been introduced to either postpone or rewire the new rules. The legislation introduced this week is Klobuchar’s third hemp-focused bill of the session. So far, none have moved forward.
But some industry insiders are cautiously optimistic about the Klobuchar-Sheehy bill, also known as the Hemp Guardrails Act. The bill would raise the potency threshold for hemp products to a maximum of 1% by weight total THC (which includes all forms of tetrahydrocannabinol, not just delta-9); empower the Food and Drug Administration to regulate hemp products and producers; prohibit sales of hemp-derived products to those under the age of 21; create packaging and marketing standards; ban synthetic cannabinoids; and allow states to enact stricter regulations.
“Minnesota is a national leader in hemp, and our state has shown that we can protect kids and support responsible hemp businesses,” Klobuchar said in a statement, adding that the measure “would keep safe hemp products on store shelves, protect consumers from dangerous products, and ensure that farmers and small businesses can continue to operate, grow and create jobs.”
Outgoing Sen. Tina Smith of Minnesota also supports reversing the new law, citing a conversation with a Minnesota brewer. The industry has embraced hemp-based drinks but faces a challenging future in that market segment if the law goes into effect.
“I was just at an event with Utepils where the owner and I agreed that this federal ban is misguided and will hurt our brewers if it isn’t delayed, or better yet, reversed altogether,” Smith said in a statement.
A major potential roadblock remains: A pair of Republican senators — who are still in the majority during the lame-duck session — are vowing to block any bill that “extends, delays or builds a regulatory framework” around hemp products.
It’s possible that no deal is reached before the new Congress is sworn in next year. With large Democratic majorities in both houses and a White House that has signaled support for regulating hemp, the law could get an update in 2027, but passing laws is typically more difficult than blocking them.
In Washington, D.C., Beecher Vaillancourt was in a taxi on Tuesday during a “hill climb” trip to lobby legislators on behalf of the U.S. Hemp Roundtable. Vaillancourt, who owns the Minneapolis-based Foundry Nation and BLNCD Naturals brands of hemp-derived products with his wife, Allison, said his sales to distributors have also dropped off precipitously in recent months. But it’s been counteracted a bit by a spike in online sales, he said.
Vaillancourt’s companies held two “warehouse sales” to move unsold product in recent months. They’re working to build up wholesale and dispensary sales in Minnesota to compensate for the potential loss of out-of-state sales. They’re also in the process of getting an adult-use cannabis license to expand their product lines into the recreational marijuana market, he said.
In the event a deal is reached, Vaillancourt has stocked up on ingredients so they can immediately ramp up production again.
“We’re hedging our bets, optimistically,” he said.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Buy Nothing Day free coat exchange in Providence turns 30
description: Head to the sprawling front lawn of the Rhode Island State House on Friday morning and you can get a warm winter coat for the attractive price of nothing. But it does cost a lot of time and effort — plus a 26-foot U-Haul — to gather the hundreds of coats to be given out […]
text:
Bags of donated winter clothing fill a 26-foot rental truck ahead of Rhode Island's 30th annual Buy Nothing Day Coat Exchange, scheduled for Friday, Nov. 27, 2026, at the State House in Providence. A volunteer stands amid the donations in the photo at right. (Photos courtesy of Lauren Testoni)Head to the sprawling front lawn of the Rhode Island State House on Friday morning and you can get a warm winter coat for the attractive price of nothing.
But it does cost a lot of time and effort — plus a 26-foot U-Haul — to gather the hundreds of coats to be given out gratis each year on Smith Hill as part of Rhode Island’s Buy Nothing Day Coat Exchange, which marks its 30th anniversary year. 
Chief organizer Lauren Testoni of East Greenwich said this year’s coat drive runs from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Friday, or until supplies run out, on the State House lawn, across from Providence Place. In the event of rain, Testoni said the event will be held in Gloria Dei Lutheran Church, right down the street.
Annual free coat giveaway set for Black Friday on R.I. State House lawn

The event’s placement across from Providence Place is somewhat ironic given its origins in the late 1990s as a local anticonsumerist effort and part of Buy Nothing Day, an anti-Black-Friday observance founded in 1992. 
The annual giveaway has historically distributed an estimated 1,500 coats a year. Testoni said she doesn’t keep a precise census of how many coats are collected or distributed, but a photo she shared of this year’s haul depicted a mountain of coat-filled bags packing into the interior of a 26-foot rental truck.
“Whatever that comes out to, I would say thousands,” Testoni said.
Demand remains substantial, Testoni noted, and seems to have grown alongside donations and the number of volunteers who help out.
“It’s grown in size, it’s grown in the amount of people that we can help, it’s grown in the number of donations we get and community partners we have,” Testoni said. “But I think the sad part is that the need has never gone away.”
Some former customers, Testoni said, have become part of the exchange’s stable of volunteers.
“We have people come year over year and truly like I only know their first names and I only see them this one day, and they are mostly people who were unhoused at some point,” Testoni said. “It’s nice to see that they stay, come back, help, give back, knowing where they were.” 
Testoni said that, beyond the holiday season when people are “very giving,” she hopes others think of people with unmet needs at other times of the year. 
“Just keep everyone in mind throughout the year would be my one thing that I would ask of everyone,” Testoni said. 
Donations are down slightly compared to previous years, Testoni said, but the items donated this year are generally of better quality. 
“I think the quality has gone up,” Testoni said. “We usually have a lot of filler stuff.”
Testoni and her mom, Pam, started leading the coat drive together about a decade ago, with the two of them working together as lead organizers for about seven years. Pam Testoni stepped down from the leadership role a few years ago, but still volunteers. Now after 10 years, Testoni is hoping to find a new leader for the charitable effort.
“I would just like to step back and be a volunteer rather than kind of running the whole show,” Testoni said in an interview Wednesday.
The most important qualification for her successor?
“Someone with a kind heart. That’s all I care about,” Testoni said.
More information, including where to donate, can be found on the Coat Exchange’s website. Testoni said the drive particularly needs children’s coats and adult sizes 3X and larger.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How prepared meals are helping fill in food aid gaps in Portland and across Maine
description: Ron Stanley has been unhoused in Portland for six years, but it wasn’t until last October that he found a reliable place to secure a hot lunch. Now, Stanley, along with dozens of others, most of whom are unhoused, gather each day on Cotton Street to get two prepared meals along with dry goods, packaged […]
text:
Volunteers package hot meals at Cotton Street's food distribution site on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)Ron Stanley has been unhoused in Portland for six years, but it wasn’t until last October that he found a reliable place to secure a hot lunch. Now, Stanley, along with dozens of others, most of whom are unhoused, gather each day on Cotton Street to get two prepared meals along with dry goods, packaged food and drinks.
“I don’t know how people are going to get a hot meal if these guys don’t show up,” Stanley said, gesturing toward the volunteers handing out food.
“It’s always a pretty good meal too,” he said. “They’re always hot, they’re nutritious and they have people here that can support and counsel us, too.”
Ron Stanley at Cotton Street’s food distribution hub on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
The meals come from nonprofit Preble Street, which prepares everything served on site at its Food Security Hub in South Portland. The City of Portland collaborates with the nonprofit, providing tables, chairs and a canopy for people to sit under and eat their meals. Volunteers from Milestone Recovery and various faith-based organizations often hand out meals.
“This fills the gap for people who are staying outside for consistent meal services, and it’s the lowest barrier option for consistent food in the city, especially with SNAP changes,” said Andrew Volkers, Preble Street’s director of health services and Street Outreach Collaborative. “In these times, hot food can really feel like a privilege.”
The need for services like the one on Cotton Street comes as food insecurity continues to rise across Maine. According to the latest national food insecurity data from Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap study, 14.5% of Maine residents experienced food insecurity in 2024, up from 13.8% the previous year.
Since then, President Donald Trump’s administration has cut access to federal food assistance for thousands of Mainers. Combined with rising costs for food, energy and other essentials, an even larger percentage of people currently have limited or uncertain access to food. 
But for people who rely on services like those at Cotton Street, access to food is only part of what makes them important. The opportunity to sit down, share a meal and spend time with others can be just as meaningful, particularly during the holidays, Volkers said. Last year was the first Thanksgiving meal the nonprofit offered in downtown Portland.
“Last year on Thanksgiving when I was here, it just felt happy and lively, and there was a lot of camaraderie,” Volkers said. “Not only food-centric holidays, but family-centric holidays bring up a lot … like trauma, lack of social support, lack of family. So offering hot meals and pie, and just sitting with them for the afternoon I think is really important.”
The Cotton Street location is part of a broader effort by Preble Street to expand access to prepared food across Maine, which accelerated after the nonprofit opened its Food Security Hub in South Portland in 2025. 
There is more demand than ever among food pantries for prepared meals, according to Colin Freeman, the organization’s chief director of community partnerships. Now that the organization has a facility in which it can cook up to 2,000 meals a day, and store thousands of frozen fully prepared meals, they can come closer to meeting it. The kitchen has the capacity for them to eventually scale up to 10,000 meals every day. 
Volunteers and staff prep mushrooms at Preble Street’s Food Security Hub on Nov. 25, 2026. (Photo by Eesha Pendharkar/Maine Morning Star)
Those meals are prepared with produce donated by Maine farms and are distributed within Preble Street’s Portland shelters, on Cotton Street and — most recently — through Good Shepherd Food Bank to pantries across the state.
“Pantries really need to fill this market where there’s people that don’t have the time to be able to produce their own meals, because if you see the kind of food that they’re receiving, it’s dried beans and things that are laborious and take time to really create delicious meals out of,” Freeman said.
“So for somebody that’s trying to work, take care of their kids, keep a house over their head, and cook for their family at the same time, this kind of meal is such a helpful thing.”
Last month, Preble Street announced the partnership with Good Shepherd funded by a $150,000 grant from Hannaford Bros. The program, called Harvest to Home, has already offered more than 10,000 meals in the month since it launched, with the goal being 100,000 meals a year.
“Access to nutritious food means more than having something to eat, it means having food that supports health, well-being and dignity,” Good Shepherd Food Bank President Heather Paquette said in a statement announcing the partnership. “Together, we can reach communities across all 16 counties and strengthen our collective response to hunger.”

title: Commentary: Imagining a future for New Hampshire’s youth
description: New Hampshire has an age problem. This problem would not be entirely solved by more housing, higher-paying jobs or better transportation. In my career as a community developer, I am convinced the problem is not an aging workforce but a youth-retention issue. Young people growing up in New Hampshire are not filling those workforce positions […]
text:
"Young people need to imagine becoming the adults they want to be right here in New Hampshire. These aren’t just dreams but rather questions of belonging, opportunity and agency." (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)New Hampshire has an age problem. This problem would not be entirely solved by more housing, higher-paying jobs or better transportation. In my career as a community developer, I am convinced the problem is not an aging workforce but a youth-retention issue. Young people growing up in New Hampshire are not filling those workforce positions in the numbers we need to thrive as a state. 
A new report from the New Hampshire Fiscal Policy Institute reveals some concerning trends. Undergraduate enrollment within the University System of New Hampshire has declined by more than 19% over the past decade. The percentage of recent high school graduates pursuing higher education dropped from approximately 61% in 2014 to 54% in 2024. Among those pursuing four-year degrees, 3 in 5 leave New Hampshire to attend college.
Additionally, the number of education degrees awarded by New Hampshire’s public colleges and universities has declined by more than half since the 2010–2011 academic year, raising additional concerns about the workforce that supports young people’s development.
Of course we need greater investment in public education from early childhood through college. We need attainable housing, livable wages, expanded and consistent transportation, and affordable childcare from birth through middle school and beyond.
Even if all that took shape and we made it possible for young adults to stay, wanting them to stay are two different ideas.
Through my work in youth development, workforce partnerships and community engagement at Monadnock United Way, I have been questioning how we approach youth retention on the local, regional and state level. We spend substantial time and resources exploring what young adults need to establish themselves here, but far less on the experience of growing up here, and how that might influence their desire to stay or leave more permanently. 
In the years before proms, college applications and first jobs, youth are actively developing an understanding of their communities and their place within them.
Research shows that youth need welcoming places to gather that do not cost money. They need safe and meaningful relationships with adults outside their families and opportunities to explore their interests, followed by various pathways to pursue their aspirations. Youth need spaces to express their opinions and know that it matters. Then they need to be shown it matters.
Most significantly, young people need to imagine becoming the adults they want to be right here in New Hampshire. These aren’t just dreams but rather questions of belonging, opportunity and agency.
Research from our own state suggests that these connections matter. The University of New Hampshire’s 10-year Coös Youth Study found that young people who felt heard and respected by adults were more inclined to want to remain in the region as adults themselves. Additional research identified family ties and community support as important factors in young adults’ decisions about staying or returning.
After-school and summer programs, paid internships, mentorship, libraries, recreation, arts organizations and accessible gathering spaces help cultivate these connections, as do the trained professionals who make these experiences possible.
While these seem like fun, extracurricular activities for children and families (and yes, some are very fun!) are also part of the basic social infrastructure that connects young people to the places they already call home.
There are already plenty of organizations and initiatives doing this work in New Hampshire.
Fund IRL New Hampshire, a statewide coalition convened by the New Hampshire Afterschool Network but joined by 20 other organizations, is advocating for investment of social media settlement funds in youth well-being, including mental and behavioral health services, out-of-school-time programming, professional development and meaningful real-world experiences.
Regional initiatives such as the emerging Connecting Monadnock and the North Country’s Positive Youth Development Collaborative are recognizing the importance of community connection, belonging and participation. These projects align with the people already doing this great work instead of duplicating programs.
New Hampshire also has established models for youth leadership and civic engagement through the New Hampshire Teen Institute, YouthWell Voices, Getting to Y, the Governor’s Youth Advisory Council and the Legislative Youth Advisory Council.
These exist already. Now we need to extend these opportunities beyond the youth-serving sector. But how?
Towns and municipalities could create youth advisory councils or hold seats designated for youth representatives on local committees and boards. Regional planning commissions and business networks could incorporate youth listening sessions into community and strategic planning. Chambers of commerce and economic development organizations could engage teenagers and even college students in conversations about the future of their local economies. 
Getting youth involved requires more than simply inviting teenagers into adult-centered spaces and conversations. Engagement means physically and mentally meeting young people where they are, removing barriers to participation, compensating them when possible and demonstrating how their contributions can inform decisions.
We cannot expect young people to develop a sense of pride, place or ownership in communities they have never been invited to help influence.
One of the ways we can do this is instead of relying on what adults believe young people need, we should be asking young people themselves. What do they value about their communities, what is missing, and what would make them excited to stay or return someday?
We must also be careful not to reduce them to the value they add numerically to our future workforce. Children, teenagers and young adults are already members of our communities, deserving of investment, meaningful participation, and opportunities to thrive right now and in the future.
Many young people will be leaving the state to pursue higher education, travel, volunteer and experience the world. This is not a bad thing, and our goal isn’t to limit youth’s horizons but to position New Hampshire as a contender among all the possibilities available to them.
The New Hampshire Advantage is an outdated idea. What advantage does it actually offer to its young people if they cannot afford to live here, learn here or see a future here? We need to work on what makes New Hampshire a desirable place to grow up and build a life today, with young people themselves co-creating that advantage.
Listening and responding to youth is not just an economic strategy, but a civic responsibility that begins while they are still small. We spend considerable energy and resources trying to attract new residents to New Hampshire. Maybe we should devote just as much to becoming a place that the youth already growing up here want to call home.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Upward, hearts: Global warming and the burden of human freedom
description: My grandfather died in the heat wave of 1954 in the Midwest, specifically St. Louis, Missouri. He had a bed and dresser in a corner of our basement in the Richmond Heights neighborhood, and he tended to walk a certain route every afternoon, which included two stops, both saloons. That day, Aug. 4th, 1954, the […]
text:
Climate-induced weather disasters include record wildfires in the West, record-setting heat waves and droughts, and aggressive hurricanes. Here, smoke plumes and hurricane clouds are visible at once. (Photo by NASA Earth Observatory)My grandfather died in the heat wave of 1954 in the Midwest, specifically St. Louis, Missouri.
He had a bed and dresser in a corner of our basement in the Richmond Heights neighborhood, and he tended to walk a certain route every afternoon, which included two stops, both saloons. That day, Aug. 4th, 1954, the temperature made 104 degrees, and my mother could not dissuade him. A retired plumber and, in stature, shorter than his grandsons would be, he wore a white shirt and straw hat and made it to his second stop, likely Rowley’s on Dale Avenue, or maybe Ted’s Corner, and, as I heard it, dropped off the stool to the floor.
No one we knew had air conditioning then. Most families had a single window fan that would blow heat out of the house and suck outside air in through other windows — slightly cooler air, especially at night. The trick was to leave open only the windows you really wanted to bring in the fan-drawn breeze, which means to be selective. Focus. The fewer openings, the stronger the breeze. Often, we would gather at one or another slightly open window, like folks during the war had once gathered around a radio.
I write this at the start of the 2026 U.N. Framework Conference on Climate Change, in Antalya, Turkey, a city whose temperature in July 2025 set a record at 115 degrees Fahrenheit. This year, the United States, my country, did not send an official delegation. The problem, delegates will say, is complicated.
Sursum corda, the priest would say in the Latin Mass, and now in English, Lift up your hearts. This recent summer, 2026, the Midwest sat at the furthest edge so far of climate warming, in which weeks went by of near 100 degrees, the result of historical human causes, detailed in such places as the journal “Nature,” and traced through paleoclimate records, tree rings, ice cores and other climate proxies, to 19th-century industrialization. It didn’t just start.
The difference, crucially and morally, is that we now know the causes and inevitable effects of such warming, drought and intense storms. In the 1950s, folks bore such heat as a variation in time. Glaciers still moved glacially, aquifers pumped central-pivot irrigation, and the Rhine River ran full.
The nuns, or maybe just one, Sister Mark, promised us children that the world would not again be destroyed by flood, citing Genesis. The Lord doesn’t repeat himself. Robert Frost favors fire but soon admits “ice / is also great / and would suffice.” Some in the Bible wait for a loud bang. Perhaps the whole planet shook from that asteroid the dinosaurs could not see coming. We see this heating thing now, coming and coming.
I am no fatalist and side with a current poet, Kathy Fagan, for whom it doesn’t matter how the world ends “if it can’t end well.” Tradition No. 1 for folks wishing to relieve their addictions to drink — or, I add, addictions to power and money — reminds us that each person is a small part of a great whole. Common welfare comes first. Humility is a strength.
Upward, hearts has been commanded of us. Not of the Lord. Us, in the liturgy, at least, and apparently in tradition. So the Japanese Buddhist monk Kanzan says —
To meet with ill fortune is to meet with good fortune.
To meet with submission is to meet with an enemy.
Ill fortune and good fortune, says scholar R.H. Blyth, are only fortune. “We make it ill or good ourselves.” That’s the point.
Writer Meghan O’Gieblyn — alluding to Simone Weil’s hope in the 1930s that workers could achieve the freedom and dignity they deserve — poses the idea that humans are but “conscious beings who are increasingly helpless against the unconscious (social) forces that are carrying us toward some uncertain destination.”
Helpless, you say. I say that O’Gieblyn “poses” the idea, not “posits,” because her suggestion appears diagnostic and investigatory. I posit this, however: If the tradition encourages humility, subservience to a higher will, such choices remain ours.
I know and have known a fair number of alcoholics, most of whom no longer drink — usually, as they often say, after they “found their bottom.” Their cases go from one-too-many blackouts to Friday nights in a cell. A certain monk might say, they had met the enemy. Some found community support. Some decided to be done and were. Some continued. The question for people who have other cravings — for fossil fuels, profits above all and mammoth data centers — is which track do we take?
The moral complexity of my grandfather’s death admits his routine of a beer or two, maybe more, with buddies. I was too young to know if he had alcoholic tendencies and do not presume. I do know that plumbing work could be rough duty in those days, made a bit easier now with PEX and plastic and glue.
My grandfather’s life was in lead and clay, cast iron and black-steel pipe, in shoulder-width ditches where flies and dirt landed or dropped on his neck and back. In time, the union relieved him of having to break concrete with a sledge, consigning that job to a specialty known now as plumbers’ laborers. He and they put forth their bodies.
I speak of the mortal body and its burden of freedom. The priest this morning identified certain moments in what he called our “salvation history,” which includes, he said, a virgin birth and the son’s resurrection. “The sea is his,” meaning the Lord’s, “for he made it, and his hands formed the dry land,” says the psalm. 
Salvation history, even in context, demands human participation, if you still believe in the will. In the preface to the eucharistic prayer, during the transubstantiation of bread into the physical body, the priest invites our participation, calling to us: “Lift up your hearts.”
Not until my 40s did I hear that call, so tepidly do most priests utter those words. I had been spending time alone in St. Petersburg, Florida, living on a friend’s sailboat, secure in its marina, for study and writing and meditation. The sailboat, I should say, had air conditioning.
My first Sunday there, I walked to St. Mary Our Lady of Grace church a few blocks from Harborage Marina, where I learned that most of the priests there had surnames like McNulty, Donahue and O’ Riordan. One of those — I am sure by his accent — at the consecration of the host and soon-to-be body, commanded, with growing emphasis and cadence that brought us all to attention, “Lift up your hearts.”
It is said that John Frederick Stewart, my grandfather, was a good craftsman, which meant he could read a blueprint. He could read it once and lay out the job in his mind. He could prefabricate a 100-plus-pound configuration of soil-pipe fittings of Ys, sweeps and traps, caulked with oakum and lead, and, with his apprentice, shoulder the unit up a ladder and bolt it into pipe hangers.
That was his work, and his lines at City Hospital or City Hall flow 100 years later.
I don’t know if he was devout, but I did, as a boy, join him and my father sometimes at College Church for Mass, and I heard then, and often over time, a reading of Jesuit Matteo Ricci, saying “When the wise man follows heaven’s decrees, fire does not burn him.”
That’s meant figuratively, not literally, for any cynics reading this. The other side of such decrees is earthly. A plumber often waits on an inspector to check blueprints against the job — the accuracy of measurement, placement of sleeves in cement, the distance from frame to faucet. As I heard it, that meant something. My grandfather’s job was to be selective, to focus. His tender was integrity.
He did not save the planet from heating that was, then, underway, but he modeled a life of choice, even if one choice tracked that fateful bar stool. It’s complicated. He did, in a certain way, lead by example. The question I pose is, “What follows?”
The mid-20th-century world, as now, included injustice and compassion, passions and suppressed passions. Society, nevertheless, learns from those who came before, and that learning heightens our responsibility to oneself and community.
My grandfather’s life sanctifies the goal Simone Weil wished in “Oppression and Liberty” for workers such as he, and really, all people — to put a small stamp on the world with the little seal of his will.
Robert Stewart edited the literary journal New Letters at The University of Missouri-Kansas City for many years. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. name: Maryland Matters
title: Officials grant more flexibility in Medicare Part D, but some state retirees still mourn state plan
description: Prescription drug coverage is a still touchy subject for thousands of state retirees who were moved from a state plan to Medicare Part D, so when state officials announced new plan options this year to provide more flexibility, some of those retirees were still wary.
text:
For some of the thousands of state retirees moved from a state plan to Medicare Part D felt a "breach of trust," so when state officials unveiled new plan options this year to provide more flexibility, those retirees were still wary. (Photo by Christine Cabalo/U.S. Marine Corps)Prescription drug coverage is a touchy subject for thousands of former state employees who lost access to a popular state drug plan and were shifted over to a federal plan in a cost-savings move.
So even as state officials announced new prescription drug plan options this year that will provide more flexibility for former workers who may have struggled during the switch to Medicare Part D, some of those retirees are still sore from that “breach of trust.”
“We lost something in that exchange,” James Roberts, president of the Towson University Retiree Association Working Group, said in a recent interview. “On the whole, people are getting their drugs covered – it’s just that it’s going to be more expensive, we’re going to have fewer drugs covered.”
His comments came in the middle of the Medicare open enrollment period, when retirees can shop and select prescription drug plans available through Medicare Part D for the 2027 plan year. Open enrollment ends Dec. 7.
New prescription benefits contract to yield ‘modest’ initial savings to state

Workers who were hired before June 30, 2011, and who retired by Jan. 1, 2020, can qualify for a state-funded Health Reimbursement Arrangement benefit, which gave a state retiree $900 a year toward out-of-pocket prescription drug costs. Households with two Medicare-eligible retirees get $1,900 a year if they qualify for HRA.
But retirees had to to through a state-contracted broker, Via Benefits, which only provided four of the available Medicare Part D plans approved by Maryland officials.
The state Department of Budget and Management addressed that this year, telling retirees could select coverage offered outside of Via Benefits, providing “greater flexibility while continuing to make Via Benefits’ expertise and support available to you,” a letter to retirees said.
Qualifying retirees now have access to nine Maryland-approved Medicare Part D plans, either through Via Benefits, directly from insurance carriers or through the federal marketplace called medicare.gov. The change is expected to let 6,000 to 7,000 more retirees take advantage of the HRA benefit now that they are not limited to plans covered by Via Benefits. And the 42,000 retirees already using the HRA benefit can shop for plans outside of Via Benefits that may be more advantageous to them.
Will the expanded coverage heal the “wound” from the shift to Medicare Part D? That depends, Roberts said.
“If someone is only taking three medications, then they’d be better off taking the cheapest plan they can find because they’re not going to be spending much on medicine anyhow,” Roberts said. “If they’re taking, like I am, many, many medications – and I know people who are taking more than twice of what I’m taking – they’re going to want a plan that’s not necessarily cheaper month by month, but they’re going to want a plan that’s cheaper in the long run by virtue of the coverage.”
Drugs covered and annual cost of coverage differ by plan and, with more options outside of the four Via plans, some retirees could come out ahead.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“This gives them many more options,” Roberts said. “There’s more flexibility by going outside of Via Benefits, so I think as a whole retirees will find that this is an improvement for them.”
But for other retirees, it’s a “hassle” to have to shop around for different plans in the first place, especially for older retirees who were used to the broad coverage offered by the former state prescription drug plan.
“Some of the people are totally confused,” said Kathlyn Miller, a board member of the Wisdom Institute, the retiree association for University of Maryland, Baltimore County.
“This is very difficult for elderly people to do,” she said. “These people are all of a sudden slammed with Medicare, and they have to understand it … These people are cautious, and they don’t want to change — change is not in their vocabulary at this age.”
The shift in coverage has roots in Maryland’s 2011 pension reform legislation, particularly part that aimed to end the state’s prescription drug coverage for Medicare-qualified state employees and move them to Medicare Part D.
Some workers wanted to stay with the state plan that they agreed to when they were hired, and feared that Medicaid Part D would not adequately cover their prescription drug costs.
The shift was supposed to occur in 2019 but a cohort of retirees sued the state, arguing that by revoking the benefits they signed up for when they were hired, the state broke its contract with them. A federal judge agreed in October 2018 and blocked the shift while their case continued. But the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals reversed that ruling in February 2023, allowing the state to move forward on the change.
Md. retirees receive notice of prescription drug benefit change despite years-long battle, lawsuit

Despite ongoing concerns raised by affected retirees, state officials said they would be moving to Medicare Part D starting in the 2025 plan year.
In the time since, Roberts says, some retirees’ fears have come true. While the old state plan covered all of the 17 prescription drugs he takes, the current Via Benefits options would have only covered up to 14 of those, meaning he has to pay for the others out of pocket.
And he’s not the only one. He collected survey results from five other groups representing state retirees about their Medicare Part D coverage options, and found just under half were not satisfied with their coverage in 2025 and 38.5% were satisfied. The rest were neutral. He cautions that it was not a survey using random sampling methods, but feels the results “reflect the feelings and responses that people sense in their coverage.”
Almost 58% said they were paying more under Medicare Part D than under their previous state drug coverage. Roberts said state officials should do their own, formal survey of retirees.
“We’re going to continue to ask for some kind of external study of the real effects of this,” he said. “I can give you some anecdotal information but I can’t give you the actual numbers.”
Meanwhile, Miller urges state retirees to shop their various Medicare Part D options before open enrollment closes to ensure that their plans are still available next year and that it is best for their situations.
“Make sure you compare your plans and check to make sure that the plan you are enrolling in next year —  don’t just let it roll over. You might be surprised by what you find,” she said. “If you don’t do that, you might find that some of your drugs aren’t covered.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pennsylvania food banks struggle to meet heightened Thanksgiving demand
description: This year’s holiday season has many organizations facing hard decisions.
text:
Two children help their mother pick up food from a food bank in Wilmington, Ohio. Some experts cautioned that Tuesday’s census data on poverty doesn’t reflect the effects of new federal policy changes that will be hitting households hard this year. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Across the commonwealth, food banks and food pantries are helping struggling Pennsylvanians enjoy a Thanksgiving dinner.
But this year’s holiday has many organizations facing hard decisions. Cuts to federal programs like The Emergency Food Assistance Program and the Local Food Purchase Assistance Cooperative Agreement Program have made it harder for food banks to stock their shelves. And cost-of-living increases tied with cuts to programs like SNAP and Medicaid mean more people are relying on their services.
Still, for some in the charitable food system, Thanksgiving is an opportunity to provide their clients with everything they need to prepare a proper holiday meal for their friends and families.
“Just because somebody doesn’t have the means, doesn’t mean they shouldn’t be able to have the same family experiences, the same celebrations,” said George Matysik, director of the Share Food Program, which serves the greater Philadelphia region. “We want to provide the types of food that bring people together and bring people around the table. There’s no holiday that does that in the United States quite like Thanksgiving.”
Food banks across Pennsylvania are struggling to keep up in the face of SNAP cuts, economic pain

This year, the Share Food Program is providing more than 30,000 turkeys, chickens and other poultry products to households, distributed through a network of food pantries and partner organizations. Preparations began in the summer.
“I’ll tell you is it’s still not enough,” Matysik said.
For Jim Reece, executive director of Friend, Inc. CommunityServices, which serves northeast Berks County, it’s about providing dignity for people who had to make difficult choices in turning to the charitable food system.
“When [money] is so tight that the things that maybe some of us take for granted aren’t available to you, what a better gift than to at least allow these families to experience some of what we all take for granted,” he said.
Reece says Friend, Inc. focuses year-round on providing people who rely on the charitable food system dignity. One way they do that is through a self-service food pantry. Unlike many others, people can come in and select what they want off a shelf like a traditional grocery store. Reece says it both helps people feel comfortable and prevents waste.
“Asking for anything, much less asking for food, has got to be one of the most humbling things that there is,” he said. “We’re seeing people who are not destitute, but have finally gotten to a point where they’ve let their guard down. They’re between a rock and a hard place. At a lot of dual income households, that check is lasting until the beginning of the fourth week of the month.”
The Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank has found another way to help. For Thanksgiving, they partner with Pittsburgh television station KDKA for an annual Turkey Fund that helps pay for gift cards at local grocery stores.
“It really goes such a long way providing the level of dignity that we really strive for,” said Erin Kelly, the director of partner and distribution programs at the Greater Pittsburgh Community Food Bank. “It just speaks to the importance of people being able to have choice, and be in the primary food system buying foods that are appropriate for them and their families.”

Turkey production bounces back but prices still rise


The $25 gift cards that their clients get are meant to supplement the food they receive at food pantries or buy through traditional grocery stores. 
Like others, Kelly noted that this year’s holiday is hitting at a time of increased need, driven in large part by increased costs and changes to federal safety net policies.
And that’s on top of the annual increase in traffic charitable food organizations see during the holiday season. Usually, there’s around a 27% increase between October and November, and the increased demand generally lasts through the winter.
“The reality of food insecurity is that a household’s food security status is often tenuous,” she said. “There are a lot of people who are food secure, but maybe only marginally. And then having an additional expense, whether it’s having to start heating your home, or preparing for winter holidays like christmas, or gearing up to have a bigger meal around thanksgiving — those are expensive. I think we all feel that personally.”
Kelly said the organization won’t be able to quantify the increase in households served this holiday season until around the end of the year, but they’re expecting a larger than usual number.
The organization’s on-site food pantry serves as many as 40,258 households. That’s not including the roughly 80% of the food they procure that’s sent to partner food pantries and organizations in the area.
“The current climate is just one of heightened anxiety around these safety net programs that people really rely on,” she said. “I think the current climate and changes to public benefits, especially the SNAP program, paired with increased costs of basic needs, is leaving people in a really tough spot.”
Matysik said one thing that helps is the increased awareness of food insecurity around the holidays. But he hopes that people remember hunger isn’t only a problem around the holidays.
“We need resources just as much in the summer time, when kids are home from school and not getting school meals, as they do in the holidays,” he said. “It’s just something for us to continue to work towards, having the type of attention that’s paid to it now paid year-round.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Deer hunting down, DNR encourages hunters to test for CWD and practice gun safety
description: For many Wisconsinites, deer stands and hunting are as much a part of the Thanksgiving season as pumpkin pie and turkey. Estimates released by the Department of Natural Resources, however, suggest that there are fewer hunters in the woods this year. Meanwhile, new cases of chronic wasting disease were reported over recent months, including in […]
text:
A whitetail deer. The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources reported this week that preliminary numbers of hunters in the 2026 deer gun season were down slightly. (Wisconsin DNR Facebook page photo)For many Wisconsinites, deer stands and hunting are as much a part of the Thanksgiving season as pumpkin pie and turkey. Estimates released by the Department of Natural Resources, however, suggest that there are fewer hunters in the woods this year. Meanwhile, new cases of chronic wasting disease were reported over recent months, including in counties that reported CWD for the first time.
On Tuesday, the DNR released preliminary figures suggesting that the number of deer hunters in Wisconsin decreased by 1.5% from  2025. The decline included gun, archery, crossbow, conservation patron and sports licenses for the deer season, which opened for guns on Saturday, Nov. 21. Out of the over 766,000 sales for deer hunting licenses issued so far this year, 405,895 were for gun privileges only. 
Final licensing figures will be available in January, the DNR stated in a press release. During opening weekend for the gun season this year, hunters registered 80,145 deer, compared to 90,720 in 2025. That’s a 11.7% decrease since last year, and 12.7% below the five-year average. Antlered deer registered by hunters during opening weekend decreased by 5.4%, and antlerless deer harvests declined by 19%  from last year. 
Temperatures during opening week were generally warm and wet across most of Wisconsin on Saturday. There was moderate rainfall in western regions of the state, while northeastern areas received the most rain. By Sunday, temperatures fell and winds picked up. The preceding warmer weather may have been more tolerable for hunters, but is known to decrease deer movement as well. 
Some areas saw deer activity while others reported little or no daytime movement, according to the DNR, and  generally deer sightings and harvests were down. Whether that changes before the end of the deer season Nov. 29 won’t be clear until  after the full nine-day gun season.
Deer hunting contributes upwards of $1 billion to Wisconsin’s economy, and popular game species like deer help support conservation efforts for other species — making chronic wasting disease in deer a pressing matter.
CWD, which first emerged in 2002 in Wisconsin, is a fatal neurological disease which is gradual and degenerative for deer, elk, and their relatives. An infected deer may look gaunt, unhealthy, may have discharge around the mouth, or may behave in a listless or unalert manner. 
In 2024, the DNR completed an “unprecedented” study which found that due to CWD  a female deer’s chances of survival decreased from 83% to 41%, and a male deer’s chances from 69% to 17%. The study also found that once the prevalence of CWD among female deer surpasses 29%, that the deer population in Wisconsin is expected to decline.
DNR officials have not calculated the current prevalence of CWD in Wisconsin deer.
CWD can occur in both farm-raised and wild deer. On Monday, the Department of Agriculture, Trade and Consumer Protection reported that two 3-year-old bucks at a Price County deer farm had tested positive for CWD, and that the area has been quarantined. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, the DNR announced that CWD had been detected in a wild deer from Pepin County for the first time, in an adult buck, and that a feeding and baiting ban in Pepin has been extended for three as a result. The ban will remain in effect until no additional signs of CWD are detected within 10 miles of Pepin and adjacent counties, according to DNR.
In October, a deer farm in Taylor County detected CWD in a young buck. That same month, another young buck in Marinette County, near Peshtigo, was found to have CWD, representing the first case for Marinette County. A similar baiting and feeding ban in Marinette County has also been extended for three years. 
State officials say hunters should test their deer for CWD. Although no cases of CWD jumping to humans have been reported, officials say vigilance is important to track the spread of the disease, because some hunters participate in the DNR’s deer donation program, which stocks food pantries around the state with deer meat.
According to the Wisconsin Department of Health Services, almost 900,000 Wisconsin residents, about 15% of the state’s population, received food assistance at least once in 2025.
Marcus Rufledt, the DNR deer donation program manager, said that with community food pantries across Wisconsin seeing a rise in demand for food assistance, the program is encouraging hunters to donate venison to the program. 
The DNR reported a 58-year-old man who was injured when he was shot in the leg when two deer entered the field during a group hunt. Both the shooter and the victim were wearing blaze orange. Last year there were two firearm-involved hunting incidents which resulted in injuries, according to the DNR. 
The DNR uses  the acronym TAB-K to remind hunters on the four rules of firearm safety:

T- Treat every firearm as if it is loaded
A- Always point the muzzle in a safe direction
B- Be certain of your target, what’s before it and what’s beyond it
K- Keep your finger outside the trigger guard until you are safe to shoot

The DNR’s Citizen Deer Advisory Council, which focuses on deer management, hunting, and conservation, is accepting applications for new members until Monday, Nov. 30.  Council members meet annually to review deer management data, hear public input and provide recommendations to the DNR and the Natural Resources Board. 
“White-tailed deer are an iconic species in Wisconsin, bringing forward a variety of perspectives in how they should be managed,” said Steve Burns, a deer and elk specialist with the DNR. The advisory councils allow for public involvement in deer population management, he said, and members receive “an in depth look at deer management issues and meet with DNR staff as representatives of their community.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: 2026 was a mixed bag for Georgia pecan farmers
description: Here’s something fun you can argue with your family about on Thanksgiving: What’s the right way to pronounce “pecan?” Lenny Wells, a pecan grower and horticulture professor at the University of Georgia, says he’s a pecan code switcher. “It varies a lot. I use both, it kind of depends on the audience I’m talking to […]
text:
Pecans are a major Georgia crop, and growers are reporting a good harvest so far this year. This 2017 photograph shows the pecan harvest at Pearson Farm in Fort Valley. Robert Holmes/Getty ImagesHere’s something fun you can argue with your family about on Thanksgiving: What’s the right way to pronounce “pecan?”
Lenny Wells, a pecan grower and horticulture professor at the University of Georgia, says he’s a pecan code switcher.
“It varies a lot. I use both, it kind of depends on the audience I’m talking to or what I’m doing,” Wells said. “If I’m talking to a group, I usually say pih-KAHN. If I’m in an orchard, a lot of times I’ll say PEE-can. It just kind of depends on how it hits me.”
Executive director of the Georgia Pecan Growers Association Bailey Segars is team PEE-can, but she says what you call the crisp, buttery little nuts may largely depend on where you grew up.
“Usually most people in South Georgia call them PEE-cans,” she said. “Alabama is strong on pih-KAHNs. Texans call them pih-KAHNs. PEE-cans is probably a Georgia thing.”
“But from a promotional standpoint, I don’t care if people call them PEE-cans or pih-KAHNs, as long as people are buying and eating them, we’re definitely happy,” she added with a laugh.
However you pronounce them, Georgia’s official state nuts are big business in Georgia – in 2024, pecans were the state’s tenth most valuable commodity bringing in more than $400 million, according to the University of Georgia’s Center for Agribusiness and Economic Development. Georgia is the nation’s largest pecan supplier, accounting for a third of all U.S. production, according to the university, and the state’s average annual harvest is enough to bake 176 million pecan pies.
Right now is prime pecan harvest time, and while 2026 had its ups and downs, Segars said so far pecan growers are seeing a decent harvest this year compared with the last few years.
Part of that comes down to the weather. A lack of rain this fall has made the harvest more efficient, Segars said.
“If they can get in the field and stay in the field harvesting, shaking trees and then blowing and harvesting them and getting them to where they need to be, shelling and cleaning plants and things like that, it’s obviously better,” she said.
And after Hurricane Michael in 2018 and Hurricane Helene in 2024 destroyed hundreds of thousands of trees, the Atlantic was quiet this hurricane season, sparing Georgia’s orchards. And many of the trees planted to replace those lost to Michael are yielding their first pecans this year, further boosting the good harvest.
“We’ve got a lot more younger trees out there, and those younger trees are generally going to be much more productive and more consistent in production,” Wells said. “The quality is going to be better for those nuts, and the varieties that we’re planting now are just a lot better than the older varieties.”
But Georgia pecan growers are also dealing with problems. In some parts of the state, especially the west, they are fighting a nasty fungus called pecan scab that can wipe out a crop.
“The fungus kind of grows on the nuts and you get little black spots that form on them.,” Wells said. “And eventually, if it gets bad enough, it can turn the whole nut completely black, and they just fall off the tree.”
And pecan farmers are not immune to issues plaguing nearly all U.S. farmers this year like tariffs and high diesel prices.
“Certainly the fuel prices have affected us like they have everyone over the last several months,” Wells said. “And for farmers, it doesn’t only affect the fuel, the diesel that you have to buy to run the tractors and equipment to do different things in the orchards and fields and things, but it also drives up the cost of fertilizer, drives up the cost of nitrogen fertilizer, drives up the cost of even the irrigation, the material that we use for irrigation, the PVC pipe.”
“Growers are kind of getting through and certainly looking a lot closer at their budgets and trying to not do anything extra that they don’t really have to do,” he added.
Still, Segars says when she gathers around the Thanksgiving table, she’ll be grateful for a solid harvest and for all those who have helped with the hurricane relief efforts.
She says she’ll be digging into a traditional pecan pie this turkey day, but her wish for the new year is for pecans to grow in popularity beyond the holiday sweets season.
“A pecan is very versatile, and you can use it obviously in baking, but it’s a great snack,” she said. “You can encrust it in protein. You can use it as a salad topping. There’s been a lot of promotion pushed to make pecans higher in consumption all year round, not just around the holidays, but we definitely continue to see the highest consumption of pecans around the holidays in pies and people making pecan pralines and things like that.”
