name: Daily Montanan
title: Federal judge strikes Montana’s drag ban as unconstitutional
description: A federal court found Montana’s 2023 drag ban to be unconstitutional and permanently stopped the state from enforcing it. But the bill’s sponsor said Montana Republicans aren’t done trying to protect children from “sexually explicit performances.” In an order Wednesday, Chief U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris said House Bill 359 from the 2023 Montana […[...]
text:
Raymi Samson performs as Eunice Exx during a drag show and protest in front of the Montana State Capitol in Helena on Thursday, April 13, 2023. (Photo by Mike Clark for the Daily Montanan)A federal court found Montana’s 2023 drag ban to be unconstitutional and permanently stopped the state from enforcing it.
But the bill’s sponsor said Montana Republicans aren’t done trying to protect children from “sexually explicit performances.”
In an order Wednesday, Chief U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris said House Bill 359 from the 2023 Montana Legislature violates constitutional protections of free speech, equal protection and due process.
Morris said the bill is missing some definitions, and others are too vague to be permissible.
For instance, he pointed to “drag queen,” defined as “a male or female performer who adopts a flamboyant or parodic feminine persona with glamorous or exaggerated costumes or makeup.”
The judge said the definition could cover many theatrical or artistic performances.
“It could include a performer portraying a character like Ursula from ‘The Little Mermaid.’ It could have included Dolly Parton herself,” the order said.
The U.S. Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals had affirmed a preliminary ban on the bill, signed by Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte.
Rep. Braxton Mitchell, R-Columbia Falls, sponsored the bill and said legislators continue to have an interest in protecting children from sexually explicit performances and “inappropriate drag story hours in public schools and libraries.”
“Once again, a far-left federal judge appointed by Barack Obama has struck down a common-sense law passed by Montana’s elected representatives,” Mitchell said in a text message.
He said a Google search will show why parents have concerns, and Montana Republicans “will not back down from protecting children.”
A group of plaintiffs led by the Imperial Sovereign Court of the State of Montana sued Attorney General Austin Knudsen; the superintendent of public instruction; a city official who had canceled a transgender woman’s talk at the Butte public library; and the City of Helena, which debated whether to grant a permit for Montana Pride events and whose city attorney said the law put the city in an untenable position.
The Imperial Sovereign Court of the State of Montana has a mission to educate and advocate for the LGBTQIA+ and allied community and promote tolerance through drag performances.
In a statement, Diana Bourgeois, of the Imperial Sovereign Court of the State of Montana, said drag artists all over Montana gathered at the Capitol in April 2023 to protest the attempts to “eradicate drag and drag artists” and hold a drag story hour.
“We swore that day that we would not be erased,” Bourgeois said in a statement from Upper Seven Law. “Today, with Upper Seven’s help, we have made good on that promise. Drag is not going anywhere, and we will continue to celebrate joyfully and authentically with our community.”
Upper Seven, a nonprofit law firm dedicated to holding the powerful to account, represented the plaintiffs.
A spokesperson for the attorney general did not comment on the order when reached by email.
The bill would have banned performances in drag and other costumes in schools, libraries, bars, theaters and other venues.
Under the law, convicted business owners would have faced fines of as much as $10,000 and license revocation, and public employees such as teachers would have faced fines of as much as $5,000 and license suspension.
The judge said the law unconstitutionally restricted content, failed to provide adequate notice of prohibited conduct, and wasn’t narrowly tailored to address a legitimate government interest.
The order also said the language in the bill made interpretation so subjective it would risk “seriously discriminatory enforcement.”
For example, the law would have banned “stripping,” but even a performer who removed outer layers of clothing might be in violation if they did so in a way “someone subjectively believes” was done “in a sexual manner,” the order said.
“Vagueness proves especially problematic for a law with expansive criminal and civil sanctions,” the order said.
It also said the law encouraged members of the public to “make individual judgments” about who is a “drag queen,” which is a problem.
“This vagueness creates significant risk of arbitrary enforcement against people who are not drag performers but who do not conform to traditional gender norms,” the order said.
For example, a transgender man who had surgery to remove breasts might be subject to enforcement “on the basis that the state considers his bare chest ‘female’ breasts,” the order said.
In a statement, plaintiff Montana Book Company co-owner Chelsia Rice said drag and costumes are “speech,” and the way people dress is political, artistic and “highly individual.”
“The decision today confirms that the First Amendment protects everyone, and the Montana Legislature is not allowed to make exceptions,” Rice said in a statement from Upper Seven.
The order noted the defendants suggested ways the court might revise the law, but the order said the court could not do so without deviating from the intent of the legislature.
Legislators are already submitting requests for bill drafts in advance of the 2027 Montana Legislature. One of those draft requests would revise laws on “hypersexualized shows,” but it is listed as being on hold, and the sponsor could not be reached for comment by email late Wednesday.

name: VTDigger
title: Montpelier apartment fire leaves one teenager dead
description:
A nearby fire hydrant, which is privately owned, appeared not to be working properly Tuesday night.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Montpelier apartment fire leaves one teenager dead.
text:
A firefighter fights the flames on 23 Cummings St. from a fire ladder on Tuesday, Nov. 24. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger
MONTPELIER — Joseph Santamore stayed at the scene of Tuesday’s Cummings Street fire until midnight, waiting for his daughter to emerge. He came back at 7 a.m. Wednesday morning.
Hours later, a black Chrysler arrived. 
“My daughter was a good person,” Santamore said after the minivan took his daughter away. “She didn’t deserve it. Not much more to say.”
Santamore’s 14-year-old daughter, Taidance Santamore, was unaccounted for all night after a house fire broke out on Cummings Street Tuesday. 
City officials confirmed a death in a Wednesday afternoon statement, but did not confirm the victim’s identity.
Santamore, a Barre resident, told VTDigger around 3 p.m. Wednesday that she had been found dead. He said the authorities allowed him to see her body before the car carried her away. She and her younger sister had been staying with her mother and her mother’s boyfriend at the time of the fire, he said. His younger daughter was outside when the fire broke out.
Two individuals — the mother and boyfriend, Santamore said — were seriously injured and are currently being treated in Boston, the father said. City Manager Kelly McNicholas Kury wrote in a statement at 4:30 p.m. Wednesday that the individuals were transported to local hospitals by ambulance after the fire began.
The cause of the fire remains under investigation, according to Kury’s statement. 
Vermont State Police’s Fire and Explosion Investigation Unit was on the scene Tuesday night and Wednesday morning working with Montpelier Police to investigate the origin and cause of the fire, State Police Public Information Officer Adam Silverman told VTDigger Wednesday. The victim’s remains were removed from the structure at around 12:40 p.m. and transferred to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner for investigation, according to Kury’s 4:30 p.m. press release.
The fire began at approximately 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, when residents said they heard an explosion. 
“It felt like a big tree fell on the house,” resident Amanda Grandfield told VTDigger as the fire burned Tuesday evening.
On the other side of the adjoined apartments, Julie Griffin heard a loud boom.
“I looked out my back window, and I saw all the flames like in the woods,” Griffin said. “And I heard a little girl next door yelling for help. So I came out front to try to get a ladder, and when I came out front, I saw the number two on fire, and it got, like, caught my place.”
Emergency services planned to remain on scene through the night to monitor the situation, Kury wrote in a statement Tuesday evening.
Grandfield was one of around 20 neighbors, friends and family members who stood vigil outside the charred building Wednesday morning as firefighters in masks worked. One shoveled ash out of the blackened door frame of unit two, where neighbors believe the fire originated. 

A Vermont State Fire Marshall and a member of the State HAZMAT Team survey the sight of Tuesday’s Cummings Street fire on Wednesday, Nov. 25. Photo by Emma White/VTDigger

Onlookers stood quietly amid the hum of a fire truck. In the bright morning sunlight, icicles hung from police tape and the building’s edges, remnants of the jets of water that doused the flames the night before.
Grandfield lived in an adjoining unit with her 10-year-old child, her two teenage children and one of her daughters and her grandchild. She was waiting to see what belongings could be retrieved from the building once the search was complete.
The family is staying with Grandfield’s son at the moment, she said. Later on, they will transition to her oldest daughter’s apartment down the street, so the kids can be closer to their school.
Three adjoining units in the 20-unit complex appeared badly damaged. All three roofs had caved in. Unit two was charred from the flames with several windows missing.
Two residents of the state-managed apartment complex independently told VTDigger that they smelled propane in the weeks leading up to the fire. 
Grandfield, whose unit was burned, said she reported the smell to the Montpelier Housing Authority and Montpelier Police about a month ago. VTDigger could not independently confirm her reports.
Another resident, who identified himself as Tyler J, told VTDigger that he suspected something was wrong with the nearest fire hydrant, as fire departments transported water from a fire hydrant about a half mile away on Elm Street using a tanker and connected hoses. He said he saw someone come to check that fire hydrant several times over the summer.
Kurt Motyka, the city’s public works director, said the fire hydrant nearest to 21 Cummings St. is privately owned. “The inspections were likely performed by the housing authority or their contractors,” he wrote in an email to VTDigger.
Josephine Romano runs a program called Neighbor for Neighbor, where she helps supply gifts and provide mentorship to children on Cummings Street. Romano said she mentors Taidance’s younger sister. 
Romano said Tuesday evening that the housing complex has been neglected, and concerns ignored by the Housing Authority for years.
“I’ve come to this neighborhood for years,” she said. “These people are people just like you and me and anyone else, and they’re living in the kind of housing that nobody is paying attention to. Jo Ann Troiano is supposed to be in charge. We’ve written letters to her. There’s mold in every single room. You can see out between the hallway and the door.”
Troiano, executive director of the Montpelier Housing Authority, declined to comment on complaints from residents until the investigation is complete, she wrote in an email to VTDigger Wednesday. 
The American Red Cross was dispatched Tuesday to support impacted families. Four members of the organization were on scene with immediate support for families and emergency service workers. 
The Red Cross continues to work with city officials, helping families establish emotional, financial, health and long-term support, according to a statement from the Red Cross Wednesday.
An initial statement from Kury Tuesday afternoon identified the building impacted by the fire as 23 Cummings St. In her email to VTDigger, Troiano wrote that the impacted units are located at 21 Cummings St., which Google Maps appears to confirm.
City Communications Coordinator Evelyn Prim directed all of VTDigger’s questions to public statements from the City Manager’s office Wednesday afternoon.
Montpelier Fire Chief Derek Libby could not be reached for comment Wednesday. Officials refused to comment on the scene.
Santamore’s family surrounded him Wednesday morning. His dog came along as well. His daughter was a good student, Santamore said. Her favorite subject was math. She had great friends and a way of making people smile, he added.
“She was a good girl,” Santamore said. “She was outspoken. Very good person to get along with.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Montpelier apartment fire leaves one teenager dead.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: Surprise! The PSC approves the acquisition of NorthWestern Energy
description: Well, to no one’s surprise, the Montana Public Service Commission approved another major energy transaction that will have long-term and likely negative consequences for Montana customers. One would think we would have learned a lesson from electric deregulation in the 1990s. Pennsylvania Power and Light was allowed to buy Montana’s electric plants, includin[...]
text:
A power line is pictured crossing Beck Hill Road in Powell County, Montana on Thursday, June 11, 2026 (Jordan Hansen / Daily Montanan)Well, to no one’s surprise, the Montana Public Service Commission approved another major energy transaction that will have long-term and likely negative consequences for Montana customers.
One would think we would have learned a lesson from electric deregulation in the 1990s. Pennsylvania Power and Light was allowed to buy Montana’s electric plants, including the dams on our rivers. They jacked up our power rates and then sold the hydro system back to us at a hugely inflated price. All with the approval of the Montana PSC.
This time around, Black Hills Corporation, a South Dakota utility, took over NorthWestern Energy. The parties involved, the media, and the PSC all referred to it as “the merger docket.” The truth is that this transaction is an acquisition of a smaller corporation by a larger one in the same line of business. Some people might even call it “corporate consolidation.”
NWE entered into an agreement with two entities, not just one. The one we never heard about is River Merger Sub, Inc. This corporation was a wholly owned subsidiary of Black Hills, created specifically for this acquisition. The agreement between the parties provided for River Merger Sub, Inc. to merge with NorthWestern. River Merger disappeared, and NWE became a direct and wholly owned subsidiary of Black Hills. That’s right . . . a wholly owned subsidiary.
Then Black Hills changes its name to Bright Horizons Energy. And presto chango, the merger that isn’t really a merger is complete. If we’re honest about it, NorthWestern has had its heart in South Dakota for a long time; it’s just that most of its customers are in Montana. NWE CEO Brian Bird has worked out of the corporate offices in Sioux Falls for a long time. And now, as CEO of Bright Horizons, he will still be headquartered there.
Of course, the acquisition will make the need for a lot of former NWE executives evaporate. Before the ink was even dry on the PSC order approving the acquisition, the cuts began. Sharon Heim, NWE’s Vice President of Government Affairs and General Counsel, left her position at the utility. She joins John Hines, NWE’s Vice President of Supply and Montana Government Affairs, who left earlier this year.
“Although I am disappointed in the outcome for myself, I completely supported the merger. The combined company will continue to bring excellent service to our customers and our employees,” Heim said.
Don’t cry any tears for Sharon Heim. She received a “payout” of $2.9 million, plus a continuing consulting contract. Hines received a similar severance benefit earlier in the year.
Of course, this is not news to anyone who has been paying much attention to this deal. A slew of executives are entitled to the same treatment if Bright Horizons terminates their employment. It was all right there in the filings before the PSC.
Private utilities point out that severance benefits don’t come out of ratepayers’ pockets. It’s the stockholders who shoulder this burden. But who provides the “revenue stream” that makes utility stock attractive in the first place? Customers, that’s who. No one can get their power from a competing electric company. They don’t exist in this private utility monopoly system. All customers have been getting from NWE recently are ever-increasing rates. This should be prevented by the PSC, but the commissioners are too busy fighting among themselves.
The truth is that all privately owned “public utilities,” like Bright Horizons, are monopoly cash cows with legal protection against losses and guaranteed rates of return on everything they spend producing power. They are rooted in the electrification efforts of the early part of the last century and have a long history of questionable dealings. Electrification in rural America was left to the government, which stepped up to the challenge and created the customer-owned cooperatives that exist today.
Mark Johnson, CEO of Flathead Electric, the largest electric cooperative in Montana and one of the largest in the Pacific Northwest, receives a little more than $1 million per year in total compensation. As CEO of NWE, Brian Bird received five times as much. We don’t yet know what he will be paid as the “new” CEO of Bright Horizons Energy.
So, the deal is done, and the PSC has signed off. But wait! Who do we hear still knocking at the door? Montana Farmers Union and 350 Montana. Two scrappy nonprofits, one representing farmers and the other representing conservationists, are appealing the PSC’s decision to district court. They are represented by attorney and recently elected legislator Monica Tranel, who is every bit as scrappy as her clients.
It’s a long shot, but it’s the best shot we have.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: For CT Dems, avoiding shutdown not the only priority in lame duck
description: Congress has three weeks to sift through a long to-do list. The top priority is funding the government, but CT legislators want more.
text:
In their final weeks as the minority party, Democratic members of Connecticut’s delegation have a list of priorities they’d like to see clear Congress before the end of the year.
But even if some of them don’t make it across the finish line, they feel optimistic about their legislative prospects as they gain larger-than-expected majorities in the House and Senate on Jan. 3.
Still, their 11th-hour sprint faces a tight timeframe. And Congress’ mandatory priorities — namely, funding the federal government — will take up the early part of the calendar when lawmakers return from the Thanksgiving recess on Nov. 30.
That leaves lawmakers with only three work weeks to tackle must-pass legislation and a growing number of priority bills for both parties, especially for Republicans, who have a limited time left in the majority.
The early days of the lame-duck session were dominated by the new member orientation for the incoming freshman class, including Luke Bronin in Connecticut’s 1st Congressional District, House leadership races, and a delayed vote regarding the impeachment of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, which House Republicans ultimately blocked.
For any bills that don’t reach President Donald Trump’s desk by the end of the year, the clock will start over when the 120th Congress convenes in the new year. But some bills have more time pressure than others.
Must-pass legislation
At the top of the congressional to-do list is government funding, which runs out after Dec. 11. Full-year appropriations bills or a short-term resolution will be needed to head off a shutdown right before the holidays.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the top Democrat on the House Appropriations Committee, is one of the players at the center of negotiations to fund the government.
If they go the short-term route on some or all of the spending bills, DeLauro has said she’d like a continuing resolution that runs only until February. She’s poised to return as chair of the Appropriations Committee and acknowledges she and Democrats will have more leverage next year.
“I want it to be sometime in February. I want the shortest possible timeframe,” DeLauro told reporters from the U.S. Capitol in mid-November before the House left for recess.
One of the biggest sticking points for Democrats is whether to cut off funding for the war in Iran in any funding deal. DeLauro wants to end funding for the months-long conflict, but she also fears what a protracted shutdown could mean for Democrats next year.
“I don’t want to provide millions or billions of dollars for this war of choice in Iran. I think we will take a look at what we can do in the short term,” DeLauro said. “But I will look for all the opportunities to curtail funding.”
“A government shutdown for me means that in the majority, we cannot move forward with the agenda that I certainly want to do in appropriations,” she continued. “I want to use the Appropriations Committee to deal with affordability issues, which we can do in education, in housing, energy and all of this.”
As defense funding remains an issue, Congress also needs to pass a defense policy bill. For Connecticut, the National Defense Authorization Act gives a boost to the state’s defense contractors that work on submarines, helicopters and military jet engines. The NDAA, which has passed every year for decades, authorizes military funding, and congressional appropriators need to allocate it.
U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services’ Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee, said in a recent interview that “this is going to be as challenging an NDAA as I’ve ever seen.”
Courtney noted that Senate appropriators recently proposed $1.1 trillion in defense spending for fiscal year 2027. In what he called a “partisan budget” that didn’t include Democratic input, he said the proposal “took money out of the submarine account to offset” other priorities.
“I just think somebody who did it didn’t understand how it works. We’re making such great progress in terms of hiring,” Courtney said, noting that Electric Boat’s workforce has grown to about 29,000. His eastern Connecticut district includes the Groton-based submarine manufacturer.
Courtney said he has concerns about the NDAA in regards to the AUKUS defense pact between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States.
Online safety legislation
In the Senate, some see the possibility of attaching online safety legislation to the NDAA. A Senate Judiciary Subcommittee recently held a hearing on child exploitation as it relates to the online gaming platform Roblox. U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., introduced bipartisan legislation allowing families whose kids were harmed by tech companies to pursue legal action in court even if they agreed to private arbitration.
And this wouldn’t be the first time Blumenthal sought to get the Kids Online Safety Act, or KOSA, done in the lame-duck session.
In late 2024, KOSA got some last-minute momentum as Republicans and Trump were on the precipice of returning to power. The bill overwhelmingly cleared the Senate that year, and in the final weeks, it secured endorsements from tech executives like Elon Musk — shortly before he headed up the Department of Government Efficiency. But KOSA ultimately fell short.
Blumenthal’s KOSA aims allow children and parents to disable addictive online features like infinite scroll and autoplay of videos, enable privacy settings and opt out of algorithmic recommendations.
This summer, a Senate committee once again approved the bipartisan bill, but it still hasn’t come to the floor for a full vote. And differences remain between the Senate and House versions of the legislation.
“I am still hopeful that the Kids Online Safety Act may be passed, possibly as part of another measure. I can’t predict what may happen there,” Blumenthal said in a recent interview before the recess. “If it doesn’t pass this Senate, I’ll be a happy warrior in the next one, when we will have much more control over the kind of act that we pass.”
Blumenthal predicted that supporters of the bill may have a better chance of passing the Senate’s version of KOSA over the House’s once Democrats are in the majority.
The biggest point of contention between the chambers is over “duty of care.” It would require companies to “exercise reasonable care” when designing a platform and hold platforms legally responsible for mitigating certain harms to minors. Senate supporters believe the bill is weak without the duty of care; those who back the House version cite potential First Amendment and censorship concerns with the provision.
“We may be in a better position if we started to move promptly in the next session when we have a majority,” Blumenthal said.
If it gets pushed into the next Congress, KOSA will need to once again go through the committee process. And Blumenthal will be pushing for the Senate version without his co-author, Republican Marsha Blackburn, who will become the governor of Tennessee.
Veterans benefits
While there was drama over a party-line veterans bill in the House, another bill that would allow combat-injured veterans to collect full benefits passed the lower chamber.
All five Democrats in Connecticut’s delegation joined an overwhelming majority in the House to pass The Major Richard Star Act in mid-November. They want to see the Senate take it up in the final weeks.
Based on current law, veterans who are medically retired and served less than 20 years see a reduction in their military retirement benefits based on the amount of their disability compensation from the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. The bill could end that offset for more than 58,000 veterans.
Blumenthal, who sponsored the Senate version, has tried several times to move the bill forward through unanimous consent. But it was blocked each time, since it only takes one member to object to such a request. He hopes Congress can get this fully passed next month and said it “should be passed right away no matter who is in the majority.”
Reauthorization of a surveillance law
Reauthorizing a controversial surveillance law is also possible in the lame duck session.
Section 702 of the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act, or FISA, expired over the summer, but the authority certified by a court lasts until mid-March. The law got caught in the crosshairs of Trump’s appointment of Bill Pulte as the acting director of national intelligence.
U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, the likely chairman of the House Intelligence Committee next year, called for the reauthorization of FISA 702 in the final weeks of the session.
Himes recently told Politico he spoke with Senate leadership about taking it up in the lame duck rather than waiting until next year when Democrats regain both majorities. “If that fails, we’ll do something in the first quarter,” he told the outlet.
FISA 702 allows the U.S. to monitor foreigners outside of the country without obtaining a warrant. The program’s renewal has consistently been a challenge since it was first enacted in 2008. And it’s one of the few issues that seemingly unites the left and right flanks of both parties over concerns about privacy rights and the Fourth Amendment that have been even more heightened for Democrats during the Trump administration.
Other last-minute items
There are also a number of bills that have passed one chamber and need approval from the other before reaching the president’s desk.
One is a bipartisan permitting reform bill that passed the Senate days before the recess. The bill now heads to the House, where it’s expected to face hurdles.
The bill, named the “Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act,” would speed up energy and infrastructure projects by overhauling permitting laws. It could open the door to faster development in industries including fossil fuels and renewable energy alike. The artificial intelligence industry is also likely to benefit, though the bill would make large data centers that power AI pay for the power they consume.
The legislation has secured support across various business and industry groups as well as those in labor. But it’s also attracted criticism from climate groups and tribal communities over changing the environmental regulations.
As the bill made its way through the Senate, Blumenthal initially voted to advance it. But in a later procedural vote, he voted no and opposed the legislation in final passage. Blumenthal cited concerns about weakening Connecticut’s water quality, including Long Island Sound, as well as historic sites.
“I have listened to constituents who share these concerns and others who support the bill,” Blumenthal said in a statement. “Ultimately, I could not vote for this legislation without changes that better safeguard our water supply, protect tribal sovereignty and secure other vital interests.”
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., didn’t vote on the measure. Since his release from the hospital in early November after experiencing a stroke, he’s missed votes as he’s spent the past few weeks at a rehabilitation center.
Another bill that’s already cleared the Senate is bipartisan legislation to regulate college sports. Both Blumenthal and Murphy voted against it in late September, arguing that the bill doesn’t adequately prioritize student athletes.
In its current form, the bill would change unlimited transfers of students to one penalty-free transfer — with exceptions if sexual assault or misconduct occurred, a program shuts down or a head coach leaves. It would set five years of eligibility for players with an age cap of 24 and provide an antitrust exemption to the NCAA and conferences to enforce standards.
It also sets standards around revenue sharing regarding name, image or likeness deals known as NIL. Under the bill, students must report compensation from NIL agreements that exceed $600. It also caps agent fees to 5% regarding such deals.
Connecticut schools like the University of Connecticut support the bill, known as the “Protect College Sports Act,” and want to see the House pass it quickly without changes to the Senate-passed version.
House Republican leadership is aiming to bring up the bill the first week of December. Lawmakers are also eyeing some changes to help increase the odds. If the House passes an amended version, it would get sent back to the Senate for passage again.
For Republicans, they’ll have their final moments in the majority to shepherd through things that’ll be much tougher in the next session. The most likely item on that list is the Senate confirmation of nearly two dozen of Trump’s judicial nominations.
Trump has also been pushing Republicans to pass a new Farm Bill before Democrats take over Congress. That legislation authorizes funding for nutrition and agricultural programs for five years and has a history of bipartisanship, but Congress hasn’t been able to pass a new one since 2018. That five-year bill ran through 2023 and was extended multiple times. The Farm Bill extension expired on Sept. 30.
To accomplish many of the must-pass and priority bills for Republicans in the waning days, they’ll need full attendance — and the votes — which tend to become a problem in the lame duck as members who retire or lost reelection head for the exits early.
Outgoing House Speaker Johnson made a plea to his party ahead of the final weeks: “We need every Republican to be here to faithfully complete our full two-year term.”

title: Utah’s avalanche season is here. Here’s how to get informed on being safe
description: The Utah Avalanche Center is preparing a series of events across the state in December as part of Avalanche Awareness Week, including safety classes and other activities. “The goal of Avalanche Awareness Week is to save lives through avalanche education,” the organization wrote in a news release. “Utah has been leading the country in avalanche […]
text:
The mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon is pictured on Sunday, March 31, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)The Utah Avalanche Center is preparing a series of events across the state in December as part of Avalanche Awareness Week, including safety classes and other activities.
“The goal of Avalanche Awareness Week is to save lives through avalanche education,” the organization wrote in a news release. “Utah has been leading the country in avalanche awareness, and we hope other states will follow in the coming years.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The organization will kick off the state’s eighth annual Avalanche Awareness Week in Salt Lake City’s Sugarhouse Park, at the big field pavilion on Sunday, Dec. 6 from noon to 3 p.m. 
The event will be available for free and will include practice avalanche rescue drills for beginners and experts, as well as lessons on how emergency responders, search and rescue teams and avalanche rescue dogs respond to avalanche accidents.
There will also be wilderness first aid training, gear demos and activities for children, the organization said.
Just this month the Utah Avalanche Center has recorded almost 40 avalanches in the state. During the 2025-2026 season, over 550 avalanches were reported by the center, according to KUTV. About 200 were triggered by people and four died in avalanche accidents.
The center is hosting other events as part of its awareness campaign, including:

Dec. 5: Utah Snow and Avalanche Workshop at Wasatch Jr High School, Salt Lake City.
Dec. 8: Pray For Snow at The Cache, Logan.
Dec. 12: Winter Kick-Off at the Moab Arts and Recreation Center (The MARC), Moab.

More information on the events can be found on the Utah Avalanche Center’s website.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Office of Housing touts nearly 2,800 new housing units in first year of operation
description: In its first fiscal year of operation, the New Mexico Office of Housing has spent more than $135 million and helped create nearly 2,800 new housing units across the state, leaders announced this week.
text:
The New Mexico Office of Housing on Nov. 24, 2026, announced it had spent more than $135 million and supported the creation of 2,758 housing units in its first year of operation. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)In its first fiscal year of operation, the New Mexico Office of Housing has spent more than $135 million and helped create nearly 2,800 new housing units across the state, leaders announced this week. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The New Mexico Legislature created the Office of Housing in 2025 and attached it to the state Department of Workforce Solutions. The office, which employs a handful of full-time housing officials, has received more than $150 million in funding in a time of historic housing-related investments from the Legislature. 
Prior to that, lawmakers and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham had worked for several years to create a statewide housing entity that coordinated projects, collected data and worked on state-level housing solutions. The state currently lacks at least 58,000 affordable housing units, and homelessness and rents have increased in recent years above the national average. 
Department Secretary Sarita Nair, who will soon become New Mexico Gov.-elect Deb Haaland’s chief of staff, announced Tuesday that the office had completed an annual report for its first year of operations and launched a new data-sharing website that details its spending and operations.
“Addressing New Mexico’s housing challenges requires coordination, transparency, and sustained investments,” Nair said in a statement. “The website gives New Mexicans a way to see the work underway, understand how state resources are being used, and access information that can help communities move housing solutions forward.”
According to the department, the office has helped fund 2,758 new housing units. That includes affordable rental and homeownership units, as well as 156 units of supportive housing, which pairs shelter with access to services like case management or mental healthcare:
The department has also supported more than 1,000 shelter beds, according to the report. 
New Mexico governor once again tries to create Office of Housing

It’s also supporting work to gather more information about the larger housing landscape.
New America, a nonprofit public policy think tank, selected New Mexico as one of 11 states to join its Eviction Data Response Network, which aims to strengthen eviction information systems. 
The Office of Housing in turn provided the New Mexico Center on Law and Poverty $150,000 in matching funds for the center to take on a two-year eviction data collection initiative. Maria Griego, the center’s economic equity director, told Source NM that the aim is for a public-facing website with as much information about eviction trends and local data as possible.
Currently, researchers or advocates like Griego have little access to data regarding approximately 13,000 New Mexicans who were evicted last year. Information regarding their demographics, household size or how they owed in rent is difficult to collect and parse, Griego said. 
Data related to evictions affecting children is of particular interest, Griego said, including which school districts experience the largest number of evictions. 
Griego also said she hopes the data will highlight the state’s three-day eviction notice period. Under current law, landlords can move to evict a tenant three days after serving them notice of nonpayment.
“Even if you have the money available on the fourth day, they don’t have to accept it and you can be evicted,” she said. “We think that this new project will really help shed a light on how much are folks in arrears, how much investment we need to be making into eviction prevention.”
Griego said she expects lawmakers will introduce legislation at the upcoming session that will lengthen the three-day period, which she said is one of the shortest such periods in the country. 
Lawmakers and advocacy groups have also called for legislation during the upcoming 60-day session beginning Jan. 19 that strengthens the office or potentially transforms it in statute to a state housing division, one with more resources and authority. 
“We’re so excited that they exist,” Griego said of the new housing office, which she described as a “great step forward” in looking at the state’s housing issues. “And we look forward to continued partnership with them, hopefully, working on a number of housing initiatives.”

title: King tides bring flooding to WA and OR coasts
description: Washington and Oregon are dealing with some of the highest tides of the year this week.  For the second day, king tides along the coast are causing flooding. The high, seasonally occurring tides aren’t expected to cease until Nov. 30.  In Washington, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning stretching from Grays Harbor County […]
text:
The coast in Westport. (Photo courtesy of Washington State Parks)Washington and Oregon are dealing with some of the highest tides of the year this week. 
For the second day, king tides along the coast are causing flooding. The high, seasonally occurring tides aren’t expected to cease until Nov. 30. 
In Washington, the National Weather Service issued a flood warning stretching from Grays Harbor County to Whatcom County, the northernmost county along the state’s coast, for Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. 
In Oregon, the same warning is in effect for the northwest coast and the south central coast. 
Immediate flooding will occur along the water, but could stretch further depending on elevation. 
In Washington, “we’re anticipating about in general three to four feet of inundation,” said Anna Lindman, meteorologist at the National Weather Service. 
“There could certainly be closed roads,” she said. “We’re just trying to urge people to never drive through water because one, you can’t tell how deep it is, and two, these are strong tides, so there might be a strong current associated with it.”
On Tuesday, the first day that the king tides arrived, a video of a man and his dog getting swept up by waves at Cannon Beach circulated online. Both were uninjured, but the video demonstrates how strong the pull of the tides can be. 
Washington is facing the combination of a storm system, seasonally occurring high waves and the El Niňo, which warms water, pulling it into the coast. 
But, Lindman said, “we’re lucky” because the weather event did not turn into a bomb cyclone.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Interim chancellor picked for permanent job at LSU New Orleans
description: After a national search for a new leader for its New Orleans campus, LSU will hire the local person who’s been in charge on a temporary basis since July.
text:
Jeanette Weiland has been named chancellor at LSU New Orleans, a role she's held on an interim basis since July 1, 2026. She was chosen following a national search, although she was not among the finalists recommended by a search committee. (Photo courtesy of LSUNO) After a national search for a new leader for its New Orleans campus, LSU will hire the local person who’s been in charge on a temporary basis since July.
Jeanette Weiland has been named the permanent chancellor for LSU New Orleans, LSU System President Wade Rousse announced Wednesday. He chose her from four finalists who had gone through a public interview process earlier this month, though Weiland was not among the candidates a search committee had advanced from the more than 50 applicants for the job. 
Rousse inserted Weiland as a finalist and ultimately chose her over University of North Texas professor and dean Michael Savoie, Winthrop University provost Sebastian van Delden and Kent Willis, a senior vice president at Stephen F. Austin State University. 
“In the interim position, Jeanette provided steady leadership stabilizing the campus’ cash flow while at the same time developing trust and respect from LSU New Orleans’ students, faculty and staff,” Rousse said in a statement. “These accomplishments set forth a foundation for her to continue to build a strong future for the university and provides proof that continuing our course towards improvement is a decision firmly rooted in the LSU System’s goal of changing the way we educate Louisiana.”
Last year, state legislators agreed to move what was the University of New Orleans into the LSU System in an attempt to stop the bleeding of its enrollment and finances. Its student body reached 17,000 before Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and there are about 5,500 enrolled for the current fall semester.
As of midyear 2024, the university was operating at more than $9 million in the hole.
Its switch from the University of Louisiana System became official this July 1, after UNO had attempted to stem its losses through layoffs, furloughs, program consolidations and building closures. Enrollment continued to trend downward in process, further exacerbating the school’s fiscal problems in a public higher education system highly reliant on tuition revenue rather than state funding. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Weiland has continued to implement stricter financial practices and emphasized student recruitment since being named interim chancellor. She’s also overseen the school’s rebranding, including a switch in school colors from blue and silver to LSU’s omnipresent purple and gold.
It’s a familiar look, as Weiland received her bachelor’s degree in international trade from LSU and earned master’s degrees in arts administration and business administration from UNO. She does not hold a Ph.D., a degree commonplace among most university leaders.
Weiland’s only previous experience in higher education is at Tulane University, where she was hired in 2023 to start its first venture capital fund. She was later named the first chief business officer for its science and engineering school.
Before that, Weiland was senior vice president at the New Orleans Business Alliance, a public-private economic development entity. She was previously a financial growth manager for the Ochsner Health System and worked in the investment and insurance fields. 
Weiland, who has also authored three children’s books, becomes the latest in a series of unconventional higher education leadership hires in Louisiana since Gov. Jeff Landry took office in 2024. The Republican chief executive has gradually exerted more control over the boards that oversee the state’s public colleges and universities, handpicking the system presidents himself.
Last week, Matt Napoli was named president of his alma mater, Louisiana Tech, without any prior experience in education. His resume includes a Ph.D. in public policy and administration, and he was most recently an appointee of President Donald Trump in the U.S. Department of Energy.  
Similarly, state Sen. Mike Reese, R-Leesville, was put in charge at McNeese earlier this year, following a career in real estate and logistics. He holds only a bachelor’s degree from the University of Louisiana at Monroe. 
Landry also had a hand in the transition of Louisiana Supreme Court Associate Justice Jimmy Genovese to president at Northwestern State University, the first and only academic role Genovese has held. Lake Charles attorney Cade Cole, with campaign support from the governor’s political action committee, replaced Genovese on the state’s highest court last year.

title: New Mexico announces recipients of state creative arts grants, totaling $1M
description: A mural festival, folk art apprenticeships and new art spaces on Santa Fe’s developing Midtown campus are a few of the eight projects receiving state funding through a new “creative industries” initiative grant.
text:
The New Mexico Economic Development Department on Nov. 23, 2026, announced the recipients of the state’s Creative Industries Public Development Projects Grant: $125,000 each for eight awardees statewide. Above: a digital rendering by Limotta Designs of a plan to repurpose buildings for art spaces on the Midtown Santa Fe campus, one of the project recipients. (Photo courtesy of the Santa Fe Metropolitan Redevelopment Agency)A mural festival, folk art apprenticeships and new art spaces on Santa Fe’s developing Midtown campus are a few of the eight projects receiving state funding through a new “creative industries” initiative grant. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The state Economic Development Department’s Creative Industries Division in March issued a call to local governments, municipalities, Tribal nations and Pueblo governments statewide to apply for a new Creative Industries Public Development Projects Grant. Creative industries, the agency said in a news release, account for $6 billion of New Mexico’s economy annually.
Each of the eight project recipients will receive $125,000. They include the City of Albuquerque for a new art mural festival on the city’s Rail Trail; the state’s New Mexico Arts for professional development workshops and an expansion of its Folk Arts Apprenticeship Program; and the City of Santa Fe and the Metropolitan Development Agency to rehab more than 17,000 square feet of vacant building space at the former Santa Fe University of Art and Design campus — now called Midtown Santa Fe —  to create spaces for community and arts organizations. 
Santa Fe Metropolitan Redevelopment Agency Deputy Director Carly “Cav” Venditti told Source NM that the project will help local artists by providing access to “below-market rent for workspaces and workforce training,” ultimately supporting more than 10,000 community members annually, within the culinary, film, new media and other art mediums.
“Creative organizations are not just cultural assets; they have the capacity to be employers, educators and drive economic activity,” Venditti said, adding that the project creates a space “to really make room for folks that are driving the economy and will help train the next generation.”
Other recipients include: Gallup, to create a walking tour downtown that combines augmented reality with Indigenous art; Las Cruces, for workforce development for local artists, as well as a new immersive art experience festival; Los Alamos County, for an initiative to provide expanded artist residency and literary festival programming; Taos County, to create an online career portal to connect youth with paid art internships; and Santa Fe County — in partnership with the Arts, Culture and Creative Economy Council — to launch “a series of pilot initiatives to strengthen and connect its creative economy, focusing on rural and underserved communities.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: Hinds DA candidate files overdue campaign disclosure reports
description: Darla Palmer, a private attorney running to be Hinds County District Attorney, in her office on County Line Road on Nov. 19, 2026.
text:
Darla Palmer, who is vying to become the next Hinds County district attorney, filed long overdue campaign finance reports Wednesday, a day after Mississippi Today reported she could be blocked from taking office if she wins Tuesday’s runoff.
The defense attorney is competing against prosecutor Gwen Agho to finish out the term of former Hinds DA Jody Owens, who resigned over the summer after pleading guilty to a federal corruption charge.
State law bars candidates who have not submitted all their required campaign finance reports from taking office. If a candidate has not filed all their required reports within the past five years, they could also be prevented from appearing on a ballot. 
On Wednesday, Palmer filed seven reports to the Secretary of State’s Office showing she received and spent $28,854.52 in campaign contributions during her 2023 campaign against Owens. 
Palmer called the failure to file reports “an oversight” and said she would pay any Ethics Commission fines. 
“None of this is willful or deliberate,” she told Mississippi Today on Tuesday. 
Palmer’s outstanding reports from 2023 covered funds she was raising through a political committee she formed for that election. 
On Wednesday, Palmer filed the outstanding reports as a candidate, not through her 2023 political committee.
In a text message, Liz Jonson, a spokesperson from the Secretary of State’s Office, wrote the reports Palmer filed as a candidate “will suffice for the committee.” 
But Palmer did not file a termination report for her 2023 political committee, meaning her committee is not exempt from future reporting requirements and could be at risk of more fines, Jonson added. 
The Mississippi Ethics Commission fined Palmer $3,700 because of the late reports. 
The commission sent nine letters about the fines to addresses that Palmer provided to the Secretary of State’s Office, said Tom Hood, the commission’s executive director. 
Palmer said she did not receive any letters notifying her of the penalties.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Former Nebraska lawmaker Kermit Allen Brashear dies at 82
description: Kermit Allen Brashear II, a former state lawmaker who served 12 years in the legislature – including two as speaker – died Sunday
text:
Former Nebraska state legislator Kermit Allen Brashear II (Provided photo)LINCOLN —  Kermit Allen Brashear II, a former state lawmaker who served 12 years in the legislature – including two as speaker – died Sunday. He was 82.
Brashear represented Legislative District 4 from 1995 to 2007. He also served as chairman of the state Republican Party from 1983 to 1985. Among his achievements was creating the Community Corrections Council in 2003. He also was behind the creation of learning communities, which helped with school funding. 
Nebraska elected officials offered condolences.
Nebraska Attorney General Mike Hilgers said one of his first political memories was that Brashear visited his house when Hilgers was in high school.
“He was friendly and engaging, and left a positive impression of the political process,” Hilgers wrote. 
Nebraska 3rd Congressional District Rep. Adrian Smith said Brashear “was one of a kind.” 
“His commitment to growing Nebraska took root in Crawford and only deepened over years while serving Nebraskans from east to west,” Smith said. “My heartfelt condolences to his family, his friends, and all who loved him. I will miss him.” 
Gov. Jim Pillen also paid tribute to Brashear, saying the longtime legislator was dedicated to public service and committed to making Nebraska a great state 
A funeral service will be held next month in Omaha.

text:
Democratic Senate nominee Troy Jackson speaks in Deering Oaks park in Portland on October 17 as part of the national No Kings day of action. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)Sen.-elect Troy Jackson has officially announced his support for Chris Van Hollen, the Maryland senator challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer for majority leader. 
In a statement Wednesday, Jackson said he would back Van Hollen when the caucus meets on Dec. 1 for the closed-door vote. “Mainers voted for change in November, and they ought to get it,” Jackson said. 
Throughout his Senate campaign, Jackson said he would not back the current minority leader, but had withheld support for Van Hollen because he wanted “to make damn sure that my vote counts.”
“I’ve talked with Mainers about what they need from the Senate, and I believe it’s time for a change in leadership,” Jackson said in the Wednesday statement. When he spoke to Van Hollen he “told him Maine needs a seat at the table when the caucus decides what gets funded and what we’re going to fight for,” he added.
He said he and Van Hollen agreed on working to end the filibuster, pass Medicare for All, and increase the minimum wage.
“I want a leader who’ll bring those fights to the floor,” he added.
Several grassroots groups that turned out Democratic voters for the midterm elections have been pressuring Sen. Angus King to rescind his support for Schumer, and back Van Hollen. Nearly 2,000 people have signed a petition that was delivered to the independent’s office earlier this week.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Healthcare advocacy coalition takes its Medicaid expansion campaign digital
description: Florida Decides Healthcare is going digital. After its campaign to put Medicaid expansion on the ballot was upended in 2025 by the Republican-led Legislature and Gov. Ron DeSantis, the organization had to rethink its strategy. It could no longer rely on its original plan to use petition gatherers after a 2025 law that changed the […]
text:
A push to put a Medicaid expansion on the ballot in 2028 has gone digitalFlorida Decides Healthcare is going digital.
After its campaign to put Medicaid expansion on the ballot was upended in 2025 by the Republican-led Legislature and Gov. Ron DeSantis, the organization had to rethink its strategy.
It could no longer rely on its original plan to use petition gatherers after a 2025 law that changed the rules for citizen petition drives was mostly upheld by a federal court. 
Florida Decides Healthcare Executive Director Mitch Emerson said at the time that the law “wasn’t an attempt to make citizen-led ballot initiatives harder, it attempted to make them impossible.”
But the impossible became possible this week after the group — joined by former U.S. Senate Democratic hopeful and state legislator Angie Nixon — announced a renewed effort to place a constitutional amendment that would expand Medicaid to lower-income childless adults on the ballot in 2028. 
If successful, it would allow the voters, and not the Legislature, to decide.
“So, what we did was make a strategic decision to pivot away from the petition method and go to a digital request,” Emerson said during a Tuesday night Zoom call with Nixon. 
Emerson, who was a field director for Nixon’s 2026 U.S. Senate campaign, said the group is working in tandem with the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network and the American Heart Association to place Medicaid expansion before Florida voters during a presidential election year.
In lieu of a people-powered boots on the ground campaign, the coalition is instead encouraging people to fire up their screens by visiting MedicaidFlorida.Org to request a petition or scanning the QR code it developed and has released.
“You just request the petition. Put in some information. You verify that you are a registered voter. We will mail a petition to you … and the step-by-step instructions on how to fill it out and a return envelope that is pre-paid,” Emerson said.
Senate Democratic hopeful Angie Nixon talks to reporters Tuesday night in Jacksonville following her concession speech. (Photo credit: Christine Sexton/ Florida Phoenix)
Impediments 
Over the past two decades, the Republican-controlled Florida Legislature has adopted a series of measures that make it harder to qualify for the ballot, including steep fines for violation of technical requirements. One of the major steps is to gather more than 880,000 petition signatures from registered voters — a figure tied to the last presidential election and set in the Florida Constitution.
Although Nixon’s campaign for Senate wasn’t as well funded as that of her opponent, Republican Ashely Moody, the Jacksonville Democrat took advantage of social media platforms like TikTok and Instagram to buoy her efforts.
Those platforms can also help bolster the coalition’s efforts to collect the required signatures to place a Medicaid expansion on the ballot.
“If you’ve already done that [signed up for the petition] you should go on social media and share the link to the petition and tell people that you signed it and you want others to sign it as well,” said Nixon, who made healthcare a top priority in her senatorial effort.
Nixon and Emerson used the Zoom call to discuss next steps with her recently formed political action committee, called Never Scared.
The 42-year old Nixon, who lost to Moody by about 2% points, was a champion of Medicare for All on the campaign trail. But she previously served as an organizing director at Florida Decides Healthcare. And until or unless Medicare for All becomes a reality, Nixon said, Medicaid expansion — a key part of the federal Affordable Care Act remains an option.
“Though they cut ACA subsidies, Medicaid expansion is still in play because it was always in play. And it will actually save us money if we go ahead and expand it because we’re winding up paying that on the back end when people use primary care,” Nixon said. “They use emergency rooms as their primary care, so I’ll put that out there.”
The ACA was an omnibus law with the purpose of providing Americans with healthcare coverage, either through a Medicaid expansion or by purchasing subsidized health insurance policies in the health care marketplace, sometimes referred to as the exchange.
Former President Barack Obama’s signature legislation, the 2010 law withstood a sweeping legal challenge known as NFIB v. Sebelius, a 2012 challenge that originated in Florida.
Although the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the law, it did rule that the section requiring states to expand Medicaid or lose matching federal healthcare dollars amounted to unconstitutional coercion.
As a result, the Medicaid expansion became optional. That has created a coverage gap in states that didn’t expand Medicaid. Falling into the gap are people whose incomes are too low to qualify for ACA marketplace subsidies but too high to qualify for traditional Medicaid.
Florida, one of 10 states that has not expanded Medicaid, has an estimated 388,000 residents in the Medicaid coverage gap.
By not expanding Medicaid, Nixon said, the state has lost access to $14 billion in federal Medicaid funds over the past decade. 
“That is billions of taxpayer dollars that have been left on the table. That is our federal tax money currently funding healthcare infrastructure and services in 40 other states that have already expanded Medicaid,” she said.
People in Florida who fall into the gap are “construction workers, our service employees, our caregivers and single parents who work hard every day only to be forced between seeing a doctor and paying rent. But this is not a partisan issue. It’s common sense,”Nixon said. 
Florida Phoenix reporter Mitch Perry contributed reporting for this story.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: NC opts into 6-month grace period for Medicaid work requirements
description: North Carolina is opting into a six-month federal grace period that will temporarily prevent Medicaid expansion enrollees from losing health insurance coverage because they fail to meet new work requirements, state health officials announced Wednesday. The new federal requirements are still set to take effect Jan. 1, and will apply to more than 740,000 North[...]
text:
About 3.1 million North Carolinians are enrolled in Medicaid.  (Photo: Getty Images)North Carolina is opting into a six-month federal grace period that will temporarily prevent Medicaid expansion enrollees from losing health insurance coverage because they fail to meet new work requirements, state health officials announced Wednesday.
The new federal requirements are still set to take effect Jan. 1, and will apply to more than 740,000 North Carolinians. But the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services recently gave states the option to adopt a grace period through June 30, 2027.
During the grace period, counties will still check whether applicants and enrollees meet the new requirements or qualify for an exemption. But Medicaid recipients will not lose coverage or face any penalties for failing to meet the new work requirements or submit any required paperwork during the first six months. 
N.C. Department of Health and Human Services Secretary Dev Sangvai said the grace period gives county departments more time to help enrollees understand how to comply with the new rules. 
“Our goal is to make sure people keep getting the care they need while we help them navigate these federal changes,” he said. 
North Carolina lawmakers this year also adopted a stricter eligibility standard than the federal rule, which was passed as part of H.R. 1, also known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act.”  
While federal law requires states to confirm that enrollees and new applicants met the work requirement for at least one month before they can be covered, state law requires enrollees and new applicants to show they met the requirements for three months. 
During the April debate over the three-month lookback period, opponents said it would be the strictest work requirement in the country. But it won’t take effect until the federal requirement does.
New campaign aims to help NC Medicaid recipients keep coverage under new rules

The work requirements apply to adults ages 19 to 64 without disabilities who receive coverage through Medicaid expansion. Enrollees are required to work, attend school or participate in other approved activities for a minimum of 80 hours per month. People with disabilities, pregnant women and parents of children under 14 are exempt. 
Critics of the new rule say the vast majority of people covered under Medicaid expansion already work, but some may have difficulty gathering and submitting the necessary evidence to keep their coverage.
Earlier this year, Gov. Josh Stein urged North Carolina’s congressional delegation to reverse the new Medicaid rules in an open letter, saying more than 250,000 people could lose coverage, and counties will have to shoulder the added administrative costs. 
Stein renewed that call in Wednesday’s announcement. 
“I am committed to doing everything I can to help people keep their health coverage,” Stein said in a statement. “We will take this brief reprieve, but it isn’t nearly enough.”

title: Former Idaho senator and insurance director to lead state Health and Welfare agency — for now
description: Idaho’s top insurance official and a former legislator will temporarily lead Idaho’s largest state agency, the governor announced Wednesday.  Idaho State Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron will serve as interim director of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare starting Nov. 30, according to a press release. Cameron had a prior stint as interi[...]
text:
The Pete T. Cenarrusa state office building in Boise, the longtime headquarters for Idaho Department of Health and Welfare and the Division of Medicaid. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Captial Sun)Idaho’s top insurance official and a former legislator will temporarily lead Idaho’s largest state agency, the governor announced Wednesday. 
Idaho Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron, right. (Photo courtesy of Idaho Department of Insurance)
Idaho State Department of Insurance Director Dean Cameron will serve as interim director of the Idaho Department of Health and Welfare starting Nov. 30, according to a press release. Cameron had a prior stint as interim head of the health agency when a former director retired in 2024. 
Idaho Gov. Brad Little also appointed Weston Trexler as interim director of the Idaho Department of Insurance until Little selects a permanent Health and Welfare director after the 2027 legislative session. The session begins Jan. 11 and typically lasts about three months. 
Former Health and Welfare Director Juliet Charron stepped down, after just over a year leading the agency. 
“Dean Cameron and Weston Trexler bring decades of experience, strong leadership, and a deep understanding of their respective agencies,” Little said in the press release. “Both have a proven commitment to serving Idahoans, and I have confidence in their ability to provide steady leadership during these transitions. I appreciate their willingness to step into these roles and continue the important work of delivering important services to the people of Idaho.”
Trexler has served as deputy director as an actuary at the insurance department since 2019 and has been at the agency since 2012, according to the release.  
As interim director during the legislative session, Cameron will be tasked with working with state legislators on a proposal to restore budget cuts for disability caregivers, as outlined in the agency’s budget request for the upcoming session. The 2026 legislative session was marked by deep cuts government-wide to avoid a projected budget shortfall. 
Cameron has led the Department of Insurance since he was appointed by former Gov. Butch Otter in 2015. Prior to his appointment, he served in the Idaho state Senate for 25 years, during which he co-chaired the state’s powerful budget-writing committee. 
Health and Welfare has more than 3,000 employees and oversees public assistance programs such as Medicaid, food benefits through the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and the Women and Infant Children program, known as WIC. The agency also provides public health services, regulates long-term care facilities, runs the state’s mental health hospitals, oversees child welfare and provides services for people with developmental disabilities. 
The agency’s total budget is more than $5 billion of mostly federal funds.
The new director will oversee a major shift to administering Idaho’s entire Medicaid program through private managed care companies, as directed by the Idaho Legislature’s House Bill 345. 
The full transition to managed care oversight of Medicaid is expected to happen by 2030.
The Health and Welfare chief will also see the state’s administration of around $183 million in grants for the second year of the five-year federal Rural Health Transformation program. 
The new permanent director will be the fourth since Little took office in 2019. 
Prior to Charron, Alex Adams served a little over a year in the position before President Donald Trump appointed him to lead the federal Administration for Children and Families under Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. 
Adams’ predecessor, Dave Jeppesen, led the agency for five years before retiring in 2023.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa State University researcher traces corn’s past through animal bones
description: In a lab at Iowa State University, faculty and students carefully shave material off of bones dating back thousands of years to understand how societies lived all through one thing — their diet. People and animals are literally made of what they eat, ISU professor Andrew Somerville said, and analyzing the matter they leave behind […]
text:
Iowa State University professor Andrew Somerville shows samples of bone mineral. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)In a lab at Iowa State University, faculty and students carefully shave material off of bones dating back thousands of years to understand how societies lived all through one thing — their diet.
People and animals are literally made of what they eat, ISU professor Andrew Somerville said, and analyzing the matter they leave behind gives important clues as to how they spent their lives, and how that would change over thousands of years for different groups.
His research has focused on the birthplace of corn as it is known today and sites with some of the oldest corn findings in the world. It can be easy to forget the immense role agriculture plays in society with the ease of modern-day conveniences like grocery stores, but Somerville said his and other researchers’ work underscores the importance of agriculture as a base of society.
“You can just see that there’s before farming and there’s after farming — religion comes and iconography and art and ceramics, and dogs. They didn’t have dogs until they started farming. Like in theory, they were somewhere around the Americas, but you don’t see them in the archeological record until people start farming,” Somerville said. “You don’t see domesticated turkeys until people start farming. You don’t see as much war and conflict until people start farming. So, like everything we think about civilization doesn’t even start until people start planting in this region. It’s corn.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Before Somerville and his wife moved to Ames to work at the university in 2018, Somerville said he spent time as a postdoctoral research fellow studying different archeological sites in Mexico, with a focus on Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley in the State of Puebla.
This valley is home to some of the oldest recorded food and feats in the world, Somerville said, from corn to avocado pits and chili peppers to turkeys, as well as this hemisphere’s oldest dam. The rain shadow cast by nearby mountains leaves this cave-filled valley very dry, allowing “anything that any human ever dropped in these caves or left there” to be preserved for thousands of years.
Iowa State University professor Andrew Somerville shows bone samples soaking to isolate the collagen. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
Researchers discovered corn preserves in the valley in the 1960s, Somerville said, with layers showing how the crop changed not unlike the ground layers that show sediment and soil changes over time.
“You can see the whole history of corn evolution from this site. The cobs at the very bottom are like an inch long, they’re primitive, barely domesticated, and then through time, as you move up in the levels, you can just see the cobs getting bigger,” Somerville said. “Amazing archeological site.”
Since no one had touched the found animal bones “since literally 1963” and animal bone chemistry is a specialty of his, Somerville said he decided to focus his research in that area; however, he had to find them first. He spent a year before going to Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley emailing and calling people about the artifacts, but it wasn’t until he physically looked around a lab himself that they were spotted and given to him to study.
Studies show corn domestication and travel
The work he and others conducted in Mexico has led to multiple studies about the environment and climate of the valley over time, with the researchers looking at stable isotope ratios of carbon, nitrogen and oxygen to draw conclusions about how much grassland and moisture was around, as well as rainfall and temperatures.
The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley sits in highlands around 1,700 meters above sea level, Somerville said, and domesticated corn arrived there between 6,300 and 4,550 years ago. Using deer and rabbit bones from the time, the team found that the window when corn was brought to the valley was “the wettest, most favorable, warmest climate conditions for thousands of years.”

 Corn is everywhere in Iowa
In order to study the DNA of ancient corn, one of Somerville’s students had to work with the samples across the world in Vienna. Somerville said ancient corn DNA cannot be analyzed in Iowa because there is so much ambient corn in the air that any ancient samples will get contaminated by it.
“We’re breathing corn right now, like it’s everywhere,” Somerville said. “There’s little cells just floating around.”

“Humans are able to expand the range of corn cultivation for the first time during this exceptionally wet period, this exceptionally favorable climate,” Somerville said. “So that’s the kind of the part we thought was the coolest because it really helps us understand the history of corn and the expansion and how and why people started farming in the first place.”
Once the lowland variety of ancient corn, called parviglumis teosinte and the first ancient corn plant to be domesticated, was brought to highlands, it was crossbred with another breed of highland corn. Somerville pointed out that once domesticated, corn cannot reproduce on its own, meaning that humans had to have a hand in its spread.
Somerville said this hybrid is the basis for modern corn, with all modern corn having 20% of genes from the highland variety and the rest from parviglumis teosinte. He added that scientists are “pretty sure” that corn first came from the modern Mexican state of Guerrero around 9,000 years ago.
“As soon as that cross happened, that’s when corn exploded all over the Americas, basically,” Somerville said. “Once it had those extra genes to help it be more adaptive, then it just went all the way down to Peru all the way up to Canada.”
Future corn study could shift to Iowa
Somerville credited the Mexican researchers he worked with and continues to collaborate with today as a major reason why this research is being completed successfully. He said he has further projects with these colleagues to look at diets of different demographic groups and migration history.
Somerville’s time in Mexico grew his interest in corn, and it is still a central focus of his research today. His colleagues in Mexico sent him human bones, such as wisdom teeth, from around 1,400 years ago to analyze the ancient people’s diets and where they grew up.
Iowa State University professor Andrew Somerville shows samples of bone collagen. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)
The researcher is also looking into how corn cultivation and other early farming practices changed the relationships between humans and other animals, like dogs and turkeys. Another study from the Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley showed that the diets of dogs started departing from other animals as agriculture practices intensified and they had more access to corn.
Eight students worked with Somerville in his lab this semester, where he taught them how to separate bone shavings into either just its mineral or biological components.
Somerville said that thousands of years from now, scientists could be doing the same kind of work he’s completing now but in Iowa rather than in Mexico. Iowa, despite its seasons bringing either quite warm or freezing temperatures, has amazing preservation abilities, Somerville said, seen from his work analyzing bison and other animal bones.
“Now we’re the most important corn-producing region in the world, yeah, future archeologists will probably be pretty interested in Iowa because our corn is in China, our corn is all over the country,” Somerville said.
