name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: The future of energy is the future of Alaska
description: The election is over, and a new administration and Legislature will soon get to work. Whatever else divides them, Alaska’s leaders and the voters who elected them share a goal: a stable, affordable energy future for this state. A gas line is how we get there. I say that as an Alaskan first. I serve […]
text:
The Trans-Alaska Pipeline is seen in the northern Brooks Range on June 20, 2007. Alaska. Running along the pipeline is the Dalton Highway. (Photo provided by the U.S. Geological Survey)The election is over, and a new administration and Legislature will soon get to work. Whatever else divides them, Alaska’s leaders and the voters who elected them share a goal: a stable, affordable energy future for this state. A gas line is how we get there.
I say that as an Alaskan first. I serve as an independent member of the board of 8 Star Alaska, the company developing Alaska LNG. Glenfarne owns 75% of 8 Star, and the State of Alaska, through the Alaska Gasline Development Corp., owns 25%. My role is to keep the focus where it belongs: on project benefits for the people of this state.
Here is what is at stake. For more than 50 years, Cook Inlet gas has heated homes and kept the lights on in Southcentral. That supply is running down. Our utilities have been clear that without new gas, Alaskans face higher bills, imported fuel and real uncertainty within the next few years.
Energy is not an abstract policy debate. It decides whether a young family stays in Kenai to raise their kids, whether a small business in Fairbanks makes payroll through the winter and whether a retiree in Anchorage remains in the home they built. Too many Alaskans have already left for places where life costs less. 
Affordable, reliable energy gives the next generation a reason to stay. Alaska LNG is the project positioned to bring North Slope gas to Alaskans. It means gas for Alaskan homes and businesses first, thousands of construction jobs and new revenue for the state for generations.
But a gas line will not be built by a single vote. It will be built, or stalled, one decision at a time. Over the next several years, state agencies and the Legislature will weigh leases, permits, tax terms, contracts and financing approvals. Each deserves real scrutiny. And each should be measured against the same question: Does this decision bring affordable, reliable energy and new state revenue closer, or push them further away?
One of those decisions is in front of us right now. The Department of Natural Resources is converting the project’s two state right-of-way leases from conditional to standard leases. It sounds like paperwork, but it isn’t. Investors and lenders deciding whether to finance a gas line want to know that its land rights are settled and that the state stands behind its own project. Converting the leases answers that question through the state’s own process, at no cost to Alaskans.
Under Gov. Sean Parnell, the Legislature passed the framework that made the State of Alaska a partner in the project rather than a bystander. Under Gov. Bill Walker, the state took the lead when others stepped back and carried the project into federal permitting. Under Gov. Mike Dunleavy, Alaska brought in a private developer to finish the job.
Three governors, from different political traditions. But each one kept the project alive and moved it forward. Legislators from both parties voted to keep the door open. That continuity is rare in Alaska politics, and it is worth protecting.
Today, preliminary gas supply agreements are in place with North Slope producers. Pipeline engineering is further along than ever. Buyers in Asia are at the table because energy security has moved to the top of the agenda. Serious work remains, but the question has shifted from whether to how fast.
That is why the decisions ahead matter so much. New administrations bring fresh eyes, and that is healthy. They should ask hard questions. The South Korean government is doing its own independent review right now, and Alaskans should welcome that kind of rigor. A project this important should stand up to scrutiny – and Alaska LNG has.
But scrutiny is not the same as starting over. Every reset costs time we no longer have. Our economy will not wait, and neither will the families deciding whether their future is here.
So my request to our newly elected leaders is simple. I would like to see them get briefed early, ask every question they have and  — at every decision point — ask whether the choice in front of them moves Alaskans closer to secure, affordable energy or sets them back. Then I hope they help finish what three governors and the Legislature started.
And to Alaskans who want a gas line: These decisions are made by people who listen. Your voice is an essential part of state policy.
Alaskans have waited a long time for this gas line. With steady, bipartisan leadership, we can be the generation that builds it.

title: Vermont Conversation: ‘We are taught to hate.’ Author and artist Dana Mashoian Walrath sees patterns in genocides and warns of echoes in America today
description:
For her latest graphic narrative work, “Book of Genocides,” Walrath’s research took her to 10 regions where she met survivors, descendants, and communities struggling with the legacy of violence.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘We are taught to hate.’ Author and artist Dana Mashoian Walrath sees patterns in genocides and warns of ech[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Author, artist, and anthropologist Dana Mashoian Walrath with her new book, “The Book of Genocides.” Courtesy photo
Books can preserve memory. They can also sound an alarm. In “The Book of Genocides,” author, artist, and anthropologist Dana Mashoian Walrath confronts some of the darkest chapters in human history. In her 424-page graphic narrative, Walrath asks what happens when societies forget, deny, or repeat the lessons of the past.
Walrath argues that genocide is not an isolated historical event but a recurring process, one marked by familiar patterns of dehumanization, discrimination, land seizure, and political manipulation.
Her work blends scholarship, personal history, travel reporting, and graphic art to examine 10 genocides spanning five centuries, from the destruction of Indigenous peoples in North America and Australia, to atrocities in Armenia, Rwanda, Bosnia, Cambodia, and Gaza. Just last week, the International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority, which Walrath depicts in her book. 
For Walrath, whose family survived the Armenian genocide, the project is deeply personal.
“The book has been lurking within me for decades and decades,” she told me. She traced the origins of the work to a moment in high school when a beloved history teacher asked her, “What is it I’m supposed to know about the Armenians besides the rugs?”
“That meant that there were other histories out there getting suppressed,” Walrath said. “Since then, I’ve been on a mission to link us across genocides.”
Walrath, who holds a doctorate in anthropology from the University of Pennsylvania, said her academic training helped her understand the structural forces behind mass atrocities.
“The act of writing a dissertation empowered me to start really telling stories,” she said. Anthropology, she added, gave her “the vocabulary to understand all the injustices that I was perceiving in the world.”
Walrath’s award-winning works also include “Aliceheimer’s,” a graphic memoir about her mother’s dementia journey, and “Like Water on Stone,” a novel about the Armenian genocide. She has published comics, essays and poetry in The Nation, The Lancet, Slate, and NPR.
Central to Walrath’s argument is her insistence that genocide be understood not simply as mass killing but as a process. Drawing on the United Nations Genocide Convention, she defines genocide as “acts committed with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group.”
Too often, she said, public discussions focus only on massacres.
“Genocide tends to just get used for massive massacres, and it loses track of all the processes that underlie those massacres,” she said.
Among those, Walrath identifies land theft, institutional discrimination, dehumanization, and denial.
“The mass killing is always about taking over land,” she said. “Dehumanization is always part of what leads to the violence of massacre.”
Her research took her to all 10 regions featured in the book, where she met survivors, descendants, and communities struggling with the legacy of violence.
In Rwanda, she spoke with both perpetrators and survivors living together in a reconciliation village. In Cambodia, she met one of the few child survivors of Phnom Penh’s notorious Tuol Sleng prison. In Bosnia, she walked through Sarajevo and experienced the tunnel that once sustained the besieged city.
“Every one of them has a story,” she said. “It was the physical experience of the place that gave me the visual voice for each of the chapters.”
The emotional toll was severe. After visiting Auschwitz, Walrath became physically ill.
“I was so broken from the grief,” she recalled. “To watch the industrial scale of what was going on there, it undid me.”
Yet Walrath says the act of drawing and storytelling became a form of resistance to despair.
“I had a concrete way every day to contribute something to counter the violence that is happening in the world,” she said.
The book also ventures into contemporary political territory. Walrath pointed to the rise of polarizing rhetoric and attacks on democratic norms occurring in the U.S. today.
President Donald Trump “uses the phrase ‘enemies within.’ That was one of the main terms that Hitler was using.”
“The parallels are really quite frightening,” she added.
Despite the grim subject matter, Walrath ends on a note of optimism. She rejects the idea that violence is humanity’s natural state.
“We are hardwired to care for each other, rather than hardwired for violence,” she said. “We are taught to hate. It’s not that we’re hardwired to hate.”
Her next book will explore reconciliation, forgiveness, and the possibility of healing historical wounds.
Humans created systems of conquest and domination, Walrath said. “That means humans can undo them.”

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: Commentary: Nerding the numbers: What Louisiana’s Nov. 3 voter turnout numbers reveal
description: Official voter turnout data from all 64 parishes for the Nov. 3 election offer insight into how Jamie Davis made it a far closer contest than Julia Letlow anticipated.
text:
An election worker holds an “I Voted” sticker at the polling location in the East Baton Rouge Public Library branch in Zachary branch on Tuesday Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Elise Plunk/Louisiana Illuminator)The Louisiana Secretary of State recently provided official voter turnout data from all 64 parishes for the Nov. 3 election, and the numbers offer insight into how Democratic candidate Jamie Davis made it a far closer contest than Republican U.S. Sen.-elect Julia Letlow anticipated.
Before we jump into the analysis, let’s take a moment to recognize Iberville Parish, where a state-leading 62% of voters took part in the midterm elections, followed by West Feliciana at 61%. They were the only two parishes to outperform the 50.25% state turnout rate by more than 10 percentage points.
Democrats didn’t exactly dominate, but …
When you look at turnout numbers by party, Democrats outperformed Republicans in just nine parishes, and Davis only won in five of them.
But Democrats posted their biggest advantage where it mattered the most — Orleans Parish, where 54.5% of its party members cast ballots compared with 48.8% of Republicans. Throw in the 41% of unaffiliated and third-party voters in Orleans (who are more than likely left-learning), and it becomes clear how Davis secured nearly 90% support there.    
Letlow lags behind Trump performance
It was expected that Letlow would not match the dominating vote totals President Donald Trump received in his resounding Louisiana win from 2024, when he carried 60% of the vote. Turnout for presidential elections is consistently and significantly higher than in midterms, with two-thirds of Louisiana voters taking part two years ago.  
But what’s worth noting is that Letlow’s percentages lagged behind Trump’s by double digits in 18 parishes, with Davis claiming wins in five of them where Trump had finished first in 2024.
In those five parishes that Davis “flipped” from Trump, turnout among Republicans was less than 50% in just one: St. Bernard, where the GOP barely outperformed Democrats, 48.1% to 48.07%. This all points to disenchantment among a consequential number of Republicans with their president and U.S. Senate candidate. 
Statewide, 56% Republicans went to the polls compared with 53% of Democrats and 38% of no-party and third-party voters. It explains Letlow’s less-than-2% victory margin compared with Trump’s 22-point win in 2024.
Eight parishes flip red to blue
Not only did Davis claim wins in eight parishes where Trump finished first two years ago, he also outperformed or matched the president’s showing in four of them. We’re going to call those strong flips.
It’s not entirely surprising that Davis pulled 61% support from his home Tensas Parish, where Trump received 51% backing in 2024. His other strong flips came in Iberville, St. James and West Baton Rouge parishes.
Davis was just a single percentage point away from a strong flip in Jefferson Parish, the state’s second most populous parish, where he received 54% of the votes to Trump’s 55%.
The other parishes that turned from red to blue were Bienville, St. Bernard and St. Landry. 
‘Other’ voters matter
Louisiana stopped recognizing the Independent Party in August 2025 ahead of this year’s closed congressional party primaries, meaning unaffiliated voters had to choose a Democratic or Republican ballot in May and June if they wanted to take part.
The Supreme Court’s landmark redistricting ruling in April allowed Gov. Jeff Landry to edit the election calendar so Louisiana’s U.S. House districts could be redrawn. As a result, the Nov. 3 elections for those seats were an open primary with candidates from all parties on the ballot.
Did the scrambled schedule deter unaffiliated and third-party voters?
In 23 parishes, the “other” voter turnout was 40% or greater. Iberville and West Feliciana were again the stellar standouts with 50% and 53% showings, respectively. Eleven parishes saw less than one-third of their “other” voters show, with the smallest share in Morehouse Parish at 28%, while 30 parishes recorded turnout between 33% and 39% for non-Democrats and non-Republicans. 
Turnout  trends
The Secretary of State’s figures show overall voter turnout exceeded the statewide rate of 50.25% in 33 parishes. Only five parishes had rates lower than 45%, with West Caroll at the bottom with 41%. The other laggards were Madison, Morehouse, St. Bernard and Vernon parishes.
Statewide turnout was just under 47% for the previous midterm elections in 2022, when only 25 parishes saw more than 50% of their voters cast ballots.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming education chief ‘baffled’ governor moved to deny school-choice funding
description:
The embattled program that gives up to $7K per student for private school expenses is also tied up in a legal challenge. The state on Monday asked the Supreme Court to weigh in anew on the case. 
The post Wyoming education chief ‘baffled’ governor moved to deny school-choice funding appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Wyoming Superintendent of Public Instruction Megan Degenfelder is “baffled” by Gov. Mark Gordon’s move to deny funding for the state’s embattled school choice program in 2027, she told WyoFile. 
Gordon recently released his supplemental budget, which seeks additional funding after the Legislature approved a two-year budget in March. In his budget book, he recommended funding $0 of the $32.5 million the Wyoming Department of Education requested to operate the Steamboat Legacy Program for 2027-28. 
It’s the latest blow to the universal school voucher program, which the Wyoming Legislature passed in 2025. Through the program, Wyoming residents can apply to receive up to $7,000 in state money per student to pay for costs associated with private K-12 education. Students must be disenrolled from public school to qualify.

Gov. Mark Gordon during his 2026 State of the State address at the Wyoming Capitol in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

The program has been dogged by questions about its constitutionality since its inception. A 2025 lawsuit challenging the program delayed its implementation one year, but more than 4,000 students enrolled this fall. The court has yet to determine whether the program violates Wyoming’s constitution.
That ongoing litigation was a major factor in Gordon’s decision to deny the funding request, he said in a statement to WyoFile. 
Now, he added, “the funding of this program is rightly in the hands of the Legislature, and they can decide, as they did last year, if they wish to fund the program now or wait for the ruling of the courts.”
For Degenfelder, who has championed the school-choice program, Gordon’s decision was surprising, “especially given the Governor’s celebratory signing of the act.” Gordon called it a “remarkable achievement for Wyoming” when he signed into law in March 2025. 
“Over 4,200 students enrolled in the program once again have their education disrupted by partisan politics, through no fault of their own,” Degenfelder said. 
As Gordon indicated, the funding issue will now go to the Wyoming Legislature. Once the governor finalizes his request, it moves through the statehouse during the legislative session. The Joint Appropriations Committee will begin holding budget sessions in January. 
Meanwhile, the court case continues with no clear end in sight. On Monday, the state asked the Wyoming Supreme Court to weigh in anew.
Laramie County District Court Judge Peter Froelicher refused in early November to dismiss the lawsuit against the state of Wyoming, Degenfelder and Treasurer Curt Meier. In the latest filing, defendants asked the Supreme Court to review that order.
A rocky path
The Steamboat Legacy Scholarship Act significantly expanded school choice in Wyoming by replacing an income-qualified 2024 “education savings account” program. The 2025 law passed amid objections it would violate the Wyoming Constitution, which bars the state from handing out public funds to individuals, corporations or associations “except for necessary support of the poor.”
When the state opened Steamboat Legacy Scholarship applications in 2025, nearly 4,000 applicants signed up to receive the money for the 2025-26 school year. Then in June 2025, a group of parents and the Wyoming Education Association sued to halt the program.
The lawsuit set off a flurry of motions and hearings. Asserting the program would cause irreparable harm to plaintiffs, the lawsuit asked the court to block the voucher program while the case proceeds. Defendants, meanwhile, asked that the case be dismissed.
Co-owner Tiffany Gamble talks with students after outdoor activities at Powder River Prep. (Dan Cepeda for WyoFile)
Froelicher granted that plaintiff’s preliminary injunction request in July 2025, barring the state from releasing any money while the case was litigated.
The state, however, fought his injunction, and further challenges led to the Supreme Court taking up the matter. The high court in May reversed the injunction, concluding the group of parents challenging the state program “failed to clearly show they might be irreparably and personally injured.” 
The Supreme Court determination that plaintiffs failed to make a clear showing of such possible injury spurred defendants to ask Froelicher once more for dismissal. For the second time, he rejected the request, moving the case closer to a trial. 
In the latest filing, defendants asked the Supreme Court to review and reverse Froelicher’s November order. 
Constitutional questions
The lawsuit argued the voucher program violates the Wyoming Constitution, which makes public education a paramount state commitment. The constitution’s education clause states, “the legislature shall provide for the establishment and maintenance of a complete and uniform system of public instruction.”
A previous Wyoming Supreme Court ruling on education funding “found that … ‘all aspects of the school finance system are subject to strict scrutiny,’ and that ‘any state action interfering with [the right to equal educational opportunity] must be closely examined before it can be said to pass constitutional muster,’” the current lawsuit states.
This voucher program, it asserted, does not pass that muster. That’s because “the state cannot circumvent those requirements by funding private education that is not uniform and that meets none of the required state constitutional standards for education.”
The program will draw students away from public schools, the Wyoming Education Association also asserts, and shrinking enrollment leads to smaller state budget apportionment. Critics have also questioned whether the program aligns with constitutional language prohibiting public school funds to be used to assist private or parochial schools.
Kindergarten students line up behind teachers at Gannett Peak Elementary School in Lander on Aug. 29, 2024, during the first week of the school year. (Katie Klingsporn/WyoFile)
Defendants, however, argue that plaintiffs lack standing because they have failed to show irreparable harm posed by the program. More broadly, supporters of the program say it provides parents with adequate options for finding the best learning opportunities for their children.
The ultimate result could prove disruptive for the families that have enrolled their children for costs related to everything from tutoring to online classes, supplies and private school tuition.
After the Supreme Court ended the injunction in May, the state relaunched the program for the current school year. Again, several thousand applications were submitted.
In a Nov. 20 post on X, the Wyoming Freedom Caucus alluded to the fact that pressure on Wyoming legislators can influence the Steamboat Legacy Scholarship’s fate. 
“If you’re among the 4,500 families who opted into WY’s universal school choice program, you likely just learned that Gordon’s supplemental budget would DEFUND it,” the post read. “Meanwhile, the budget crams $100M into the state’s savings account. What will the 69th Legislature do?”

name: Source New Mexico
title: PNM seeks 19% rate increase
description: Most residential customers of New Mexico’s largest electric utility will see an average jump of 19% in monthly costs under a proposed rate increase PNM filed Tuesday with state regulators.
text:
New Mexico’s largest electric utility filed paperwork Nov. 24, 2026, that seeks to collect $172 million from ratepayers, which would amount to a 19% increase in monthly electric bills for most residential customers. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)Most residential customers of New Mexico’s largest electric utility will see an average jump of 19% in monthly costs under a proposed rate increase PNM filed Tuesday with state regulators. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The utility’s filing, estimated to be more than 13,000 pages, cites a number of costs — like modernizing the electrical grid, investing in renewable energy and mitigating against wildfire risk — that compelled the utility to collect $172.2 million from ratepayers in the form of higher utility bills. 
If the Public Regulation Commission approves PNM’s request, approximately two-thirds of residential ratepayers across the state will see a roughly $22 increase in monthly electrical bills, according to the filing.
Lisa Goodman, vice president of investor and community relations at TXNM Energy, PNM’s parent company, told Source NM on Wednesday that the price hike is necessary in part due to rising costs the utility is experiencing, as well as growing demand for electricity across the state. 
“You’ve got an inherent increase in the underlying costs. We’re not making up the cost of steel or aluminum or those sort of things, right?” she said. “Then you’ve got the other side of that. Things are growing. Our system hit multiple new system peaks this summer. So people are using more energy. There is an increase on the grid.”
PNM’s filings say the increase is needed to pay approximately $87 million needed to “harden, improve and expand” the electric system, along with $90 million in renewable energy and energy storage costs. The utility also needs $54 million due to increased operating and maintenance expenses, in addition to and other costs “associated with wildfire mitigation, cybersecurity protections and technology advancements.”
The proposed rate increase would take effect Oct. 1, 2027. PNM in 2024 also sought and received PRC approval for a rate increase that averaged $11 more a month for most ratepayers. That increase started appearing on electric bills in July 2025. 
While PNM is turning again to ratepayers to pay for what amounts to a 13% increase across the board, it is also rolling out a first-ever program that would shield some customers from the price hike.
A law the New Mexico Legislature passed in 2025 enabled PNM to establish a program targeted toward low-income ratepayers. Under the new program, customers whose income is 200% or less of the federal poverty limit will see, on average, only a $1 increase each month in their electric bills. 
That income threshold amounts to $66,000 for a family of four. Goodman estimated Wednesday that one-third of New Mexico residential ratepayers would qualify.
“We’ve really worked to incorporate that low-income discount to offset any impact to customers from this,” Goodman said. “So it’s negligible to them.”
New Mexico utility regulatory officials pave the way for PNM acquisition hearings to continue

The filings initiate a hearing process at the PRC that is expected to take between 10 and 13 months. Customers can weigh in via written or public comments at meetings, and the PRC will hold a public hearing at some point before approving the increase. 
The request for a rate hike drew swift criticism from Mariel Nanasi, executive director of clean energy organization New Energy Economy. In a statement Tuesday, she called it “outrageous” that PNM would seek a rate increase at the same time the PRC is considering whether private equity firm Blackstone should be allowed to acquire PNM.
“These proceedings cannot be treated as though they have no relationship to one another,” she said. 
PNM officials said Tuesday that the requested rate increase and the potential acquisition are “separate regulatory processes with different purposes” and that its proposed increase reflects “investments needed to serve customers, regardless of the acquisition.”

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: Sugar industry, Hoeven applaud tariffs targeted at Brazil
description: MOORHEAD, Minn. — The federal government is seeking to protect U.S. sugar producers from unfair competition from Brazil and other countries.  U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., held a press conference Wednesday at the headquarters of American Crystal Sugar in Moorhead to highlight plans for an additional tariff on sugar imports.  The Red River Valley of […]
text:
Trucks go in and out of the American Crystal Sugar beet processing plant at Hillsboro, N.D., on May 4, 2025. (Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)MOORHEAD, Minn. — The federal government is seeking to protect U.S. sugar producers from unfair competition from Brazil and other countries. 
U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., held a press conference Wednesday at the headquarters of American Crystal Sugar in Moorhead to highlight plans for an additional tariff on sugar imports. 
U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, right, discusses sugar imports on Nov. 25, 2026, in Moorhead, Minnesota. With Hoeven is Tom Astrup, center, president and CEO of American Crystal Sugar, and Rick Kasper, president and CEO of Minn-Dak Farmers Cooperative. (Photo by Jeff Beach/North Dakota Monitor)
The Red River Valley of North Dakota and Minnesota is a prime sugar beet growing region. Hoeven said the domestic industry needs to be protected from foreign dumping of sugar into the U.S. market or consumers will be affected. 
“If these unfair trade practices wipe out our industry, the consumer is disadvantaged because then we’re at the mercy of whatever price they want to charge,” Hoeven said of sugar-exporting countries.
U.S. Trade Representative Ambassador Jamieson Greer said in an announcement that an increase in sugar tariffs is aimed at Brazil but will apply to other countries.
Written comments on the policy are due Dec. 30. The trade agency will hold a hearing about the proposed tariff modification Jan. 14.
Hoeven noted a study by the North Dakota State University Agricultural Risk Policy Center that found that sugar imports going over quotas resulted in an estimated loss of up to $1.8 billion for the U.S. sugar industry last year. 
Hoeven was joined at the press conference by representatives of American Crystal Sugar and the Minn-Dak Farmers Cooperative based in Wahpeton, North Dakota. 
“We will urge USTR to take this opportunity to update the sugar tariffs, thereby ensuring that foreign producers are not enriched at the expense of American farmers and workers,” Minn-Dak President and CEO Rick Kasper said. 
In May, 112 members of Congress, including all three members of the North Dakota delegation, sent a letter to the trade agency calling for action on sugar imports.

text:
An economic assistance application for the South Dakota Department of Social Services. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota Department of Social Services plans to enforce Medicaid work requirements by the original deadline of Jan. 1, even though the federal government is giving states six more months.
The U.S. Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services announced the six-month grace period earlier this month. Top congressional Democrats had said states need more time to build systems that keep eligible people from losing coverage.
Arkansas and Indiana are among other states that plan to start in January. Connecticut, California, New York and Kentucky are among the states planning to use the delay, according to Becker’s Hospital Review. Some states, such as Nebraska and Montana, have already implemented work requirements.
Voters reject measure that could have triggered repeal of Medicaid expansion in South Dakota

Brenda Tidball-Zeltinger, South Dakota’s interim social services secretary, said in a statement that changing the state’s plan now “would require significant programming changes in a short amount of time.” 
Medicaid expansion enrollees ages 19 through 64 will be required to work, do community service, or attend an education program at least 80 hours a month to stay enrolled, under the 2025 federal law known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. There are exemptions for pregnant people, caregivers of young children, people with complex medical conditions and tribal members, among others.
Medicaid is a joint federal-state health insurance program. In South Dakota, it traditionally covered low-income groups such as children, elderly people and disabled people. In 2022, South Dakota voters approved expanding Medicaid eligibility to low-income adults. 
South Dakota voters approved a constitutional amendment in 2024 allowing work requirements for Medicaid expansion. The state drafted its own rules but withdrew the proposal after Congress and President Donald Trump passed federal requirements in 2025. 
As of October, 31,606 South Dakotans were enrolled in Medicaid through expanded eligibility, among roughly 142,000 Medicaid enrollees in the state. The Department of Social Services estimated in April that about 1,200 South Dakotans would lose coverage because of work requirements.
Medicaid enrollees have been notified of the upcoming change, according to the department.
Liz Schenkel, external affairs manager for Community HealthCare Association of the Dakotas, said in an emailed statement that the organization is “disappointed” with the department’s decision, but will work with the department to support a “successful implementation and minimize unnecessary coverage disruptions.”
“We viewed it as a tool that would have protected both Medicaid members and the state,” Schenkel said, “by providing additional time to identify implementation challenges, test systems, and ensure communication efforts were working as intended before coverage consequences took effect.”

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: For the first time, Utah has 2 unaffiliated legislators. Who are they and who will they caucus with?
description: For the first time in Utah’s modern history — perhaps ever — two unaffiliated legislators will be taking up seats in the Utah House next year.  They come from very different backgrounds. Patrick Belmont is a water, earth and climate professor at Utah State University in Logan. Sergio Sotelo, of West Jordan, is an electrician […]
text:
Sergio Sotelo (left) and Patrick Belmont won election to the Utah House as the state's first unaffiliated legislators. (Photos courtesy of Sergio Sotelo and Patrick Belmont)For the first time in Utah’s modern history — perhaps ever — two unaffiliated legislators will be taking up seats in the Utah House next year. 
They come from very different backgrounds. Patrick Belmont is a water, earth and climate professor at Utah State University in Logan. Sergio Sotelo, of West Jordan, is an electrician and longtime labor union member and organizer. 
For both, it’s not yet clear whether they’ll caucus with Republicans, Democrats or neither. That means they could act as political wildcards in a 75-member chamber where this year’s blue wave election flipped 18 Republican legislative seats — doubling Democrats’ caucus from 14 to 28 and shattering Republicans’ two-thirds supermajority for the first time in more than 30 years. 
When the Utah Legislature’s session starts in January and the new slate of lawmakers are sworn in, House Republicans will have lost 16 seats to 14 Democrats, Belmont and Sotelo, slashing the GOP ranks from 61 to 45 members. 
Utah’s 2026 election results are certified, solidifying Democrats’ gains in the Legislature

In the Senate, Republicans lost two seats, so they’ll still hold a supermajority in that chamber, while House Republicans will hold a simple majority. 
However, newly elected GOP legislative leaders from both chambers have said they’re listening to voters’ rebuke of their party, and they have promised to work collaboratively rather than combatively with the stronger Democratic caucus. 
Knowing that they could play a role in helping certain legislative efforts to cross the finish line — or stop them in their tracks — Belmont and Sotelo both say they want to focus on solutions that matter for Utahns, like housing affordability, living wages, and sustainable water policy for the Great Salt Lake.
What they don’t want is more divisive, two-party politicking.
Belmont said he’s worried about the possibility that Republicans and Democrats will “dig their heels in harder” and become even more polarized under the Legislature’s new makeup,  but he said “I will be doing everything I can to make it more collaborative.” 
“I really do deeply believe that that is the only way forward,” Belmont said. “Having honest conversations that span ideologies.” 
Both Belmont and Sotelo said they haven’t decided who they’ll caucus with when the session starts on Jan. 19. Belmont floated the possibility of “engaging with people, perhaps as a third caucus” that includes members from both parties. But that remains to be seen. 
Sotelo said he and Belmont  “both need to be very cautious on how to carry ourselves up there” on Capitol Hill. 
Analyzing Utah’s blue wave: Many Republicans didn’t turn out; others crossed over to vote blue

“I think we’re both aligned on the same thing, that the one thing we’re going to do is prioritize our constituents, prioritize our communities and caucus to favor and benefit those constituents and those communities that put us there,” Sotelo said. “What’s going to be best for them.”
While it’s common for independent and third-party candidates to run for legislative office, Belmont and Sotelo’s wins are the first unaffiliated candidates to be elected to the Legislature in the state’s recorded history. The state’s only third-party legislator, Sen. Emily Buss, a Forward Party member, narrowly lost her seat to Republican Brooks Benson. 
Belmont and Sotelo’s elections came during a year when unaffiliated Utah voter registrations ticked upward. This year, the state’s active unaffiliated voters rose to 519,252, up 41,275 from 477,977 in November 2025, according to state records. 
Republicans still make up the majority of the state’s active voter registrations with 912,989, but that’s down slightly from 926,455 in 2025. Democrats have 260,867 voters, up from 241,063 last year.
The increase in unaffiliated voter registration could have been a small factor in helping Belmont and Sotelo. However, both candidates mostly attributed their success to hard work knocking doors — but also a growing sentiment among voters frustrated with the status quo. 
“There’s probably a lot of people out there who feel the same way that I do, that partisan politics is just not going to get us where we need to go,” Belmont said. There isn’t a single party that has all the answers. We have to get back to a place where we’re having real conversations.”
While the blue wave clearly helped them this election, Sotelo said he saw it more as a working class wave — propelled by people who “voted with their pockets.” 
“When I was out knocking doors, I was knocking on independent doors, Democrat doors, Republican doors, and you know what? They’re all working families,” Sotelo said. “They all need to put food on the table. They all need to go out, work, and earn a living.”
Patrick Belmont poses for a photo in front of the Utah Capitol in Salt Lake City. (Photo courtesy of Patrick Belmont)
Who is Patrick Belmont?
Belmont won the House District 3 seat this year by a wide margin, beating Republican incumbent Rep. Jason Thompson with more than 59% of the vote, according to certified election results. 
Belmont’s race this year wasn’t his first foray in politics. Rather, it was his third time running for the seat after two previous unsuccessful campaigns in 2022 and 2024. 
On election night, Belmont had hosted about 20 of his closest campaign volunteers for a home-cooked, Thanksgiving-style feast — with a big turkey — at his house in downtown Logan. 
As they waited for results, Belmont said he had “nothing but good feelings and deep gratitude” for his campaign. He had lost before, but he said he felt like they ran a strong campaign. 
Utah House Democrats shake up leadership after the blue wave doubled their caucus

But when the results came out, the room “erupted,” he said. 
“We were not expecting to be ahead with that kind of margin,” he said. 
His lead not only held, but grew as more ballots were tallied. 
“It was just overwhelming. … I’m an ultra marathoner. I run a lot of really, absurdly long races. And this felt like a whole different level.” 
After five years and multiple campaigns, Belmont said it felt like the work finally paid off. 
Belmont said he’s been an independent most of his life, but in 2022, he ran as a Democrat because “I thought I needed a party behind me.” But that year, he said “people immediately kind of put me in a box, and it just shut off a lot of conversations.”
So when he decided to run again in 2024, Belmont opted to run as an independent, “and it felt so much better, so much more authentic to me and who I am, and it just opened up so many more conversations.” That also meant some Republicans also decided to support him that year. 
“I’m an independent because I am accountable to evidence, my conscience, and my constituents,” he said. “That’s what I really want to be accountable to, and that’s the way I’m going to work in the Legislature.” 
The 48-year-old water scientist and professor at Utah Valley University was born in Chicago but moved to St. Louis when he was young. He lived in Texas, Pennsylvania and Minnesota while earning his undergraduate, graduate and postdoctoral degrees before moving to Logan, Utah. He’s lived there for 17 years. 
Belmont said he decided to run for public office out of a desire to maintain Utah’s quality of life while also becoming frustrated that “when science is asking something hard of us, it gets ignored or — worse — buried.” 
Utah Gov. Cox: Republicans ‘suffered a historic defeat.’ Now, he says they have to ‘listen’

“It was the harder lessons from science that were not making its way into management policy in a way that I think they need to,” he said. 
As an example, he pointed to the shrinking Great Salt Lake. 
“The science has been done for a long time. We know what we need to do there. We’ve thrown over $1 billion at the lake now, passed two dozen bills, and it’s worse off than we started seven years ago,” he said. “And it’s because a lot of the people in elected office right now don’t want to have the harder conversation.” 
Belmont said he’ll be pushing a “conservation first” strategy when it comes to water policy. He said he’d like to see the conversation shift away from “how can we create more supply to how can we save water,” and he said he wants to ensure “excessive” water users actually pay for their use. 
Water in Utah, one of the driest states in the country, is far too cheap, he said. 
“We’re the second-driest state in the country. We have the highest per-capita water use in the country. It’s absolutely bizarre,” he said. “And any economist would look at that and be like, ‘Well, of course, you’re basically giving it away for free. What do you expect?’” 
Who is Sergio Sotelo?
Sotelo was taking out the trash from his election night watch party when results were posted. When he came back inside, he said everyone was cheering. 
The 43-year-old, who lives in West Jordan with his wife and two children, said he never doubted that he would win, even though some told him he was crazy to run for House District 38, expected to be firmly red. 
“We never had any doubt that we were going to pull this off because we worked so hard,” Sotelo said of his campaign. But like Belmont, he was caught off guard by the margin. Sotelo won with more than 56% of the vote to Republican Chris McConnehey’s nearly 44%.  
Utah House Democrats’ wins come with mixed feelings over loss of some moderate Republicans

Sotelo said as he and his campaign workers would knock doors, they’d come back surprised by how many people were excited to engage with his campaign — not just because they liked his message as a blue collar worker and union supporter, but also because they felt like sitting politicians hadn’t campaigned in their neighborhoods for years. 
“Instead of telling me to go pound sand and kick rocks, they’d say, ‘Hey, you want a water? Want a gatorade? Thanks for coming by,’” he said. 
Sotelo grew up in Chicago after his parents immigrated there from Mexico. He said he moved to Utah in the early 2000s. He worked for more than 15 years as an electrician, both working in the trade and representing workers through a local chapter of the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers. He currently serves as treasurer of that chapter and runs a small accounting business with his family. 
Sotelo said his involvement in politics dates back to his early days with the union, helping track bills and advocate for labor-friendly policies. 
He said the Utah Legislature has had a long history of anti-union legislation. But the controversial bill banning collective bargaining for public unions that lawmakers passed in 2025 — only to repeal it soon after amidst a successful referendum effort — was the final straw that prompted him to run for the Legislature. 
Utah Legislature approves repeal of anti-collective bargaining law

The sponsors of that bill — Senate Majority Leader Kirk Cullimore and Rep. Jordan Teuscher, R-South Jordan — both lost re-election this year to Democrats. 
While his margins surprised him, Sotelo said frustrations had brewed for a long time — and this was the year where people had enough. 
“The Republican party got way too comfortable with that supermajority,” he said. 
While he said some of his progressive ideals align with the Democratic party, Sotelo said he chose to run as an unaffiliated candidate because he sees himself as an advocate for the working class, which spans all political stripes.
“They don’t care if it’s red; they don’t care if it’s blue … they vote with their pockets,” he said. 
Polling data showed his campaign that “people were upset with both parties,” he said, “so we needed to let the people know that there was an alternative.” 
“We can have different solutions and not just rhetoric of switching the ball from one court to another,” he said. “Just the constant bickering and blaming, it’s just like, let’s stop that. Let’s just have conversations on solutions.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado submits new waiver to exclude sugary drinks from SNAP benefits
description: Colorado once again is trying to limit the use of federal nutrition assistance money on sugary drinks and soda. The state submitted a waiver to the U.S. Department of Agriculture on Nov. 20 to begin a five-year pilot program that would exclude some drinks from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the food benefit program for […]
text:
Soda on display in a grocery store. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)Colorado once again is trying to limit the use of federal nutrition assistance money on sugary drinks and soda.
The state submitted a waiver to the U.S. Department of Agriculture on Nov. 20 to begin a five-year pilot program that would exclude some drinks from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, the food benefit program for low-income people. Under the waiver, sugary drinks are defined as having at least 5 grams of sweetener per 12 ounces.
“SNAP plays an important role in helping every Colorado family put nutritious food on the table,” Gov. Jared Polis, a Democrat, said in a statement. “Sugary beverages like soda have no nutritional value or health benefits, and lead to negative health outcomes like higher rates of obesity, diabetes, and worse dental health. By supporting Coloradans to make healthy choices we can improve our health, fight chronic disease, and lower healthcare costs.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The drinks covered by the waiver do not include baby formula, natural fruit or vegetable juice, meal replacement drinks, drinks with milk as the main ingredient and beverages for medical use.
Colorado initially submitted a waiver for sugary drinks in May 2025, and the federal government approved a handful of state’s, including Colorado’s, requests that summer. A federal judge then blocked five of the state plans this June, however, after SNAP recipients sued. The plaintiffs included a Colorado woman with diabetes who worried the waiver would prevent her from using her SNAP money to purchase the drinks she regularly uses to maintain her blood sugar. The USDA is appealing that decision.
A new class action lawsuit now seeks to block similar SNAP restrictions in 18 other states.
The new waiver elicited criticism from Hunger Free Colorado, the nonprofit policy organization that strongly opposed the first waiver attempt.
“Regardless of how this proposal is structured, restricting food choices does nothing to address hunger or the barriers Coloradans face in accessing health food,” policy advisor Mariah Guerrero said in a statement. “Instead, it increases stigma, creates confusion for families and retailers and exacerbates hunger. We question what this effort will accomplish beyond wasting valuable time and resources that should be spent supporting Colorado families and protecting SNAP from the very real threats it faces.”
Colorado’s revised waiver comes after consultation with the USDA, Polis’ office said. About 588,000 Coloradans use SNAP benefits, according to the state’s Department of Human Services. That’s down about 30,000 people from last year, following eligibility changes passed by Congress.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: A statue for Shaumpishuh, the Indigenous leader who helped shape Guilford
description: A six-person committee is trying to raise $60,000 to commission a statue of the female sachem.
text:
Ellen Creane still remembers the first time she heard about Shaumpishuh, a female sachem of the Menunkatuck Band of the Quinnipiac Tribe. She was in the audience at a book talk, and the story of Shaumpishuh’s life resonated with Creane, who often thinks about the long arc of Guilford’s history, and the people who lived there long before 1639. 
Four years later, she’s working to make sure friends, neighbors, educators and students know that name too — and that Shaumpishuh receives some of the historical due she is owed.    
That’s the goal of the six-member Shaumpishuh Statue Committee, a Guilford-based crew of retired educators, local historians, cultural workers, writers, and tribal leaders that in May received unanimous approval from the Guilford Board of Selectmen to install a sculpture at 55 Park St., beside the Jedediah Lathrop House and directly across from the Guilford Town Green. 
This fall, the committee has launched its first fundraising campaign and released a call for artists that ends Jan. 31 of next year. While the group does not yet have a formalized budget, it has set a fundraising goal of $60,000, and is applying to the Mellon Foundation for grant funding. 
Committee member Kevin “Red Eagle” Brown, who served as chairman of the Mohegan Tribal Council from 2013 to 2019, said that the Mohegan Tribe has pledged support to the campaign but that the specifics are not yet public.  
“It’s about reconciliation, respect, knowledge, and learning,” he said. “And about recognizing that these were among the first peoples here.” 
“We want this to be a permanent message, not only to people of the shoreline, but nationally,” added Creane, a longtime educator and writer who is now the committee’s board secretary. “We expect this to be as nationally important as the story of Pocahontas or Sacajawea.”   
Shaumpishuh, of whom an actual likeness is not known, lived and died in the 17th century, and in that time became a persuasive advocate for the Quinnipiac people. Her brother, Momauguin, was a grand sachem, or chief, who lived in what is now recognized as New Haven and East Haven. Her uncle, Qussuckquansh, was a sachem in the villages of Kuttawo and Totoket, or what is now recognized as Branford, according to maps from the Massachusetts Historical Society. 
By the 1630s, she had become the sachem of the Menunkatuck Band, a fact that Creane is still often amazed by when she thinks of it (Shaumpishuh also mothered three children, including a daughter who became a chief sachem, according to John Menta’s 2003 book “The Quinnipiac: Cultural Conflict in Southern New England”). In 1638, she advised Momauguin on what historians now widely call the New Haven Agreement, in which white, English colonial settlers — likely benefitting from the fear and fallout of the Pequot War — offered ostensible military protection and material possessions such as hatchets, knives, and bowls in exchange for land. 
The following year, Shaumpishuh helped broker a trade agreement with the Rev. Henry Whitfield that would become a founding and foundational document of the Town of Guilford. In the deed, Shaumpishuh granted settlers access to land in exchange for goods including stockings, shoes, hats, and cutlery, according to the 19th-century account of librarian and professor Bernard Christian Steiner. Between the scribbled words “squaw” and “sachem,” her signature is a bow and arrow.    
How much agency she had in this decision isn’t directly known: a smallpox epidemic in 1633 devastated Indigenous communities across the state, wiping out what historian James “Jim” Powers estimated was 85 percent of the Indigenous population. Then from 1636 to 1638, the Pequot War showed the militarized violence of which colonial settlers were capable: hundreds of Pequot were killed, and others were enslaved, a practice that historian Margaret Ellen Newell explores further in her book “Brethren by Nature: New England Indians, Colonists, and the Origins of American Slavery.” 
In between, “the Pequot attempted to subjugate other tribes throughout Connecticut and the islands offshore,” according to the Mashantucket Pequot Museum & Research Center’s resource “Battlefields of the Pequot War.” 
By the time Shaumpishuh was navigating negotiations with Whitfield, she would have been keenly aware of the potential violence that could follow an unwillingness to negotiate and sign an agreement, as English colonists encroached on Quinnipiac land. Or as historian and professor Nathan Braccio recounts in a 2023 essay for the Massachusetts Historical Society, “when Shaumpishuh sold rights to her land to the English two years later, it was to a people who had amply demonstrated their penchant for violence.”     
The deed itself seems to reflect this imbalance of power: it is written in English in Whitfield’s neat script (read a transcription here), with the signature that confirms her presence.    
“She played an incredible role in the history of protecting the rights of her people,” said Powers, a retired high school history teacher who now serves as the committee’s president. “I’ve always been an incredible fan of hers, especially at a time when the English Puritans considered women to be the property of their husbands.”       

Shaumpishuh Statue Committee members Cheryl Buckley, Ellen Creane, Courtney Cucinotta, Kevin “Red Eagle” Brown, Mike Bracken, and James (Jim) Powers pictured inside the Quinnipiac Dawnland Museum at a committee meeting in November 2026.   Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

The committee, which officially incorporated as a nonprofit in May of last year, started with that history. In 2021, Powers published “Shadows Over Dawnland,” a work of historical fiction about the culture, land stewardship, and ultimate displacement of the Quinnipiac people, using the very real and equally calamitous 1633 smallpox epidemic as a launchpad into millennia of history. 
In the book, Powers follows a Quinnipiac boy named Ponaim, whose parents have both died of smallpox, as he becomes the student of a Quinnipiac shaman named Commossuck (the main characters are fictionalized, but the name “Ponaim” comes from Whitfield’s historical records). Those years of research, through which he also became a founding member and advocate of the Quinnipiac Dawnland Museum, also gave him an education on Shaumpishuh.
In 2022, Powers gave a book talk that Creane attended, and at which she learned that West Lake, an area of the town that she calls home, “is the last known place the Quinnipiac lived,” Powers said. That same year, she was part of a small group that began meeting to discuss the possibility of a statue or memorial in the town. By last year, those efforts had grown into the formalized committee, which sought nonprofit status as a way to begin its fundraising efforts. 
During that time, it also became increasingly clear that the committee needed to have Native voices. Brown, who currently lives in Guilford, and Courtney Cucinotta, a Branford-based herbal therapist and gardner who has Nipmuc and European ancestry, now sit on the committee. In addition, the committee reports to an advisory council comprising roughly 20 people.
When the committee initially brought its request for a statue to the five-member Guilford Board of Selectmen in the fall of 2025, the biggest question became not whether the statue would ultimately materialize (the committee has yet to select an artist; more on that below), but where the artwork might go. While the town is not providing financial support for the statue, Guilford First Selectman Matthew T. Hoey III said that the board is in agreement that the project contributes to the rich and complex history of the town. 
“It feels wonderful for us to have been able to accommodate what was a really great idea that ties our current community to the foundation of Guilford, and the role that this woman played as the sachem, the chief, of the Menunkatuck Band,” Hoey said in a phone call Tuesday morning. “This can serve as an educational statue, so that more of our youth, and our adults, can learn about the role this woman played in allowing Guilford to become what Guilford is today.”
Selectmen debated different locations: the historic Town Green itself, which houses monuments to Guilford residents lost during the Revolutionary, U.S. Civil, and Korean Wars; the “Great Plain” of Guilford, which sits beside the Long Island Sound and which the Menunkatuck Band once considered vital to their way of life; the Henry Whitfield House itself, where Whitfield began to make a home for himself following the 1639 signing. 
Across the street from that house, there is also a spot memorializing the 1639 Guilford Covenant, which acknowledges the beginning of a colonial settlement known as Guilford. None of them felt right. 
Then “we were looking for other properties around the Green,” and ultimately landed on the Major Jedediah Lathrop House, remembered Hoey. That location felt significant to both committee members and the Board of Selectmen: the Lathrop House is home to several municipal offices, and owned by the town. 
It is right next to the town’s public library, a building dedicated to the pursuit of knowledge and curiosity, and close to the town’s First Congregational Church, which does a fair amount of social justice work. It also sits just across the street from the Town Green.    
“It satisfied and fulfilled what the committee felt would be the most appropriate location, with Shaumpishuh looking West across our beautiful Town Green,” Hoey said.

The Major Jedediah Lathrop House in Guilford. The town’s Board of Selectmen unanimously approved a spot for the Shaumpishuh statue in front of the house’s porch (where the American flag is) in May of this year.  Credit: Lucy Gellman / CT Mirror

   In May of this year, the Guilford Board of Selectmen unanimously approved their request. By then, the committee had secured an outpouring of support that came from university professors, museum curators, Connecticut town and city historians, and State Rep. Moira Rader and State Sen. Christine Cohen, both of whom represent the district.    
In addition, and perhaps most movingly, members of the Native American Cultural Heritage Council — that includes representatives of the Eastern Pequot Tribal Nation, the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation, the Mohegan Tribal Nation, the Golden Hill Paugussett Indian Nation, and the Schaghticoke Tribal Nation — voiced their strong support for the project. 
Last month, committee members released a request for proposals open to artists of all backgrounds requesting sketches for an adult, life-sized representation of Shaumpishuh, which they plan to ultimately cast in bronze. According to the request for proposals, the rendering should “reflect the time period (1630’s) (Northeast Woodland Culture)” and “reflect a welcoming and healing community.” It closes January 31; Powers said in an email Tuesday that no artists have submitted to date. 
Because there is no known image of Shaumpishuh that exists, committee members said they are open to artistic interpretation; the committee currently has an AI-generated image as its logo on social media. In each application, they have also requested a proposed budget, and materials, including an artist’s statement and statement of purpose (read the full request through the National Sculpture Society here). The request does not specify whether or not having a Native artist is a core principle of the project, although both Creane and Cucinotta expressed interest in that at a recent committee meeting.
During a committee meeting at Guilford’s Dudley Farm (the Quinnipiac Dawnland Museum sits on the property), Cucinotta sketched out a rendering showing Shaumpishuh kneeling gently on the ground, hands out in a gesture of offering and gratitude. When asked, she smiled and said she doesn’t consider herself an artist, and simply had turned out the sketch as one potential direction an artist might go in. But as she passed it around the table, she spoke about the context in which she images the statue.
“I’m thinking about her spirit,” she said. “That prayer of offering, of listening to receive.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: West Jackson is home to ‘the worm guy’
description: Matt Casteel, founder and managing partner of WurmWorks, talks about his farm in Jackson on Thursday, June 4, 2026. Casteel’s farm sits near land targeted for rezoning as a developer seeks approval to build a large heavy-industrial data center campus on about 230 acres in northwest Jackson.
text:
Matt Casteel is known around Jackson as the worm guy. 
Although he thinks of himself as a farmer first, Casteel has come to embrace the name.
“Worm guy. Yeah, I don’t mind anymore. I used to be like, ‘Well, I’m kind of a micro farmer.’ Worm Guy. No, it’s good, it’s fun, it’s delightful,” Casteel said.
Casteel runs a worm farm called Wurmworks on a little less than 2 acres of land in west Jackson where millions of earthworms compost food scraps, coffee grounds and other organic food waste from across the city into soil. 
Wurmworks sells the soil, plants and a composting service.
For the composting service, Casteel collects food scraps from residential customers who gather their kitchen waste in plastic bins. Once the bins are full, they leave them at one of the drop off locations around town, and Casteel takes the scraps back to the farm and feeds them to the worms. 
“Everything that we use to make our compost, it’s sourced from right around here,” Casteel said.
There’s no city-run curbside compost collection, so organizations such as Wurmworks have stepped in to fill the gap for Jackson residents.
Before becoming a farmer, Casteel, who grew up across Mississippi, worked in international hunger relief for almost 10 years. His father, Steve Casteel, said the business came out of his son’s passion for people being able to grow their own food. 
“When he started his first worm bed in the garage he said, ‘Dad, I think this is what I want to do, and I want to do it in Jackson. I love Jackson,’” Steve Casteel said. 
“For the last eight-ish years of my life building this from literally a bin with worms I ordered on the internet to millions of earthworms. And around a 25 to 30% growth rate every year,” Casteel said.
Since Wurmworks started in 2018, it has moved around. It was on a friend’s farm in Terry when he was starting out. For about three years it was at the Eco Shed, a now defunct coworking space in Jackson, where Casteel worked alongside another farmer as he continued to build out his composting and earthworm operation.
But it was important that Wurmworks owned its own land. 
“New, young small farmers really have a tough time accessing land, which is their means of production. When you don’t own your means of production, it’s kind of hard to build a successful, sustainable business,” Casteel said.
He bought the land Wurmworks is on in 2023.

Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayWurmWorks, seen in Jackson Thursday, June 4, 2026, sits near land targeted for rezoning for a proposed large heavy-industrial data center campus on about 230 acres in northwest Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi TodayWurmWorks, seen in Jackson Thursday, June 4, 2026, sits near land targeted for rezoning for a proposed large heavy-industrial data center campus on about 230 acres in northwest Jackson. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“What’s just been miraculous is that 1.7 little acres is so big. It’s just so fruitful,” Steve Casteel said. “You just couldn’t think all this could be in this one little piece of land.”
The farm now has around 25 large raised wooden beds filled with earthworms. At first glance, the beds look like they’re just holding dirt, but when Casteel runs his hands through the dirt, he uncovers a multitude of worms just below the surface. 
“It looks really dry, right? Kind of like worms don’t live in there, right? But all you got to do is pull all that (dirt) back and you see all the wormies are just right on the surface,” Casteel said. 
Casteel, who lives in Jackson, wanted a place that was in the city but was away from herbicides and other things that could disturb the worms.
“Any type of contamination affects earthworms. They’re very sensitive to contamination. They’re very sensitive to oxygen percentages. They’re very sensitive to moisture content,” Casteel said.
Earlier this year, 230 acres of land surrounding Wurmworks was slated to be rezoned from residential to industrial use, and a developer was interested in building a data center there. 
In July, the city council ultimately passed a six month data center moratorium, to develop guidelines for any data center that would come to Jackson, although no serious projects have materialized. And controversy has continued. 
Casteel is worried about the impact a data center could have on his farm and the water he uses for his worms and plants. He initially favored a “measured, thoughtful, moratorium period” during which the council or other leaders could engage with the community, dig into the science and make sure there were appropriate regulations in place.  
But over five months later, Casteel said the process has not gone smoothly.
“We’re finding the whole process of the moratorium has been frustrating to say the least,” Casteel said, citing a lack of transparency, clarity and communication from the city and other officials. 
While the council fights and deliberates, Casteel continues his work.
On Saturdays, he and his dad are a regular fixture at the Mississippi Farmers Market in downtown Jackson. Customers can drop off their bins of food scraps, buy soil and plants that Casteel cultivates on the farm.  
Casteel never planned to start a nursery or sell plants but he now sells succulents and fruit trees. His work has continued to expand. He is involved with summer camps, urban gardens and a farm to school initiative. 
“Watching him create this complex network of relationships and continually build community and connection,” Steve Casteel said. “There’s just this kind of organic community that just continues to develop and grow.”

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Two Georgia GOP House lawmakers are challenging November losses
description: Two Georgia House Republicans are challenging their defeats in the Nov. 3 midterm election after House Democrats flipped enough seats to hand them control of the chamber with a slim majority in January. State Rep. Soo Hong, a Lawrenceville Republican, narrowly lost her race to sports agent Chris Luchey just 35 votes out of nearly […]
text:
Top: Democrat Chris Luchey and Republican state Rep. Soo Hong. Bottom: Democrat David Dillie and Republican state Rep. Bill Hitchens. Hong and Hitchens are contesting their losses to Luchey and Dillie. Two Georgia House Republicans are challenging their defeats in the Nov. 3 midterm election after House Democrats flipped enough seats to hand them control of the chamber with a slim majority in January.
State Rep. Soo Hong, a Lawrenceville Republican, narrowly lost her race to sports agent Chris Luchey just 35 votes out of nearly 24,000, according to election results certified by the secretary of state’s office.
But according to a Wednesday filing in Hall County Superior Court, Hong’s lawyers say they have identified at least 93 votes cast by people not eligible to vote in the district because they had moved out of the district before Oct. 5 – the last day to register to vote – and hadn’t lawfully updated their registration.
“Because the number of illegal votes exceeds the 35-vote margin, the result of the Election is, at a minimum, placed in doubt,” reads the complaint written by attorney Bryan Tyson, who is representing both Hong and Hitchens. “Georgia law requires the Court to declare the Election invalid and order a new election.”
“I’ll be obtaining legal representation and look forward to my day in court,” Luchey said in a phone call Wednesday.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Effingham County, Republicans are challenging the results of an election in which Rincon Republican state Rep. Bill Hitchens was unseated by tradesman David Dillie. Dillie won by just over 800 votes out of more than 22,000.
That case revolves around allegations that Dillie voted in Nevada in June and was therefore ineligible to run under Georgia’s residency law. The same claims arose before the election, but a state administrative judge ruled he was eligible.
At that time, Dillie’s former foster father testified that another foster child may have filled out and returned a mail-in ballot under Dillie’s name that had been sent to his home.
In documents filed in Effingham County Tuesday, Republicans said new evidence has emerged from an expert handwriting witness who has concluded that the signature on the ballot was Dillie’s.
“I have my legal counsel, we’re looking into it, and we look forward to our day in court,” Dillie said in a phone call.
Not counting the two races being challenged, Democrats currently claim 90 seats in the 180-seat chamber.
Early voting in a Dec. 1 Southwest Georgia runoff ends Wednesday. If Republican state Rep. Mike Cheokas is able to fend off the challenge from Democrat Ethan Wolfe, a retired military officer, the chamber would be split 90-90, which would mean neither party would hold a majority.
House Democrats have already prepared to take over the majority, including by nominating longtime Columbus Democratic state Rep. Carolyn Hugley to be the next House speaker. If she is sworn in, she will become the state’s first Black speaker.
House Democrats currently claim a one-seat majority with three races unresolved, including the one that Luchey is leading in. Dillie was declared the winner of his race and is among House Democrats’ 91-seat majority.
Hong, Hitchens and the attorney representing their cases did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
This is a developing story, check back for details.
