name: Rhode Island Current
title: A tie for the Glocester School Committee highlights a shortcoming in state law
description: Every vote counts. Unless there’s a tie. Two Glocester School Committee candidates received the exact same number of votes in the Nov. 3 election after a recount and final certification by the Rhode Island Board of Elections Tuesday. The board’s 5-0 vote to accept a previously disqualified extra ballot  created a tie between candidates Gary […]
text:
Glocester School Committee candidates Sheri Lynn Chandler, left, and Gary King, right, tied for the third and final open seat on the school board following a recount and reconsideration of an additional ballot by the Rhode Island Board of Elections Tuesday. (Courtesy photos)Every vote counts. Unless there’s a tie.
Two Glocester School Committee candidates received the exact same number of votes in the Nov. 3 election after a recount and final certification by the Rhode Island Board of Elections Tuesday. The board’s 5-0 vote to accept a previously disqualified extra ballot  created a tie between candidates Gary King and Sheri Lynn Chandler for the third and final open seat on the nonpartisan, six-member school board.
Now it’s up to Glocester Town Council to fill the seat by a majority vote within 30 days, according to the town charter.
How and when the council will choose is still undetermined, as town officials await guidance from Town Solicitor Dave Igliozzi. Igliozzi said Wednesday morning he needed to review the town charter before contacting council members.
But what would have happened if the tie had been in a state legislative race?
Rhode Island’s expansive election law never addresses how to break a tie in a state legislative race, according to John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island.
“This is something I’ve known was going to happen for a long time, and we need to be better prepared for,” Marion said in an interview Tuesday. “When incidents like this happen, a window opens to do some policymaking.”
Secretary of State Gregg Amore’s office offered a different interpretation in an email to Rhode Island Current Wednesday.
Even though there is nothing in state law that explicitly mentions a tie, there is a section on what happens when there is a “failure to elect” state officeholders and legislators. If there is no state general officer elected, including if no candidate gets a plurality of election votes, the Rhode Island General Assembly chooses between the top two vote-getters. In the case of no election for a state legislative seat, there is a new election
Marion said the absence of an election, as stated in the law, is not the same as a tie and stressed the need for further clarity.
From coin tosses to card flips, runoff elections or new elections altogether, the intrigue and excitement of settling an election tie has attracted attention in local and state races nationwide. Yet neither Marion nor the Rhode Island Board of Elections could recall any previous examples of a tied race in Rhode Island.
Despite the extraordinary chain of events that led to the deadlock, King was calm and nonchalant when contacted by Rhode Island Current Tuesday night.
“I guess we’ll see,” he said.
King, a 55-year-old millwright and welder, previously served one term on the Glocester School Committee, from 2003 to 2007. His now-adult sons both attended town and regional public schools.
His comeback bid came from his frustration over the regional school district’s handling of a former Ponaganset High School teacher accused of having an inappropriate relationship with a student. The teacher was indicted on two counts of third-degree sexual assault following an investigation by the Rhode Island State Police and Attorney General’s office. The incident also spurred an independent investigation by the regional school committee — which includes all the members of the Glocester school board –- along with staff training and other policy changes.
“I don’t tolerate that behavior,” King said of the former teacher. He also criticized the school committee for “overspending” on various budget items.
Chandler, a first-time candidate with two children still in the public school system, also emphasized student safety and fiscal responsibility in an interview with The Valley Breeze.
Chandler did not attend Tuesday night’s election board meeting due to a scheduling conflict. In a statement to Rhode Island Current Wednesday morning, she thanked the voters who supported her and other school committee candidates.
“A tie shows how deeply our community cares about our schools,” she said. “As election officials work to resolve this properly, my focus remains on fully supporting students and schools, keeping communication clear for families and taxpayers, and asking critical questions to analyze options before making informed, sound decisions.”
The Rhode Island Board of Elections on Tuesday, Nov. 24, voted 5-0, with one abstention and one absence, to accept a previously disqualified ballot in the Glocester School Committee election, putting two candidates at a tie. Facing them is candidate Gary King. (Screenshot)
No hesitation 
In the initial tally of Nov. 3 election results, Chandler led King by two votes for the third-place spot on the school committee.
King requested and was granted a recount by the Rhode Island Board of Elections. After refeeding every ballot into the tabulating machines on Nov. 13, he was still one vote behind Chandler.
Recounts are open to the public. King observed and identified a single ballot that went initially uncounted, though he thought it should be counted. The ballot, cast at Ponaganset High School during the 20-day early voting period, was rejected because the voter appeared to select four of the seven school committee candidates, when the maximum choice allowed was three.
One of the four ovals was only partially filled in. The other three — including the one in front of King’s name — were completely darkened.
The ballot-counting machine initially flagged the submission as an overvote, but the error was overridden, meaning the voter chose to not alter their choices when they had the chance. As a result, the voter’s school committee picks were left out of the initial results, and the recount.
King contended the fourth selection counted as a “hesitation mark” under the state elections board’s voter intent guide, meaning it was not an actual selection, and that the ballot should count based on the voter’s selection of the three other candidates.
“I believe this board will see it the same way,” he said in an interview before the election board’s meeting.
They did. Following a brief discussion and review of the rest of the ballot in question, the board voted unanimously to accept the previously uncounted ballot, putting King and Chandler in a deadlock at 1,293 votes apiece.



Quotation







This is something I’ve known was going to happen for a long time, and we need to be better prepared for. When incidents like this happen, a window opens to do some policymaking.


– John Marion, executive director of Common Cause Rhode Island


The elections board certified all results, including in the school committee race, at the same meeting, leaving it up to the Republican town council to break the tie.
Rhode Island Current contacted all five members of the council. Councilor Jonathan Burlingame, a former school committee chair before he won a seat on the council in 2022, remained noncommittal. He knew King, but not Chandler, and said he wanted to learn more about both candidates’ views before making a decision.
“It’s definitely an important position, where a lot of our money is put forth in the town,” he said of the seat. “They control a good 50% of our taxes.”
The other four council members had not responded as of early Wednesday afternoon.
In search of solutions 
Inspired by the Glocester case, Marion is looking ahead to the start of the 2027 legislative session in January to advocate for changes to state elections law.
In local races, he said, it makes sense for municipal officials to determine the winner in the event of a tie. But enshrining that practice in state law would be a good idea, he concluded. 
As for statewide races that end in a tie, Marion suggested something that gives both candidates an equal chance. At least 28 states use random methods like drawing lots or dice rolls, while another 12 hold runoff elections, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
The cost and historically low turnout associated with runoff elections make them problematic, Marion said. 
Miguel Nunez, executive director for the elections board, deferred to the election board’s legislative subcommittee to review and make recommendations on potential policy changes.
Marion’s legislative to-do list includes setting more comprehensive guidelines for how to determine voter intent on ballots like the one King brought forward. 
The elections board currently relies on a single-page ballot interpretation guide, developed by Common Cause in 2022 as part of its input on the state’s risk-limiting audit, a biennial post-election review to confirm accuracy of ballot tabulator machines.
But the guide offers few examples of overvotes, undervotes, stray marks and other scenarios where a voter’s choices on the ballot might be open to interpretation.
“We need to develop regulations for voter intent before this becomes a bigger controversy,” Marion said.
He hoped to incorporate a better detailed voter intent guide into forthcoming legislation enshrining federal protections against voter suppression into state law.
A  Rhode Island Voting Rights Act was introduced during the 2026 session but failed to advance out of committee in either chamber, despite strong support from good government advocates. At the time, advocates pledged to reintroduce the bill in 2027, with the intent of passing protections before the 2028 election cycle.
Louis DeSimone Jr., vice president of the election board, abstained from the vote on whether to include the additional ballot in the Glocester School Committee race because he participated in the original audit determination to reject it.
Election board member Marcela Betancur did not attend the meeting.

name: National
title: Veterans’ abortion restrictions likely to stay in place for months as lawsuit timeline stretches
description: Despite a lawsuit and opposition from newly empowered congressional Democrats, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ tight abortion restrictions are likely to remain in place for at least six months, if not longer. The VA policy, in effect for nearly a year, has drawn significant criticism from some veterans and other groups. But the timeline […]
text:
The U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs medical campus in Rapid City, South Dakota. A lawsuit challenging the VA’s decision in 2025 to end nearly all abortion care and abortion counseling is ongoing, but will likely extend late into next year before any action from the appeals court. (Photo by Seth Tupper/South Dakota Searchlight)Despite a lawsuit and opposition from newly empowered congressional Democrats, the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs’ tight abortion restrictions are likely to remain in place for at least six months, if not longer.
The VA policy, in effect for nearly a year, has drawn significant criticism from some veterans and other groups. But the timeline may be extended on the legal challenge, and there’s seemingly little that a new congressional majority can do to change the policy without passing legislation, which would take some time. 
Under the military’s medical benefits package, since the 1990s, abortion care was provided if the pregnancy was a result of rape or incest, or if necessary to save the pregnant patient’s life. Beginning in 2022, the VA provided abortions for health-preserving reasons as well, and implemented a policy allowing members to be reimbursed for having to travel for care if they were stationed in a state with a ban. 
But at the end of 2025, the VA announced it would not provide any abortion care for veterans even in cases of rape and incest, would not allow any abortion counseling, and would rescind the reimbursement policy.  
The VA responded to thousands of public comments about the proposed rule, saying it would make no changes as a result of the feedback. It was finalized on Dec. 31, 2025. One of Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s first directives when he took office in January 2025 was about rescinding the 2022 policy, and the formal rule adoption process began in August that year.
Trump administration officially ends veteran abortion access

The legal arguments surrounding the case rely on a specific section of law written in the 1990s that the VA says excluded infertility services, abortion and pregnancy care from veteran medical benefits. But those opposing the rule say even that section, which they disagree should be applied as narrowly as the administration is using it, does not exclude abortion counseling.
The department said ectopic pregnancy terminations and miscarriages are not considered abortions and can be treated. 
The policy led to a lawsuit filed in May by Minority Veterans of America, an organization with more than 3,600 members in 49 states and the District of Columbia. The organization argues that the VA made the change without a reasonable explanation, violating administrative law, and says its members have already been harmed by not being able to discuss options with care providers.  
The lawsuit is ongoing, but it may be at least six more months before oral arguments are heard in the case, making any department-level changes unlikely anytime soon. U.S. Department of Justice attorneys representing the VA asked the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit for an extension until Feb. 8 to file a response, which was originally due on Dec. 9. The court hasn’t yet approved that request, but if it does, it will extend the overall timeline of the case by several months.
Sides weigh in
In the complaint, Minority Veterans of America argued that veterans of reproductive age have high rates of chronic medical and mental health conditions that can increase risks associated with pregnancy, including post-traumatic stress disorder, hypertension and kidney disease. Those conditions can heighten the risk of hemorrhage and placental issues.  
According to a friend of the court brief submitted by 212 congressional Democrats, the VA told their staff in February 2025 that records showed about 462,000 women veterans of reproductive age were enrolled in VA healthcare, along with an estimated 112,000 women of reproductive age in the Civilian Health and Medical Program of the VA, or CHAMPVA, which provides coverage to veterans’ families, including children.  
The department has said it is complying with statute, and that it is adhering to the U.S. Department of Justice’s legal opinion issued prior to the finalization of the rule stating that the VA could not legally provide abortion care. The VA also said the government was under no obligation to subsidize or to “facilitate” abortion. The current policy also doesn’t allow reimbursement for travel expenses or special leave to seek abortion care, which was permitted under the 2022 rule. 
“As explained in this rule, VA can provide care to pregnant women in life-threatening circumstances under the medical benefits package,” the agency said in its response to public comments. “In all other circumstances, VA will not discuss options for abortions outside VA and will not refer veterans and CHAMPVA beneficiaries to abortions outside VA.”
So far, no Republican elected officials or anti-abortion groups have filed briefs in support of the VA’s policy in the lawsuit. When the rule was initially proposed, Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America, one of the leading national anti-abortion organizations, called it a “major win.”
“We thank President Trump and VA Secretary (Doug) Collins for restoring the rule of law and ending the Biden administration’s illegal policy that forced taxpayers to fund abortions through VA hospitals and violated state pro-life laws,” SBA President Marjorie Dannenfelser said in a statement at the time. “Thankfully this injustice is now corrected.” 
Culture of silence around abortions for active-duty military intensifies, researchers say

Some of the states with the highest number of service members and veterans, including Alabama, Florida and Texas, also have some of the most restrictive abortion laws in the country. According to estimates from nonprofit National Partnership for Women and Families, more than 400,000 women veterans lived in states that already had an abortion ban in place or were likely to ban it in 2023. That figure represents more than half of the women veterans in the country.
“The decision to rescind that rule was both harmful and cruel,” said Jordan Goldberg, policy director of the Reproductive Freedom Alliance, a coalition of state governors who support reproductive rights.  
All 47 Democratic U.S. senators and 165 Democratic U.S. representatives signed the brief in October asking the court to override the rule. In March, those senators voted in favor of a resolution that would have allowed Congress to block the rule, but it failed to pass in a 48-50 vote.
Although Democrats will hold nine more seats in the Senate in January, Goldberg said there is a limited window of a few months during which an agency’s rules can be challenged, and that time has passed. 
Goldberg said some states with Democratic leaders, such as California, are working to adopt state-level policies that help veterans who need abortion care and can’t get it from the VA, but that has its limits too. 
“A state cannot take the place of the federal government,” Goldberg said. 
‘In a precarious position’
When Sylvia Andersh joined the U.S. Air Force in 1974, women were so new to the military that there were still enlistment limits, and Roe v. Wade, the 1973 U.S. Supreme Court case that affirmed a constitutional right to abortion access, was barely a year old.
Just before the end of the four years she spent on active duty, Andersh needed an abortion.
At the time, she said military personnel were supportive of her decision and helped her access care at a private clinic. But if she were serving today, with the military’s current stance toward abortion and 13 states with restrictive laws, she doesn’t know what that might have meant for her care. She went on to have a son in 1986, and four years after that, she had a miscarriage at 13 weeks and needed treatment. 
“It’s been very painful to see that women who have served their country do not deserve the respect of having control over their own bodies,” Andersh said.
Andersh, who left home at 18 to join the military as one of few women service members, said she thinks the new policy is designed to drive women away. 
“It puts them in a precarious position, because when you’re in the military, you’re supposed to be combat ready at any time, and how do you navigate that when you have responsibilities as a mother and a parent?” she said.   
Stateline reporter Kelcie Moseley-Morris can be reached at kmoseley@stateline.org.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan legislators challenge prison officials over inmate’s medical care and mold claims
description: Following an October federal appeals court ruling allowing a lawsuit alleging toxic mold conditions within the state’s only women’s prison, one of the plaintiffs is seeking a permanent transfer from the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. That plaintiff, Krystal Clark, has become a focal point of criticism of the Michigan Department of Corrections, a[...]
text:
Women's Huron Valley Correctional Facility in Saline Township, Michigan. | Photo by Jon King/Michigan AdvanceFollowing an October federal appeals court ruling allowing a lawsuit alleging toxic mold conditions within the state’s only women’s prison, one of the plaintiffs is seeking a permanent transfer from the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility.
That plaintiff, Krystal Clark, has become a focal point of criticism of the Michigan Department of Corrections, as she faces what her attorneys described as a medical deterioration from toxic mold exposure, which led to an emergency court motion to transfer Clark to Duane Waters Health Center in Jackson in July.
But in laying out their own findings of fact in court proceedings, the department is expressing doubts that Clark has many of the health conditions cited in her request for a more longstanding court order keeping her out of Women’s Huron Valley, describing Clark’s claims as “exaggerated and inaccurate.”
This includes doubts about Clark suffering from mold growing in her ears, which was the centerpiece of testimony from state Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) at a House Oversight Committee hearing in February.
State Rep. Laurie Pohutsky (D-Livonia) testifies to the House Oversight Committee on health and sanitation concerns at the Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility. Feb. 24, 2026. | Screenshot.
The filing from the state’s legal team alleges that Clark has refused a biopsy that would be able to conclusively confirm a diagnosis of aspergillosis, a respiratory illness or infection caused by breathing in spores of mold, and has otherwise refused treatment from the department’s doctors.
“Clark claims to suffer from several health conditions, including an ear infection, difficulty breathing, nosebleeds, a severe mold allergy, and coughing blood,” the filing reads. “At various times, she has also complained of a facial droop, vomiting blood, and difficulty walking, but these claims are based on Clark’s self-reported symptoms and lack corroboration in her medical record.”
Pohutsky, as well as state Rep. Emily Dievendorf (D-Lansing), both of whom have openly criticized the department, were critical of the department’s categorization of Clark’s claims as fabricated.  
“MDOC has already drawn the conclusion that Krystal Clark is healthy and that her complaints are part of a grand manipulation towards getting money out of the department,” Dievendorf wrote in a statement to Michigan Advance. “The assumption of ill intent toward Clark may be the most disturbing and dangerous of MDOC’s responses because it hangs questions over legitimate health conditions that require a serious response and likely require improvement on the part of MDOC to prevent the same health issues in other incarcerated individuals across MDOC’s facilities.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Department of Corrections has repeatedly denied any issues with mold at the facility and released findings of independent environmental testing done by a private contractor, which concluded the facility did not have dangerous systemic black or toxic mold conditions. In response to the emergency motion that temporarily removed Clark from Women’s Huron Valley, the department released a response that disputed the medical need for that transfer.
“Allegations contained in the plaintiff’s motion are not supported by the medical evidence or facts known to the department,” a spokesperson for the department wrote to the Advance in response to the concerns raised by the legislators. “Extensive medical records have been publicly released as part of the response to the plaintiff’s motion for emergency relief. Ms. Clark was not experiencing any emergent medical condition that warranted transfer from Women’s Huron Valley Correctional Facility (WHV).”
However, both legislators state that they have personally seen Clark and attested to her need for medical care outside of Women’s Huron Valley. 
“I have witnessed Krystal’s physical condition myself,” Dievendorf wrote. “Krystal has very real health issues that require action, yet her necessary care is being pushed to the month she is expected to be paroled, almost 6 months from now.”
For years, Clark has alleged that black mold at Huron Valley has made her sick. She said she has struggled to breathe and developed rashes, swelling and headaches. (Jay Love/Survivor Speaks)
Clark will be first eligible for release on May 9, 2027, according to Michigan’s Offender Tracking Information System, but could be incarcerated up to a maximum date of May 9, 2040. 
Pohutsky described what she witnessed of Clark’s condition, specifically the alleged mold in her ear, saying, “It is black and fuzzy, and it completely covers her ear.”
Both legislators also contested the department’s claims that there are no issues of mold within the facility, with Pohutsky calling it “laughable” and adding, “The idea that they’ve eliminated the mold, so she must be lying about any of these conditions being linked to it, is absurd, and they know it.”
Pohutsky added that she sees the statements made by the department in Clark’s case as demonstrating a broader issue with medical care in MDOC facilities. 
“Their insistence that none of these symptoms or issues can be true because there’s no medical record of them being true. The whole point is that none of these folks, not Krystal Clark, not anyone else that has been at Huron Valley, not anyone else that is in any of the other MDOC facilities, is getting adequate medical care. So the fact that they keep pointing back to their own medical records, or lack thereof, is sort of beside the point, because they’re not getting adequate medical care,” she said. “People are not receiving adequate care, and their immediate tactic is to act as though it is just simply not happening, and everyone who characterizes it other than completely sufficient and appropriate medical care is wrong. I think it’s insulting.”
Dievendorf added that, when they have expressed concerns to the department, “I have yet to hear MDOC take any responsibility for unsafe infrastructure, unfair conditions of confinement, and inadequate medical care. I have yet to witness MDOC admit it can and should do better.”

name: VTDigger
title: Elderwood at Burlington settles racial harassment suit with federal government, averting trial
description:
The nursing home’s operators agreed to pay $450,000 to staff members who faced racial harassment and to institute racial discrimination prevention measures.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Elderwood at Burlington settles racial harassment suit with federal government, averting trial.
text:
The Elderwood at Burlington nursing home in Burlington on Monday, November 30, 2020. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
A federal racial harassment case against the operators of a Burlington nursing home is no longer slated for trial. 
The U.S. Equal Employment Opportunity Commission — which enforces federal civil rights and workplace discrimination laws — agreed to a settlement with the Elderwood Administrative Services, LLC and 98 Starr Farm Road Operating Co., LLC, which does business as Elderwood at Burlington, according to a statement the federal commission released Tuesday.
“This settlement sends a clear message that employees in healthcare and long-term care settings do not surrender their federal civil rights when they come to work,” Katie Linehan, trial attorney for the federal commission’s Boston Office, said in the statement. 
Under the settlement, the nursing home operators will pay $450,000 to a group of six Black former staff members of Elderwood at Burlington who were alleged to have experienced sustained repeated racially-motivated attacks, including racial slurs and physical violence, from white residents in 2020, according to a complaint filed by the federal commission in 2022. The commission further alleged in the complaint that nursing home managers and supervisors did not address the racial harassment in an adequate or timely manner, violating Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, which protects against employment discrimination on a basis of race. 
The settlement and federal monitoring will continue for two and half years, during which the nursing home must institute racial harassment prevention measures. This includes updates to the nursing home’s anti-discrimination policy, maintaining a discrimination hotline and annual anti-discrimination training for staff members of Elderwood at Burlington and Elderwood’s Corporate offices, with additional training for supervisors and managers.  
Most of the affected staff members were traveling nurses who arrived at Elderwood at Burlington to help fill staffing shortages during the peak of the Covid-19 pandemic. The federal complaint came after Seven Days reported on the staff members’ allegations. 
A federal judge in Vermont denied the operator’s request to resolve the case without going to trial in March. Before this settlement was reached, a jury trial was set to commence in December. 

READ MORE

Chief District Judge Christina Reiss wrote in March that, based on the evidence, a reasonable jury could find that the extensive racial discrimination faced by staff caused a hostile work environment that was not sufficiently remediated by Elderwood. 
Understaffing remains a concern at Elderwood at Burlington, and care issues have cropped up as well, according to a recent state inspection. 
Elderwood at Burlington is rated two out of five stars, based on health inspections, staffing and quality measures, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services database. The facility had to pay around a $221,000 penalty to the federal government in 2024, and was denied Medicare payment on the same date, but the database does not specify the reason for the fine. 
Federal ratings can be unreliable, as the ratings are based on self-reported data and tend to be inflated rather than underrated, said Kaili Kuiper, Vermont Legal Aid’s state long-term care ombudsman. 
The most recent state inspection of Elderwood at Burlington in October by the Vermont’s Division of Licensing and Protection found that the facility failed to properly report a resident’s allegation of sexual abuse from a staff member and that short-staffing has affected response times and care provided to residents. 
The ombudsman’s office has fielded ongoing complaints about delayed response times to resident call bells at Elderwood at Burlington, Kuiper said, but she does not consider it to be among the facilities in the state providing the worst care. Kuiper could not speak to the allegation of sexual abuse because she didn’t have information about it. 
“We hate to see issues with responses to call bells because that’s such a fundamental duty of a long-term care facility to be responding to requests for assistance,” Kuiper said. “Unfortunately, it is something we hear a lot from residents in a lot of our facilities.”
Elderwood has submitted an acceptable plan of correction to the Division of Licensing and Protection, and so the nursing home is currently in good standing with the state and soon will be in “alleged compliance” by Nov. 27, Pamela Cota, the division’s survey and certification director, wrote in an email to VTDigger. 
The nursing home has a 45-day window after the inspection to implement the plan of correction. After that period, the division will conduct an unannounced, on-site inspection to determine if the facility is in substantial compliance. 
The racial harassment suit is outside the scope of the Vermont Department of Disabilities, Aging and Independent Living, and so the Department and its associated Division of Licensing and Protection declined to comment on the settlement. 
Elderwood at Burlington and the operator’s legal team did not respond to requests for comment by Wednesday morning.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham releases universal childcare ‘blueprint’ for other states
description: Outgoing New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Tuesday released a “blueprint” for the state’s nascent universal childcare program intended to help other states implement their own.
text:
New Mexico Gov. Lujan Grisham on Nov. 25, 2026, released a ‘blueprint’ detailing the state’s universal childcare program to help other states develop their own. Above, Olga Grays reads to children in her class at Mrs. Olga's Daycare in Las Cruces in September of 2026. (Photo by Leah Romero for Source NM)Outgoing New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham on Tuesday released a “blueprint” for the state’s nascent universal childcare program intended to help other states implement their own. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Lujan Grisham signed the universal childcare program — the country’s first — into law in March. In a statement on Tuesday, the governor said that since then “we’ve heard from public policy leaders and experts across the country who want to learn how they can implement similar programs in their states.” The 32-page document, she said, “provides a step-by-step approach to tackling one of the biggest affordability challenges of our time.”
The document lists five key elements of the program, including establishing a single early childhood state entity; creating state-based funding streams, such as a trust fund; developing a compensated and credentialed workforce of early childhood providers; and expanding family access and investments to bolster the supply of childcare facilities. Each element includes detailed implementation actions and timelines.
Growing Up New Mexico President and CEO Kate Noble urged other states to follow New Mexico’s lead, during a phone call with Source NM. The organization operates an early childcare center in Santa Fe and has advocated for the program for several years. 
“This is the best thing you can do to transform a society,” Noble said. “Investing in early childhood is the game changer, from school achievement to reduced crime.”
The governor’s office highlighted that more than 40,000 families and 50,000 children in the state already benefit from the program
But the program has also faced challenges. In October, the chief legislative economist told lawmakers that the state’s early childhood trust fund is forecast to be empty and unable to support universal childcare by 2048 because of increased payouts and funds meant for the trust fund being diverted. The New Mexico Early Childhood Education and Care Department plans to hold a hybrid public hearing on a proposal to require co-pays for high-earning families using the program on Dec. 3. Meeting demand has also been a challenge for childcare providers. 
Despite the challenges, Noble said she hopes more states form their own programs and highlighted the work that went into creating New Mexico’s.
“I’m waiting for the screenplay of this cast of characters who have had different perspectives and different talents who have come together through time to build this system and make it possible,” Noble told Source NM. “We all believe in it.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: US Supreme Court to weigh bans on AR-15s in 2nd Amendment case
description: The case, known as Viramontes v. Cook County, involves two lawsuits: one challenging Cook County’s ban and another challenging CT's ban.
text:
After a man used a semiautomatic rifle to kill five children and wound dozens of others at a California elementary school in 1989, officials in sprawling Cook County, Illinois, banned what they called assault weapons — certain firearms such as the AK-47 and AR-15.
Decades later, the U.S. Supreme Court is set to decide whether Cook County’s ban — and similar restrictions across the country — violate the Constitution.
The Supreme Court will hold oral arguments on Dec. 2 in a potentially landmark gun rights case that could sweep away the power of states and localities to prohibit popular models of firearms used in numerous mass shootings. The decision could also stop Congress from imposing new prohibitions on some semiautomatic weapons after a previous ban expired in 2004.
“The safety of our communities is at stake,” Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke said in a statement. “There is absolutely no reason that AR-15s, AK-47s and other weapons of war that were designed to inflict mass carnage should be available to the public.”
States at odds
The case has pitted red and blue states against each other. Democratic state officials have urged the Supreme Court to uphold the bans, while Republicans say they must be invalidated under the Second Amendment.
Eleven states and the District of Columbia ban “assault weapons,” according to the advocacy group Everytown for Gun Safety, which defines them as high-powered semiautomatic firearms. They include California, Connecticut, Delaware, Illinois, Maryland, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington state.
Several major cities, such as Denver, Indianapolis, New York and Philadelphia, also have restrictions. Chicago is the county seat in Cook County.
The Supreme Court has spent nearly 20 years bolstering Americans’ rights to have guns and limiting the government’s power to restrict them. The justices first ruled in 2008 that the Second Amendment guarantees an individual right to bear arms for self-defense. 
The court then said in 2022 that restrictions must be rooted in the country’s historical tradition of firearms regulation. The new standard spurred fresh challenges to modern-day laws limiting guns.
The justices will now decide whether bans on AR-15s and similar semiautomatic weapons — high-powered guns that fire and automatically reload each time the trigger is pulled — clear that high bar.
Suits by gun rights advocates
The case before the Supreme Court has been known as Viramontes v. Cook County, but it involves two lawsuits: one challenging Cook County’s ban and another challenging Connecticut’s ban. After oral arguments, the justices will likely release a decision in the case in the spring.
Cook County residents Cutberto Viramontes and Christopher Khaya, members of the Firearms Policy Coalition, a gun rights advocacy group, first sued over the county’s ban in 2021. On Oct. 29, Viramontes asked the Supreme Court to drop him from the case without providing a reason. The court granted the request on Nov. 23, but Khaya and other challengers remain and the case will proceed for now.
Gun rights advocates argue that under the court’s previous decisions, guns in common use, such as the AR-15, cannot be banned.
A nationwide online survey of more than 51,000 adults this summer found that 25% of gun owners currently own an AR-15- type rifle. In total, 30% of gun owners own at least one rifle commonly referred to as an “assault weapon,” according to an analysis of the results by William English, a political economist at Georgetown University.
“This is one of the most important Second Amendment cases in American history,” Brandon Combs, president of the Firearms Policy Coalition, said in a statement. “The question is simple: Can the government ban some of the most popular firearms in America?”
For the Firearms Policy Coalition the answer is an emphatic “no.” 
In a brief to the Supreme Court, the FPC and other petitioners say there are many reasons why Americans may prefer AR-15s and similar semiautomatic rifles, including that they tend to be more accurate than handguns and are lighter and have less recoil than other rifles and shotguns.
The brief says that “by any objective measure the handgun is the most dangerous weapon to modern society,” given its use in violent crimes. And because the Supreme Court already struck down the District of Columbia’s handgun ban in 2008, the semiautomatic rifles in question should also be protected by the Second Amendment, the brief argues.
Regulations of dangerous weapons
Supporters of the ban counter that the right to keep and bear arms under the Second Amendment, like other constitutional rights, is not absolute. The nation’s history is filled with examples of regulations of especially dangerous weapons, they say.
In their brief to the Supreme Court, Cook County officials trace the AR-15’s military origins as the civilian version of the M-16, the rifle widely used by the U.S. military in the Vietnam War. They highlight the history of gun sellers marketing the firearms as “assault weapons” or “assault rifles.” 
The Chicago-area ban on the AR-15 and similar weapons is compatible with the nation’s historical tradition of firearm regulations, Cook County argues, because the rifles are offensive weapons of war designed for maximum lethality and not typically used for self-defense.
During the 2010s, just over a third of mass shootings involved semiautomatic assault weapons, according to data from the Gun Violence Archive, a nonprofit group that tracks incidents of gun violence, that was analyzed by The Trace, a news organization focused on gun violence. Mass shootings were defined as incidents that took place in public areas where four or more people died.
“When weapons are introduced into society that have the capability to perpetrate some of our most tragic and frightening crimes, from mass shootings to assassination attempts, democratically elected legislators are permitted to respond with appropriate regulation,” Cook County’s brief says.
Federal appeals courts have issued conflicting decisions about the constitutionality of the bans, though most appellate decisions have upheld the restrictions.
The U.S. 7th Circuit Court of Appeals found Cook County’s ban acceptable in a 2025 decision. Two months later, the 2nd Circuit sided with Connecticut in a challenge to its ban. But the 3rd Circuit ruled against New Jersey’s restrictions in July 2026 — a month after the Supreme Court decided to take the cases involving the Cook County and Connecticut bans.
Dem, GOP attorneys general weigh in
States have jumped into the fight on both sides of the Supreme Court case.
Democratic state attorneys general in 18 states filed a brief urging the justices to reject arguments by gun rights supporters that AR-15 and similar semiautomatic weapons should be protected because of their popularity. Such a standard would break with common sense, they wrote.
“It would risk opening the floodgates for other unusually dangerous weapons — just because sales of those weapons have cleared some arbitrary popularity threshold,” the Democrats argue.
Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell and New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport led the brief. They were joined by Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Hawaii, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, and Washington, in addition to the District of Columbia.
On the Republican side, Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach, Tennessee Attorney General Jonathan Skrmetti and 25 other state attorneys general have pressed the Supreme Court to strike down state and local bans on AR-15s and similar weapons. They argue the weapons are commonly used for lawful purposes.
The GOP state officials also reject comparisons between the AR-15 and military-issue weapons. In a brief to the Supreme Court, they note that the AR-15 semiautomatic rifle has never been issued to military service members.
“The superficial similarity in appearance between the AR-15 platform rifle and standard service rifles simply reflects that certain ergonomic and design features translate well to both military and civilian use,” their brief, led by Kansas and Tennessee, says.
Other states signing on to the brief include Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, South Dakota, Texas, Utah, West Virginia, and Wyoming.
Trump administration opposes bans
President Donald Trump’s administration has also asked the Supreme Court to strike down the bans. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer and other U.S. Department of Justice officials in their brief urge the justices to reject the term “assault weapon,” arguing that it is a political term that wasn’t in use prior to 1989.
Sauer’s brief refers to FBI estimates that of the nearly 13,700 homicides in 2025, about 38% were committed with handguns. By contrast, just 3% involved rifles of any kind — semiautomatic or otherwise.
“Holding that the Second Amendment protects handguns but not rifles would be ‘backwards,’” the brief says.
But Julia Schardt wants the Supreme Court to listen to her experiences and those of other shooting survivors. 
Schardt was a second-grade teacher at Cleveland Elementary School in Stockton, California, on Jan. 17, 1989, when a 24-year-old man shot and killed five children and wounded some 30 others — at the time the worst non-college school shooting in U.S. history. The shooter had an AK-47 and other weapons.
The shooting prompted a national outcry that helped lead to limits on some semiautomatic weapons across the country, including a nationwide “assault weapons” ban passed by Congress in 1994.
Schardt and more than a dozen other survivors of shootings have signed on to a brief urging the Supreme Court to uphold the bans. They say their stories underscore the danger and lethality of the weapons.
The brief recounts Schardt’s experience that day, including one student telling her that another was dead. The next day, Schardt viewed the body of an 8-year-old to help confirm the child’s identity and saw the massive head wound left by a bullet.
“In Julia’s view, the assault weapons used allowed for so much carnage in so little time,” the brief says. “She believes it is hard to understand the damage these weapons can do to a child’s body without seeing it with your own eyes.”
This story was first published Nov. 25, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: VTDigger
title: Around Vermont this week: Nov. 25-Dec. 2
description:
Seven Days’ Magnificent 7 highlights seven events in and around Vermont this week, including Winter Lights, Shelburne Museum’s showstopping holiday spectacle.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Around Vermont this week: Nov. 25-Dec. 2.
text:
Courtesy of Adam Silverman Photography
This story was first published in Seven Days on Nov. 23, 2026.
VTDigger is teaming up with Seven Days. Each week, we’ll share their Magnificent 7, a hand-picked roundup of must-see, must-do events happening around the state. This is a new experiment, so please take our quick survey at the bottom of the page and tell us what you think.
It’s Lit
Opens Friday, Nov. 27
Bundle up tight for Winter Lights, Shelburne Museum’s highly anticipated seasonal display. The grounds’ iconic landmarks — including the historic Ticonderoga steamboat and the 1871 Colchester Reef Lighthouse — transform into twinkling titans to light up even the darkest night. New this year: artist Calvin Laituri’s menagerie of illuminated forest friends in the Beach Woods.
Flip the Switch
Friday, Nov. 27
Tree-Lighting Ceremony Credit: Courtesy
How lovely are these branches! Burlington’s beloved Tree-Lighting Ceremony sets hearts aglow at the top of Church Street, where revelers gather to gawk at this year’s 30-foot wonder, direct from Shelburne. Community caroling and a reading of Clement Clarke Moore’s 19th-century holiday touchstone, ’Twas the Night Before Christmas, honors the perennial symbol of the season.
Shine On
Friday, Nov. 27
Cheetatah Credit: Courtesy of Ali Kaukas Photography
This Black Friday, skip the big-box store blowouts and treat yourself to House of Sparkle at Higher Ground in South Burlington instead. Studio 54 vibes collide with Green Mountain glam at a sequined showcase of spinning prowess, including Burlington vinyl master Tad Cautious, members of DJ Love’s Amplify Collective, and 2026 Burning Man performers Cheetatah (pictured) and Vetica.
Fowl Play
Friday, Nov. 27-Sunday, Nov. 29
A Family Thanksgiving Courtesy
Looking for a new Turkey Day tradition? Give thanks the 1890s way at Billings Farm & Museum’s A Family Thanksgiving in Woodstock. Visitors step back in time at a Victorian-era extravaganza complete with butter and piecrust making, apple tastings, wool-weaving crafts, and horse-drawn wagon rides through scenic pastures. It’s sure to put some gratitude in your attitude.
Downhill From Here
Friday, Nov. 27-Sunday, Nov. 29
World Cup Saturday Killington ResortWinter 23/24 Credit: Courtesy
The world’s fastest female technical Alpine skiers flex their muscles at the 10th annual Stifel Killington Cup. The nail-biting slalom showdown is expected to feature history-making gold medalist Mikaela Shiffrin and 2026 Winter Olympics bronze medalist Paula Moltzan. Live tunes by roots-rock outfit the Revivalists and other top names keep fists pumping between runs.

READ MORE

Dream Weavers
Saturday, Nov. 28
At the Flynn Main Stage in Burlington, Albany Berkshire Ballet entertains by leaps and bounds with its rendition of Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky’s magnum opus, The Nutcracker. Distinguished dancers from around the country bring to life the enchanting holiday spectacle about a young girl named Clara and her journey through the Land of Sweets.
The Male Gaze
Tuesday, Dec. 1
“Breastplate Rock” by Theodore (Ted) Kerr Credit: Courtesy
In observance of World AIDS Day, Brooklyn writer and educator Ted Kerr speaks on “The Partial Figure: Visualizing HIV/AIDS” at the University of Vermont’s Fleming Museum of Art in Burlington. The edifying exploration takes stock of historical and contemporary depictions of the crisis, with special attention paid to the Western world’s use of the male torso as subject.

name: California
title: CalPERS está cambiando las reglas para los jubilados con trabajos de medio tiempo. Te explicamos por qué
description: California limita la cantidad de horas que los jubilados pueden trabajar mientras reciben una pensión, pero tanto las personas como los empleadores suelen cometer errores. CalPERS está tratando de aclarar las reglas con dos nuevas políticas.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Trabajar a tiempo parcial después de la jubilación puede resultar contraproducente para los ex empleados del gobierno de California que están cobrando pensiones.
 Tanto ellos como sus empleadores deben cumplir con la ley de pensiones de California o se arriesgan a costosas sanciones que pueden arruinar sus planes.
 Tomemos como ejemplo Sacramento, que despidió a 41 agentes de policía de la reserva el año pasado tras una auditoría realizada por el Sistema de Jubilación de Empleados Públicos de California.
 O bien, empleados públicos que recibieron cartas de su fondo de jubilación exigiéndoles que devolvieran cientos de miles de dólares en ingresos de pensión por haber infringido esas normas.
 CalPERS está intentando simplificar las normas con dos nuevas políticas que aclaran quién puede trabajar mientras recibe una pensión y durante cuánto tiempo. Su junta directiva aprobó las propuestas la semana pasada, pero no son definitivas y están sujetas a un período de consulta pública.

 La primera disposición establece un cronograma claro sobre cuánto tiempo puede una agencia gubernamental contratar a lo que CalPERS denomina un jubilado beneficiario de una pensión, es decir, alguien que trabaja mientras recibe una pensión. Anteriormente, los jubilados que trabajaban a tiempo parcial podían hacerlo por un período limitado. Si CalPERS adopta formalmente la nueva política, las agencias podrían contratar a un jubilado beneficiario de una pensión durante dos años y luego solicitar hasta dos prórrogas de un año. Si la agencia aún no puede cubrir el puesto, podría solicitar una exención limitada que le permita al jubilado trabajar hasta 120 horas al año.
 El segundo cambio facilitaría que los policías y bomberos jubilados accedan a puestos de trabajo a tiempo parcial, al clarificar su edad de jubilación . Elimina un conflicto con la legislación fiscal federal y establece que la edad de jubilación de un empleado es la del lugar donde desarrolló la mayor parte de su carrera profesional.

 «Estas regulaciones propuestas brindarían a los empleadores y jubilados un marco más coherente a seguir y ayudarían a prevenir infracciones evitables», declaró la presidenta de CalPERS, Theresa Taylor, en un comunicado escrito tras la aprobación de las dos políticas por parte de la junta. «Igualmente importante, harían que el proceso de aprobación e informes fuera más transparente y responsable».
 Sin embargo, los empleadores gubernamentales tienen reservas.
 Cory Sazillo, director legislativo de la Asociación de Alguaciles del Estado de California, intervino en la reunión de la junta directiva de la semana pasada para destacar que, en ocasiones, las agencias policiales recurren a agentes jubilados para cubrir puestos difíciles de llenar. Instó a la junta a mantener cierta flexibilidad en aras de la seguridad pública.
 “Las oficinas del sheriff del condado utilizan a los jubilados de muchas maneras, en casos sin resolver, unidades especializadas y servicios judiciales”, dijo.
 Los agentes de la reserva de Sacramento que perdieron sus empleos a tiempo parcial el año pasado son un buen ejemplo. La ciudad no pudo recontratar a ninguno de ellos tras la auditoría, según declaró un portavoz.
 Organizaciones que representan a ciudades, condados y distritos especiales escribieron a la junta de CalPERS solicitando modificaciones , incluida una prórroga por dificultades para los puestos que no se puedan cubrir después de la contratación de un empleado a tiempo completo.
 Pero las agencias también elogiaron a CalPERS por intentar aclarar las normas.
 “No nos oponemos a que se establezca un límite definido para el servicio posterior a la jubilación. Un estándar claro beneficia más a los empleadores y a los jubilados que la ambigüedad, y también responde al interés del sistema de prevenir abusos”, escribieron las agencias.
 Las disputas sobre cómo CalPERS aplica las normas sobre el trabajo después de la jubilación se han ido acumulando durante varios años. En agosto, el gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó una ley respaldada por uno de los sindicatos de empleados públicos más grandes del estado, la Asociación de Empleados Escolares de California, que exigirá a CalPERS notificar con mayor antelación cuando audite una agencia.
 Además, varios jubilados de CalPERS están demandando al fondo de pensiones por las notificaciones que recibieron cuando se determinó que habían infringido las normas sobre trabajo después de la jubilación. Una de ellas recibió una carta exigiéndole que devolviera un millón de dólares en ingresos de pensión que percibió mientras trabajaba a tiempo parcial. La demanda se está tramitando en el Tribunal Superior de San Francisco.
Esta noticia se actualizó para incluir más información sobre las prórrogas para los puestos de pensionistas jubilados.

name: California
title: California presenta demanda para bloquear la norma de Trump que niega la ayuda a familias con estatus migratorio mixto
description: Alrededor de 7,000 familias californianas podrían perder sus viviendas subvencionadas debido a una política de la administración Trump que niega la asistencia del Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano (HUD) a los hogares con estatus migratorio mixto.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
California, junto con otros 21 estados y Washington D.C., presentó una demanda el lunes impugnando una norma de la administración Trump que impediría que decenas de miles de hogares de bajos ingresos recibieran asistencia federal para la vivienda, incluidos más de 7,000 en California.
 A principios de este mes, la administración Trump finalizó una norma para prohibir que todos los hogares con estatus migratorio “mixto” —es decir, aquellos con algunos miembros que son ciudadanos o residentes legales y otros que viven en el país ilegalmente— reciban vales de vivienda o vivan en viviendas públicas.
 La nueva norma pondría fin a la ayuda para todos estos hogares el 14 de diciembre. La demanda presentada por los estados ante el Tribunal de Distrito de los Estados Unidos para Massachusetts argumenta que la administración Trump se extralimitó en sus funciones al anular una ley del Congreso y solicitó al tribunal federal que suspendiera la entrada en vigor de la nueva norma.
 Durante décadas, los inmigrantes indocumentados han tenido prohibido recibir subsidios federales para vivienda. Sin embargo, a partir de la administración Clinton, el Congreso exigió al Departamento de Vivienda y Desarrollo Urbano de EE. UU. que proporcionara asistencia proporcional al porcentaje de miembros con estatus legal. Por ejemplo, una familia con dos padres indocumentados y dos hijos ciudadanos recibiría la mitad de la ayuda a la que tiene derecho.
 “California no se quedará de brazos cruzados mientras la administración Trump obliga a las familias a elegir entre permanecer juntas y tener un techo sobre sus cabezas”, dijo el fiscal general Rob Bonta en una conferencia de prensa en la que anunció la demanda.
 En una respuesta por escrito, la oficina de prensa del HUD afirmó que la norma “pone fin a la explotación del dinero de los contribuyentes”.
 «Esta norma garantiza que SOLO los ciudadanos estadounidenses y ciertos no ciudadanos que cumplan los requisitos residirán en viviendas financiadas por el HUD», continuaba el comunicado, atribuido al secretario Scott Turner. «Este cambio representa una reasignación de hasta 218 millones de dólares que ahora se destinarán a los estadounidenses que cumplen los requisitos y que actualmente se encuentran en lista de espera».
 Desde que la administración Trump publicó la versión final de la norma a principios de este mes, las agencias locales de vivienda pública se han apresurado a encontrar la manera de cumplirla, minimizando al mismo tiempo el desalojo de residentes y las pérdidas económicas para las propias agencias. Algunos advierten que muchos ciudadanos estadounidenses y residentes legales podrían tener dificultades y, en última instancia, no lograr cumplir con los requisitos más estrictos para demostrar su elegibilidad. También advierten que las agencias de vivienda se verán presionadas financieramente al desalojar a hogares de estatus mixto de bajo costo y reemplazarlos con hogares que tienen derecho a todos los beneficios.
 Agencias de vivienda y gobiernos locales de todo el país , incluidos Los Ángeles, San Diego, San Francisco, Fresno, Santa Bárbara y el condado de Santa Clara, presentaron su propia demanda el lunes.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear dark money committee raised $892,550 in 2025, down from year before
description: Gov. Andy Beshear’s dark money political committee Heckbent, Inc. got $892,550 in donations from unnamed donors in 2025. The total is listed in Heckbent’s Form 990 filed this month with the Internal Revenue Service and released by Heckbent to the Kentucky Lantern late Tuesday. The contribution total was down about 35 percent from the $1,378,250 […]
text:
Kentucky Governor Andy Beshear will have a tighter timeline to consider clemency requests from people on Kentucky's death row, thanks to a new constitutional amendment. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)Gov. Andy Beshear’s dark money political committee Heckbent, Inc. got $892,550 in donations from unnamed donors in 2025.
The total is listed in Heckbent’s Form 990 filed this month with the Internal Revenue Service and released by Heckbent to the Kentucky Lantern late Tuesday.
The contribution total was down about 35 percent from the $1,378,250 that Heckbent reported a year ago that it raised in its first year – 2024.
But largely because it made no big donations of its own in 2025 as it had in 2024, Heckbent was able to report that it had $1,058,552 on hand as of the start of 2026.
Heckbent is one of two political organizations created by Beshear soon after he won reelection as governor in 2023 and began exploring a campaign for the 2028 nomination of the Democratic Party for president. It is a nonprofit “social welfare” organization which reports to the IRS and whose stated purpose is “advancing policies that help working families.” The IRS requires that most spending of such groups be for social welfare, if so, and does not require them to disclose names of donors.
Beshear’s other political organization is a super PAC called In This Together, Inc., which must disclose names of its donors to the IRS and Federal Election Commission. Since its creation through mid-October of this year In This Together has reported $10.7 million in contributions.
Party takes position against big money
The release of Heckbent’s latest annual IRS report comes as the Democratic National Committee is asking campaigns of Democrats seeking the party’s 2028 presidential nomination to sign a pledge denouncing advertising by super PACs (that can raise contributions of unlimited amounts) and dark money groups (that keep names of donors secret.) According to many news reports, the party will require its presidential candidates to sign the pledge as a condition for participating in its presidential debates beginning next summer. A report in Politico, for instance,  called this “a significant move by DNC Chair Ken Martin after a midterm in which voters empowered Democrats who vowed to curb money in politics.”
Eric Hyers, who managed Beshear’s two campaigns for governor and serves as political strategist for Heckbent and In This Together, did not immediately reply to an email this morning from the Lantern asking for Beshear’s response to the DNC’s new policy and how it might affect Heckbent and In This Together.
The recent Heckbent report
While donors’ names are not listed, Heckbent’s report for 2025 does show amounts for each of 38 contributions adding up to the $892,550 total. The largest contribution was $100,000. Another unnamed donor gave $75,000, seven gave $50,000, others smaller amounts.
Unlike 2024, Heckbent reported making no major program grants or donations of its own in 2025. It reported spending $294,475 of which the report says $155,183 was spent for the group’s unsuccessful effort to advocate for legislation to enact a universal pre-kindergarten law in Kentucky.
 (In 2024 Heckbent reported two major donations: what it described as a “social welfare” expense of $400,000 to Kentuckians for Public Education, a group that advertised for defeat of a constitutional amendment that would have allowed spending public dollars on private schools; and a $175,000 “political” donation to Kentuckians for Good Judges which advocated the election of Pamela Goodwine to the Kentucky Supreme Court.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: State Supreme Court upholds social media ban for man convicted of felony threats, stalking
description: A man who threatened to kill convenience store occupants in a June 2022 incident and later pleaded guilty to making violent threats and stalking one of the store’s employees won’t get to use social media once he’s out of prison and placed on extended supervision, the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled Wednesday. The social media ban […]
text:
The Wisconsin Supreme Court chambers. (Photo by Henry Redman/Wisconsin Examiner)
A man who threatened to kill convenience store occupants in a June 2022 incident and later pleaded guilty to making violent threats and stalking one of the store’s employees won’t get to use social media once he’s out of prison and placed on extended supervision, the Wisconsin Supreme Court ruled Wednesday.
The social media ban won’t violate Jonathan James Petersen’s free speech rights, Justice Annette K. Ziegler wrote for a unanimous court. The ban is a condition of Petersen’s extended supervision term scheduled to start late next year.
Ziegler rejected Petersen’s argument that with “the ubiquity of social media in modern life,” the ban should be modified to allow him social media access under the supervision of a monitor.
“We conclude that the ‘no social media’ condition here is not overly broad and is reasonably related to Petersen’s rehabilitation and thus does not violate the First Amendment,” Ziegler wrote.
Petersen was sentenced to prison after an incident in June 2022, when the Kenosha County Sheriff’s Department reported he brandished a gun at a Kenosha County Kwik Trip, threatening to kill five employees and four customers in the store and himself.
Sheriff’s deputies arrested Petersen after using a Taser. The gun turned out to be a pellet gun, the sheriff’s department reported.
An employee of the store had a restraining order against Petersen after reporting that he had stalked her for an extended period, according to court records.
In February 2023, Petersen was sentenced in Kenosha County to more than 4 1/2 years in prison, followed by 6 years of extended supervision, after pleading guilty to four felony counts: two for making terrorist threats and one each for stalking and false imprisonment, all with the use of a dangerous weapon, according to court records. 
Petersen remains in prison, and the extended supervision term is scheduled to begin in December 2027, according to Department of Corrections records
Ziegler wrote in the decision that Petersen’s trial attorney agreed to the social media ban as a condition of extended supervision.
Petersen later petitioned the court to modify the ban and allow him to use social media with the approval of the agent supervising him. The circuit judge and subsequently the state Court of Appeals rejected Petersen’s petition, and Wednesday’s Supreme Court ruling affirmed the lower courts.
“Petersen relentlessly harassed and stalked the victim even after court intervention. Prohibiting him from using social media is a direct response to the facts underlying his convictions and serves to protect the victim,” Ziegler wrote.
She added: “Prohibiting Petersen from using social media greatly reduces the chances that he can begin other harassment and stalking campaigns against the victim here and other potential victims.”
In a concurrence, Justice Rebecca Dallet endorsed the opinion’s conclusion, writing that the nature of stalking and Petersen’s use of social media to stalk the victim justified the ban during his extended supervision.
She added, however, that such a sweeping ban could be too broad under different facts, circumstances and alleged offenses.
“Considering how universal social media has become and its many legitimate uses, imposing a blanket ‘no social media’ condition of extended supervision should be a last resort for circuit courts when they use their broad discretion to impose conditions on extended supervision,” Dallet wrote.

Delmarva Power and Chesapeake Utilities lowered their gas supply rates Nov. 1. How much you save depends on how much gas you use.
WILMINGTON, Del. — A typical Delaware household that heats with natural gas could save about $11 to $13 a month this winter. The cuts lower the price of the gas itself. Delivery charges are set separately, and gas supply rates remain higher than they were before last fall’s increases.
What the cuts mean for your bill
Delmarva Power estimates that a typical household using gas for heat would save $13.04 in a winter month, or about 9%. For a household using 7,800 cubic feet of gas, the sample monthly bill drops from $143.92 to $130.88. The residential supply rate fell from 80.647 cents to 63.922 cents per 100 cubic feet.
Chesapeake Utilities estimates that a household using 120 therms of gas in a winter month would save $10.91, or about 5%. The residential supply rate fell from about $1.30 to $1.21 per therm, the unit Chesapeake uses to bill for gas.
Why the rates fell
The cuts follow steep increases last fall. In 2025, Delmarva asked to raise its gas supply rate by 43%, and Chesapeake asked for an increase of about 30%, according to the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate. Those requests were projected to add $11.33 a month to a typical Delmarva household’s bill and $16.51 to a typical Chesapeake household’s bill.
This winter, the U.S. Energy Information Administration expects a benchmark U.S. wholesale gas price to average 36% below last winter’s level. A warm start to November and more gas in storage than expected helped ease prices. The agency also expects growing U.S. gas production to put downward pressure on prices. A long cold spell or a supply disruption could push prices back up, the Public Advocate’s office said.
Delmarva and Chesapeake use the supply charge to recover what they spend buying, transporting and storing gas. They earn no profit on that charge. The Public Advocate reviews those costs on behalf of customers, and the Delaware Public Service Commission makes the final decisions. The lower rates are in effect while the commission reviews both cases.
To Go Box

Who is affected — Delaware customers who buy natural gas from Delmarva Power or Chesapeake Utilities.
How to follow the cases — Search DelaFile for Delmarva docket 26-0880 or Chesapeake docket 26-0883. Written comments or objections in the Chesapeake case are due Dec. 18.
How to get heating help — Eligible homeowners and renters can apply for winter heating assistance through March 31, 2027. Apply through the Delaware ASSIST portal or call 302-255-9875.
Who to call about your bill — Start with your utility. If the issue remains unresolved, call the Delaware Division of the Public Advocate at 302-241-2555.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Iowa dentist sanctioned for recommending unneeded treatments
description: An Aspen Dental dentist from Ottumwa, accused of recommending extensive but unnecessary treatment for a patient, has been ordered to take a course on ethics. The Iowa Dental Board alleges that at some unspecified time in the past a complaint was filed against Dr. Jon Dyer of the Aspen Dental Clinic in Ottumwa. According to […]
text:
The Aspen Dental in Ottumwa, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)An Aspen Dental dentist from Ottumwa, accused of recommending extensive but unnecessary treatment for a patient, has been ordered to take a course on ethics.
The Iowa Dental Board alleges that at some unspecified time in the past a complaint was filed against Dr. Jon Dyer of the Aspen Dental Clinic in Ottumwa. According to the board, the complaint alleged Dyer diagnosed a patient with periodontal disease and that he “emphasized the need for extensive treatment, despite a subsequent dentist finding that there was no evidence of periodontal disease.”
As part of its investigation, the board says, it asked a consultant analyze the records of other patients treated by Dyer. According to the board, the patient records “showed a pattern of findings” that involved recommendations for treatment beyond what was indicated by the patients’ condition.
The board charged Dyer with failing to exercise the degree of care that is ordinarily exercised by the average dentist.
To resolve the case without a hearing, Dyer and the board recently agreed to a settlement that calls for Dyer to complete a comprehensive, board-approved remedial education program focused on ethics, periodontal diagnosis and recordkeeping.
In its decision, the board said Dyer has “voluntarily taken steps to identify areas of improvement and to implement procedural changes to improve consistency and accuracy in periodontal assessments.”
Dyer declined to comment on the case when contacted by the Iowa Capital Dispatch.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Tuberville inauguration will not include parade
description: Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville’s inauguration in January will not include a parade, his transition committee said Wednesday, citing previously low attendance and high security costs.  In lieu of a parade on Jan. 18, which is also Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Tuberville’s transition committee – which will sell sponsorship packages to cover other inaugural costs –[...]
text:
The Alabama State Capitol photographed during inauguration ceremonies at the Alabama State Capitol in Montgomery, Alabama on Monday, Jan. 16, 2023. Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville's inauguration celebrations will not include a parade, the transition committee said Wednesday. (Stew Milne for Alabama Reflector)Gov.-elect Tommy Tuberville’s inauguration in January will not include a parade, his transition committee said Wednesday, citing previously low attendance and high security costs. 
In lieu of a parade on Jan. 18, which is also Martin Luther King Jr. Day, Tuberville’s transition committee – which will sell sponsorship packages to cover other inaugural costs – plans to arrange a donation to Montgomery’s civil rights museums to cover costs of inauguration attendees. 
“We’re not coming to Montgomery to throw ourselves a big party. We’re coming to work,” Tuberville said in a statement Wednesday. “We’ve got a great team coming together, and on January 18, we’re going to ask God for His guidance, thank the people who put their trust in us, and get started by signing our first executive orders immediately following the ceremony.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
King lived in Montgomery from 1954 to 1960 while serving as pastor at Dexter Avenue King Memorial Baptist Church, one block west of where Tuberville will take the oath of office at the Alabama State Capitol. King led the Montgomery Bus Boycott following the arrest of Rosa Parks in 1955, and delivered his “How Long, Not Long” speech on the steps of the Capitol after the 1965 march from Selma to Montgomery.
The sponsorship packages, which range from $10,000 to $500,000, include VIP tickets to the inauguration ceremony, inaugural ball and regional celebrations in Mobile and Huntsville the week prior. 
According to the statement, free tickets to the events will be made available through a public lottery next month.
“Inauguration Day is not about me, but it’s about the people of Alabama,” Tuberville said. “We’re bringing the festivities beyond our capital city so more Alabamians can join us in celebrating the state we’re so blessed to call home.”
The transition team is led by Elliot Maisel, CEO of a distributing company based in Mobile. He said in a statement that the “peaceful transition of power” is an American tradition that all should have access to.
“As a third-generation Alabamian who has built a business and raised my family here in Alabama, it is a tremendous honor to help lead this historic and peaceful transition of government,” Maisel said. “Our country is built on different backgrounds, vigorous debate and the ability to come together.”

title: SC state parks offer free admission, ranger-led hikes for Black Friday
description: The deal coincides with the start of the agency's annual Dashing Through the Parks scavenger hunt, which runs through New Year's Day.
text:
Paris Mountain State Park, pictured, is among the parks where visitors can get free admission for Black Friday. (Provided by SC Parks, Recreation and Tourism)COLUMBIA — For Black Friday, the state parks system is offering a 100% discount on admission to any of its parks.
People of all ages can visit any of the 51 state-run parks for free Friday as part of an annual tradition for the state agency. This is the sixth year the state Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism has offered the deal.
The idea began with outdoor retailer REI, which since 2015 has closed its doors on Black Friday in an effort to encourage employees to spend more time outside. The retailer dubbed the event #OptOutside, which the South Carolina parks department altered to #OptOutsideSC for the annual promotion.
Three parks will offer guided hikes for Black Friday.
At Colonial Dorchester State Historic Site, a ranger will lead an hourlong historical walk beginning at 10 a.m. Oconee State Park will offer a two-hour, family-friendly hike also starting at 10 a.m. And for late risers, Oconee Station State Historic Site will have a two-hour hike beginning at 2 p.m.
Five parks will offer Black Friday 2026 stickers between 9 a.m. and 5 p.m. Anyone who stops by can pick up an exclusive sticker at Croft, Lake Greenwood, Sesquicentennial, Givhans Ferry, or Little Pee Dee state parks, according to the agency.
Visitors can get a jumpstart on the parks department’s annual Dashing Through the Parks scavenger hunt, which starts Thanksgiving Day and ends New Year’s Day.
The online scavenger hunt awards points for people who visit certain parks and landmarks, attend events, or complete missions from home during that time. Anyone who racks up enough points can receive a free shirt or enter a drawing for state parks gift cards, according to the agency.
