name: Michigan Advance
title: Battleground poll reinforces what Lawrence heard from voters about healthcare
description: Beginning in January, Democrats will hold majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, taking power back from Republicans as voter frustrations over everyday costs resulted in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump and Republican policies. While inflation and prices were a top issue for voters, polling from Hart Research commissioned by the advocacy [...]
text:
Democratic Congressional candidate William Lawrence announces his final push to mobilize voters as he stands outside of U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett's (R-Charlotte) former office in Lansing on Oct. 27, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)Beginning in January, Democrats will hold majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, taking power back from Republicans as voter frustrations over everyday costs resulted in a nationwide rebuke of President Donald Trump and Republican policies.
While inflation and prices were a top issue for voters, polling from Hart Research commissioned by the advocacy group Protect Our Care and the Service Employees International Union, found that frustrations around healthcare helped deliver wins for Democrats in battleground districts across the country. 
Between Nov. 4 and Nov. 8, Hart Research surveyed 1,230 voters from 59 congressional battleground districts. Survey results found that healthcare was a “very important” factor in deciding 71% of participants’ votes.
When voters were asked to rank their top issues, healthcare ranked second only to inflation and prices, polling above concerns around the war in Iran and jobs and wages.
On a press call discussing the survey’s findings, U.S. Rep.-elect William Lawrence (D-Lansing) who ousted U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett (R-Charlotte) in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, said the polling data tracked with what he heard on the campaign trail. 
“We talked to tens of thousands of voters and we heard again and again that healthcare is simply unaffordable, unreliable and it creates this cloud of anxiety over people’s lives,” Lawrence said. “Even those who have high-quality coverage now have no confidence that they’re going to be able to keep that coverage in the future, or that it will remain affordable because of how much volatility there has been in the healthcare markets and how Republicans have made this a political football that they seek to cut at every opportunity.”
Polling from Hart Research shows affordable healthcare was a top concern for battleground voters. (Screenshot)
Guy Molyneux, a partner at Hart Research, explained that while Democrats held a modest 6% advantage among the voters they polled, with 52% voting for Democrats and 46% voting for Republicans, voters who rated healthcare as their top issue overwhelmingly voted for Democratic candidates.
Additionally, when voters were presented with a list of policy actions Republicans and President Donald Trump had taken in recent years, the three items that voters largely rated as a reason to vote against Republicans in Congress were all tied to healthcare.
The poll also asked voters which issue was a higher priority, healthcare or lowering taxes – a major theme in Republican campaigns. Sixty-three percent of voters rated healthcare as their personal priority, while 34% said cutting taxes was more important.
When asked which issue was of higher priority to each party, a broad majority of voters said healthcare was more of a focus for Democrats, while Republicans were more concerned with cutting taxes.
Looking ahead to what voters want from their elected officials, 83% of voters said it was important for Congress to take action on the cost of healthcare. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
While 95% of Democrats surveyed said they’d like to see Congress act on healthcare costs, Molyneux noted that this issue was also vital to most Republicans, with 71% saying Congress should take action.
As for what Congress should do specifically, the survey presented voters with six issues that Democratic candidates and party leadership have identified as possible priorities for the caucus. 
Each proposal drew support from at least two-thirds of the voters surveyed, with participants showing particularly strong support for capping insulin costs at $35, adopting reforms to bar insurance companies from overriding decisions made between doctor and patient and restoring funding to local hospitals.
While survey data showed voters trusted Democrats far more than Republicans to deliver on affordable healthcare, the survey also found that voters were more concerned with Republicans blocking solutions than Democratic overreach.
Forty-eight percent of voters said they were concerned about congressional Republicans or the president impeding efforts to make healthcare more affordable while 34% worried that Democrats would go too far in imposing government-run healthcare.
Polling from Hart Research examines voter priorities on health care and tax cuts, as well as which they felt was a higher priority for the two major political parties. (Screenshot)
Lawrence also noted that healthcare costs have put the squeeze on small business owners who provide healthcare to their employees, placing them in a situation of having to choose to either cover these rising costs or pass them on to their employees.
Additionally, 23 Michigan health facilities have announced cuts, closed, or are at risk of closure, Lawrence said, while noting that care itself is becoming less available.
Upon joining his Democratic colleagues on Jan. 3, Lawrence said he looked forward to undoing Republican cuts to the Affordable Care Act and Medicaid, “and doing so immediately before those cuts begin to bite deeper.”
From there, Democrats need to work toward expanding healthcare access and increasing affordability, working down the road to universal and guaranteed healthcare, Lawrence said.
Gabriella Jones-Casey, an executive vice president for SEIU Healthcare Michigan stressed that the voters gave members of Congress a mandate to put people first, and deliver affordable healthcare.
“We are not asking. We are not begging. We are not pleading,” Jones-Casey said. “We voted for those who committed to improving care for our families in our communities, and we will not back down. Lawmakers must put care ahead of corporate tax breaks and strengthen the care that allows Michiganders to be healthy and to thrive.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: Give thanks for the extraordinary natural world South Dakotans have inherited
description: The South Dakota countryside never seems to be in much of a hurry. Spend an afternoon walking a windswept prairie trail, sitting beneath an old cottonwood or wandering through a thick Black Hills forest, and before long the landscape begins to slow you down. There is something about these places that draws us in. It […]
text:
An October 2026 view of South Dakota's Black Hills. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)The South Dakota countryside never seems to be in much of a hurry.
Spend an afternoon walking a windswept prairie trail, sitting beneath an old cottonwood or wandering through a thick Black Hills forest, and before long the landscape begins to slow you down.
There is something about these places that draws us in. It may be the peacefulness of a quiet morning sunrise, the raw power of a thunderstorm, or a roaring blizzard. Nature has a way of absorbing us.
Long before homesteaders carved dugouts and built sod houses, Native people understood that the land is more than a place to live. The changing seasons, the movement of wildlife, the wind, the stars and the weather are part of a spiritual relationship with the natural world that requires respect, observation and patience.
Hope brought the homesteaders here. The prairie taught them that survival demanded hard work and a respect of nature.
Perhaps that’s why Laura Ingalls Wilder’s “The Long Winter” still speaks to so many readers. It wasn’t simply a story about surviving one of the harshest winters on the northern Plains. It was about making difficult decisions and depending on neighbors.



Quotation







There is something about these places that draws us in. It may be the peacefulness of a quiet morning sunrise, the raw power of a thunderstorm, or a roaring blizzard. Nature has a way of absorbing us.


When the town’s food supplies were nearly exhausted, Almanzo Wilder and Cap Garland risked their lives traveling across the open prairie to find wheat. They recognized the signs of an approaching blizzard and took great risks to beat the storm. Their courage and judgment helped carry the community through the winter.
Harvey Dunn understood those same lessons. Growing up on a South Dakota homestead, he painted women carrying water, children helping with the harvest, a father hunting to supplement the table, and families enduring drought, wind and loneliness.
Decades later, Terry Redlin made us long for a simpler time.
A pair of deer standing at the edge of a farmyard at twilight. Warm light spilling from the kitchen windows of a farmhouse. An emerging moon illuminating the fresh tracks etched into crystalline snow.
His paintings make us think about warm childhood memories, conversations around the kitchen table and the importance of wildlife and churches to our wellbeing.
Maybe that’s why Redlin’s paintings continue to resonate.
The natural world offers those experiences every day.
Each fall, enormous flocks of snow geese move south across the Dakotas, riding cold north winds. Their great chorus draws us to something larger as they follow ancient migration routes.
The same sense of wonder can come from watching a deer emerge from the safety of a grove of trees or seeing a pheasant scratching for pebbles along a country road.
Whether it’s a prairie lake alive with whitecaps or a quiet bend in the Missouri River, or the timeless Badlands, the landscape has a way of putting our daily concerns into perspective. Nothing is as urgent as it seems.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sit quietly long enough marveling at the landscape and the distance between generations begins to disappear. The people who broke this ground, built these farms, planted shelterbelts and watched similar sunsets stop being memories and once again walk with us down familiar paths.
They left us physical reminders of what was important in life. It might be an old wooden toolbox like the one tucked into the corner of our garage, filled with unusual tools, rusty bolts, worn hinges and bent nails that no hardware store would bother to stock anymore.
An old farmer understood the value of saving something that might someday be useful.
Perhaps wisdom works much the same way.
Every generation leaves the next a kind of toolbox. Patience. Humility. Careful observation. Respect for the land. The willingness to listen before speaking, to think before deciding and to recognize that our actions have consequences.
As Thanksgiving approaches, perhaps there’s something else the landscape offers us. Gratitude.
It is not simply gratitude for a successful harvest, another fall migration, a warm home or another year with family and friends, important as those blessings are. It is a deeper appreciation for the extraordinary natural world we’ve inherited.
Maybe that’s something worth remembering as we slow down and gather around Thanksgiving tables this week.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Commentary: Hall of Fame finds Machine Gun Molly
description: Timing had never been Molly Bolin Kazmer’s friend. On the basketball court, sure, when she could stop and start and pull up and score with such ease and precision that anyone who saw it could only feel their jaw drop. But away from the court? She played in an era when few cared about girls’ […]
text:
Molly Bolin Kazmer, left, as a player for the Iowa Cornets of the Women’s Professional Basketball League (1978-81) and on a 2025 visit to the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame in Knoxville, Tenn. (Photos courtesy of Molly Kazmer)Timing had never been Molly Bolin Kazmer’s friend.
On the basketball court, sure, when she could stop and start and pull up and score with such ease and precision that anyone who saw it could only feel their jaw drop.
But away from the court? She played in an era when few cared about girls’ and women’s basketball outside her native Iowa, she played professionally in a league that only lasted three years, she couldn’t play in Europe because she had a child to raise, and because she’d gone pro, she never had a shot at playing in the then-amateur-only Olympics.
In early November, though, after decades of flying under the radar as an early pro women’s basketball superstar, the player once known as “Machine Gun Molly” got a stunning, unexpected call that informed her that her time had come at last.
She was a Hall of Famer.
On Nov. 5, Kazmer was named to the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame Class of 2027. She’s part of a group that includes former UConn and WNBA legend Diana Taurasi, who became the WNBA’s all-time leading scorer in a 21-year career and was a six-time Olympian. Rounding out the class are veteran WNBA coaches Sandy Brondello and Mike Thibault, official Dee Kantner and longtime UCLA administrator Judith Holland.
“It came out of the blue, it was very shocking. And I was a completely blithering idiot,” Kazmer said. “When I was being told, I was like, ‘What? What?’
“It was an overload of emotions. All these years of not thinking I was ever going to get in. It was definitely cool, though. Very, very cool.”
Unlike the processes at the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame, for which Kazmer has twice been a finalist, or the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame, the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame didn’t announce its nominees or finalists. Kazmer was out celebrating her wedding anniversary with her husband, John, hardly expecting a phone call to tell her she was a Hall of Famer.
Kazmer will be part of interesting class that includes just two players – one who rewrote the WNBA records book and got to play pro basketball for 21 years and one whose brief career yielded records that, even now, few people know about.
“It’s like the opposite ends of the spectrum, but yet it shows the start of the journey and how, with excellence, how far someone could take it,” Kazmer said.
The latest inductees, announced Nov. 5, into the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame. (Image courtesy of Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame)
It’s a personal moment for Kazmer but also a nod to the short-lived Women’s Professional Basketball League (WBL), which in its three-season run from 1978-81 was the first women’s professional basketball league. Kazmer was the first player to sign a contract for the league, which also included future Hall of Famers such as Ann Meyers, Nancy Lieberman and Carol Blazejowski. Seventeen former WBL players are in the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame, as well as nine Olympians, but there are also dozens of others who disappeared into the annals of history like Kazmer did.
“Now I have an opportunity just to say their names,” Kazmer said of the pioneering players of the WBL.
For a generation of Iowans, it’s a happy moment, too. Kazmer was a popular — downright beloved — player for the WBL’s Iowa Cornets, based in Des Moines and Cedar Rapids. The Iowa native seemingly came from nowhere (Grand View College, now University but back then a junior college) by way of Moravia, Iowa, to become the WBL’s leading scorer and MVP.
Molly Van Benthuysen averaged 50-plus points at Moravia High School and once scored 83, but her team never made it to the state tournament. Few colleges outside of Iowa recruited girls from the state because of its six-on-six style of play. She headed to Grand View but played in nonconsecutive seasons after taking off a year to get married and give birth to her son, Damien.
In 1978, the Women’s Professional Basketball League, which eventually went just by WBL, was founded with eight teams, including the Iowa Cornets. Then known as Molly Bolin, Kazmer quickly became one of the most popular and marketable players in the league. In her second season, she led the league in scoring (32.8 points per game) and was the league’s co-MVP with Ann Meyers.
Posters of Machine Gun Molly were popular, and Kazmer appeared in commercials with Larry Bird and in a film with Pete Maravich. On the court, she set a record with a 55-point performance against the Minnesota Fillies — a mark no WNBA player has topped. (She also scored 54, 53 and 50 points in other games.)
“The WBL was totally legitimate. You can’t tell me it wasn’t the best players in the world in that league,” Kazmer said. “Ann Meyers, Nancy Lieberman, Carol Blazejowski, these were the biggest college stars coming in, and I was playing at their level and competing with them.
“And then, boom, just like snap of the fingers, it was gone. And it was like, you’re a pro player, a pro without a league.”
But it was a league without much money and the Cornets folded after two seasons. Kazmer moved to the West Coast and joined the WBL’s San Francisco Pioneers. A year later, the whole league was done. Another league, the Women’s American Basketball League, formed in 1984 but lasted just one year. Kazmer stayed active with basketball, including trying to start up other leagues, but her playing days were done. She was 27 years old. Thirteen years later, in 1997, the WNBA launched.
“I had to shut it off for a while because it was just too hard to see it take off without me after all those years of trying to make it happen,” she said. “That lasted about eight or 10 years.”
Kazmer stayed in California. She lives near Palm Springs and works in real estate.
The players of the past have built connections with the WNBA and Unrivaled, the winter 3v3 league about to begin its third season. In 2018, former WBL players founded Legends of the Ball Inc. (LOB), a nonprofit with a mission to educate fans and current players about the WBL and its impact on the game. Former players have been honored and recognized at WNBA games.
“We’ve been treated like royalty,” Kazmer said.
Kazmer is the organization’s vice president; her former rival and now good friend, Elizabeth Galloway-McQuitter, is president.
It’s likely the organization’s work to raise the WBL’s visibility helped pave the way for Kazmer’s nomination and entry into this hall of fame. Galloway-McQuitter, who played for the Chicago Hustle, is a tireless advocate for the WBL and its former players, and Hall of Famer Meyers also has championed Kazmer.
“If somebody told me when I was playing against them, ‘One day, they’re going to help you get into the Hall of Fame,’ I never would have believed it,” Kazmer said. “That’s a thing that’s so cool about the passing of time and our shared experience with the WBL.”
Kazmer’s and the WBL’s stories are starting to be told more now. The entire WBL was inducted into the Women’s Basketball Hall of Fame in 2018 in its Trailblazers section. Former San Francisco Pioneers were invited to celebrate the Golden State Valkyries’ WNBA title at their massive championship parade on Nov. 4. (Kazmer could not go because of prior commitments; another one-time Pioneer, former Iowa Hawkeyes star Cindy Haugejorde, did attend.) Kazmer’s Iowa Cornets jacket and swag are in the Naismith Basketball Hall of Fame in Springfield, Mass.
There’s a documentary, “Blazers,” in production about the WBL. Kazmer is working closely with filmmaker Matt Fife. Production is about one-third complete, Kazmer said, and the filmmaker is working on funds to bring Kazmer to Iowa to film in Moravia, Des Moines and Cedar Rapids. There’s also a script for a biopic of Kazmer, she said.
Kazmer said the documentary would likely have wrapped up production early next year, but now it’s been delayed – for a good reason. The Hall of Fame induction ceremony is scheduled for June 26, 2027, in Knoxville, Tenn.
“I was hoping it would be done sooner, but these things take time,” she said. “And, you know, that’s kind of a cool new ending.”
More about Molly

Stephen H. Provost wrote a biography, “The Legend of Molly Bolin: Women’s Pro Basketball Trailblazer,” that was released in 2019.
Former Des Moines Register columnist Daniel P. Finney wrote a wonderful profile of Kazmer in 2020.
In a 1980 televised WBL game between the Iowa Cornets and Minnesota Fillies at Veterans Memorial Auditorium in Des Moines, Kazmer (then Molly Bolin) scored 54 points. Video highlights survive on YouTube, with Iowa broadcasting legend Jim Zabel on the call.
Women’s Professional Basketball League (WBL) history and statistics have been compiled on a website, Remember the WBL.

title: US economy heats up on AI investment, consumer spending
description: The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released today shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult.  Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as […]
text:
People shop at an Ohio Walmart in April. Consumer spending driven by tax cuts and refunds, along with business investment in AI data centers, helped boost U.S. economic activity in the third quarter. (Photo by Marty Schladen/Ohio Capital Journal)The U.S. economy grew at an unexpectedly high annual rate of 4.3% in the third quarter, the biggest bump in three years, federal data released today shows. It raises the likelihood of interest rate hikes that make borrowing for homes and investments more difficult. 
Increases in business investment and consumer spending led the bump, as the artificial intelligence boom fueled investment while tax cuts and refunds kept shoppers going. The increase in gross domestic product could be a temporary bump, economists say. 
“This level of GDP probably won’t be sustained in 2027. A slowdown in AI investment is likely, and many consumers don’t have much cushion left to handle higher prices,”  Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, wrote in a post on social media platform X. 
The federal Bureau of Economic Analysis announced the revision Wednesday for inflation-adjusted GDP, a measure of economic activity. The third-quarter estimate was up significantly from an earlier estimate of 3.4%. 
Western, Southeastern states see economic bumps in first quarter

The 4.3% increase was the highest since 2023, when it was 4.5% in the third quarter. 
The bureau said the increase was driven by gains in the value of computer software and consumer spending on pharmaceuticals, recreational goods and vehicles, while economic activity dropped in healthcare.
State estimates are not yet available for the third quarter. In the second quarter, when national growth was 2.2%, the largest annual growth was in New York (4.0%), followed by Delaware and South Carolina (both 3.5%). GDP decreased the most in West Virginia (down 2.3%), Wyoming (down 1.6%) and Alaska (down 1.3%), according to BEA statistics. 
E.J. Antoni, a conservative economist once nominated to head the BEA, wrote in an X post that the “red-hot” increase makes a Federal Reserve interest rate hike “guaranteed.” 
“Good news is bad news,” Antoni wrote. 
Stateline reporter Tim Henderson can be reached at thenderson@stateline.org.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: St. Cloud’s first Somali American legislator scrutinized over childcare center, wife’s immigration
description: Democrat Abdi Daisane, who made local history as the first Somali American elected to the Legislature from central Minnesota, now faces a barrage of allegations from conservative media and Republican officials about his wife’s immigration status, his childcare business and his political activity in Somalia. Daisane, 38, in some ways represents the political [...]
text:
Rep.-elect Abdi Daisane, DFL-St. Cloud. (Courtesy photo)Democrat Abdi Daisane, who made local history as the first Somali American elected to the Legislature from central Minnesota, now faces a barrage of allegations from conservative media and Republican officials about his wife’s immigration status, his childcare business and his political activity in Somalia.
Daisane, 38, in some ways represents the political and economic achievements of the Somali diaspora in Minnesota. Born in a war-torn Somalia, he grew up in a Kenyan refugee camp and immigrated to the U.S., becoming a citizen in 2014. He has two degrees from St. Cloud State University and owns a childcare center and a consulting firm for small business founders, according to his campaign website and LinkedIn profile.
And on Nov. 3, he achieved a remarkable political upset, flipping House District 14A after losing by over 12 points in 2024. His victory mirrors the nationwide blue wave while underscoring the changing demographics of a city once nicknamed “White Cloud.”
With the upset victory has come new scrutiny, however: Local outlet Alpha News resurfaced a 2023 interview his wife, Ayan Ahmed Aidid, gave to Somali-language BBC News in which she described illegally crossing the border into the United States. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement then amplified the story to its 1.1 million followers on X. Aidid’s attorney says she has a pending asylum claim.
Shortly before Daisane’s election, Alpha News also raised suspicion of fraud at his childcare center Blooming Kids, citing an unnamed source who reported not seeing any children there in the past. The Reformer visited Daisane’s St. Cloud childcare center this month, and kids were visible from the outside of the center.
Blooming Kids provided meals through a federal program that was exploited by fraudsters, and its program was previously sponsored by a nonprofit accused of fraud. Neither Daisane nor his childcare business have been charged with fraud, and there is no public evidence that Blooming Kids participated in the fraud scheme. Nevertheless, Minnesota’s most powerful Republican, U.S. Rep. Tom Emmer, referred to him as “a Somali fraudster who ran a daycare and was guilty of fraud” without offering evidence.
Emmer’s comments echo a year of intensified attacks on Somali Minnesotans from Republicans, propelled by Trump, who has referred to Somali people as “garbage” and whose administration sent thousands of federal immigration agents to Minnesota last winter, ostensibly to target Somali immigrants, the vast majority of whom are citizens.
Daisane agreed to an interview with the Reformer, scheduled for Nov. 19, but canceled after ICE made its X post on Nov. 18. Daisane has not responded to a list of questions sent through the House DFL Caucus on Nov. 19.
Alpha News did not respond to emails asking for more clarification on its anonymous sourcing.
The Reformer examined the allegations around Daisane based on the information currently available. Here’s what we know.
Childcare center is part of meals program, but no evidence of fraud
Blooming Kids received $1,740 to $15,133 in federal nutrition program money per month from October 2020 to July 2026 — $598,251 total — from the Child and Adult Care Food Program, according to data provided by the Minnesota Department of Education that goes only six years back. The $15,133 went toward 1,400 free lunches in July of this year — around 60 lunches per day, which is consistent with the 85 to 90 kids that Daisane has said the daycare serves daily, according to an MPR News article.
In 2020 and 2021, Partners in Nutrition was the sponsoring nonprofit for Blooming Kids in the meals program, meaning it facilitated payments from the Minnesota Department of Education and was responsible for overseeing the meal site.
Partners in Nutrition and the now infamous Feeding Our Future, also a sponsoring nonprofit, took advantage of relaxed U.S. Department of Agriculture rules during the pandemic: Both funneled money to since-convicted meal site operators who falsely claimed to be serving thousands of kids every day.
In January 2022, the FBI executed search warrants and raided Feeding Our Future’s offices; the meal sites in the FBI’s allegations included sites also connected to Partners in Nutrition. The Minnesota Department of Education suspended payments to Partners in Nutrition the same day.
Blooming Kids, Daisane’s center, stopped billing the federal nutrition program until April of that year, when it switched to Providers Choice, a longstanding sponsoring nonprofit the department recommended to meal sites looking for sponsors after the FBI raids.
Daisane’s center has continued participating in the meals program, and there is no publicly available evidence that the childcare center participated in Partners in Nutrition’s scheme.
Blooming Kids Child Care Center, which is owned by Rep.-elect Abdi Daisane, stands in St. Cloud, Minn., Friday Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)
Daisane and Blooming Kids have not been charged with fraud by federal or state prosecutors. According to a spokesperson for the attorney general, Blooming Kids is not part of the attorney general’s investigation of Partners in Nutrition and its meal sites, which has included Partners in Nutrition paying $18.5 million as part of a civil settlement.
Blooming Kids received small amounts of federal nutrition money compared to Partners in Nutrition-sponsored meal sites that have been investigated for, charged with or convicted of fraud. Monthly payments for meal sites operated by defendants who have pleaded guilty to fraud charges and were included in the attorney general’s Partners in Nutrition civil lawsuit largely ranged from $50,000 to upward of $1 million.
Somali-run childcare centers in Minnesota came to national attention after right-wing social media influencer Nick Shirley published a video in December claiming to show Somali childcare centers that receive public funding but have no children visibly present — a claim echoed by Alpha News’ anonymous source on Daisane’s center. The video went viral, fueling the Trump administration’s attempt to freeze childcare funding to the state. Several of the businesses featured in Shirley’s video served free and reduced meals to kids under the sponsorship of Feeding Our Future, the Star Tribune found at the time; one owner has since pleaded guilty to defrauding both the childcare assistance program and the federal nutrition program.
Most of the vendors and meal site operators charged or convicted in connection with the Feeding Our Future and Partners in Nutrition fraud schemes have been Somali American. The leaders of both nonprofits are white women: Aimee Bock, the founder of Feeding Our Future, who was sentenced to 41 years in prison following a jury trial; and Kara Lomen, Bock’s former business partner who ran Partners in Nutrition and who has thus far avoided criminal charges.
Somali-owned childcare centers and unrelated businesses experienced an influx of harassment following Shirley’s video.
Childcare center has had several licensing violations
Blooming Kids also received $6.8 million total from Child Care Assistance Program since 2020, for serving between 130 and 190 kids every year, according to data provided by the Minnesota Department of Human Services. The state- and federally funded program provides financial assistance for childcare for low-income families.
Daisane’s childcare center had 12 violations from an October licensing review conducted by the state’s Department of Human Services, all of which are listed as having been corrected. The violations include a lack of proper immunization and allergy documentation for kids; an unclean and poorly maintained space; and staff not completing training requirements.
The center has had a handful of violations in each licensing review since 2023, the earliest review available for the center on the Department of Human Services’ website. (The inspections and violations also seemed to confirm the presence of children.)
The Reformer reviewed violations for the 29 actively licensed childcare centers in St. Cloud and found that most had zero to four violations from their most recent inspections. Only one other St. Cloud daycare had as many violations as Blooming Kids.
The center’s violations were reported on during Daisane’s first run for the state House in 2024. A St. Cloud Times article noted at the time that Blooming Kids’ violations were consistent since 2021, with some offenses repeating year to year.
Daisane told the St. Cloud Times in that article that he had difficulties recruiting people to work at the center, because of low pay and little benefits, and that the state could do more to help with staffing issues.
In 2025, Minnesota spent $367.8 million on its Child Care Assistance Program, with 57% of that coming from the federal government, according to the state’s Department of Children, Youth, and Families. Over 37,000 Minnesota children received financial assistance through the program in 2025.
Daisane campaigned for a parliament seat in Somalia in 2021
Alpha News recently reported on Daisane’s 2021 parliamentary bid in Somalia, linking to a campaign video posted on Jubbaland TV’s Facebook page in which Daisane pitches himself as a candidate for the Federal Parliament of Somalia.
Democratic-Farmer-Labor House leadership confirmed Daisane’s attempt to run for parliament in Somalia.
The party was unaware of the parliament run before the Alpha News article.
In a statement, Rep. Zack Stephenson, DFL-Coon Rapids, the next House speaker, wrote, “No, I didn’t know that Rep.-elect Daisane had explored a parliamentary bid in Somalia in 2021. He has explained that he never formally filed as a candidate and never held office there.”
Stephenson continued, “Voters decide who represents their district. Rep.-elect Daisane earned his neighbors’ trust, and they elected him to serve them in the Minnesota House. I am confident he will work hard for his district, and I look forward to working with him on the issues that matter to Minnesota families.”
DFL leadership did not respond to the Reformer’s questions on what the party’s vetting process looks like or whether they knew about Daisane’s wife’s immigration status or his childcare center being sponsored by Partners in Nutrition.
Daisane is likely eligible to run for office in Somalia since he was born there to Somali parents. Somali citizenship law is mainly based on patrilineal descent. Somalia’s 2012 provisional constitution and new 2026 constitution allow for dual citizenship.
There are no laws in the U.S. against citizens running for public office in other countries. The U.S. Department of State’s guidance says that becoming a foreign head of state is a potentially expatriating act, but being elected to a lower office generally isn’t. Daniel Noboa, the president of Ecuador, is a dual citizen; Pope Leo XIV is a citizen of Vatican City, the United States and Peru.
Daisane’s wife entered the country illegally in 2023
In a 2023 BBC News Somali article, Aidid, Daisane’s wife, described her migration journey from Somalia to the U.S., which culminated in her climbing over the U.S.-Mexico border wall using a ladder procured by smugglers.
Aidid describes herself as a Somali poet, MBA student and social activist on her Facebook profile. BBC News noted that Aidid’s poems have gone viral on Somali social media platforms.
Libs of TikTok, a right-wing X account, posted about Aidid’s immigration status in January and called for Aidid’s arrest.
Alpha News published an article last week, in part citing the BBC News Somali article. ICE shared the article on X in a post: “BREAKING: MINNESOTA LAWMAKER-ELECT’S WIFE IS IN THE U.S. ILLEGALLY.”
The ICE post continues: “Ayan Ahmed Aidid, the wife of newly elected Minnesota state lawmaker Abdi Daisane, is a 30-year-old Somali national who illegally crossed the southern border on April 2, 2023. She was apprehended by CBP but then RELEASED into the country by the Biden administration without proper vetting and has since remained in the U.S. illegally. Our nation’s immigration laws apply to EVERYONE, and the men and women of ICE will enforce them, regardless of political status or power.”
Aidid’s immigration lawyer, Abdiqani Jabane, posted a statement on Facebook after ICE’s X post, stating that Aidid has a pending asylum application.
“She is a mother of two, and the recent coverage has brought considerable attention to her family,” Aidid’s lawyer’s statement reads. “As her case proceeds, we ask everyone to respect the privacy of Ayaan and her family.”
Aidid, on Facebook, reshared a Global Somali Magazine profile about herself written the same day, with the headline “Ayaan Kaaba: The Poet behind the headlines.”

title: Disaster declared: Trump approves assistance for Florida floods
description: President Donald Trump has approved a major disaster declaration for the flooding inundating Florida since Oct. 31.  Much of the eastern side of Florida has been flooded by heavy rainfall since the beginning of the month. The declaration provides federal funding to residents of Brevard, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, and St. Lucie counties. […[...]
text:
One of many roads underwater after heavy rainfall in New Smyrna Beach on Thursday, Nov. 19, 2026. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)President Donald Trump has approved a major disaster declaration for the flooding inundating Florida since Oct. 31. 
Much of the eastern side of Florida has been flooded by heavy rainfall since the beginning of the month.
The declaration provides federal funding to residents of Brevard, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, Palm Beach, and St. Lucie counties. The money can go toward temporary housing, home repairs, loans for uninsured property losses, and other needs. 
FEMA instructs families to first file insurance claims then apply for federal assistance. 
Residents may apply at www.disasterassistance.gov or call 1-800-621-3362.
The federal government has made money available to local governments for debris removal, too, in Brevard, Hardee, Indian River, Martin, Okeechobee, and Palm Beach counties. 
According to a Monday update from Gov. Ron DeSantis, the state has completed nearly 500 rescues and almost 160 Florida State Guard personnel were mobilized. More than 400 Florida National Guard personnel had been mobilized, too.

name: National
title: Reproductive health providers say workforce shortage worsened by abortion bans
description: Reproductive health providers around the country say state abortion bans and federal policy changes have exacerbated workforce shortages, according to a new report.  Too few workers, especially in rural areas, as well as difficulty retaining and recruiting reproductive health providers and students, were cited as top challenges during in-person interviews wi[...]
text:
A midwife treats a patient during a pregnancy checkup at the Southern Birth Justice Network’s mobile midwifery clinic in Miami. Florida was among 13 states where reproductive health providers reported high workforce shortages as part of an ongoing study on the impacts of abortion policy on reproductive health care. (Photo by Nada Hassanein/Stateline)Reproductive health providers around the country say state abortion bans and federal policy changes have exacerbated workforce shortages, according to a new report. 
Too few workers, especially in rural areas, as well as difficulty retaining and recruiting reproductive health providers and students, were cited as top challenges during in-person interviews with the providers. They included OB-GYNs, midwives, family medicine physicians, and advanced practice clinicians such as certified nurse midwives and nurse practitioners.   
The report is part of the ongoing Reproductive Health Experiences and Access Study, led by the Urban Institute and the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s Reproductive Equity Action Lab, in partnership with SisterSong Women of Color Reproductive Justice Collective. 
In 2025, researchers interviewed 164 health care providers, advocates and policymakers in 13 states selected for their variety in geography, race and ethnicity, and access to abortion and reproductive health care. 
“Providers who deliver reproductive care are in short supply, particularly in states with restrictive abortion policies,” the report said. “These workforce shortages are occurring alongside widespread closures of reproductive health care facilities, further decaying access to care.”
Interviewees both in states with abortion protections and with bans said workforce shortages impeded broader health care access. But respondents from states with abortion limits said those policies had deterred some providers from practicing in those states.

Reproductive health care restrictions likely to repel provider workforce, research shows

“There are other states nearby like Minnesota or Illinois where you can have a similar Midwest lifestyle and not have to worry about, ‘When my patient comes bleeding in the ER, am I going to have to talk to the hospital lawyers before I treat her miscarriage?’” said an anonymous provider in Iowa, where most abortions are banned after 6 weeks’ gestation. “When you’re looking at ‘Where do I want to live?’ it’s easy to cross Iowa off the list.” 
The study interviewed providers in Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Illinois, Iowa, Maryland, Mississippi, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Wisconsin. 
Some interviewees said if there’s an emergency during pregnancy but no maternity service at the nearest hospital, patients have to go to the emergency room, where providers may not be trained in miscarriage management or not understand their state’s abortion laws.
In multiple states, interviewees expressed high levels of burnout and job dissatisfaction, especially in states with abortion bans and restrictions. Interviewees said rural areas suffered the most from workforce shortages generally and especially when it comes to providers trained in procedural abortions, including in states with liberal abortion laws like California. 
Interviewees said restrictive abortion laws deter undergraduate, medical school and residency applicants in those states, or if they do attend universities in states with bans, they are increasingly opting not to practice where they trained. The report notes that California, Illinois and Maryland have launched efforts in recent years to try to increase abortion training throughout the country. 
“I came here because I knew I would get very comprehensive abortion care training through my OBGYN residency,” said an anonymous provider who completed an OB-GYN residency program in North Carolina before a 12-week abortion ban went into effect in 2023. “I don’t know that I would make the same decision now because there are limits … on what medical students can learn in North Carolina.” 
Stateline reporter Sofia Resnick can be reached at sresnick@stateline.org.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The lowest turnout, but the biggest jumps: What new election data show about voter participation in Gateway Cities
description: Voter turnout was up in nearly all the state’s cities and towns this year compared to 2022. More than 2.7 million residents cast ballots on November 3 compared to roughly 2.5 million in 2022, nearly matching the state’s record-high midterm election turnout set in 2018. But those gains were, for the most part, even more striking in the Gateway Cities.
text:
IT’S NO SECRET that Massachusetts’s Gateway Cities — some of its most disadvantaged and diverse urban communities — have some of the state’s lowest voter turnout. In 2022, nine of the 10 municipalities with the lowest rates in Massachusetts were Gateway Cities.  
None of that changed during this year’s midterm election, according to finalized election results released by Secretary of State Bill Galvin’s office on Friday, but most of the state’s 26 Gateway Cities still have reason to celebrate.  
Voter turnout was up in nearly all the state’s cities and towns this year — 343 out of the Bay State’s 351 — compared to 2022. More than 2.7 million residents cast ballots this year compared to roughly 2.5 million in 2022, nearly matching the state’s record-high midterm election turnout set in 2018. Statewide, turnout was up by 9.5 percent. 
Those gains were, for the most part, even more striking in the Gateway Cities. Of these 26 communities, 21 saw a jump higher than the statewide increase of 9.5 percent.  
Nowhere was this truer than in the state’s lowest-turnout city. 
Lawrence had the lowest voter turnout in the state in both 2022 and 2026, but it also had the state’s third-highest growth in turnout this year, at 29 percent — more than three times as high as the state’s. (Lawrence’s rate of growth was surpassed only by a pair of towns so small that any changes in their turnout are likely outliers.)  
That majority-Latino city wasn’t the only one to see a significant jump in voter participation. Springfield, Chelsea, and Brockton — also majority-minority cities with some of the state’s lowest turnout — all saw jumps of 26 percent or more.  
“The low voter turnout has not necessarily been evidence that residents don’t care about the city,” said Julio Mejia, executive director of the Merrimack Valley Project. “For too long, cities like Lawrence have been characterized in that way, but I think the recent gains have told a completely different story.” 
Supporters of Celina Reyes for 16th Essex District state representative hold campaign signs outside of a school in Methuen on Election Day. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
The number of registered Latino voters in cities like Springfield and Lawrence continues to climb as the state’s Latino adult citizen population nearly tripled from 2000 to 2024.  
Shanique Rodriguez, executive director of the nonprofit Massachusetts Voter Table, which works to improve civic participation in Boston and the Gateway Cities, ascribed the rise in voter engagement to a list of factors, including a record-tying number of ballot questions, dissatisfaction with President Trump’s second term, and year-round civic engagement work by local organizations. 
She hopes the dramatic jump in voter participation will carry over into the 2027 municipal elections, which are notorious for low turnout.  
“It’s great to see people turn out in an election that everyone was publicizing, but if we can see that same sort of 26 to 29 percent increase in a municipal election, then I’ll feel like we are really progressing,” Rodriguez said.  
Gateway Cities — home to 38 percent of the state’s foreign-born residents — were particularly impacted by the Trump administration’s Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) raids last year.  
Both Chelsea and Lawrence are majority-Latino cities, while nearly half of Springfield’s residents identify as Hispanic or Latino. Brockton is New England’s first majority-Black city and home to a large Haitian-born population.  
“Folks are dissatisfied with the national climate, particularly around affordable housing issues, immigration, education, and health care,” Mejia said. “It has motivated people to participate, and folks are clearly paying attention in communities where we have dense immigrant populations.”  
Chelsea, which became a sanctuary city in 2007, quickly found itself a target of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown. Around 46 percent of the city’s population was born outside of the United States — the largest share of foreign-born residents of any community in Massachusetts.  
Hundreds of students and families have since left Chelsea’s public school district; some left the country. Some residents said ICE agents showed up at their doors demanding to be let in. Others were stopped in their cars and arrested in the street. Chelsea’s usually bustling downtown emptied out as agents became a regular presence.  
Latino voters were sharply critical. Pew Research Center polling from September and October found that 62 percent of Latino voters nationwide believed the Trump administration had gone too far in its deportation efforts.  
Hispanic voters represented 6 percent of all voters in Massachusetts this year, and half of those didn’t vote in the last midterm election, according to The New York Times’s voter trends estimates. That’s a larger share than any other racial or ethnic minority. And compared to 2024, when Latino and Hispanic voters across the US swung right in support of Trump, these voters shifted more than 20 points to the left in the state’s House and Senate races.  
“Latino voters are not a monolith. Their participation and political choices reflect a range of concerns, not simply about immigration or party affiliation,” Rodriguez said.  
Rodriguez said concerns over economic security and federal immigration surges “may have heightened the sense of urgency” during this year’s midterm election, and federal policy changes might have felt “particularly personal” in cities like Lawrence. 
But the unique political moment doesn’t mean turnout will stay this high, she warned. 
“A healthy democracy cannot be dependent on political crisis to get people to vote and participate. Democracy must be a regular part of community life,” Rodriguez said. “It’s not just about November 2026, it’s about whether we can sustain these gains in 2027 and beyond.” 
In Lawrence, roughly 3,000 more residents cast their ballots on November 3 than did in 2022. More than 50,000 people were registered to vote in the city this year — the highest that number has been in any election in well over a decade.  
Lawrence Community Works staff speak with a potential voter on Election Day outside of an affordable housing property at 50 Island Street. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
Mejia said organizations like his have continuously done registration outreach in Gateway Cities like Lawrence and Lowell, which may have helped expand the electorate.  
The Merrimack Valley Project’s nonpartisan civic engagement work includes door-to-door outreach, phone calls, and resource-building. The organization has also held candidate forums and public assemblies in an effort to engage residents in local elections. 
Yet Lawrence’s overall voter turnout this year was the lowest in the state at just 26.5 percent — up from 22.8 percent turnout in 2022. 
This year’s surge in voter participation is a good sign, Mejia said, but cities like Lawrence still aren’t back up to their high 2018 turnout levels, meaning there’s still room to improve. 
“Lawrence started with a very low baseline, which explains the potential for significant percentage growth. However, we shouldn’t minimize that progress,” Rodriguez said. “The important question is: What barriers remain?”  
Lawrence voters face a litany of barriers when it comes to voting, including language, transportation and economic challenges. Nearly 83 percent of residents are Hispanic or Latino, nearly half are foreign-born, and 78 percent speak a language other than English at home. 
But other factors may also have been at play in Lawrence — including numerous political scandals and campaigns that have energized residents and voters alike.  
In August, Mayor Brian DePeña’s was arrested after federal prosecutors charged him with fraud and money laundering. State Rep. Francisco Paulino, a Democrat representing Lawrence and Methuen, was also arrested and charged that month with eight counts of wire fraud and three counts of money laundering. Both men have pleaded not guilty.  
Paulino’s seat was up for grabs this year, and the race garnered some local attention after a write-in candidate from Lawrence launched his bid. And even though the mayor wasn’t on the November 3 ballot, organizers in Lawrence spent Election Day gathering signatures to recall DePeña.  
“Lawrence residents are actively organizing around other issues, and I think the city experienced a unique local political moment,” Rodriguez said. “The recall signature campaign created additional opportunity for political conversations, grassroots organizing, and engagement from community.” 
Lawrence residents collected signatures on Election Day for a citizen-led petition to recall Lawrence mayor Brian DePeña, who was arrested in August after federal prosecutors charged him with fraud and money laundering. (Hallie Claflin/CommonWealth Beacon) 
This year’s ballot also featured an unusually high number of widely debated ballot questions, including unsuccessful efforts to repeal recreational marijuana and upend the state’s primary election system. Those questions likely boosted turnout and engagement as they have in the past, Rodriguez said.  
“Midterms are sort of that in-between place where a voter in Massachusetts isn’t super engaged because we don’t have super competitive seats on the congressional level,” she said. “These elections really boil down to what’s on the ballot for the state.”  
She pointed to a successful 2022 ballot measure creating a new 4 percent tax on incomes over $1 million — commonly known as the millionaires tax — that generated widespread debate and voter engagement.  
Other factors could be contributing to higher turnout in the Gateway Cities and statewide, Rodriguez said, including the state’s permanent adoption of mail-in and expanded early voting options in 2022. But this year’s early voting data showed that Gateway City residents did not use the option nearly as heavily as the rest of the state; many preferred voting on Election Day. 
“In Gateway Cities particularly, we have folks that are working multiple jobs, hourly shifts, and they have schedules that don’t necessarily accommodate a trip to City Hall during the early voting hours,” Mejia said. “Early voting is convenient in theory, but still difficult in practice.”  
Rodriguez and Mejia agreed that the significant jump in turnout this year doesn’t mean local organizations and civic groups can let off the gas. Voter turnout is just one piece of the civic engagement puzzle, they said.  
“We cannot disappear from communities after election day and expect residents to remain connected,” Rodriguez said.
